r.x: Zenz Pipes

is the brand of handmade pipes Klaus Zenz produces under his own name in Wiener Neustadt, in Austria's Lower Austria state. Zenz, recorded as born in 1963, is a woodworker who trained as an art joiner (Kunsttischler) before turning to pipes; the brand's fondness for wooden detailing is mostly linked to this training. The workshop appears in regional handicraft directories as an independent craft record. As there is no reliable record of the founding year, no date is given in this entry.
Workshop and Production Approach

Zenz's working method is a small-scale workshop based not on serial manufacture but on bowls handled one by one. Blocks are selected from among briar imported from Italy; during sorting, the direction and soundness of the grain are considered decisive. The standard the workshop itself highlights in its promotion is a production built on detail rather than quantity.

Rather than being bought ready-made, mouthpieces are worked in the workshop. The main materials are hardened rubber (ebonite) and Cumberland, distinguished by its veined appearance; acrylic can also be used on request. The textural differences these materials leave on the mouth are covered in the mouthpiece materials entry.
Shape Idiom

The workshop's most cited pieces are freehand bowls that go beyond standard dimensions and follow the direction of the wood's grain. Both polished and sandblasted surfaces are seen; sandblasting is preferred to bring the grain texture to the surface. According to maker promotional texts, wood and brass inlays are used as thin transition rings between shank and mouthpiece; this detail has not been confirmed by an independent source. It is also stated that models are made to fit the nine-millimeter filter common in the Central European market; this information rests on a single secondary source.
Its Place in Austrian Pipe Making

Austria has a long pipe-making history, with established manufactories such as Ludwig Lorenz and the Wiener Kaffeehauspfeife tradition. Zenz Pipes sits closer not to the factory branch of this history but to the trend of single-maker workshops that gained strength across Europe toward the end of the twentieth century. The brand has been noted for the care of its craftsmanship in German-speaking pipe circles. There is no confirmed record regarding annual production count, changes in stamp form, or whether the workshop is still active today; the brand's official website is also not accessible.

r.x: R. Quagliata Pipes

is the name of a small briar pipe bench based in Phoenix, Arizona, and run alone by Ryan Quagliata. Organized records about the brand date to the late 2000s; its founding year is not documented. Its name is associated not with serial production but with a limited number of hand-shaped pieces.
The Workshop's Surroundings

Quagliata's name became known during a period when the American handmade pipe scene was growing on a broad amateur base. In this period the route to opening a bench often ran not through a school but through informal relationships built around material suppliers and tobacconists. In Phoenix, that address was the Pipe Makers Emporium run by Paul Hildebrand: a shop that sold the materials needed for briar and stem work and that, from time to time, also gave lessons. By Quagliata's own account, when he could not afford the lesson fee he found a way to learn by taking on repair jobs at the shop instead; it was there that he picked up hands-on knowledge of pipe-body engineering and the use of bench tools. Such a trade is considered a common form of learning in the growth of the American handmade pipe scene in the 2000s.

By his own statement, his occupations before turning to pipes were cabinetmaking, machining, and jewelry work; there is no independent confirmation of this background. That all three demand precision of measurement and surface finishing is cited as groundwork that eased his move to the bench. His first piece was simply a pre-drilled block bought from a tobacconist joined to a ready-made vulcanite stem.
Approach to Making

The workshop's distinguishing choice is that the stem is made at the bench together with the briar body rather than bought ready-made. For this, rod-form ebonite and cumberland were used, with the body-stem joint solved with a Delrin tenon. In these same years, hand-shaping the stem had become, for most independent American workshops, a threshold by which craftsmanship was measured. The brand's stamp, meanwhile, was applied with laser engraving rather than a steel punch; records cite the durability and clean look of the stamp as the reasoning. Among the names he looked to as a benchmark of craftsmanship, he counted Jody Davis of J. Davis Pipes and Jeff Gracik of J. Alan Pipes.
Recognition and Afterward

R. Quagliata Pipes never settled into a broad distribution network; production went directly to buyers and a narrow circle. Records on the brand stop in the late 2000s, and there is no reliable information about the period after. Whether the workshop continued operating therefore remains an open question.

r.x: GBD line names

are the line names stamped onto the shanks of the brand's pipes. In identifying a GBD, collectors look first at this name and only then at the shape number. Born from the partnership of Ganneval, Bondier, and Donninger, the brand used more than a hundred line names over its lifetime, and for most of them neither a complete production record nor a reliable date list survives.
The Documents Behind the List

The most comprehensive record on the subject is the line list Jerry Hanna compiled for Perardua.net, which Pipedia republished with permission. Hanna's material draws on three sources: correspondence that circulated on the alt.smokers.pipes newsgroup in the 1990s, Herb Wilczak and Tom Colwell's 1997 reference book
Who Made That Pipe?

, and Oppenheimer GBD catalogues from the 1970s and early 1980s that he later acquired. The compiler states openly that the record remains incomplete; many lines today are known only by name, with no record of their finish.
First Grade, Second Grade, and Private Brands

The lines fall roughly into three groups. Those carrying the GBD stamp are considered first grade, while those sold under the line name alone, without the brand logo, are considered second grade. A third group is what the catalogues gather under the heading "private brand": the body comes off the GBD bench, but the stamp carries the name of the tobacconist or chain that placed the order. This distinction is not as fixed as it appears. The same line is sometimes listed with the logo and sometimes without it in catalogues from different years; the line name alone is therefore not a reliable indicator of grade, and the grade cannot be pinned down without knowing the production year.
Grades and Recognized Lines

No official GBD quality scale is known. The order available is a list drawn up by a collector comparing the 1976-1980 catalogues, which places Pedigree, Straight Grain, Prodigy, and Bronze Velvet at the top, with Virgin, Varichrome, Prestige, Jubilee, and New Era just below. Virgin is remembered as the only GBD grade made for years with unfilled briar. Prestige and the deeply sandblasted Prehistoric line favored Perspex stems: black on the former, glass-like clear on the latter. In brand documents, the word Perspex refers to the acrylic stem material. Century's launch date is inconsistent across sources: one record gives 1950, another gives the 1960s or 1970s. Xtra is said not to have been made after the 1930s, while Seventy-Six is said to have been released in 1976 for the American bicentennial.
Finish Names, Size Codes, and Dating

In catalogue language, "take off" is the name given to a two-tone staining method: the stain darkens the softer texture of the grain while the harder grain stays light, sharpening the contrast between them. Granitan is the name for a surface that, after sandblasting, is partly sanded down to roughen like gravel, while Tapestry and Fantasy are the names for geometric areas masked off and left smooth before sandblasting. The general framework of these techniques is covered in the entry on surface finishes. The Iringa, Jenga, Kibo, and Nusi lines were not made from briar but from African meerschaum; the 1976 catalogue states that these were worked in Tanganyika. The region's sepiolite deposits, particularly the Amboseli basin, appear in mining records, and some of the names come directly from that geography: Iringa is a city in southern Tanzania, while Kibo is the highest cone of Kilimanjaro. Non-standard oversized pieces, from smallest to largest, were distinguished by the codes Conquest, Collector, and Colossus. In dating, the medallion on the stem is also a guide: the replacement of the inlaid metal medallion with a painted stamp points to production after the merger with Comoy's of London.

r.x: Bessai

is the name of a pipe shop that worked at the same address across two generations in Cleveland, Ohio. The name comes from John Bessai, who ran the shop largely on his own for many years: the same person shaped pipes at the bench, repaired incoming pipes, and tended the shop's tobacco counter. After him, his son Herb Bessai carried the business on. The Bessai name in American pipe history is associated not with a wide production network but with craftsmanship preserved within a narrow circle over many years.
The Shop in the Arcade

The shop's opening is recorded as around 1898. The address was the Arcade, the glass-vaulted passage running between Euclid and Superior Avenues in Cleveland, opened in 1890; being the city center's busiest enclosed shopping structure, this passage meant a steady flow of customers for a craftsman's shop.

The space had two rooms and was small. The front section was devoted to sales and repair, the back section to the bench. Bessai's pipes were shaped from start to finish in this back room, by a single hand; the hours at the bench were set to the shop's quieter moments. The natural result of such an arrangement was a low production volume. The small number of pipes that emerged mostly stayed within the shop's own customer circle, with very few examples reaching beyond it.
Production and Stamps

Bessai's surviving work is largely classic molds. Known examples include clean-bodied billiards, long-shanked canadian shapes, and bulldog examples. The material is briar; both smooth polish and rustication with hard, notched lines were applied for the finish.

The brand's most recognizable mark is its stamp: the letters "J" and "B" are joined so as to share a single vertical stroke on their backs, struck as though a single letter. This mark is seen both on the mouthpiece and on the left side of the shank. Shank stamps carry, alongside the maker's name, the wording "CLEVELAND, OH U.S.A." and grade markings such as "SPECIAL" and X, XXX.
Closure and the Brand's Present-Day Trace

John Bessai's exact date of death is unknown. Pipe sources only convey that he died before 1969; some collection records give the date as late 1968, though this information cannot be tied to an independent document. His son Herb Bessai took over the shop and continued making pipes. According to the same sources, the business closed around 1978.

Bessai pipes are rarely seen in secondhand circulation today. The name is known especially among collectors in Ohio and the Midwest; outside this region it is little recognized. Evaluated on a limited number of surviving examples, its craftsmanship is considered fine work among the shop-made American pipes of its period. In this respect the brand is one of the early and long-lived examples of the American handmade pipe tradition formed by independent craftsmen who worked, in those same years, behind their own shops in every corner of the country.

r.x: Mummert

is the one-man pipe workshop that Werner Mummert runs in the town of Otterbach in Western Palatinate. Two strands come together in Mummert's work: the habit of a technician fluent in measurement and tolerance, and a sense of form built entirely through observation rather than under any master. The workshop is small and its output limited; even so, its pieces are better known among collectors in North America than in Germany.
A Technician's Second Trade

Sources place Mummert's start in pipe making in the mid-1980s; the date most often given is 1987. For decades the craft stayed in the shadow of his day job: he worked as an engineering technician, only able to get to the lathe in the evenings and on weekends. Retirement reversed the balance, but output never grew large; he is reported to complete an average of about fifty pipes a year. The workshop is said to be registered with the Chamber of Crafts (Handwerkskammer) as a turnery business, and Mummert is reported to have been accepted into the European Woodturners Association, which requires sample work to be submitted to a jury for membership; neither of these records has been confirmed from an independent source.

Because he did not train under a master, he set his own standards, and they are surprisingly simple. A pipe should first be smokeable, then comfortable to hold, and it should not tip over when set down. Sculptural pursuits that sacrifice usability for appearance fall outside Mummert's interest.
Formal Language
His most cited work is his take on the bulldog: a body with sharp corners, a pronounced V at the heel, and a forward-leaning look from the side. Three other designs also carry his signature.
Barrel:
A cylindrical body where the boundary between bowl and shank is unreadable; some examples hide a reverse-calabash chamber inside.
Glass-shanked reverse-calabash poker:

A poker bowl is fitted with a shank made of heat-resistant tempered glass instead of briar, so the smoke's swirl inside stays visible. The two parts are usually joined with springs so they can be disassembled and cleaned.
Apple:
Built on an optical trick that looks flat and lean from the side but fills out when viewed from above or below.
He also has two signature surface treatments:
Deco
, drawing on Art Deco's sense of color, and
Rust

, achieved by coating the briar with iron-particle paint and accelerating its oxidation. He developed his deep, rough sandblasting technique through years of experimentation; he says his early interest in the approach was sparked by seeing the work of American makers such as Bruce Weaver and J. T. Cooke at trade shows.

His technical background shows up in the details. Some models have a small thermometer set into the bowl, and some pipes with cubic bodies have a QR code engraved into the base. He is one of the few German pipe makers with a CNC lathe, but he uses it only for certain parts rather than to produce the whole pipe — the shaping and finishing are done by hand.
Shows and Recognition

Records show his first show appearance was in Cuxhaven in 2004; in later years he appeared at Fürth, Lohmar, Cagli, and Chicago, and attended the Chengde show in China between 2016 and 2018. In 2012, at the Saint Petersburg show, he met Peter Matzhold, who encouraged him to introduce his work to American circles; this meeting is considered the start of a long-running collaboration. Today his name is known in pipe-smoking circles not just in Germany but also in Italy, France, and Denmark.

r.x: Leo Pipes

is a small-scale pipe workshop South African painter Leon du Preez set up in the early 2000s in the Goodwood suburb of Cape Town. The brand name comes from a shortened form of the maker's name, and the pipes carry the LEO stamp. Production was run single-handedly and stopped entirely with du Preez's early death; for this reason, Leo-signed pipes are counted among the rarer surviving examples today.
The Maker's Path

Du Preez's primary profession was the visual arts. Records show he completed an undergraduate degree via Port Elizabeth Technikon followed by a postgraduate art program, held his first group exhibition at the Ann Bryant Art Gallery in East London, South Africa, and curated that same gallery for years. His early paintings focused on the homeless and the solitary; in later years he turned toward work centered on the ocean. His design-forward approach to pipes is most often traced to this artistic background.

His first encounter with pipes dates to simple experiments with bamboo during his school years. The work became serious around 2001, when he met Johan Slabbert, a retired police detective who made pipes under the Jobert brand. Du Preez soon began working as an apprentice under Slabbert, and the two shared the same working space in Goodwood for years. The maker also set up a second, fully equipped workshop at his own home, which also served as a backup production site for Jobert.
Materials and Method

Because briar blocks are not locally available in South Africa, both Jobert and Leo turned to the country's own woods. The main species used were wild olive and the thorny acacia known locally as black hookthorn; lead tree, mopane, and African ebony are also known to have been tried in the same circle. This use of native hardwoods is a typical example of how making pipes from woods other than briar arose, outside Europe, out of necessity.

The workshop's method was deliberately simple. Du Preez did not use a lathe; all shaping was done with a drill press and a disc sander. This naturally produced a freehand line where every piece is unique: bodies that followed the grain of the wood rather than symmetry. No varnish was used in finishing; the surface was simply buffed to a shine. This choice both leaves the natural texture of the native woods visible and allows the surface to develop its own patina over the course of use. A similar approach is seen at many small workshops working with alternative pipe-making woods.
Aftermath

Leon du Preez died unexpectedly at a young age; sources do not give an exact date. This loss marked the end not only of the Leo brand but, by one account, indirectly of Jobert as well: Johan Slabbert is known to have stopped making pipes some time later, and the brand's website closed as well. Today Leo pipes are remembered as a short-lived but distinctive link in the small South African school of makers working with materials other than briar.

r.x: Gasparini

is a small-scale pipe workshop producing in the village of Luvinate, in the province of Varese, northern Italy. The brand is considered a typical example of the intermediate generation in Italian pipe making formed not by large factories but by family businesses: a limited number of enduring models, naturally aged logs, and a production system built on handwork. Its founding date is disputed; the Pipedia entry states that Mario Gasparini and his wife Ida began the business in 1938, while the manufacturer's own promotional material, and secondary sources relying on it, give 1948. Because the war years fall between the two dates, it remains unclear which marks the actual start of production.
Material and Production System

The workshop's main material is Italian briar, supplemented by a small amount of log of Greek origin. The principle Gasparini's own account emphasizes is drying the log naturally rather than with heat or other accelerating methods. In practice this means the blocks are left in storage for months, stretching to years for the top-quality groups; the workshop holds the view that fast drying damages the wood's fiber structure. Once dried, the blocks are carved according to the direction of the grain when shaping begins.

Production is split into two separate lines. On one side is the series line, where bowl, shank, and drilling operations are carried out partly by machine and the pipes are then sorted into groups by quality and surface finish. On the other are the "Fatta a Mano" (handmade) and "da Collezione" (collection) groups, shaped entirely by hand from selected logs; one-off pieces prepared for collectors also come from this branch. The practice that sets the workshop apart from its peers is fitting a bowl carved from solid meerschaum block into a finished briar body.
The Workshop's Course

The building housing the production section was expanded in the early 1950s, and the workshop has operated in the same structure ever since. The office and warehouse, kept in Milan for a long time for marketing reasons, were moved to Luvinate in 1971, bringing the whole business together at a single address. The information that management passed from 1977 to the founder's daughter Marisa Gasparini and her husband, and later to their daughter, rests solely on the manufacturer's own promotional material and has not been confirmed by an independent record.

r.x: Xin Li

(b. 1980, per records) is a pipe maker working in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province in eastern China. Since 2018 he has run his own Xin Pipes line by himself. His output splits into two branches: plain shapes drawn from English-French classics on one side, and, on the other, experimental work that plays with the angles of familiar forms.
From Real Estate to the Bench

Pipes were not Xin Li's first pursuit. After studying industrial design at the China Academy of Art and art history at the University of Münster in Germany, he began working at a real estate company; handcraft remained a spare-time pursuit. In the small workshop he had set up himself, he mainly made furniture. The birth of his son in 2014 upended this arrangement; there was neither time nor space left for woodworking. Around the same time, a mutual acquaintance introduced him to pipe maker Yang Zhimin. That both had graduated from the same academy made the connection easier, and Yang took Xin Li on as his first apprentice.

Training began at Yang's bench in 2015. Xin Li left the real estate business entirely in 2016 to move into pipemaking full time, and within a short time reached a level where he was also producing for his master's brand, Zhiputang.
The Zhiputang Partnership

The Zhiputang name, which initially covered only Yang's own work, turned into the joint signature of the two makers between 2016 and 2018. According to accounts, during this period Xin Li traveled to Italy with Yang and had the chance to see and buy briar firsthand at one of its main sources. The partnership ended amicably; Pipedia and LePipe.it date the split to 2018, while Smokingpipes's product notes date it to 2019. After this, Xin Li began producing under his own name at the one-man workshop he had set up at home.
Color, Proportion, and Bamboo

The first thing that sets Xin Pipes apart at a glance in the artisan scene is color. In place of the standard trio of light tan, brown, and black, body staining runs to tones such as ochre, mint green, brick red, rose, and khaki. These are not bright but matte, neutral tones; even so, since they're rarely seen in the pipe community, they stand out immediately.

According to records, from the last months of 2022 onward, plain classic shapes such as the billiard, brandy, and pot gained weight in his production. Even so, Xin Li doesn't treat these with their usual proportions; he works them with wide, plump chambers and shortened shanks, and most often uses bamboo for the section of the shank left without briar. Enlarging the chamber's share while shortening that of the shank and mouthpiece reduces the pipe's weight and helps its balance. Bamboo, thanks to its curved structure, also allows the line running from chamber to mouthpiece hole to trace sharper curves, particularly in bent models.
Influences and the Experimental Branch

The Danish School's influence is clearly legible in the work from the Zhiputang period; the S. Bang duo Per Hansen and Ulf Noltensmeier, whom Xin Li counts among his favorite makers, is the sign of this connection. In the years of his own name, a simplicity comes to the fore that avoids unnecessary elements and rests on balanced proportions and clean lines. This attitude is considered kin to the principles of makers in the Sixten Ivarsson line, though the result looks quite different. The maker's second branch, meanwhile, rests on breaking the angles and curves of familiar shapes; the resulting forms carry recognizable names but step outside their accustomed silhouettes.

r.x: Manhattan Briar Pipe Co.

was an American pipe company operating in New York at the start of the twentieth century. It did not emerge from the growth of a small workshop but from an investment decision made in the years when the tobacco industry was at its most monopolistic: according to the record, it was founded in 1902 as a New York corporation by the American Tobacco Company, the era's giant tobacco firm, following an agreement reached with the owners of the Brunswick Briar Pipe Company. Details of its founding capital and address appear only in secondary compilations and are not repeated here.
The Trust's Pipe Arm

Understanding Manhattan Briar requires knowing the company behind it. American Tobacco Company was born in 1890 from the merger of a series of tobacco firms under the leadership of James B. Duke, and because it held such a large share of the market, it became popularly known simply as the "Tobacco Trust." Adding pipe manufacturing alongside cigarette and tobacco production was a natural extension of this expansionist logic.

The takeover did not happen in a single step. Although the majority of shares passed into the trust's hands within the first year, the former partners retained a sizable minority stake for a time; it is reported that these shares too were bought out in 1906, at which point the company became entirely the trust's pipe arm. Yet this arrangement did not even last five years: when the Supreme Court's 1911 ruling broke up the American Tobacco Company, Manhattan Briar continued on as a separate business. This phase, in which large capital entered pipe production, is an American tendency that can also be traced in the example of the American Smoking Pipe Co..
Products and Stamps

The company's core business was mass-produced briar pipes. In 1913 the presidency was held by John Glossinger, who had previously run American Tobacco's pipe division; under him a comprehensive promotional campaign was run focusing on high-quality briar. The collection also includes meerschaum pipes bearing the Manhattan stamp. The possibility that these examples were made by European craftsmen and restamped in America rests solely on assessments of form and workmanship; it is not documented. Offering both materials side by side was a common choice in the American market of the period.
Factories and Patents

Manufacturing began operating in New Jersey in 1905: the company settled in Jersey City under a ten-year lease, and built the factory where the pipes were finished in Marion. When the lease expired, from 1915 onward the office and factory were consolidated under a single roof in Brooklyn. The Brooklyn era is said to have been guided by a manager named W. C. Bastian, who is reported to have been granted a patent in 1910 for a chambered mouthpiece resembling the P-Lip mouthpiece of the Peterson brand; however, which patent this refers to remains unclear even in the secondary sources.

The only patent that can be traced through documentation is John Gianninoto's. This inventor, who lived in Brooklyn, was granted a patent on December 11, 1917, for a carrying mechanism that allowed spittoons to be emptied without soiling the surroundings; the document is registered to the inventor himself rather than to the company, while the information that Gianninoto was a Manhattan Briar employee rests on secondary compilations.
Final Years

The company continued to appear in local trade directories until 1921. It is accepted that it was purchased and absorbed the following year by S. M. Frank & Co.; the details of the sale are conveyed not through primary documents but through later compilations. As the brand name gradually fell out of use, Manhattan-stamped pipes today are encountered only within collector circles.

r.x: Radice

is a pipe workshop established in the town of Cucciago, in the province of Como in northern Italy. Luigi "Gigi" Radice, whose name the brand carries, was born in 1939 and entered pipe making in the early 1960s, in the nearby town of Cantù, in the workshop of Carlo Scotti, who made Castello pipes. This apprenticeship period instilled in him all the basic habits of the Italian handmade pipe tradition.
From Caminetto to His Own Brand

After his years at Castello, Radice founded Caminetto together with his colleague Peppino Ascorti, a brand that found wide resonance outside Italy as well. By the records, the partnership began in 1968, and in the mid-1970s, with the contribution of Milanese distributor Gianni Davoli, carried the brand into the international market. Radice left the partnership in late 1979 and began production under his own name in early 1980.

The new workshop was a family business from the outset. The founder's father, Paolo Radice, took part in some of the basic stages of production; his son Gianluca was likewise at the bench from the founding years on. Another son, Marzio, joined the business in later years, and the two brothers, having trained alongside their father, gradually took on an ever-larger share of production. Gigi Radice did not step away from his own bench work throughout this period.
Material and Surface Finishes

The workshop sources its raw material from Italian briar cutters and states that it rests the blocks in its own stock for at least three years. Surface finishes are the brand's most recognizable trait; different grades of sandblast and rustication are known by their own names — "Silk Cut," "Rind," and "Underwood" — while smooth-finished pipes are gathered into a separate series. Silver bands and metal rim details are engraved by hand, with a burin; for many years this work was done personally by Luigi Radice. Special pieces with a bamboo-look shank and details in buffalo horn, mouflon horn, and deer antler also feature in the workshop's repertoire.

On the technical side, the most talked-about practice is the oil-curing process, developed by drawing on the method used in old English workshops. A "twin bore" arrangement, with two separate airways drilled in the stem, is likewise one of the workshop's own experiments. Long a user of lucite stems, Radice added ebonite (vulcanite) stems to its production as well, in response to requests from pipe smokers.
Stamps

According to accounts, a small dot-shaped mark indicating the filter arrangement can be found on the stem of Radice pipes. Also according to collector records, from the late 2000s onward a figure was added to the stamps next to the "Hand Made in Italy" inscription, showing the number of years elapsed since the brand's 1980 founding. As far as can be verified, this figure offers a handy reference point for roughly dating a pipe.

r.x: Jirsa

is a pipe workshop in the Czech Republic that carries the name of Oldřich Jirsa and today runs as a family business. Production is concentrated in the town of Rynholec, west of Prague. The brand is known among Central Europe's small-scale pipe workshops for its consistent craftsmanship and its distinctive shape interpretations.
Founding and the Maker

That founder Oldřich Jirsa began pipe making in 1994 is stated consistently both in his own account and in promotional material written about the brand. As the account has it, Jirsa trained professionally as a mold maker, and came to woodworking through souvenir items sold in Prague; a collector's commission for a figural pipe bowl is what drew him into this field. The workshop has moved location several times since its founding, keeping production at the scale of small series.

The brand is considered a late link within the Czech lands' long pipe-making tradition: workshop production, carried on in the region since the nineteenth century, was largely consolidated into state enterprises in the second half of the twentieth century and, after the 1990s, redistributed once again among small independent workshops. Jirsa is one of the businesses born within this second wave.
Production and Material

The workshop's working method rests on running numerically controlled and hand-operated equipment side by side. Rough shaping of briar blocks is done with a CNC mill, and the remaining work is carried out by hand; the maker's own account notes that the bulk of the pipes come out in small series, while a limited number of examples pass entirely through his own hands from start to finish. The recorded result of this arrangement is a repeatability in smoke-channel and tenon dimensions considered high for a small workshop.

One of the workshop's distinguishing features is that it makes its own stems. Early pipes show vulcanized rubber (ebonite/vulcanite) and cumberland stems; later production moved to the workshop's own food-grade blend, said to be somewhat softer than acrylic. The thin, light-colored insert band set between shank and stem is the brand's most easily recognized detail.
In keeping with the widespread Central European habit, nearly all pipes are drilled with a 9 mm filter seat. Both smooth-polished and rustic, sandblasted surfaces are used as finishes.
Stamp and Grading

Pipes are marked under the shank with a stylized "J" set inside an oval frame. Quality tiers are shown with stars; records indicate that at the very top of the scale sit the three-star, SG-marked examples, distinguished by grain selection.
The shape repertoire is dominated by the measured interpretations typical of Czech workshops. The workshop's work in the bulldog family is said to draw particular attention from collectors.

r.x: Dino da Campione

is the stamp Milan-born Leonardo Airaghi (1929-2010) applied to his pipes. The second half of the name comes from Campione d'Italia, an Italian enclave on the shore of Lake Lugano, surrounded on all sides by Switzerland's canton of Ticino: this small town, legally part of the province of Como, was where Airaghi carried out his main profession. Pipe making was never a livelihood for him; the production that began in 1969 never reached three hundred pieces in any of the thirty-six years it continued.
The Person Behind the Name

According to accounts, Airaghi's main profession was managing the Campione casino, and he took much of his orders while holding this position. That he ran the two pursuits side by side also explains why production never grew to workshop scale. The family is said to have descended from a line that produced painters and sculptors in nineteenth-century Milan; though this connection is often repeated around the brand, it is not documented in independent sources.

Distribution of the stamp within Italy was equally narrow: for years it ran solely through the Novelli tobacconist in Rome. Beyond that, pipes went directly from Switzerland to buyers elsewhere; the addresses they reached ranged from North and South America to Gulf countries and the Far East.
Production Scale and Stamps

Annual figures surviving from the workshop make it possible to view the scale of production numerically. In 1969, the first year, twelve pipes were made; the number first exceeded a hundred in 1978, mostly ran between one hundred sixty and two hundred forty after the second half of the 1980s, and reached its peak in 1994 with two hundred fifty-five pieces. The sum of the years present in the record exceeds four thousand pieces; since 1979 is missing from the list, the actual figure is somewhat higher. These figures come from a single record and have not been independently verified.

The stamping arrangement had several layers. The body first carries the name "Dino da Campione," and on some examples this is joined by material designations such as "Radica Extra." Pieces from the cleanest briar blocks, showing no trace of flaw, were set apart with the letters
AP

inside an oval frame; sources state these two letters are the initials of an English descriptor meaning "flawless." It is reported that up to four snail marks could be stamped on the same body, these marks indicating the internal quality ranking Airaghi set for himself. The rare pieces he considered exceptional bore the
QUEEN
stamp; this mark has a counterpart in secondhand records.
Approach to Construction

Selectivity is the starting point of this stamp: it is reported that blocks with flawed grain were set aside entirely unworked, keeping the waste rate high. In terms of shape, he did not stray outside classic families; measure and balance were preferred over startling silhouettes. The surface was mostly polished with natural wax, rustication rarely resorted to. Cutting a flat plane beneath the bowl so the pipe could stand on a table, or adding a small support foot of bone or briar to the mouthpiece, are among the details recognized for this stamp.

The problem Airaghi dwelled on most was durability. He is said to have thrown prototypes against the workshop wall to see where they broke. This pursuit found its answer in the cross-tenon mouthpiece he developed together with his son Cesare Airaghi, who set out as a designer in 1980: the shank and mouthpiece meet at an angled surface, reducing the risk of breakage on impact. Examples with this construction are few.

Production was reserved solely for family after 1999 and stopped entirely in 2005. According to records, Airaghi died on 10 December 2010 in the village of Morcote on the shore of Lake Lugano, in Ticino. Since the stamp never moved into catalogue production, it is counted among the signatures that fully fit the artisan definition within the Italian handmade pipe tradition.

r.x: Idskov Piber

is the brand under which Danish maker Carsten Idskov signs his pipes with his own name. The bench is in Aarhus and has operated at hobby scale from the start; the maker's main occupation is teaching, and he teaches mathematics and woodworking at a school. Because his livelihood does not depend on the bench, production moves at the maker's own pace rather than under commission pressure. One result of this is an imbalance in the brand's recognition: while it is considered an established name in Denmark, it has barely appeared at international shows and so has not gone beyond a narrow circle abroad.
The Maker's Path

Carsten Idskov was born in 1958 in a village in Jutland (Jylland) and later settled in Aarhus. His introduction to pipes dates to the mid-1990s; shortly after, he joined the city's pipe club. The club was not just a social circle but became, over the following years, a connection that also shaped his production habits; Idskov remains an active member of the club today.

His move into making came about through a commission. When the pipe he had ordered from Jens Tao Nielsen arrived, the package also contained a pre-drilled briar block, included so he could try his hand at it. When the result proved encouraging, Idskov turned to Poul Ilsted in Svendborg and received both new blocks and his first technical guidance from him. Exactly when he began production in earnest is unclear; dealer records cite 2001, but this date has not been confirmed by an independent source.
Materials and Surface

Block briar is sourced mainly through Kent Rasmussen. Bodies destined for sandblasting are not finished at the bench; they are sent to a workshop in Aarhus that specializes in the process. This is a customary division of labor in small workshops: the one stage requiring expensive equipment is outsourced, while all decisions about the shape stay with the maker.

Three materials stand out for mouthpieces: vulcanite, a hardened rubber; its grained variant, cumberland; and, as a colored option, synthetic amber. The differences in texture and care among these three are covered in the mouthpiece materials entry. On the decorative side, silver ferrules are the most visible choice; sperm whale tooth is also mentioned as an element frequently used on the shank.
Stamp and Scale

The stamp carries the Idskov name alongside the country abbreviation DK and the year of manufacture, so each pipe carries its own year on it. The brand uses no grading system, setting it apart in this respect from the portion of Danish school workshops that adopted tiered classification. Annual output, according to an account resting on a single source, is around 150 pipes; the figure has not been independently confirmed and may have varied over the years. Idskov is also a collector and is regularly seen at events around the Danish championship.

r.x: The Briar Workshop

is a shared bench founded in Vermont in the 1970s that had a hand in shaping the American handmade pipe tradition. The workshop's founder, Elliott Nachwalter, began the work in a cabin near Stowe with a handful of tools, working alongside Andrew Marks; he later formed a partnership with Jorg Jemelka and gave the workshop its name. The founding's exact year does not appear consistently in the sources; secondary sources cite 1976. Danish designer-maker Finn Meyan Andersen also joined the team shortly after.
The Workshop's Way of Working

The Briar Workshop was conceived not as a one-person bench but as a production setting in which more than one maker worked under the same roof. Among the names who worked here over the years are Brad Pohlmann, Jim Cooke — who would become known as J. T. Cooke — and Carole Burns. In this respect the workshop functioned as a kind of school for the American handmade pipe scene that flourished in the 1970s and 1980s: makers learned bench discipline here, then went on their way under their own names.

One distinctive side of the workshop is described as an attempt to combine handwork with machinery. According to the account, as part of a collaboration set up with Ehrlich's in Boston, pipe production machines dating from the turn of the century were acquired, and these machines were overhauled by Jemelka; however this detail rests on a single chain of sourcing. The aim was for a hand-shaped model to be reproduced without its measurements being lost. It is said that the workshop could thus work both on one-off pieces and on limited runs of certain models. In Nachwalter's own account, choosing well-rested briar blocks is the starting point of the work; vulcanite and acrylic are seen as mouthpiece materials on surviving examples.
Stamps and Periods

The workshop's pipes generally carry an oval stamp: "The Briar Workshop" on top, a phrase giving the maker designation below, and a grade mark made up of a letter or a letter-number combination in the middle. On some examples there is also a second stamp on the shank giving the maker's name and indicating that it is handmade. The "USA" wording found on the stamps and the grading letters are the main clues collectors use to place a pipe within its period.

Freehand examples hold a notable place among workshop-stamped pipes. Nachwalter opened his own shop in New York in 1980, where he designed custom pipes for his customers. After a gap of about three years, he founded, in 1996, his own eponymous workshop in southern Vermont, overlooking the Battenkill River. Today the name The Briar Workshop is not in production; the brand's trace continues in the secondhand circulation of its stamped pipes and in its founders' later work.

r.x: Lester C. Garlow

(Lester Commodore Garlow) was an amateur maker in the United States who carved figural briar pipes in the 1950s and went almost entirely unrecognized in his own time. He worked under no brand, trained in no workshop tradition, and left behind about twenty-three pipes. His name entered pipe literature only after his death, once scattered auction records and family accounts were pieced together.
From the Navy to the Bench

By one account, Garlow joined the US Navy in 1940 and served six years, reportedly spending most of that time aboard the light cruiser USS Marblehead. The ship's official record shows it was attached to the Asiatic Fleet in the Far East at the start of the Second World War, was badly damaged in an air attack in the Makassar Strait on 4 February 1942, and after repairs was assigned to the South Atlantic and, from 1944, the Mediterranean. This means the account of "throughout the war in the Pacific" does not fully match the ship's actual route. Marblehead's wartime service was also the subject of a book published in 1944.

He is said to have taken up carving aboard ship as a pastime. After being discharged, his wife Alice's purchase of a block of briar advertised in a Manhattan shop turned this manual skill toward pipes. The first pipe drew praise from those around him and was given away; the carvings that followed grew steadily more elaborate.
His Pipes and Bench

His motifs were mostly drawn from the American West and nature scenes: pioneers around a campfire, mounted Native warriors, a deer hunter, a cavalryman lying prone with a rifle aimed, the head of Lakota leader Sitting Bull, gorilla heads, and a gorilla family. One of his largest pieces exceeded 17 inches, or forty centimeters, in length. He is said to have taken seven months to complete a pipe depicting eleven wild horses galloping. According to his son's account, he finished his last pipe in 1954: the body carved with seven African elephants moving toward a tree that itself formed the chamber, with fine pieces of ivory used for the tusks; the scene is said to have been inspired by a display seen at a natural history museum in New York.

His bench was unassuming. His machine equipment consisted of a hand lathe, a few drills, and a vise; the real work was done with carving tools of various sizes, chisels, a jeweler's kit, and scrapers and picks salvaged from dentistry. His pipes reached collectors through Wally Frank's shop in New York; a set of nine pipes passed this way into a single collection. Because he could manage only one or two pieces a year on average, carving never took the place of his primary job. A 1959 Michigan newspaper article shows him living in Lansing and reports that he had carved 23 pipes by that point; the "just finished" description of a carving in that article does not entirely square with the 1954 date given by his son. Garlow suffered a stroke in 1966 and died in 1970, at fifty-two, following a second stroke.
Rediscovery

The years he worked were the golden age of series-produced pipes in the US; while brands such as Kaywoodie and Dr. Grabow filled the benches, figural carving remained a narrow pursuit entirely outside this production, drawing largely on the 19th-century meerschaum-carving tradition. At an auction held in New York on 4 April 1978, promoted in the press as the city's first sale devoted to pipes, eight of the 291 lots carried the Garlow signature; the catalogue identified him only by his surname. The pipe depicting the gorilla family was pictured in Harry L. Rinker's 1983 antiques price guide. A search post his son Tamarack wrote to a pipe forum in 2005, a magazine article by his other son Bruce in 2014, and a compilation published in 2025 pulled these scattered traces together into a single life story. Garlow's output, produced entirely alone over just a few years, is today counted among the rare mid-20th-century examples of figural narrative carved into a pipe.

r.x: The
Directory of US Pipe Brands

is an attempt to gather the scattered record of American pipe production in one place; this page holds the second part of a three-part directory, covering ninety entries from Glamp to New Jersey Briar Pipe Co. Pipe making in America ran along two tracks: on one side, series-production factories in centers such as Jersey City, Brooklyn, and Chicago, along with dozens of their sub-brands; on the other, one-man workshops working weekends in a home garage. The entries below are brief and factual; brands for which only a name is on record are kept in the list, with the gaps clearly noted.
Brands
Glamp
— American pipe making known under the name Andrew Glamp. No further information is on record; only the maker's name is documented.
Glen Court
— The work of Glen Court, living in Hadley, Massachusetts. He marked his freehand pipes with the "G Court" stamp; he also produced pipes called Royal Court.
Glenn Tinsky

— Son of pipe maker Mark Tinsky, Glenn Tinsky began working in his father's workshop on a limited basis after graduating from culinary school, then formally joined the business. Most of his pipes carry the American Smoking Pipe Co. stamp; a smaller number are marked simply "G. Tinsky."
GM Pipes

— The brand of a maker known as Gregg. Stating he has worked for more than thirty-five years, the maker specializes in three-piece pipes and has spent twenty years experimenting with different wood species. In 2009 he released the two-piece GM Signature Series pipes made of bocote wood; this line also introduced a hand-carved "GM" stamp under the bowl.
Gold Coast
— One of several sub-lines of the Lee brand, appearing in at least one Pipes by Lee catalogue. It was initially known for a distinctive gold-plated band; later models left the mouthpieces unadorned.
Golden Bull

— A small tobacconist founded in 1969 in the Old Town district of San Diego. Owner Geoffrey made some of the pipes in his own garage, marking them with the "Golden Bull" stamp and hand-carving them. The shop later took the name Racine & Laramie; the name change took place in 1974. One Golden Bull example on record turns out to be a secondhand Ben Wade imported by Lane Limited, refurbished and rebranded.
GRC Pipes

— The brand of Darius Christian; his name appears in sources under various spellings such as Erch and Eruch. He started as a hobby in 1999 after buying a PIMO pipe kit, and turned into a small-scale producer with support from colleagues such as Trever Talbert and J.M. Boswell. He works alone, making classic shapes in the Danish line with vulcanite, cumberland, and acrylic mouthpieces. The maker he uses as a benchmark is Per Hansen of the S. Bang workshop. His grading runs from A down to G; the last two letters indicate secondary quality. The brand name was chosen in honor of the maker's wife.
Hahn, Rick

— Rick Hahn of California is recorded as a name new to pipe making. He uses Greek briar obtained from JH Lowe & Co., imported in 1995 by Tim West; his mouthpieces are Italian vulcanite, and his pipes are finished with carnauba wax.
Hale
— The pipes of Rocky Hale of Mesa, Arizona. Records describe him as a locally known maker without further detail on his work.
Hampton

— Amateur maker Wade Hampton of Phoenix, Arizona. He trained under Horace DeJarnett. His stamp reads "Made by Wade" and "Handmade in Arizona," together with a serial number and date; his emblem is a stylized WH monogram.
Harmon

— Steve Harmon's pipes represent a playful approach rather than a claim to high craft. He made unusual, sometimes odd shapes, experimented with colored paints, and added colored acrylic ornaments to his pipes. Even so, most of his output stayed in light, natural tones that let the wood's grain show through. He allowed small flaws and rusticated the larger ones; some of his pipes show carved line networks covering the entire stummel. Records place him in the Henderson area of North Carolina; he was born May 4, 1960, and died suddenly.
Hayes, Robert E.

— A maker from Southport, North Carolina. He made pipes as a hobby for years before bringing his production up to a level he could sell. He sourced his briar from a well-known Danish maker; his engineering and rustication work were well regarded. His pipes were displayed on Cornell & Diehl's tables.
Haywood

— Irving "Scacy" Haywood, living in Glenarden near Washington, D.C., made decorative tobacco pipes throughout his life alongside work as an auto mechanic and photographer. He served on the Glenarden Municipal Council from 2007 to 2011. He was also known in music through Scacy and the Sound Service, an early funk and go-go band he formed in the late 1960s.
Heisenberg

— The brand of Jim Brown of Mooresville, North Carolina. He began production in 2014 under the name "Werner Heisenberg," using Mediterranean briar, olive wood, and European bog oak. Mouthpieces are hand-cut and made of vulcanite or acrylic resin; special woods and other mouthpiece materials are used on customer request.
Heritage Pipes Inc.

— Founded as a subsidiary of S. M. Frank & Co., the company was closed at the end of 1971 following the parent firm's decision to reposition its Kaywoodie brand toward higher quality. Its emblem was three small dots in red, white, and blue. Heritage Heirloom, Kaywoodie's top-tier line, was made in the 1960s and discontinued in 1970; the line was overseen by Stephen Ogdon, who came from Dunhill. According to accounts, only one in three hundred briar pieces was deemed worthy of this line, and the finest Para rubber was used for the mouthpieces.
Herskovitz

— Sandor Herskovitz, registered in Flushing, New York, is remembered for making and selling pipes in a public park in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Only isolated examples of his pipes are documented.
Herter's
— This outdoor and hunting supply company is thought to have had pipes made under its own name; the record does not go beyond this possibility.
Hew Len Pipes
— The brand of Jaden Hew Len, working in Wai'anae, Hawaii. No information is on record about production; only the maker's name and location are documented.
Hialeah

— Hialeah pipes were released before 1975 by Whitehall Products Co., then part of Helme Products. Whitehall was based in Wheeling, West Virginia; Helme was based in New Jersey. All known examples are made of Algerian briar.
Hildebrand

— Paul Hildebrand made freehand pipes in his workshop in Phoenix, Arizona. He also owned Pipe Makers Emporium, which for several years was the exclusive North American distributor of Algerian briar; most of the stock was later bought by Steve Norse of Vermont Freehand. He was a member of the Arizona Pipe Club and the Arizona Pipe Makers Society, and taught about three pipe-making courses a year. He made pipes for more than a decade and also handled restoration of estate and collection pipes. He passed away on June 29, 2024.
Holcomb

— Florida maker Mack H. Holcomb worked first in Hialeah, then settled in Sanford, where he retired. Whether he used a stamp on his pipes is unknown; at least one of his pipes is recorded as being in the Tom Dunn collection.
Hollco International

— This company in Chatsworth, California, was previously known as Hollco-Rohr. It acquired the Wally Frank company in 1969; around the same time it became the US importer of the Castello and Comoy's brands and the maker of several pipe lines, chief among them Pioneer.
Howard

— Tom Howard, a well-known comedian of the 1940s and 1950s, was a skilled pipe maker alongside his vaudeville and radio work. A 1947 Popular Mechanics article introduced him as "hobbyist of the month." Starting around 1939, in a workshop next to his home in Red Bank, New Jersey, he turned out a pipe roughly every three hours from bagged briar blocks and mouthpiece blanks. He also built scale-model ships, trains, and cannons.
Hudson Universal Pipe Co.
— An American firm that produced the Eagle, Excelsior, Harrington Park, and Hilex brands; records consist of no more than this brand list.
Hugunin's Los Angeles

— A tobacconist that operated in Los Angeles. A newspaper notice dated March 11, 1916, shows Harry L. Hugunin registering the business at 110 N. Spring Street; another notice from 1918 lists the shop under the name W.F. Ball as dealing in pipes and pipe repair, blended tobacco, and cigars. Records show the firm was founded in 1882 and continued at least until the late 1940s.
Hyaac
— Carver Abraham Hyaac (†) of Poland, Ohio. The record is limited to his name and location.
Ideal Mfg.
— A pipe maker founded in Bellefonte, Pennsylvania; details of its products are unknown.
Imperati

— The records about this maker are both scarce and contradictory. Imperati is described in some sources as a pipe maker with a shop in New York, in others as a maker working in Baltimore, in others as a craftsman supplying large New York shops such as Wilke, and in still others as a designer working mainly for Wally Frank; according to this last account he also prepared the firm's "pipe of the month" examples.
Irrera
— A pipe maker who worked in New York. No information is on record beyond his name and city.
J. Arthur Pipes
— A brand hand-carving its pipes from Algerian, Italian, or Greek briar. Mouthpieces are hand-cut from German cumberland or vulcanite. Its founder and founding date are not given in the records.
J.B. Russell

— A distribution company operating in North America, known for short as JBB. The workshops making pipes under its name are mostly Italian and French firms, one of which is Chacom. It had a privileged relationship with Sasieni and Charatan. The company was founded by a World War I colonel who opened tobacconists in London and Manhattan after his military service. After the founder's death in the 1930s, the business stayed in the family; it was bought by Daniel Blumenthal in 1970.
Jack's Handmade Pipes

— Jack Hamburg Jr. began making pipes as a hobby in 1988 with machinery he acquired from the Moss & Lowenhaupt factory in St. Louis. He works in Joliet, Illinois, producing mostly freehand pipes using Greek briar and lucite mouthpieces, and also does repair work.
Jacobson-Hardy
— A pipe maker who worked in Bennington, New Hampshire; he left no trace in the records beyond his name.
Jandrew

— The brand of J. Andrew Kovacs. He lived in the Arizona towns of Jerome and Cottonwood, and is said to have later moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Horace DeJarnett learned the fundamentals of pipe making over roughly a year at his workshop in northern Arizona (see DeJarnett Pipes).
Jasper Co.

— Pipes stamped with the brand name, the phrase "Imported Briar," and the address 104 W. 47th St., NYC. The firm does not appear to have been registered as a company in New York, does not appear to have trademarked its name, and does not appear to have advertised its pipes; nothing else is known about it for this reason.
Jemelka

— Jorg Jemelka co-founded The Briar Workshop in Vermont in 1976 together with Elliott Nachwalter, and appears to have stayed there until 1980. His real interest was pipe-making machinery and, in the long run, automation. Under a collaboration with Ehrlich's of Boston, the workshop acquired turn-of-the-century pipe-making machines; Jemelka converted these machines to produce exact copies of handmade pipes. This method is the main difference separating the workshop's Florida and Vermont branches. Nachwalter and Brad Pohlmann continued producing both series-production designs and individual handmade pipes. Jemelka advanced his automation goal further by earning a master's degree between 1980 and 1983.
Jesse Jones

— A maker who embraces the functionality, elegance, and durability of the classic English school, rarely venturing into abstract shapes. His aim is to keep handmade pipes in classic shapes at an accessible level; he designs his pipes with an eye to an open draw and comfort of use. From 2014 to early 2016 he worked on Chheda Pipes together with Premal Chheda, owner of Smokers' Haven, while also continuing his own line; he later left that collaboration.
Jimmy Mermet

— Son of Andre Mermet and a maker in his own right. He has carried on the Mermet brand that began with his father's business in France; the business's roots trace back to his grandfather. His pipes are known for being undervalued on the estate market relative to what they deserve.
Jo Davidson

— Not actually a pipe maker but a sculptor internationally known mainly for clay portrait busts. His connection to the pipe world came through the Marxman heirloom line launched by Bob Marx in the 1940s. Toured as a traveling exhibition, the collection was presented in 1947 as pipes made by hand from artists around the world, some of them famous. The line's most notable piece was the figural pipe Davidson carved around March 1947, bearing his own portrait.
Joe Case
— Joe Case, working in Kingston Springs, Tennessee, makes his own pipes alongside pipe repair and restoration. He runs his repair business under the name Briarville.
John Chapman
— A pipe maker apparently American. His known pipes are dated 1974, 1977, 1979, and 1980; no other information is documented.
John Crouch
— A tobacconist that has operated in Alexandria, Virginia, for more than thirty years. The shop has also had pipes made bearing its own name.
John Surrey Ltd.

— Based at 509 Fifth Avenue in New York, this firm produced pipes under the John Surrey brand. The Slugger Baseball Pipe it released in 1948 drew great interest: the shank and mouthpiece resembled a baseball bat, and the bowl resembled a ball.
Johnson, Richard C.

— Counted among America's highest-rated pipe makers. In 1939 he began making pipes at Weber Pipe Co., which Carl Weber had founded in Jersey City a year earlier. After leaving the firm he moved to Pennsylvania and bought a farm near Carlisle, continuing production in a small workshop set up on the farm; Weber had him make special-order pieces for years afterward. His name appeared in various books and magazines, most recently in the December 1997 issue of Smoke Shop Magazine. In the early 1980s he trained Eric C. Christie as an apprentice for three years.
Jorgenson

— Yern "Bo" Jorgenson and his wife Billie ran a shop called Gateway Pipes and Tobaccos in Wayne, Pennsylvania. Jorgenson was an authorized repairman for brands including Dunhill and Charatan. He offered his own pipes only at this shop. His pipes were noted for exceptional craftsmanship: Sardinian briar was personally selected at Carl B. Weber's (Weber Pipe Co.) New York factory, production followed a very traditional method using tools inherited from his grandfather, no filler was ever used, and finishing was done with carnauba wax alone.
Joseph B. Desjardins

— A firm working in Fall River, Massachusetts, was one of the large-scale producers of its era at the end of the nineteenth century, at one point employing sixty workers. The company declined with the Great Depression of 1929. One of its brands was JD, its initials rendered inside an oval frame. The firm held two patents, one for a pipe reamer and the other for a mouthpiece-making machine.
KEN

— A brand produced by Prim Associates of America in Chicago. The design was based on a patent by Otto Turinsky: filed in December 1939, the patent was granted in May 1941 under number 2,242,805. Its mouthpiece is lucite; the bowl chamber below contains mechanisms meant to trap tar and moisture, thereby reducing the harshness of the smoke. The pipe was featured in Popular Mechanics in 1946 with a list of six features.
Kimberly
— One of the many brands produced under Arlington Briar Pipes Corp.; the record goes no further than this connection.
Klodt

— Eric Klodt became a pipe enthusiast in 2005 and soon after discovered high-grade pipes and began researching the craft. He gained his technical and tool knowledge by watching makers such as Rad Davis, Grant Batson, Nate King, and Michael Lindner work at the bench.
Knickerbocker Pipe Co.

— Officially named Knickerbocker Smoking Pipe Company, Inc., the firm was based in Brooklyn, with a corporate address at 1271 Avenue of the Americas in New York's Time-Life Building. The company was dissolved on December 23, 1992. Alongside pipes it also sold items such as cufflinks and tie pins. Its Kool-Smok model was an aluminum pipe based on Viking and Falcon designs: airflow could be adjusted with a nut beneath the screw-in briar bowl, and the angled cooling fins cut into the shank gave the impression of a drill bit when viewed from the side.
Kowal

— Jeffrey M. Kowal of Beaver Falls, Pennsylvania, first offered his handmade pipes through his own eBay shop. Alongside pipes he also works on carved pieces such as wooden sculptures, canes, and gun stocks.
Kubik
— Pipe maker Jim Kubik of Middleburg Heights, Ohio; no documentation exists on his production.
Kuehl
— Carver Alan Kuehl (†) of Grayson, Georgia. No record exists beyond his name and location.
Laird
— Ted Laird of Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, is recorded as a new name; his pipes are known only from occasional auctions.
Lakatosh

— Carver John Lakatosh of New Columbia, Pennsylvania, worked in a home workshop in the Susquehanna Valley above Sunbury. He presented most of the pipes he made on weekdays at craft fairs across Central and Southern Pennsylvania. Following a downturn in the tobacco industry he gave up carving and returned to bus repair, later settling in Lewisburg and making furniture for family and friends. He passed away on March 8, 2018.
Landon & Warner
— A firm known for an unusual system-pipe example. Records show it filed a patent application on April 11, 1936; no further detail is documented.
Lannes Johnson

— A maker from Texarkana. A graduate in medical technology, he worked in that field for about thirty years. He began pipe making in 1997 with a kit obtained from Mark Tinsky, then learned from Trever Talbert. He prefers making traditional shapes from Greek briar with vulcanite and lucite mouthpieces. He stamps his pipes with his name or, more recently, the letters LJ set inside a heart, adding a grade, date, origin, and the words handmade. His older grading system rose in order through the letters L, T, C, G, and E, with a number from one to five added according to the quality of the wood and design; the current system relies on one to five heart marks.
Lassen
— Pipes bearing the stamp "CUSTOM MADE by Lassen," mostly in a freehand line, were made by Albert Gold of Wichita, Kansas.
Ledone

— The work of Lucille and Ralph Ledone of Wisconsin; their slogan emphasized that they made pipes for both men and women. Lucille entered the craft under her father's influence; records say she learned it from Baier. She produces fewer than sixty pipes a year; many women users have favored her pipes for their small bowls and long shanks. Her stamp consists of "Cille" and the year.
Lee

— The brand, stamped "Pipe by Lee" along with quality markings on the shank, was distributed by Stewart-Allen Co., Inc. of New York. Grading rises in order from one to five stars. On early pipes the stars have seven points, on mid-period pipes five points; on later pipes a colored gold-star stamp was used. The brand's secondary quality lines were released as Briarlee and Gold Coast, both featured in a Pipes by Lee catalogue.
Leedy

— Tom Leedy of Clayton, Ohio, is regarded as a versatile and creative American maker. His pipes are always freehand and made without a lathe; while some of his designs recall the line of the old Danish masters, most resemble no known example. The internal structure of his pipes is carefully calculated. Alongside imported briar he uses materials such as American fruitwood and olive wood; his natural, carnauba-finished sitter pipes are especially sought after.
Lewis

— Rich Lewis died of a sudden heart attack on June 1, 2023. His family had owned Lewis Pipe & Tobacco since 1969; Rich joined the business in 1972 at age twenty. In the 1980s he worked alongside leading pipe makers in Italy and England; he became nationally known both for his pipe making and as an authorized repairman for numerous high-end brands.
Lone Star Briar Works
— The brand of Mark Domingues, working in Houston, Texas; no detail on his production is documented.
Longrie

— A company founded in the 1930s by Earl J. Longrie of Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Its slogan emphasized the coolness of its pipes. Longrie held the patent for a spiral cooling coil fitted inside the mouthpiece, filed on June 27, 1932, and granted March 20, 1934, under number US1951665.
Loscalzo Pipes

— The brand of Craig Loscalzo of Lexington, Kentucky. He became interested in the craft after a visit to Kai Nielsen's workshop on the Danish island of Fyn; influenced by Nielsen, he learned the craft under Tim West and Ronni Bikacsan of Nashville. He was introduced to Danish pipes through his Danish brother-in-law, an avid pipe smoker. He produces his pipes under the Pipes by CAL label and also does cleaning and repair work.
Lucky H Pipes

— The pipe arm of Hendrick Wood Creations, founded by artist Chris L. Hendrick of Pearland, Texas. The workshop first produced hand-turned wooden bowls and single-form hollowed pieces, shifted its focus that same year toward writing instruments made from tree roots, and later founded Lucky H Pipes to turn to handmade briar pipes.
Manges
— American maker Rick Manges of Michigan is a member of the International Association of Pipe Smokers Clubs (IAPSC) and a relatively recent entrant to the craft.
Mark Stewart

— He began his career in real estate finance, management, and development in the Philadelphia area, and worked as a sports agent through his company Sports Management, Inc. In retirement he moved to the mountains of the Brevard area of North Carolina and turned to pipe making and repair, becoming a well-liked member of the pipe community. He used Cornell & Diehl's Crooked Lane blend in his own mixtures and did repair work for many venues, most notably Bruce's Pipe Shop in Asheville. His story was covered in Chuck Stanion's article in the spring 2014 issue of Pipes and Tobaccos.
Mars

— According to Wilczak and Colwell's records, Mars pipes were made in America by Otto Sevic and date to 1930; this is consistent with the July 6, 1926 patent indicated by the "MARS, PAT. 7.6.26" stamp found on the pipes. The patent covered a filter mechanism set into the base of the bowl: accessed through a black bakelite cap, the chamber held an aluminum reservoir that collected moisture from the bowl, with a tube extending from the bowl's base down into this reservoir. The cap contained a cotton-like material to absorb the moisture.
Martin Pipe Company

— The brand of Hal M. Silverstein of Albany, New York. Born in Syracuse and a graduate of Syracuse University, Silverstein served as a navy photojournalist in the Vietnam War; he died on November 7, 2003, at age fifty-nine. His pipes carry the "Martin" stamp and are quite rare on the estate market.
Martin, Sam

— A part-time maker from Little Rock, Arkansas. According to the 1987 guide to American pipe makers published by Pipe Collectors International, he made 125-150 pipes a year. He worked full-time at the phone company, making his pipes in an old garage behind his house; his pipes, made with quality briar, had a distinctly rustic look. He died in 1992.
Mayflower
— Mayflower pipes were made by National Briar Pipe Co.; see that entry for details.
McCranie's

— The McCranie's Pipe and Tobacco shop in Charlotte, North Carolina, was founded in 1979; it is today run by the founder's sons, Todd and Trent McCranie. Pipes were made for the shop under its own name by Bill Ashton, stamped MADE IN ENGLAND, and by Tonino Jacono; the sandblasting on Jacono's pipes was also carried out at Ashton.
Medici

— The brand is named in memory of Lorenzo de' Medici, the best-known figure of fifteenth-century Florence, whose patronage of the arts made the city's artistic and architectural flourishing possible. Sykes Wilford of Smokingpipes.com had long carried the goal of building a very high-quality, reasonably positioned American-made brand; when this met Todd Johnson's similar ambition, Medici was born. Adam Davidson made Medici pipes under Johnson's guidance early in his career, before he began working at smokingpipes.com.
Mehaffey

— E.A. Mehaffey ran a pipe and tobacco shop in Wheaton, Maryland. He made pipes for many years, though accounts say his own tobacco blends were more esteemed than his pipes. He continued his business into the 1980s.
MelloPure

— A pipe made by the Mellopure Pipe Company of Cincinnati, Ohio, based on a 1947 Canadian patent. It is a six-piece metal system that includes a cleaner-condenser fitted into the shank and removable from the front of the pipe. Designed as the core of the system, this piece, drawn out along discs arranged along its axis, was meant to wipe the tar and oil from inside the shank as it was removed.
Mesa Woodsman
— Hugo Mesa was the brother-in-law of LPI's Barry Levin. He made a small number of sculptural, unusual pipes.
Milan Bros.

— Milan's story began in February 1912 with a small shop J. H. Milan Sr. opened on Jefferson Street in Roanoke, Virginia. As the business quickly grew, J. H. and his new partner A. H. Milan moved into additional space at the same address. Following A. H. Milan's death in 1938, J. H. once again became sole owner; three of his six sons carried on the trade within this family business. After an unbroken forty-four years, the shop moved in 1956 into a new building of roughly 2,400 square feet on Jefferson Street, where it remained for more than fifty years. The business passed to Don and Myriam Roy in 1994, and to their daughter Renée and her husband David Meyer in 2000.
Milton
— Pipe maker Herb Milton of Margate, Florida. Whether he retired or passed away is unclear from the records; no other information is available.
Milton Brian Kalnitz

— Milton Kalnitz, father of pipe maker Brian Kalnitz, owns Bellezia. He began building his own handmade pipe line in the 1960s and formally founded his business in the 1970s. By his own account, when he began making pipes there were only six other businesses offering handmade pipes in North America besides his own. He is also teaching pipe making to his grandson David Kalnitz, who works at the shop.
Mission Briar

— A brand that emerged during World War II and vanished shortly after the war. When briar imports became difficult in 1941, Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy began making pipes from manzanita root under Kaywoodie, while Reiss-Premier Co. did the same under its own name; this is the origin of the name "mission briar." KB&B's subsidiary Pacific Briarwood Company owned plantations of this shrub in the Santa Cruz Mountains of California. Since the wood was not as high-quality as true briar, the venture was abandoned after the war. Monterey pipes were made by Kaywoodie using mission briar.
Mock
— Midwestern carver Don Mock (†) was born in Minnesota and, at the time his profile was prepared, lived in Montevideo, Minnesota.
Monarch

— Monarch Pipe Co. was founded in Hartford, Connecticut, most likely in the late 1930s, by Fred Warnke, who had received a patent for a system pipe on January 22, 1935. The company moved in the 1950s to Tulsa, Oklahoma, and later to Bristow, also in Oklahoma. Monarch also produced the E. A. Carey Magic Inch and Duncan Hill Aerosphere pipes.
Moon Valley Pipe Works
— The brand of pipes made by Cody Easom in Boise, Idaho; no record exists beyond the maker's name and city.
Moonshine Pipes

— The Moonshine Pipe Company was founded by Jonathan Lavezzo in a small eight-by-ten-foot cabin in Charlottesville, Virginia. Having spent most of his working life in carpentry and construction, Lavezzo, after surviving a serious motorcycle accident, sought a trade that would be less punishing on his body and mind. His interest in working with wood pointed that search toward pipes; the brand quickly drew the attention of his peers and was featured in various publications.
Murado
— Only the brand name appears in the records; no information is available about it.
N.W.R. Pipes

— The brand of Nathan Rimkus of Los Alamos, New Mexico. Rimkus works by day as a materials engineer and makes his pipes on weekends. He started the craft as a woodworking and design experiment during his university years, setting out on the path together with his father, Victor Rimkus (Rimkus Pipes).
National Briar Pipe Co.

— A firm based in Jersey City, New Jersey. Its known brands include Biltmore, Forecaster, Honeybrook, King Eric, Kleenest, Nifty, Rembrandt, Sir Sheldon, Drysmoke Silvertone, The Mayflower, and The Doodler; the last of these was created by Tracy Mincer and was produced by him for a time. Rembrandt-branded pipes carry an italic capital "N" on the left side of the mouthpiece; the same stamp is thought to have been used on the firm's other brands as well.
Neeb

— David Neeb began his working life as a maritime lawyer. After smoking pipes for many years, he retired and tried selling pipes under the name MKELAW Pipes, then learned pipe restoration, and finally pipe making. He learned the craft first from Lee von Erck and then from Rad Davis. He works in Elm Grove, Wisconsin, offering both his own pipes and pipes he has restored.
New Jersey Briar Pipe Co.

— A firm producing mostly stock-clearance, promotional, and private-label pipes. It was acquired in 1956 by S. M. Frank & Co. and continued operating as that company's subsidiary until December 31, 1972.
