r.x: Brigham Pipes

is a Canadian pipe brand founded in Toronto by Roy Brigham in 1906 and kept within the same family across four generations. The brand announced itself not so much through briar craftsmanship as through the filter mechanism based on a replaceable maple rod fitted inside the mouthpiece.
From Repair Shop to Factory

Having completed his apprenticeship under an Austrian pipe master settled in Toronto, Roy Brigham opened his own repair shop in 1906. In the early years earnings came almost entirely from repair work. Within twelve years the workshop grew to a team of six and became an address known beyond Toronto for its craftsmanship. Pipes bearing his own signature also began to appear during this period; as the product of a workshop that knew exactly where breakage most often occurred in repairs, they were designed with points such as the bowl-shank joint reinforced without sacrificing lightness.

Pipes coming in for repair were at the same time an archive of complaints. The conclusion Roy Brigham drew from this archive was that what bothered smokers most was the burning sensation left on the tongue (tongue bite). The common explanation of the era attributed the problem to the temperature of the smoke.
The Maple Filter

In the second half of the 1930s, Roy and his son Herb, who took over the business's helm around 1938, sought the explanation not in temperature but in chemistry: the tars and acids carried by the smoke left a mild burning effect on the tongue. The target that followed from this was to find a porous material that could trap this residue without dulling the tobacco's flavour. Most of the experiments came to nothing, and some even mixed their own taste into the smoke. Only two materials met the criterion: bamboo and hard maple. The latter, reliably available in Canada, was chosen.

The result was a cylindrical maple rod, bored lengthwise through the middle. The rod sat inside a shank recessed to match it, and was replaced with a new one once filled. Because the narrowness of the cross-section did not restrict the draw, the pipe remained light-drawing, while a significant portion of the residue was trapped before reaching the mouth. The mechanism was patented in Canada under number 372982, and later pipes were stamped "CAN PAT 372982." For the general logic of residue-trapping mechanisms, see the entry on pipe filters and systems.
Growth and Production Moving to Europe

The filtered models opened the way for the brand. Production staff had grown to over forty by the 1960s; in 1970 the company moved to a larger facility, and its network of points of sale across Canada came to be counted in the hundreds. For a long time, the great majority of pipes made in the country carried the Brigham signature. Bowls were predominantly briar-based, and a wide range was produced, from the classic billiard family to freehand pieces.

Quality tiers were indicated by brass dots set into the shank; as the number of dots increased, so did the grain flawlessness of the briar. This system, run on eight tiers for more than forty years, was reorganised in 1980 into seven tiers, and the separate series names were dropped. For mark and dot details, see the entry on dots, marks, and dating on Brigham pipes.

Roy's grandson Mike Brigham joined the company in 1978. Herb Brigham died in 2010 at ninety-four. As Toronto's production staff dwindled in the early 2000s, bowl production moved first to Italy and then to France; maple filter rods, however, continued to be produced in Canada. Records indicate makers who later became known under their own names, such as Philip Trypis and Julius Vesz, learned the trade at this workshop.

r.x: Hamric

is the brand under which American pipe maker Zack Hamric produces handmade pipes under his own name. The workshop operates in Sarasota, Florida, and is also known as "Z Hamric Artisan Pipes." It is not a mass-production outfit but a one-bench craftsman's workshop; its style leans not on the American workshop tradition but on the flowing lines of the Danish School.
Two Separate Production Periods

Behind the brand lies an interrupted craft history. Hamric learned pipe carving while working as a carpenter at Opryland USA in Nashville after college, producing mainly Danish-line freehands during this first period. A long stretch of corporate work and family life followed, and the bench stayed closed for roughly thirty years.

The second period began when the maker took over equipment from a pipe repair shop. Records indicate that in the 2010s he aimed to raise his annual output to around seventy pipes, a scale that placed the brand within a period when American artisan pipe making was expanding rapidly. The workshop is known to continue at this scale today, still as a one-man operation.
Material and Approach to Making

The priority Hamric describes is sourcing material directly. The briar he uses is bought from a supplier who has been cutting in Italy's Calabria region for three generations. Mouthpieces are not made from ready molds but hand-cut solely from SEM ebonite or Cumberland rod; being limited to just these two options among mouthpiece materials is one of the brand's distinguishing features. The bamboo used in shank extensions is also sourced directly from China.
Shape Repertoire

The second period's output is not limited to freehands. Secondhand pipe listings show volcano, reverse calabash, and author bodies, sandblasted and semi-sandblasted surfaces, decorative details like antler rings, and examples made from bog oak. This repertoire points to a manner that shifts between freehand form and classic proportion. Blending Danish influence with classic silhouettes is regarded as a common tendency seen among most independent American makers who came to prominence after the 2000s.

The low annual output has meant the brand is largely known through individual pieces rather than catalog series; for this reason the Hamric name is associated not with catalog runs but with individually signed bodies.
There is a minor spelling inconsistency in the name: while some records give the surname as "Hamrick" or "Hameric," the signature the maker himself uses is "Zack Hamric."

r.x: Von Erck

is the handmade pipe brand Lee von Erck runs single-handedly out of his workshop in Negaunee Township, in a wooded area near Lake Superior in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. The brand takes its name directly from its maker, and is also found in records as "von Erck's Classics."
A Craftsman Who Came to the Trade Late

Von Erck is not a maker who went straight into pipe-making. By his own account, after his military service he worked as a ski instructor and ice hockey coach, and spent a period breeding dogs. Having smoked a pipe since his youth, he first turned to repair work, and production followed from there. Records state he began making pipes regularly in the late 1980s. He first showed his products at fairs and dealers in the Midwest, and in later years took part in fairs in Europe and Asia; his pipes are known to have reached Denmark, Italy, Russia, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan.
Oil Curing and Surface Work

The most talked-about part of the brand is the oil-based curing method applied to briar. Von Erck does not disclose the composition of the oil mixture, which aims to draw out tannins and resinous residue from the root. For this reason the order of production is unusual: after the bowl and shank are drilled, shaped, and polished, the pipe is set aside for a long curing and drying process, and only after this stage is finished is the mouthpiece specially carved for it.

The maker uses plateau briar, and says the shape is largely left to the direction of the grain in the block; this attitude explains why the catalog leans toward large-chambered, freeform pieces. In surface treatments, along with smooth polish, sandblasting and partial rustication take up a broad place; the deep-pored sandblast surface is called "morel" at the workshop. According to information compiled by Pipephil, annual production has stayed at the level of 150-250 pieces.
Stamps and Grading

Every pipe is stamped with its own serial number at the end of the process. The first two digits of the number are the year reversed, the last three give the sequence within that year; for example, pipe no. 20010 is the tenth piece of 2002. Quality grades are shown with letters: AAA is the top tier, and according to the maker's own records only three examples have ever been made at this level; AA goes to pieces with no visible flaw to the naked eye, A to the bulk of production. Grade C is not offered for sale, while the letter R marks pipes reworked after having already been considered finished. Additionally, the stamp "MINE" indicates that piece was, for a time, the maker's own pipe.

The stamping system also records the briar's source. According to the list the maker has published, TVC indicates Greek briar brought in in 1970, ALG Algerian briar, CORS a block reported to be of Corsican origin, and PM material obtained from Peter Matzhold. Pipes without any mark are from Greek briar brought in in 1997. The abbreviations TSPTC, GKCPC, and MAPS, used for club orders, are added by the same logic.
Recognition

Von Erck received the Chicagoland Pipe Collectors Club's annual honorary "Doctor of Pipes" title in 2013; the other recipient that same year was Rex Poggenpohl. He teaches at pipe-making seminars held at the Chicago pipe show, and also hosts short-term students at his workshop.

r.x: PipesMD Pipes

is the name of the signature under which American maker Charles "Charlie" Sharp gathers the pipes made by his own hand. Records give Rio Rancho, in the state of New Mexico, as the workshop's address. PipesMD is not a factory-scale brand; it is one of the small workshops built around a single bench, of which there were growing numbers in the United States in the second half of the 20th century.
A Maker Who Came from the Machine Shop

Sharp did not enter pipe making from wood but from metal. He spent most of his working life in tool-and-die work and machining. This background carries over directly into pipe making: both the smoke channel and the stem socket demand precise alignment, an area where years spent at the lathe and milling machine pay off directly. Such a career shift is not uncommon among independent American makers; a good share of the names who turned to pipe making in the postwar period learned their trade either in a woodshop or in a machine shop.

Records show he took over a tobacco shop that changed hands in the eastern part of the country in 1971 and used it as a bench where he could display his own pipes. The shop closed in 1980, but production continued.
The New Mexico Period

After the shop closed, Sharp moved his workshop to New Mexico and continued production there. Besides pipes, he also made fountain pens from exotic woods and acrylic; acrylic is a plastic also widely used among stem materials in pipe making. His work was promoted largely online, through a dedicated promotional site.

By the maker's own description, pipes are made to order from briar burls of Corsican and Algerian origin. These two regions long served as Europe's main source of raw material for pipe making after the briar revolution; Algerian briar was very common in the mid-20th century, and supply became increasingly difficult in later years. That an American workshop cites these two names is a sign it drew its raw material from the European trade chain.

No fixed model catalog is known. As is customary in one-person workshops, shape is determined by the order and by the grain of the burl on hand; the resulting production pattern is that of a small-volume bench working directly with customers.
State of Knowledge

Almost everything known about PipesMD rests on a short promotional text written by the maker himself; independent documentation is next to nonexistent. The promotional site fell out of use over time, and those asking about the brand on pipe forums have likewise been unable to find detailed information. Stamp forms, production numbers, and the workshop's current status are undocumented; for this reason PipesMD is counted among the workshops known not for their catalog but solely through their founder's professional story.

r.x: Waughtel

is the name given to the pipes of Robert Waughtel, who worked in Harrisburg, in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania. Waughtel was known first as a tobacconist and, in the last years of his life, as a pipe maker; the number of pipes he produced is small, and today these pieces circulate only among collectors. Nearly everything known about the brand comes down through his family and those who knew him; the information below has not been cross-checked against independent archival records.
A Craft From a Tobacconist Family

By family accounts, the Waughtels had been in the tobacco trade for several generations. Robert's father, Preston Waughtel, ran cigar shops in York County, Pennsylvania; it was in this environment that Robert learned to hand-roll cigars, and his interest in tobacco lasted a lifetime. In later years he ran pipe shops in Lebanon, Lancaster, and Harrisburg. His own blends stood out at these shops, including ones named "Waughtel's Best" and "Waughtel's Delight." According to a 2009 account from his daughter, some of these blends went on living at the Wingenroth Pipe Shop in Lebanon even after the business changed hands twice more following his own departure.
The Move Into Pipe Making

Waughtel had long collected fine pipes, but his own wish to make them found an outlet only in the late 1980s; by family account, he had spent the two years after leaving the shop playing poker professionally. He's said to have bought both workshop equipment and a large quantity of aged briar from a pipe maker who was retiring from the trade, which he then stored in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room. As covered under curing, resting a cut log for a long time is a stage that reduces the wood's later movement; the ready-made stock on hand let Waughtel work with well-matured material even from his very first pipes. As he advanced in the making process, his sense of shape sharpened too.
Design Language and the End

In the accounts of those who knew him, pipes coming from Waughtel's hand are distinguished first by their voluminous stummels: the form leans on classic pipe shapes, but the proportions push past catalog measurements. Two pieces described by one collector can be dated: a semi-scoop marked 1991 with a slightly curved (quarter-bent) shank, and a brandy that came into his hands in 1996, with even less curve (an eighth-bent). By his daughter's estimate, total production stayed under two hundred pipes; the toll of the long labor each piece demanded is cited as one reason for the small number. Because the count is so small, his pipes turn up only through the estate pipe market.

Robert Waughtel died in 1997; two different accounts give different months. A friend who knew him places the death in the early months of the year, while his daughter points to July and a sudden heart attack. By the same account, Waughtel was in the process of passing his equipment and accumulated knowledge to an apprentice in the Harrisburg area at the time; whether that transfer was completed is unknown. No new pipes bearing his name followed; what remains is a limited number of signed pieces and the blend names left over from his tobacconist years.

r.x: Davorin

is the small-scale workshop signed under his own name by a Croatian pipe maker working in Zagreb. The maker's surname appears in sources as Denović; the diacritical spelling has not been confirmed by independent records. Within the community, the workshop's name is associated above all with morta — oak that has turned semi-fossilized after thousands of years in swamps and riverbeds. The maker has also served as chairman of the Zagreb-based "Lula" Pipe Smokers Association, keeping pipemaking as a pursuit alongside his main profession.
An Identity Built on Material

The workshop's current identity is the result of a search for material. The maker first worked with briar, then tried olive wood, and finally made morta his main material. The briar he uses comes mainly from the Adriatic coast; by his own account, Croatia is a country favorable for both briar and olive wood, and was in the past considered a significant region for clay pipe production.

For sourcing morta, he works with a carpenter known in records only by the first name Darko; no surname is given. The material is drawn mainly from the valleys of the Sava River and its tributaries, with pieces ranging in age from a few centuries to thousands of years. In the workshop's own promotional material, the oldest piece is said to come from the Krapina River and to be roughly 8,290 years old; this figure has no independent confirmation. Time spent underground enriches the wood mineralogically, darkening or otherwise altering its color accordingly. Alongside black, the maker's account mentions tones he calls "gold" and "copper," as well as experiments with rarer red and blue veining. For the material's general properties, see the entries on morta and pipemaking from morta.
The Glagolitic-Letter Stamp

The second detail that makes the workshop recognizable is its stamp. The pipes carry a hot-stamped letter "D" stylized from the Glagolitic alphabet (Glagoljica). According to the maker's own explanation, this choice grew from a wish to draw a symbolic link between a very ancient material and the oldest writing system of the Slavic world. The Glagolitic alphabet is the first Slavic writing system, dated to the mid-9th century; traditional accounts trace it to the Byzantine monk Saint Cyril of Thessaloniki. Croatia is the region where this alphabet survived longest: in some areas it remained in use until the 19th century.
Production and Reputation

Davorin pipes are not mass-produced; they are shaped one at a time by hand and remain limited in number. In early promotional texts, the maker describes pipemaking not as a commercial business but as a pursuit through which he gives gifts to those around him. Over the years his work has also come to be seen outside Croatia, and he has become one of the few names invoked when morta pipes are mentioned.

Sources do not agree on how many years the maker has been making pipes: promotional texts published at different dates give figures such as fifteen, twenty and twenty-nine years. These figures should be read against the date they were written; no precise starting year appears in the records.

r.x: BBJ piber

is a one-person pipe workshop signed by Danish maker Børge Blume-Jensen with the initials of his own name. Blume-Jensen began carving pipes regularly in 1996 and has worked ever since at his rural workshop in the south of the island of Sjælland. Production has never scaled up to a factory level; the brand has stayed limited to a few dozen pipes a year, making BBJ a typical example of small-scale signature workshops within the Danish school.
The Master's Path

Records place Blume-Jensen's birth in the mid-1950s and his first contact with pipes in his youth. He carved his own first pipe at fifteen from a pre-drilled "hobby block" bought from Brakner, a pipe factory operating in his hometown of Sorø. This was not his profession: he completed his training as a jeweler in the early 1980s, ran his own workshop in that field until the early 1990s, and afterward spent many years directing a music and culture school in Ringsted. As long as he held a full-time post, pipe making remained a leisure pursuit; the time he devoted to the bench increased markedly after his retirement in the late 2010s. At his fresh start in 1996, guidance from a local pipe master was decisive. He sourced his first briar blocks and stems from the Stanwell factory in Borup. In later years he has himself stated that he drew on the assessments of well-known Danish masters such as Jess Chonowitsch, Kjeld Sørensen (Red Hat), and Tom Eltang.
Production and Stamping

The workshop's primary material is briar; records note that the master occasionally uses olive wood as well. Vulcanite is preferred for the stems, with acrylic used from time to time. Most pipes are finished smooth; contrast staining is applied to bring out the grain. Blocks with minor flaws or confused grain are instead finished with sandblasting or rustication.
The shape repertoire is largely classic; the master says he interprets these familiar molds with his own sense of proportion. Products are stamped with the word
BBJ
and the brand's logo. Quality grading runs in three tiers: A, B, and C. The top grade, A, is reserved for pipes with a flawless surface and even grain structure.

Annual output has varied from period to period depending on the master's professional obligations. Sources give figures ranging anywhere from forty to a hundred, so a fixed number cannot be stated; in any case, what is involved is a limited output entirely finished by hand. Because every stage from design to final polish comes from the same hand, no two BBJ pipes are identical copies of one another; even examples gathered under the same model name show variation in size. Blume-Jensen continues to attend Danish pipe gatherings once or twice a year to introduce his work to the community. Such gatherings are considered the main avenue of visibility for one-person Danish workshops that have no distribution network.

r.x: Jeantet

is one of the oldest family names in Saint-Claude pipe-making. The family entered the record as owners of a wood-turning workshop in an era when the briar pipe did not yet exist, grew over the nineteenth century into one of the town's largest producers, and in 1988 stopped being an independent maker and became the brand of a group.
From Family Bench to Partnership

The Jeantet name is recorded in connection with a business in Saint-Claude from as early as 1775. The firm's work at the time was not pipe-making but woodworking generally: wooden shanks fitted to porcelain bowls, and pipes made from wild cherry wood in particular. The firm took the name Jeantet-David in 1816, and in 1837 became a partnership uniting numerous small workshops scattered across the town under a single trade name.

The change in material came in 1858; from that date onward, briar became the firm's main raw material. Growth was rapid: by 1890, more than fifty people were working for Jeantet. Once the limits of working with scattered workshops were reached, construction of an integrated factory that would concentrate production in a single site began around 1891 on Rue de Bonneville; the building took several years to complete. In 1898, Maurice Jeantet reorganized the business and expanded the facility by buying the neighboring workshop to the south. Another branch of the family would, a few years later, found Paul Jeantet SA, a factory devoted to stem production. Having rough shaping and polishing and other intermediate steps circulate among home-based subcontractors was standard practice in Saint-Claude at the time.
Peak and Closure

The company converted to a limited-liability status in 1938. In this period there was also a branch workshop at Montréal-la-Cluse, in the Ain department, where finishing was done on the cheaper models. By the 1948 census, the Saint-Claude workforce appears to have exceeded a hundred, part of whom worked from home. The facility was modernized around 1950 with additions such as freight elevators.

Production reached its peak around 1969, then declined sharply within less than a decade. Even though a steam-based facility for drying briar — quite modern for its day — was built in the factory yard around 1979, the trend did not reverse: by 1987, the workforce had fallen to twenty-two.
Handover of the Brand

Wanting to keep the name alive, the family sat down with Yves Grenard — once Jeantet's chief designer, head of Chapuis-Comoy since 1971, and said to be a distant relative of Pierre Comoy of Comoy's of London. As a result, Jeantet joined the Cuty Fort group in 1988, alongside the John Lacroix and Emile Vuillard brands, under the leadership of Chacom, founded in 1987. The factory was closed; its buildings were purchased by the Saint-Claude municipality in 1989, and when alternative use plans failed to materialize, the structures were marked for demolition, with the southern workshop disappearing before 1992.

The brand name itself, however, is not lost. Following the closure, Jeantet was carried on as one of Chapuis-Comoy's secondary brands, and Saint-Claude-made pipes continue to be marketed under this stamp.

r.x: Moretti

is a handmade pipe workshop founded in 1968 by Igino Moretti in the town of Recanati, in Italy's Marche region. The founder's son-in-law, Marco Biagini, has headed production for more than forty years; today his son Luca joins him as well. Working olive wood and bog oak alongside briar, and a small briar dot inlaid into the stem, are the brand's most distinctive features.
The Pipe Tradition in Recanati

Pipe making in this small Marche town near the Adriatic is considered to date back to the 1850s. At the start of the twentieth century, the town's established workshop was Hully Briars. According to the manufacturer's own history, the firm worked with about forty employees, made half of the pipes it produced for other companies, and sold the remaining half under the brand BEP-SON, derived from the first syllables of the owners' names, Beppe and Sonia. Igino Moretti and his wife joined the workshop in its most crowded period, when the number of employees approached fifty; Igino gradually became its principal pipe maker.

Hully Briars's closure brought Moretti to the brink of a career change: he had passed the railway examination, and working as a train engineer offered a concrete livelihood. Choosing to stay in the craft, the master founded his own brand, Moretti Recanati, in 1968. Sources give 1950 as the year Hully Briars closed; the manufacturer's own history does not state a year.
The Marco Biagini Era

Marco Biagini, who married Igino Moretti's daughter, is said to have been a former gendarme (carabiniere) who began making pipes alongside his father-in-law in the early 1980s, gradually taking over the workshop entirely. In the brand's early years, its livelihood depended largely on contract production for other firms; Biagini gradually reduced this work, consolidated production under his own brand, and moved toward distributing directly, without intermediaries. The brand name was simplified in the mid-2000s to simply "Moretti."

The workshop's way of working suits this scale: the block is not fixed to a lathe jig; the chamber and smoke channel are drilled with the wood held by hand. This slow-moving method, demanding a high degree of manual precision, is a detail underscored both by the maker and by those who write about the brand.
Materials and Series

Moretti pipes are made from Italian briar naturally aged for at least ten years; sources state that the blocks used come from Calabria. The workshop also works with olive wood and with bog oak (morta); it is counted among the few workshops able to work bog oak. The maker states that no chemicals are used in the finishing, and that color is left entirely natural.

The catalog is tiered according to surface treatment and grain quality: rustic and sandblast pipes, smooth groups separated by size number, above these the Collection and Emblem series, and at the top the Marco Biagini series bearing the master's own name. Olive wood and bog oak bowls are grouped under separate headings; 9mm filtered models and reverse-calabash examples are also available. The top series is represented by only a limited number of pipes each year.
Identifying Clues

The small briar dot inlaid on the side of the stem is regarded as the brand's hallmark. For a long time the word "Recanati" appeared below the brand name in the mark; this line has not been used on pipes made since the mid-2000s, and collectors treat this as a rough dating clue. Another known preference of the workshop is leaving the interior surface of the chamber without excessive sanding; the aim, as reported, is to let the carbon layer build up more quickly. Biagini's practice of not filling sand pits in the briar with putty, and instead setting aside blocks with serious flaws from the start, is also frequently cited. In all these respects, Moretti sits closer to the artisan pipe tradition than to the large Italian firms that mass-produce.

r.x: Sydney P. Ram

is a pipemaker and tobacconist who worked in Chicago through the 1930s and into the early 1940s. His shop stood at 59 West Monroe, in the city's Loop business district. Ram's name is remembered today both for the pipes he left behind and for a handbook he wrote on pipe smoking; because the pipes he made were limited in number, he is mostly known through secondhand collecting.
Shop and Production

Ram's business was not just a point of sale but also a small-scale production and service workshop. A sixteen-page promotional catalogue from the shop's era survives, and it stands as the most concrete document of how the business operated. The catalogue states that the pipes' briar blocks came from Algeria and Corsica. According to the same document, the business prepared its own tobacco blends and also handled pipe repair on-site; a customer could thus find pipes, blends, and maintenance all under one roof.

The pipes generally bear the "Sydney P. Ram" stamp in a script style. In addition, the stamp set includes phrases such as "straight grain" or "imported briar" indicating the quality of the block. Ram's pipes were finished with a light polish; it is said this surface would darken to a deep brown at an unusually fast rate with use.
The Book and Life After Chicago
In 1941 Ram published a guide on pipe smoking titled
How to Get More Fun Out of Smoking; A Guide and Handbook for Better Smoking

. The book remains accessible today, having been reprinted years later, in 2011. The text is a practical handbook written in the tobacconist idiom of the period, and it has made Ram's name a reference point beyond his work as a pipemaker.

The Chicago shop closed in 1942. According to records, Ram moved to California after this date and continued making pipes for a while using the old block stock he brought with him. For this reason examples made from Chicago-era material after his "retirement" are also in circulation; around 2013, unused old-stock pipes of California origin were reported to have surfaced.
Two Spellings of the Name

One detail noted by those who study the brand is that the maker's name appears in two different forms: "Sydney" on the pipe stamps, but "Sidney" in his catalogue and correspondence. This duality causes confusion in source surveys; when identifying a given example, one must account for both spellings while reading the stamp on the shank and stem — see the entry pipe anatomy for those parts.

Ram's workshop stayed at the scale of a tradesman serving his own city's customers, not a large factory. This scale is the main reason his name is remembered in American pipe history not as a major producer, but as a well-documented small business of its era.

r.x: Roland-Briars

is the brand under which German pipe maker Roland Schwarz produces pipes bearing his own name. The brand emerged in the first half of the 2000s and is a typical example of the path from hobby to profession. Before he began producing, Schwarz had smoked a pipe for roughly thirty years, yet during all that time he had never taken an interest in how the pipe he used was made; his profession was not pipe making but media design.
From Repair to Production

What changed direction was a secondhand pipe collection given to him. Schwarz began accumulating and reconditioning these pipes in 2000. Repairing an estate pipe involves, on a small scale, many of the operations of production, from cleaning the chamber to reshaping the mouthpiece; this pursuit gradually turned into a desire to make his own pieces.

The decisive name in this transition was German maker Jan Harry Seiffert. Schwarz carved his first pipe under his supervision, and nearly all the pipes he made in his early period passed through Seiffert's review. The second guiding figure was Belgian collector Erwin Van Hove, whose contribution concerned not so much the technique of pipe making as when and to which circles the work should be announced. According to records, within two days of the brand's website going live, several well-known American and European enthusiasts had placed orders.
Approach to Making

According to the brand's own promotion, only long-rested plateau briar is used in production, and the bodies contain no fills. Mouthpieces are hand-shaped, with the bit left flat; for the tenon, teflon is preferred for its resistance to breakage. This choice runs in the same direction as the general approach among lathe-turned synthetic tenon materials.

According to a German-language review from January 2004, the pipes were made in two types, with and without a filter chamber, no lining was applied to the inside of the bowl, and the smoke channel ran centered along the shank, terminating at a hole at the bottom of the bowl. The same source notes that on some oval-shanked pieces, the mouthpiece was fitted so it could be rotated. At the time the pipes were not graded and were signed with a single stamp, the words ROLAND HANDMADE.
Position and Aftermath

Schwarz has positioned himself not as a high-grade master but as a maker working at the mid-tier; he has stated that what he intends to develop going forward is not technical craftsmanship but a shape language of his own. Contemporary community reviews found the internal construction and mouthpiece work of the pipes strong, while accepting that the style was still in a formative stage. The brand's pipes were never given to intermediary dealers, being announced solely through his own website. According to a note on Pipedia, this site has been inaccessible since 2012; whether the brand continues production cannot be traced through independent records.

r.x: Johny Pipes

is a handmade pipe workshop founded by Meysam Jahani in the city of Babol in northern Iran. Records indicate that what began in 2018 as a one-man bench turned within a few years into a recognized signature reaching retailers beyond Iran as well. The workshop's visibility owes largely to a maker from a country without a deep-rooted pipemaking tradition reaching international collectors through self-taught skill.
Founding and the Maker

According to the account given, Meysam Jahani sat down at the bench not with a career goal in mind but as a side pursuit during a period when his university work had stalled. The maker never went through an apprenticeship at any workshop; he is said to have developed his hand skills largely by watching instructional videos online, receiving support during this process from fellow Iranian pipemaker Aref Rahimi. What began as a part-time pursuit quickly turned into a full-time occupation, with production gathered under the Johny Pipes signature. The workshop's visibility outside Iran grew as it entered the collections of pipe retailers based in the United States.

This path is considered a typical recent example of the artisan pipe versus factory pipe distinction: small-scale, single-maker production can reach international buyers directly without being confined to its home country's domestic market.
Production and Shape Language

The workshop uses briar for its stummels. Which material is preferred for mouthpieces is not specified separately in the promotional texts; the range covers the mouthpiece materials common among artisan workshops. Surface finish ranges from plain-polished bodies to rustic textures; where sandblasting is applied, care is taken to raise the grain's texture.

The shape considered the maker's signature is the calabash arrangement. Both the traditional calabash and the reverse-calabash structure — in which smoke expands and cools in the cavity beneath the chamber — make up the workshop's best-known work. The calabash arrangement is also adapted to classic silhouettes such as the billiard, poker, pot, rhodesian, and volcano; a body outline that looks familiar from the outside is thus paired with an unconventional interior structure. Calabashes worked in short, plump proportions are treated as a separate heading within the workshop.
Collections

Johny Pipes groups its work under series names. Among the headings listed in the workshop's own promotional material are the straight grain, cumberland, plateaux, and rustic series devoted to plain-grained bodies, along with the calabash and reverse-calabash series. To these are added titles such as Azar, Sadaf, Palas Cat, and Toca. A separate heading is also used for pieces made as one-of-a-kind pieces.

This naming is not a shape classification: the series are distinguished more by surface finish, mouthpiece material, or chamber arrangement. It is therefore possible to see the same silhouette across more than one series, and the series name alone does not indicate the shape of a given pipe. The workshop's range moving back and forth between traditional lines and freer designs is likewise tied to this flexible arrangement.

r.x: CO-Pipes

is the joint brand of two makers working in Hamm, in Germany's Westphalia region. The workshop, which takes its name from this partnership, is run by Kelvin Pohler and Thorsten "Toto" Klemme; the pair have presented the pipes they produce under their own names since 2015. Both pursue pipe-making alongside other work, so production moves not in series but piece by piece.
The Danish Line

By the workshop's own description, its benchmark is the formal approach developed in Denmark; CO-Pipes is in this respect counted among the German followers of the approach known as the Danish school. The concrete expression of this is that, rather than fixed classic shapes, mostly freeform bodies are worked. In such production, the material is what decides: the direction of the grain revealed when a briar block is opened largely determines which way the body will extend and which surface will be brought to the fore. Every body thus remains a one-off.

Another point the manufacturer's texts highlight is that concern for form does not overshadow ease of use; accordingly, even a sculptural-looking pipe is expected to have balanced weight distribution, a comfortable bite, and a properly opened smoke channel. The workshop is said to have become recognized relatively quickly within the German community; this assessment currently rests on manufacturer and retailer texts.
Way of Working Together

What sets CO-Pipes apart from similar small workshops is that its division of labor is not organized as "your pipe, my pipe." Pohler and Klemme work on the same body sometimes in turns, sometimes together; rough shaping, sanding, fitting the shank to the mouthpiece, and final surface work all pass through both makers' hands. The resulting pipe carries not one maker's signature, but the pair's shared signature.
A Bond Built Through Tobacco

The brand name is also tied to two tobacco blends: in a collaboration with German blender HU Tobacco, blends called "The Bullet" and "The Swan" were produced. By the manufacturer's descriptions, The Bullet is a ready-rubbed flake dominated by dark Virginia, with a small amount of Perique and a spicy character. The Swan, meanwhile, is presented as an English-type blend with a pronounced smoky side, adding Cyprus Latakia, black Cavendish, and a pinch of Perique to the Virginias. According to the story told, the starting point for the two distinct blends was that the two makers' tastes in tobacco differ from one another.

Directory of Japanese Pipe Brands

is a collective list of workshops and brand names that have made pipes in Japan. Production in the country draws on two distinct veins: on one side, the centuries-old craft tradition of the traditional Japanese pipe made of metal and bamboo; on the other, one-person benches that, in the second half of the twentieth century, discovered the Scandinavian shape idiom and developed their own style working in briar. The entries below briefly summarize the documented basic facts about each brand; those with a standalone article on the site are linked.
Brands
Goisagi Pipes
— Records mention only the brand name; no documented detail exists about the workshop, maker, or production.
Hachiro

— Seiji Hachiro grew up among pipes as the son of a Japanese pipe dealer and made his first pieces at age fourteen. At fifteen he displayed his work at his father's stand at the 2005 Chicago show, catching the attention of noted makers such as Teddy Knudsen and Edward Andrew Jurkiewicz of the E. Andrew Briars workshop. He continued his training over the following summer holidays at the sides of makers such as Tonni Nielsen and Lee von Erck in the United States, and later began working in his own workshop in Nishinomiya, Hyogo Prefecture.
Hasegawa

— Toyohei Hasegawa is a maker of the traditional Japanese pipe, the kiseru. He started out in Tsubame, one of the main production centers for this pipe, apprenticing to master Zengoro Hattori at age thirteen. He went out on his own in 1926, at just eighteen; in periods of high demand he produced as many as three hundred tin and copper kiseru a month. In the final stretch of his career, in the 1990s, he made pieces inlaid with gold and silver; after winning numerous awards, he was named among Tsubame's living cultural treasures.
Hattori
— Zengoro Hattori was one of the respected kiseru makers of the twentieth century. In his workshop in Tsubame he trained many craftsmen, including Toyohei Hasegawa.
Higuchi

— Born in Tokyo in 1930, Junichiro Higuchi moved to the bench in 1974 and returned that same year with first prize from a handmade pipe competition he entered. His annual output is around fifty pieces. His approach to shape sits close to the Danish school; besides briar he also works in ivory, horn, and bamboo.
HiRo
— HiRo-branded pipes are made by Yorozutoshi Hiroyuki, born in 1958. The maker works in Hokkaido.
Ichi

— Ichi Kitahara founded his bench in 2004, but has a long artistic background before that date. He trained in fresco painting in the Baroque style, and spent several months in South Dakota studying Native American silversmithing. Throughout the 1990s he made custom jewelry and ornamental pieces on commission, selling them through galleries in Tokyo. He is a student of Hiroyuki Tokutomi and makes pipes on a part-time basis.
Komatsu

— Having worked as a hairdresser for twenty years before moving to the bench, Komatsu draws a parallel between hair cutting and pipe making as crafts, saying balance is the decisive criterion in both. He has also worked on how smoke exits the stem, using an air-channel shape of his own design at the stem's end for even smoke dispersal.
Maruyama
— Hajime Maruyama is a young pipe carver not widely known outside Japan. No further detail is available on his style or production volume.
Miyasaka
— Pipes are known to have been made under this name; no record exists of the maker or workshop.
Namiki

— Namiki Manufacturing Co. Ltd. worked with Dunhill on lacquer (urushi) coated pipe production. The company has a technique of its own; pipe bowls are mostly decorated with various motifs and figures drawn from nature imagery.
Roland

— The name Roland has been used by several independent firms. A known example bearing this name in Japan was likely made by Fukashiro Tsutomu, who is said to have signed some of his more modest pieces with this brand. The same pipe also bears the stamp of Kikusui, one of Tokyo Ginza's longstanding tobacconists — a store-brand arrangement of the kind common at shops in the West too.
Tokutomi, Yuki

— Yuki Tokutomi is the daughter of Hiroyuki Tokutomi, a leading figure in Japanese pipe making, and has been making pipes since mid-2005. She grew up at her father's bench, learning the material and the process by helping him in the workshop. Her style reflects her father's while retaining its own character; her cited shape influences include Danish maker Gert Holbek and her father's own teacher, Sixten Ivarsson. She made her debut at the CPCC show in 2007.
Yanagihara

— Shigeyoshi Yanagihara is a maker whose career at the bench spans thirty years. After retiring from his career, he continued production as a pastime, making one to three pipes a year. He lives in Tokyo.
Zousan

— The maker's real name is unknown; the nickname "Zousan" can be translated into English as "Mr. Elephant." Said to have been making pipes since the early 1990s, he is among the Japanese makers little known in America and Europe.

r.x: Buescher's

was one of the best-known workshops making corncob pipes in the United States in the middle of the twentieth century. It was based in the town of Washington, in Missouri, the state regarded as the world capital of the corncob pipe. The "World Famous Pipe" stamp it used on its products still makes the brand identifiable on the secondhand market today.
Founding and the Town's Competition

The company was founded by George Buescher, Jr. Records indicate production began informally in 1939, with formal registration completed in 1941. This date coincides with the peak of Washington's corncob pipe industry: workshops opened one after another in and around the town during the first half of the twentieth century. Buescher's competed not only against Missouri Meerschaum, regarded as the industry's founder, but also against workshops such as Hirschl & Bendheim that had begun production far earlier. The newly founded company operated at the disadvantage of entering a market that had been established decades before it.

It is said that George Buescher worked for a time at Missouri Meerschaum and held a position in that company's management, though this has not been confirmed by documentation. Because of this connection, it was long assumed that Buescher's was sold to Missouri Meerschaum in the late 1940s. This scenario, which held true for many of the town's small producers, did not apply to Buescher's, which remained independent.
Production and Product Range

The workshop was built around mass production rather than individually handmade pipes. Its main product was the corncob pipe: dried and aged corn cobs were turned into bowl shapes, coated on the outside with a plaster-like filler, and then fitted with a simple stem. This method allowed for production that was far faster and cheaper than the handwork required by briar pipes. It was precisely this economic equation that made the corncob pipe so widespread in twentieth-century America: the raw material came from surrounding fields, the production steps could be mechanically replicated, and the broad public that could not afford a briar pipe ended up with a smokable pipe all the same. Buescher's was built exactly on top of this demand.

Between the 1940s and the 1960s the workshop also worked with other materials: hardwood pipes made from hickory, maple, and cherry wood joined the product list. The company also added various corncob-based novelty items to its production line, of which salt-and-pepper shaker sets are the best known. By 1976 the founder's son, David Buescher, had taken on the role of vice president and come to run most of the day-to-day operations and distribution.
Closure

By the late 1980s most of the corncob pipe makers in Washington had withdrawn from production; the only major name left standing in the industry was Missouri Meerschaum. Buescher's survived this contraction for a while longer, but closed its doors around 1990-1991. Today the brand lives on only in collectors' cabinets and old catalog pages; examples bearing the "World Famous Pipe" stamp are considered a tangible memento of the crowded era of the American corncob pipe industry.

r.x: Curtz

is the one-man bench American pipe maker Arley G. Curtz ran under his own name in Salt Lake City, the capital of Utah. The brand is the product neither of a factory nor of a family tradition passed down through generations; it was built on a pursuit taken up late in life. Curtz's actual profession lay in a field unrelated to pipe making, arts administration; he took up the bench after retiring as director of the Bountiful Davis Art Center in Bountiful, Utah.
From Repair to Making

Curtz's first regular contact with briar came not through making but through repair. He worked as a pipe repairman at Jeanie's Smoke Shop, a tobacconist in Salt Lake City, and entered into the structure of the pipe while working through broken shanks, burnt rim edges, and deformed mouthpieces. Because repair requires taking a pipe apart down to its inner channel and airflow to understand it, it is an unusual but solid school for the transition into making. Exactly which year he began producing his own pipes is not clear in the records; sources only note that he moved into making following his time as a repairman. In later years he gathered his work under the name "Curtz Handmade Pipes and Pipe Repair," running making and repair side by side on the same bench. This dual way of working resembles the small benches set up in the American scene after retirement.
Material and Working Pace

The workshop worked with briar blocks coming from the Mediterranean belt; sources mention Greek and Italian briar in particular. These two sources were the block suppliers small American workshops turned to most at the end of the twentieth century. Curtz kept his annual output limited to about seventy pipes; this figure corresponds to a pace in which every piece, on a one-man bench, passes through drilling, shaping, and polishing by a single hand. Small next to the thousands-counted output of serial production, this number is considered normal among handmade workshops.
Stamp and Recognition

Curtz pipes are known to bear a stamp carrying the maker's name under the shank. What the numbers seen alongside the stamp mean is not settled; while interpreted in collector circles as a quality grade, no primary record confirms this reading. His repertoire of shapes stayed within classic families, favoring measured, usable forms over showy designs.
Legacy

Arley G. Curtz died in May 2025, and the bench closed with the maker's death. Curtz is a typical example of the fairly numerous one-man workshops of late-twentieth-century American pipe making that turned out limited but good work without chasing fame. That his name is not widely known is the common fate of such makers: output is small, distribution is regional, and the brand more often than not ends together with the maker himself.

r.x: E. Andrew Briars

is an American pipe workshop run at a one-man bench in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The maker behind the brand appears in official records as Edward Jurkiewicz; in pipe circles he was known as "Andrew," and the brand name grew out of these two names. Sources do not agree on the spelling of the surname: the funeral home's and the local newspaper's notices give "Jurkiewicz," while pipe literature uses "Jurkieweicz." According to his obituary he was born on 29 May 1936 and died in Milwaukee on 23 December 2017 at the age of eighty-one.
From Machinist to Pipe Maker

Jurkiewicz's actual profession was not pipe making. He worked for thirty-seven years as a machinist at the Allen-Bradley plant, a maker of automation equipment. According to the obituary, his interests were not confined to the bench; he studied English literature at Marquette University, made oil-pastel paintings, and made time for history reading and learning Japanese. He kept up pipe making alongside these pursuits, as an after-hours occupation.

He learned the craft around Milwaukee's long-established tobacconist Uhle's. Jack Uhle, who guided him, had himself learned the trade directly from Achille Savinelli, founder of the Savinelli brand. In this way, the family tree of a Milwaukee bench connects, two generations removed, to the main line of Italian pipe making. No source gives the exact year he began making pipes under his own name; according to accounts this falls around the early 1980s.
Production and Style

The workshop's scale stayed small throughout. According to accounts, annual production did not exceed about 150 pipes, and the briar blocks he worked came from Italy, Corsica, and Greece; it is reported that he obtained these blocks not directly from log dealers but through Danish makers he knew. He used vulcanite, cumberland, and lucite for his bits.

He is not considered tied to a single style; alongside measured classic shapes he is also credited with freehand work. Surface finishing offered only two options: smooth and sandblast. It is said that in his sandblasts there was no concern to hide the wood's natural flaws, and the texture was left as it was. He also stayed within earth tones for staining; the information that he worked across a range from yellow to red, dark brown to black rests on the brand's own old promotional text and has no independent confirmation.
Stamp and Distribution

It is reported that the pipes carry a script-style "E. Andrew" wording, the word "BRIARS," and a date giving the year of manufacture. This layout of the stamp rests on a single source and has not been independently verified; if accurate, the date stamp would be the most practical way of putting surviving examples in order.

Jurkiewicz distributed his output for many years directly through tobacconist shops; alongside work under his own name, it is also reported that he made pieces for shops under more modest names. The brand never moved to a factory scale, and production stopped entirely with the maker's death. Today E. Andrew pipes circulate only in the estate market and are counted among the quiet examples of the American one-man-workshop tradition.

r.x: Phil Rivara
is an American pipe maker working alone, who rebuilds classic pipe shapes with proportions longer and thinner than usual. His pipes are recognized by a plain
PR
stamp struck on the body; because no series production is done, every piece is unique.
From the Navy to the Bench

Rivara's introduction to the pipe long predates his profession. He served three years on active duty and five years in the reserves in the United States Navy; records indicate he took up pipe smoking in 1989, during his reserve years. In the years spent between Northern California and the Pacific Northwest, he built up a working history running from repair work to auto body work, from a partnership in a business to various handcraft jobs, becoming accustomed along this path to tools and machining.

His move into pipe making, however, came quite late and by chance. According to a 2013 interview, his first time sitting at the bench was roughly three years before that; to be able to make a long-stemmed "Gandalf" pipe a friend wanted, he spent more than six months researching, watching footage of factory production and taking guidance from experienced American makers such as Mark Balkovec and Chris Morgan, largely teaching himself. His workshop is shown in the 2013 interview as being in Sacramento, and in more recent sources in Eagle Point, Oregon; the exact date of the move is not documented.
Shape and Material

The common thread across Rivara's work is stretched proportions. Long-stemmed shapes, especially the Canadian family and Cutty interpretations, are the forms that most often come off his bench; thinning the body without breaking the classic mold and lengthening the shank gives his pipes a silhouette that stands out at first glance. By contrast, he keeps his distance from the Oom Paul shape; by his own account, getting the smoke path right in this form is a challenge for him.

In block choice, he relies on two sources: in interviews he speaks of Greek briar and of briar blocks known as "Mimmo." For mouthpieces he uses acrylic, ebonite, horn, and other natural materials; he has stated that he has also experimented with morta and aluminum. That the turning and milling part of the work relies on machine equipment he has set up himself lets him reproduce fine details with repeatable precision.
Work Beyond Pipes

The workshop does not produce pipes alone. Rivara also makes wood-handled pipe reamers, tools used to correct the carbon buildup in the chamber. He also makes hand-shaped canes and walking sticks. That all three are produced with the same lathe and milling setup shows that Rivara builds his work more on a machine-shop discipline than on carving alone.

The maker is one of the American independent makers who shares his working process on his own video channel; because these recordings serve as documentation of a one-man workshop's day-to-day operation, they are among the sources frequently cited within the community.

r.x: Meissen Porcelain

is the name of the manufactory where hard-paste porcelain was first produced on a serial basis in Europe. Founded in workshops at Albrechtsburg Castle in the Saxon town of Meissen, the enterprise marked a technical turning point on a continent that had until then depended on porcelain from the Far East. Its significance for pipe history dates back to its earliest years: shortly after its founding, the manufactory also produced bowls for smoking tobacco, making it one of the earliest links in the German branch of the porcelain pipe tradition.
Porcelain's Riddle Solved in Europe

The composition of hard-paste porcelain remained unsolved in Europe for a long time; the continent made do with expensive imported pieces from China and Japan. Augustus the Strong (Augustus II), Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, kept Johann Friedrich Böttger, known for his claims of alchemy, working under supervision. After 1704 Böttger was drawn into the ceramic and glass experiments of the mathematician and natural scientist Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus. Tschirnhaus died in 1708; Böttger, continuing the research, soon arrived at a usable paste composition.

The manufactory was founded in 1709 under the name Royal Polish and Electoral Saxon Porcelain Manufactory, with workshops set up at Albrechtsburg Castle in Meissen, and official production began in 1710. The first product to emerge was not white porcelain: it was a reddish-brown and extraordinarily hard paste known as Böttger stoneware (Böttgersteinzeug). This paste had two practical advantages: it held fine detail from the mold without distortion and could be polished before firing. Silver vessel shapes of the period and Far Eastern ceramics could therefore be imitated with relative ease. White hard-paste porcelain that could be glazed and painted reached the market in 1713; roughly a decade later the overglaze enamel colors developed by Johann Gregorius Höroldt opened the manufactory's classical period. The crossed-swords mark, derived from the Electoral coat of arms, began to be used in the 1720s, became mandatory in 1731, and is still considered one of the oldest trademarks in continuous use today.
Meissen and the Pipe

According to reports, the manufactory's records from around 1712 list tobacco pipe bowls and whole pipes among the products it sold; this information has not been independently verified. Early-dated examples were not made of white porcelain but of the reddish Böttger stoneware. As the account goes, one such piece survives in a private collection: a fixed-stem bowl of Dutch form, unmarked. Which master's hand produced these pieces is unknown; attributing them to the workshop pipe maker Johann Müller remains no more than a hypothesis.

Meissen's involvement with the pipe never grew into a dedicated production line. Yet the painted porcelain-bowled pipes that spread through German and Central European workshops from the eighteenth century onward rest technically on the hard paste solved here. Porcelain is not porous like clay pipes; it does not absorb smoke, and so requires a water chamber to collect condensing moisture and a long stem. This constraint shaped the distinctive form of porcelain-bowled pipes, positioning the material within the world history of the pipe more for its painted surfaces and ceremonial value than for its smoking performance.
Today

After passing through various periods of ownership, the enterprise took the name Staatliche Porzellan-Manufaktur Meissen GmbH in 1991; its sole shareholder is the state of Saxony. Production today is centered on tableware, figurines, and art objects; the early pipe bowls survive as historic pieces studied in museums and private collections.

r.x: Hynick

is the name of the one-man workshop American pipe maker Tim Hynick runs in the greater Boston area of Massachusetts. This workshop, which has nothing to do with mass production, is counted among the artisan makers who turn out a limited number of pipes a year. Rather than achieving broad recognition on a national scale, the brand has remained a name that circulates among collectors around New England.
The Start of the Path

No clear record fixes the year the workshop was founded; the available dealer and club records suggest that Hynick began production sometime in the 2000s. It is said that the maker learned the craft not through trial and error on his own but at the bench of established American makers. Dealer profiles mention, among these names, J.M. Boswell and Joe Skoda, founder of the Skoda Pipes workshop; since this information rests on a single dealer source, it should be read with caution. Hynick has himself acknowledged the support he received from other makers early on.

On the raw material side, the workshop works with culled briar blocks bought from the suppliers that top-tier American makers turn to. This selection is also the main factor determining production volume in one-maker workshops: tightly culled blocks mean few but consistent pipes.
Approach to Form

Two groups make up the bulk of the workshop's output. The first is freehand pipes carrying the influence of the Danish school; bodies that develop according to grain direction and deliberately move away from symmetry are the defining line of this group. The second is classic shapes kept to medium and large scale. In both groups, keeping the dimensions on the large side is considered a choice that makes the maker's handwork visible.
Surface and Mouthpiece Work

The application that most defines the workshop is the rusticated surface treatment Hynick developed himself. Leaving deep, irregular indentations instead of a repeating regular texture, this treatment gives the bowl a rough, unfinished-stone-like appearance and is counted as the brand's signature. Mouthpieces are not bought ready-made either; the maker shapes acrylic and Cumberland rod on his own lathe. According to dealer records, some examples have silver and copper spacer rings fitted between shank and mouthpiece.

There is no organized institutional source on the brand. The most detailed text is a workshop-visit article published around a Boston-based pipe club; information beyond that relies largely on dealer records and collector posts. What level the workshop is currently operating at has likewise not been confirmed by any current source.

r.x: Innerschwyzer-Pfeifen

is the name of a local pipe tradition kept alive in the Muota valley (Muotathal) of central Switzerland, and of the family workshop that represents it today. The workshop's signature product is the pipe known locally, in short, as "Yps." The name comes from the local pronunciation of
Gips
, meaning plaster, and points directly to the bowl's classic material. In terms of shape, the Yps is considered a valley-specific interpretation of the broader "Schwyzer" family of peasant pipe.
A Local Type with a Plaster Bowl

What sets Yps pipes apart from mainstream briar production is that the bowl is cast in plaster rather than shaped from wood. This choice is considered an extension of the habit, from before briar spread across Europe, of working with materials that were easily found and cheaply worked in the Alps; the same logic is seen in the clay pipe tradition, with its porous earthenware bodies. After casting, the plaster bowl is finished and dressed by hand. A significant portion of the workshop's output is completed with metal fittings; the metal band and lid fitted to the bowl's rim serve both to protect the soft material and to give the pipe the region's familiar look.
The Break in the Tradition and Its Revival

Andreas Heinzer, the name behind today's workshop, did not come to the trade from pipe making. As a young man he trained as a machinist at the Victorinox factory in Ibach, the firm known for its Swiss army knives, and changed careers years later. Being cut off from handwork weighed on him, and this, combined with seeing that no one was left in the valley making the Yps, led him to decide to restart production.

The last maker before the break, records say, was Paul Betschart, who ran the craft for many years and was known locally by the nickname "s' Wiselis Pauli"; as the story goes, Betschart gave up the work in 1996, and shortly before his death approached Heinzer with an offer to carry the craft on, though the proposal found no response at the time. When the workshop was set up, the venture was shaped from the start as a family undertaking; as it is told, the support of Heinzer's brother Paul and his sister-in-law Silvia, a goldsmith, proved decisive at this stage. Heinzer is regarded today as the last pipe maker still carrying on this craft in Muotathal, and says he learned it largely through his own effort.
Product Range

The workshop's output is not limited to the plaster-bowled Yps. The same traditional molds are also worked in wood; the materials used include rosewood (Palisander), whitebeam (Mehlbeerbaum), boxwood, and deer antler. Alongside these, handmade pipes in contemporary shapes not tied to the local molds are also produced. For the place of these non-briar woods in pipe making, see the woods other than briar and alternative woods used in pipe making entries.

The pipe is not the workshop's only pursuit: knives with handles of natural material, rings, chains, and other jewelry made of cow and deer horn, and horn-framed eyeglasses also come off the same bench. That every piece is one of a kind is a working principle the workshop states for itself. The Heinzer family is a regular participant in the alpine cheese fair held every year on the last weekend of October in Muotathal; Swiss television programs on traditional crafts have also featured the workshop on several occasions.

r.x: Learned

is the name identifying the handmade pipes of pipe maker Sam Learned (1936-2015), who worked in York, in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania. Learned took up the craft at fifty-nine, while running an established patent law practice. Over a production span approaching twenty years he became known for his horn shapes and his "Hunter" pipes, which set a crown of deer antler at the end of the shank. Within the American handmade pipe tradition, he is counted as a small workshop with a distinctive style.
From Engineering to Patent Law

Sam Learned was born in Seattle on 17 September 1936; his family moved to Phoenix in 1946. In 1960 he earned a chemical engineering degree from New Mexico State University and joined the army as a lieutenant that same month; his introduction to pipes dates to these years. Leaving the army in 1964, he settled in York and worked as an engineer. Holding patents on several machine inventions of his own steered him toward law: in 1973 he earned a doctorate in law from the University of Baltimore, and after 1975 practiced patent law on his own. Pipe making continued alongside this demanding profession, carried on as a pursuit confined to certain days of the week at a workshop in his home's basement.
Apprentice to Mr. Groum

Learned had seen the pipes of Jim Margroum for years at Adams County's apple harvest festival, and in December 1995 proposed to apprentice under him. Margroum (1921-2001), who worked in Hanover and stamped his pipes "Mr. Groum," was a self-taught maker known for figurative carvings — a bitten apple shape in particular. The apprenticeship began on 4 January 1996 and ran for a year in sessions of four hours, twice a week. Greek plateau briar sat at the center of the training: reading a block's grain, spotting a flaw in advance, and drawing the shape from where the wood allowed it. In later years, the ties he built with American makers such as Ed Burak, J. M. Boswell, and Mark Tinsky shaped his style. Records indicate that under this circle's influence he moved away from stained surfaces, increasingly leaving pipes in their natural color, finished with polish and wax alone.
Lines and Grades
The maker's output was gathered into a few named lines:
Horn
— horn shapes he developed by way of Danish and Italian interpretations. He is known to have set aside his largest and cleanest blocks for this line.
Hunter
— pipes in which the mouthpiece seats into a crown of horn at the end of the shank. Since every piece of horn differs, no two examples are alike; bark-topped plateau bowls also appear in this line.
Free Style
— free-form shapes not tied to a classical mold.
Large Mouth Bass
— figurative pipes finished by hand from large, near-flawless blocks.
Mule
— a plain entry line marked with a single-star grade, made to introduce his work to new buyers.

Quality grades ran three tiers based on the wood's quality: Star (select), Crescent (superior), and Sun (first class). Hunter pipes were made mostly at the first two grades, and at Sun grade where the wood allowed it.
Stamp, Mouthpiece, and Dimensions

Learned signed his pipes with an interlocking "SL" mark, accompanied by a two-digit year, so dating can be read directly off the shank. On pipes from later years a grade mark was also added to the stamp. He used lucite for the mouthpiece in early years but later switched to vulcanite, which he found lighter and easier to work; he is known to have deferred to buyer preference on mouthpiece material. Chamber diameters were mostly around 2 centimeters; he also made large chambers exceeding 2.5 centimeters in his Hunter and free-form pieces. He tried to source his briar directly at origin: alongside an Algerian connection, records show he planned supply trips to Corsica and Italy. By 1997 he had completed around 350 pipes; in his prime he turned out about twenty pipes a month. Sam Learned died on 5 October 2015.

r.x: Pipes JAS

is the name of a small pipe bench run single-handedly by Juan Antonio Salhus Rodríguez in the city of Curicó in Chile's central region. Among the few workshop-scale producers in Latin America, the brand stands out for relying entirely on a local wood rather than imported briar. Because thorough records about it long remained scarce, it is listed in most catalogs under "brands of uncertain identity"; even so, the maker's own publications and interviews in the Spanish-language pipe press lay out with reasonable clarity who founded the brand and how.
The Founder and the Birth of the Bench

Salhus spent his working life in information technology, running a small computer business in Curicó. In a 2012 interview he says he began smoking a pipe more than twenty years earlier, returned to it after a gap, and made his first pipes about two years before that interview; on this basis the bench can be said to have been founded around 2010. The founding year is nonetheless not fixed; dates in the maker's own publications do not line up exactly with this calculation. The start was less a business plan than a response to dissatisfaction with ready-made pipes: Salhus and his physician friend Marcos Benavente tried making pipes for their own use, and interest from those around them turned production into a regular practice. In the same interview he says monthly output at that time ran between thirty and forty pipes, and that he promoted the brand mainly online and at local craft fairs; this figure rests on a single interview and cannot be taken as valid for later years.
Espino: A Native Alternative to Briar

The brand's defining choice lies in its material. Like many producers who work with woods other than briar, Salhus turned to what was at hand and chose the heartwood of espino (Vachellia caven, formerly Acacia caven), native to Chile's arid interior plains. This squat, thorny acacia is the typical tree of the Chilean matorral scrubland and has traditionally been used mainly for firewood and charcoal. Salhus gathers and selects the wood himself directly from where it grows; he cites hardness, grain texture, and heat resistance as his selection criteria. These criteria echo the reasoning frequently put forward in the history of woods sought as alternatives to briar.

The same simplicity is kept in the finish: no paint, colorant, or varnish is applied to the body, color and pattern are left entirely to the wood's own grain, and only carnauba wax is used as the final coat. Salhus says the wood distributes heat well and forms a soft carbon layer in the bowl; this is the maker's own assessment and does not rest on independent measurement.
Method and Stamp

Every stage of production is carried out by hand, using simple hand tools rather than mass-production machinery. Salhus lists his process as: selecting the wood, rough-cutting, drilling the tobacco chamber and airway, centering the stem, shaping with a rotary hand tool, fine sanding, branding the stamp, and waxing. The stylized "JAS" letters burned into the shank are the brand's only identifying mark; no catalog number, shape code, or year stamp is used. The distinction between handmade and machine-made is usually debated at factory scale; Pipes JAS, by contrast, stays within the natural limits of a one-person bench. Because production is irregular and small in scale, the brand's recognition outside Chile is limited, and whether the workshop is currently active has not been confirmed.

r.x: Barling

is an English pipe house founded in London in 1812, counted among the oldest surviving names in the pipe world. At the outset stood not pipe carving but silversmithing: Benjamin Barling, a silversmith working in Marylebone, founded the firm by making mounts, bands, and lids for meerschaum bowls. When his sons William and Edward joined the business, the firm took the name B. Barling & Sons. Records show the company exhibited silver-mounted meerschaum sets at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London and used the medal it won there on the cover of its later catalogs.
From the Silver Workshop to the Briar Lathe

When briar was introduced to English smokers in the 1850s, Barling turned to this material as well. The path it followed at first was the common method of English pipe houses of the day: bowls were roughly turned at French production centers such as Saint-Claude, finished at the London workshop, and completed with silverwork. Exactly when the firm moved to turning its own bowls is disputed; sources give years ranging from 1906 to 1909. Even this transition was not absolute: according to testimony given during a legislative hearing in 1928, the company was still forced to keep buying semi-worked bowls (stummel) from Saint-Claude in order to meet demand.
Algerian Wood and Grades

The brand's reputation rests to a great extent on the wood it used. For many years Barling favored slow-grown, air-dried Algerian briar; this material, known among enthusiasts as "old wood," is regarded as the chief explanation for the pipes' reputation for a cool, mild smoke. The "YE OLDE WOOD" mark struck on the shank, along with the T.V.F. mark — which collectors read as an abbreviation of "The Very Finest" — is part of the same claim. The 1962 catalog lays out the product hierarchy starting from plain models and running through the sandblasted finish known as "fossil," Guinea Grain, Ye Olde Wood Special, and two separate straight-grain classes. When this source narrowed with the outbreak of war in Algeria in 1954, the company, by its own account, shifted its supply to France, Italy, Sardinia, Spain, and Greece.
The Family's Departure and the Change in Stamps

On October 3, 1960, the family sold the company to its largest customer, Finlay, though it continued to run the business itself until mid-1962. Forty-nine percent of Finlay's shares belonged to Imperial Tobacco, and in early 1963 Imperial acquired the remaining share as well, bringing Barling under its direct control. Reading this transition from the product alone is not easy, because for roughly twenty months after the sale, the pipes continued to leave the hands of the same makers, stamped exactly as before. The real dividing line appeared in 1962: with the 150th-anniversary catalog, the first digit of the model number began indicating length, and in the retailer catalog published at the end of that year, the arched "BARLING'S MAKE" stamp was replaced by the script "Barling" logo. Collectors' distinction between "Pre-Transition," "Transition," and "Post-Transition" rests on these thresholds; exactly where the boundaries should fall is still debated.
After London

Imperial Tobacco closed the Barling factories in London in 1970 and outsourced production; brand-stamped pipes were made first at English workshops such as Charatan, then in Denmark by Erik Nørding. Records indicate the naming rights passed to Bucktrout in 1980, and production continued for a time on the Isle of Man; in later years, Barlings clearly made by Peterson also came onto the market. In 2020, German pipemaker Oliver Kopp brought the brand's European and American naming rights together under a single owner and restarted production.

Family-era Barlings remain one of the most closely researched areas of English pipe collecting. Which period an example belongs to is generally determined by comparing the form of the stamp, the digit arrangement of the model number, and additional marks such as T.V.F.
