r.x: Ailarov

is the name of the workshop the Russian pipe maker Sergey Ailarov runs alone in Moscow. Pipe making in Russia, compared with established centers such as France or Denmark, is a pursuit not even half a century old; Ailarov is counted among the few names from this young craft best known outside the country.
Before the Workbench

Ailarov was born in 1973 in Vladikavkaz, in the Caucasus. His first professional training was in music: he studied jazz guitar and composition. At twenty-five he settled in Moscow and worked for a time in photography; it was also in this city that he began making pipes.

According to records, the start of it all was a pipe given to him as a gift on his thirtieth birthday. Ailarov first turned to collecting pipes, then tried growing his collection with pieces of his own making, carving his first pipe by hand from a block of briar. Through the introduction of a Moscow tobacconist he is said to have met Michail Revyagin, one of the established figures in the Russian pipe circle, learned the basics of the craft at his workshop for a time, and, after acquiring the necessary tools, set up his own workshop once that period ended.
Production and Shape Language

Ailarov's work does not come from a production mold but from decisions made block by block, which is why the number of pipes he produces each year is limited. Sources describing the maker's craftsmanship emphasize balanced proportion, grain quality, and the internal dimensions that determine the smoke. His surface treatment includes both high-polish examples and sandblasted finishes; natural materials such as horn are also known to appear in his mouthpieces.

Production is not tied to a single family of shapes: alongside forms close to classic molds, such as the billiard or the brandy, there are also freehand interpretations that grow as free as the block allows. Ailarov is known to consider the "classic versus freehand" debate unproductive, arguing that every handmade pipe carries the maker's own sense of form.
Standing

Ailarov is regarded as one of Russia's representatives of the generation of independent artisan workshops that spread worldwide over the past two decades. Since his pipes reach the market through specialist channels in Europe and North America, he is also known among collectors outside his home country.

r.x: Salim Şener

is a meerschaum pipe carver raised in the Eskişehir region. His name appears in international records, with Turkish letters dropped, as "Salim Sener"; the stamp on his pipes most often shows only "Salim" or "Sener." Records show he entered the craft in the early 1970s, and over more than forty years of production has become known both for figural carving and for ornamental arrangements associated with his own name.
From Quarry to Bench

According to records, Şener's childhood ambition was not carving but teaching; he stood out for his aptitude in drawing. In 1970, at age thirteen, he began working alongside his father in the meerschaum quarries near his village of Margı. After a year at the quarry he turned toward the bench: in 1971 he began an apprenticeship under Ahmet Gök in his village, and from 1972 to 1974 worked in Eskişehir at the workshop of his uncle Ekrem Şener. His listing as born in 1957 in auction records is consistent with these dates.

This route is typical of the pattern in Eskişehir meerschaum carving. In quarry villages, children mostly first took on the extraction and sorting of the stone, moving on to carving only after years of rough-shaping and finishing work alongside a master. Şener's passing through two separate benches is part of this same pattern; moving from a village workshop to a city workshop meant a change in scale and subject repertoire within the craft.
Ornamental Arrangements

Sources state that he began carving the flower ornaments distinctive to his pipes in 1985, and the arrangement known as "reverse claw" from 1989 onward, continuing to work on this theme since. The claw motif is among the oldest subjects of meerschaum carving; it has been worked since 19th-century workshops in the form of a bird of prey's claw gripping the bowl. Şener's treatment of this classic subject in his own arrangement is what has earned his name a separate heading in catalog listings.

Among the subjects seen on pipes bearing his signature in secondhand and catalog records are dragons, eagles, tigers, goat heads and human portraits; these pieces are gathered under the heading "Autograph Series" in dealer catalogs. The number of carvers able to sign a pipe with their own name in Turkish meerschaum production is limited, and Şener is counted among the makers who carry this distinction.
Partnerships and State of Sources

He is noted as having worked jointly in the past with Şevket Gezer and Yunus Ege, and as having run a partnership since 1999 with Erdoğan Ege. His work reaches outside Türkiye mainly through two channels: the Eskişehir-based MeerschaumStore, and SMS, which carries Turkish block meerschaum pipes to the United States. In American dealer listings of master carvers, his name appears alongside those such as Erdoğan Ege, Yunus Ege and Sadık Yanık.

Sources note that he has won various awards, though the names, the granting bodies and the years of these awards are not documented. There is likewise no verifiable record of the workshop's present arrangement, the apprentices he has trained, or whether production continues; what is known rests on short entry listings and the secondhand records his pipes circulate through.

r.x: Lorenzetti

is a pipe workshop founded in 1934 by Otello Lorenzetti in the town of Recanati in Italy's Marche region. Starting at home with a few rented lathes and twenty to thirty pipes a day, the business grew across later generations into a family firm turning out tens of thousands of pipes a year and exporting to many countries. Production has since stopped.
The Birth of a Workshop in Recanati

In the first half of the twentieth century, Recanati was home to several small pipe workshops; Catena Remigio, named in the records, is one of them and is cited as the place where the brand's founder learned the craft. Born in 1911 in Castelnuovo, part of the town, and with schooling that ended at primary level, Otello Lorenzetti completed eighteen months of military service in Cividale, in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region, then began working for himself in 1934. The first workshop was part of the home, the lathes were rented, and daily output did not exceed twenty to thirty pipes. Products were delivered directly to tobacconists around Macerata, San Severino, and Civitanova Marche.

The decade following its founding was interrupted twice by the war. The founder was conscripted in 1935 and sent to units in Africa, not returning until January 1937; he was called up again in October 1940 and did not return home until 1943. Marinella, whom he married in 1940, became the second defining figure of the business during and after these years.
Turning into a Family Business

The era of rented lathes ended in 1947: the founder built, with his own means, equivalents of the machines he had been using until then, and had a craft workshop in Civitanova Marche prepare the parts that were hard to shape by hand. Production sped up and diversified as a result. The 1960s and 1970s marked the beginning of exports; the founder's children Luciano, Gabriella, and Alessandro, along with a few employees, joined the business as it opened up to markets in Europe, Africa, and America. On the matter of the brand's renown, it is reported that Sandro Pertini, the well-known pipe enthusiast who served as President of Italy, took an interest in Lorenzetti pipes.

According to information given to local press in 2014 to mark the business's eightieth year, annual production ran between twenty and thirty thousand pipes, with the main export markets being Canada, China, the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany. At that time the business was headed by the founder's youngest son, Alessandro Lorenzetti. Together with the Moretti workshop, founded in the same town in 1968, Lorenzetti is counted as one of the two addresses that made Recanati the pipe center of the Marche region.
Stamps, Series, and Craftsmanship

The pipes carry a hand-script "Lorenzetti" on the left side of the shank, with "ITALY" below it; the series name, shape number, or both appear on the right side. Restoration and inventory records mention series names such as Avitus and Macerata, along with four-digit shape numbers. A hand-script "L" mark was used on the stems.

Production is built on classic English and Italian shapes made from briar; smooth, sandblasted, and rustic finishes all appear side by side. Examples with vulcanite and acrylic stems, models decorated with silver bands, and bodies suited to 9 mm filters are all part of the known catalogue. This structure places the brand closer to the scaled-up factory pipe tradition than to workshops identified by a single maker's signature.
Current Status

Records indicate the brand's production has ended; sources give no definite closing date. The business's official website, which had stayed online for many years, is also inaccessible today. As a result, Lorenzetti pipes now appear not as new production but in collections and secondhand circulation.

r.x: Pipe materials and construction

is an umbrella heading that considers together the two variables shaping both a pipe's appearance and its smoking behavior. The result changes as much with how the body is built as with what material the bowl is made from: the path the smoke channel follows, whether an air gap sits beneath the bowl, and how the stem seats into the shank. Part names and their placement are covered in the pipe anatomy entry, and a criterion-by-criterion comparison of materials is found in pipe bowl materials.
The Framework of Natural Materials

The standard material of the modern pipe, briar — the root burl of the tree heath (Erica arborea) that grows around the Mediterranean — earned its place through its resistance to fire and its ability to absorb the moisture released during smoking. Before briar settled into that position in the second half of the 19th century, Europe's dominant material was fired clay. From the 16th century, when tobacco entered the continent, the clay pipe was in the hand of smokers of every class; Westminster's pipe makers were numerous enough by 1619 to become a livery company under royal charter. Among mineral-derived materials, meerschaum stands out: its name means "sea foam" in German, and the principal deposits of this soft sepiolite lie around Eskişehir, with secondary deposits in Somalia's El Buur region. Because its porous structure draws in moisture and tar, the surface, as it is used, turns from bottom to top through tones running from yellow to amber.

At the far end of the list are rarer materials: oak blackened over thousands of years in a bog (bog oak), pipestone carved from North America's red catlinite, and fired porcelain. In the calabash pipe, the body is made from a gourd, while the bowl surface that contacts fire is usually a separate piece of meerschaum or porcelain. The workshop that turned the corn cob pipe into a cheap, mass-producible product was founded in 1869 in Washington, Missouri; the Dutch immigrant carpenter Henry Tibbe patented, in 1878, the method that boosted the cob's durability by filling its pores from the outside with a plaster-like compound. The company took the name Missouri Meerschaum in 1907.
How Construction Affects Smoking

Two pipes made from the same material do not smoke the same way if their construction differs. What defines a calabash is not the material of its body but the wide air gap left beneath the bowl; this volume is held to cool the smoke, lower its moisture, and soften its bite. Briar pipes whose outer line imitates a calabash mostly lack such a gap, so the resemblance stays on the surface. The same principle also operates in separately lined bowls, filter sockets, and moisture-collecting stem mechanisms. There is also a construction-based reason corn cob is so often recommended to beginners: it is held to deliver the expected smoke from the very first day, without the break-in period briar requires.
Metal and Synthetic Experiments

Metal-bodied pipes form a separate branch. What these designs share is collecting moisture that condenses along the shank in a separate chamber and giving the smoke a longer path to travel before reaching the mouth; the bowl in most models is an independent part that can be removed and replaced. Records list Kirsten and Falcon as the names continuing production in this branch.

Laboratory materials were also tried in the mid-20th century. Records indicate the Super-Temp Corporation began producing a model called "the pipe" in 1963, with a plastic body and a bowl lined with pyrolytic graphite; from 1965 sales ran through Venturi, Inc., and the line was withdrawn from the market around 1975. S. M. Frank & Co., meanwhile, developed Brylon in 1966, a material combining heat-resistant resin with ground wood flour; pipes made from this durable but relatively heavy material continued to be produced in later years as well.

r.x: Fader's

is an American tobacconist business that opened in Baltimore in 1891 and was run by the same family for many years. Though not a pipe factory running series production in its own workshop, it is counted among the typical examples of the US house-brand (house line) tradition through the eponymous pipe series it had other manufacturers make.
A Century as a Family Business

The founder of the shop, Abraham Fader, was born in Germany; it has often been recounted by later generations that he founded the business out of a need to make a living rather than any passion for tobacco. A small hand-rolled cigar workshop stood right next to the store. The great fire that consumed the center of Baltimore in 1904 destroyed both this workshop and the warehouse; though the city was rebuilt quickly, the manufacturing arm closed in the early 1920s in the face of the spread of machine-made cigars, and the business turned entirely to retail.

After Abraham Fader's death in 1934, the business passed to his son Ira B. Fader, who had trained in chemistry and joined the store on his return from World War I; the firm's name took the form A. Fader & Son in this period. When Ira died unexpectedly in Europe in 1959, management passed to the third generation, Bill Fader. Bill Fader remained at the head of the shop for decades and turned the business into a Baltimore chain by opening branch after branch; a second location in Towson, according to the record, opened in 1965.
Change of Hands

The 107-year-old business did not pass to a fourth generation: in 1998, at the height of the cigar boom, it was sold to a Baltimore-based cigar and tobacco retailer. According to the account, the buyer was a company called AFADCO, which after the sale merged with another investment partnership and simplified the trade name to Fader's. Bill Fader continued in the tobacco trade after the sale and held a role in the American tobacco retailers' professional association. When the cigar wave subsided in the early 2000s, most of the chain's stores were divided among different investors.
House Series

The store's eponymous pipes were never produced at its own bench; the stamp belonged to Fader's, the body to other workshops. Over the years the series that reached the market sometimes took their names from the shop itself: Fader's Calvert, from the flagship store on Calvert Street in downtown Baltimore, is the best-known example. Some series, meanwhile, were named directly for a surface or material feature: the rough-surfaced Fader's English Rough, Fader's M/L, whose bowl is said to be lined with African meerschaum, Fader's Naturals with unstained briar, and the filter-equipped Fader's Filter Pipe all belong to this group. Pipe listings also mention a model stamped simply "Fader" and a Fader's Tan Blast; these are said to have been made to order at the Shalom Pipe Factory in Israel and in Italy respectively, though these attributions are not backed by independent records.

Such stamps, as is often seen among briar brands forgotten over time, are understood to point to the retailer rather than the manufacturer. Because a tobacconist could shift its orders to different workshops over the years, two pipes carrying the same name may have come from entirely different hands, which makes dating house series difficult. It is recounted that the store employed a full-time pipemaker for a period, a tradition said to have ended in the early 1960s. Today the business stocks the pipes of many different manufacturers and no longer issues a new series under its own name.

r.x: SMS

is an import and distribution brand bringing meerschaum pipes carved in Eskişehir to the United States market. It is not a workshop producing pipes at its own bench, but an intermediary that commissions work from independent carvers in Türkiye and puts the finished pipes into circulation in the US under its own name. With a history spanning more than forty years, it is considered one of the most familiar names for Turkish meerschaum in America.
Founding and Family Business

The brand was founded in 1980 by Şamil Sermet, from Eskişehir, and his wife Beth Sermet. The business is known as SMS Meerschaums & Briars; its face online is SMS Pipes. In US trade directory records, the company appears under the title Sermet International, Inc., based in Vancouver, Washington, with a founding year of 1980. According to the company's own account, Şamil Sermet took a buying trip to Türkiye every year and personally managed the relationship with the carvers.

Following Şamil Sermet's death, the business has been carried on within the family: his wife Beth Sermet is credited on the office and ordering side, their son Mert Sermet in day-to-day operations, and Şamil Sermet's sister Emel Sağtekin in quality control. Sağtekin is stated to have held this role since 1988. According to records, SMS is considered a supplier reaching close to five hundred tobacconists nationwide.
Import Model and the Eskişehir Connection

SMS's business model rests on the scattered workshop structure of Eskişehir meerschaum carving. The company buys pipes from master carvers, most of whom work in and around Eskişehir. According to the brand's own promotion, it maintains an ongoing working relationship with about ten masters; the names mentioned include Salim Şener, Erdoğan Ege, Sadık Yanık, İsmail Bağlan, Yunus Ege, Ramazan Karaca, Tekin Gök, and masters from the Gezer family. It is emphasized that only pipes carved from natural block meerschaum are used, and that material obtained by pressing stone chips is not employed.

The pipes generally do not carry the carver's signature; the only mark on them is SMS. This is a common arrangement among importer brands, and it creates a difficulty for collectors: which master a given SMS pipe came from can only be guessed at from its shape and workmanship style. This same circumstance also explains why the distinction between artisan pipe and factory pipe is not easily drawn in the Turkish meerschaum market.
Products and Distinguishing Marks

The catalogue draws on two strands. On one side are meerschaum interpretations of classic pipe shapes such as the billiard and bent billiard; on the other are the figural carvings that are the true specialty of the Eskişehir school: motifs such as bowl held in a claw, sultan and pasha heads, animal figures, and skulls fall into this second group. Lattice work, where the body is pierced in an openwork technique, is also common.

Acrylic and vulcanite are used for mouthpieces, and the brand name is inlaid on the left cheek of the mouthpiece. The pipes come with a hard presentation box lined in golden fabric; the round label inside the box carries SMS at the center, surrounded by English wording noting hand-carved block meerschaum and Türkiye. This box-and-inlay arrangement is the main clue used to identify a pipe circulating on the secondhand market.
The Briar Line

SMS's second line of business is pipes made from briar: the company handles US distribution for the Italian brand Lorenzo. Lorenzo's origins trace back to the Fratelli Lana workshop, founded in 1900 in the town of Gallarate, Lombardy; the business passed into the hands of the Tagliabue family in 1946, and the brand took its current name in 1969. In this way, SMS brings meerschaum and briar together under one roof, as its business name itself suggests.

r.x: Italian pipe making

came of age after the war not in a single center but in two separate nuclei hundreds of kilometers apart. One was Pesaro on the Adriatic coast; the other was the Lombardy line north of Milan taking in Como, Cantù, Cucciago, and Varese. Untangling the kinship between brand names most often comes down to knowing which of these two nuclei a given brand is tied to.
Pesaro: From Master to Master

In Pesaro, small workshops that knew one another sprang up during the 1960s and 1970s; the region's brands were born largely in the hands of people who broke away from these workshops. The name at the center of the network is Giancarlo Guidi. After making pipes as an amateur for a time, Guidi founded the Mastro de Paja workshop in 1972; when he and his partner Giannino Spadoni parted ways in 1981, he left the workshop and founded Ser Jacopo the following year. Bruto Sordini, who trained under Guidi, also left with him in 1981; in later years he would become known under the name Don Carlos. Giorgio Imperatori, who founded Il Ceppo, had known Guidi since Pesaro's earliest years; the brand's production begins in the late 1970s. Names that emerged later, such as Rinaldo and L'Anatra, are likewise extensions of this same web of kinship.

The region's style is considered neoclassical. What is renewed is not the mold but the proportion: established English shapes such as the billiard or the bulldog remain recognizable, but the transitions between shank and bowl, the stance, and the balance of volume are reworked. Following the direction of the briar's grain during cutting is also a habit credited to the region.
The Como Line: From Factory to Workshop

The story in the north begins in 1947 with the Castello workshop Carlo Scotti opened in Cantù; the region's high-end pipe tradition spread out from there. Peppino Ascorti joined Castello's benches in 1959, Luigi Radice in 1961. Ascorti left at the end of 1968 to start his own business and brought along his neighbor in Cucciago, Radice; once Milan tobacconist Gianni Davoli took on distributing the pair's pipes, the brand came to be known by the name Caminetto. The trio broke up at the end of 1979: first Radice, then Ascorti left the workshop. Radice founded the brand bearing his own name in 1980; the Caminetto name, in time, passed to the Ascorti family.

The region's second strand is the factory tradition. Achille Savinelli and Enea Buzzi entered into partnership in 1947; Savinelli took charge of sales, Buzzi of production, and the pipes reached the market under the Savinelli name. The manufacture Buzzi ran in the town of Brebbia, near Varese, began being stamped with the Brebbia name from 1953 onward; the link between the two names broke off completely in 1956. The Rovera family workshop, founded in Varese in 1911, meanwhile turned in 1974 into the Ardor brand, taking its name from Angelo and Dorelio Rovera, and moved entirely from series production to fully hand-finished pipes.
A Question of Scale

What separates the two traditions is a matter of scale as much as geography. The Radice family's annual output stays under two thousand; Caminetto's production rose from three thousand to seven thousand a year over the course of the 1970s. Brebbia and Savinelli, by contrast, were founded from the outset as factories meant to produce at a steady volume. Scale alone, however, does not determine style: factory-rooted makers went on to develop hand-finished top series over time, and, as in the case of Ardor, some turned their production over entirely to handwork.

r.x: Celius

is the pipe workshop Svend Axel Celius founded in 1963 on Denmark's small island of Bogø. The brand was born during the years when postwar Danish pipes were rising in the American market, and it was among the first to profit from that rise. The maker's name is best remembered today for the Chess series, graded after chess pieces.
From Suhr's Workshop to His Own Factory

Records indicate Celius began his career around 1959-60 at Suhr's Pibemageri in Copenhagen. This workshop was one of the early centers of the hand-shaping approach known as the Danish school. He trained under Poul Rasmussen and the workshop's foreman, Sven Knudsen. A few years later he left to start his own business, moving his production into a former dairy building in Bogø By.

The years the factory was founded coincide with the period when interest in Danish-made freehand pipes was growing rapidly in the United States. Celius was among the first Danes able to ship such pipes overseas in meaningful numbers. Smaller quantities also went to Germany, though the brand's real recognition took shape in the American market. At its most productive, the factory employed close to twenty workers. Contract production for the Copenhagen house of W. Ø. Larsen is also said to have taken place during the same period.
Series and Stampings
Celius production gathers into three main lines:
Chess:

The brand's most important group. Its grades are taken from chess pieces: the lowest, Pawn, was reserved for sandblasted-surface pieces, followed by Rook, Knight, Bishop, Queen, and King. When the natural bark of the briar was left on the rim of the bowl, the pipe additionally received a "Root" stamp. Numbers also appear in the stamping; those recorded so far range from 1 to 31. Though these numbers appear to indicate a shape, they are not binding the way another maker's shape numbers might be: what is held onto is a starting point, a base form that was frequently stretched at the workshop.
Fantasy / Fancy:

Bolder interpretations of the freehand approach. Part of this output is stamped "Fantasy," part "Fancy." From the surviving examples it has not been possible to work out in what order, or in which years, the two stamps were used. Both are graded by number.
Zenia:
A series of classic shapes named after the maker's daughter, produced only for a limited stretch of time.
Change of Ownership and Aftermath

Celius left Bogø around 1970, handing his workshop and the brand name to an entrepreneur named Jens Peter Ransborg. Ransborg kept the business running until 1975-76, and some pipes from those years carry a "Ransborg" stamp. After the shop closed, Svend Axel Celius briefly returned to the trade. In this second period, Henning Andersen from his original crew joined him part-time; small-scale handmade production for Stanwell is also said to have been carried out in the same years. The comeback did not last. The maker moved to Fyn in the late 1980s and, according to records, died around 1999-2000.

There is no consensus on the reasons for the brand's decline. Workshops such as Preben Holm and Karl Erik, which produced semi-freehand pipes on a far larger scale with machine assistance during the same years, created heavy competition for a small island factory.

The level of workmanship remains a point of debate today: since it operated close to series production, finish quality varies noticeably from piece to piece, and it is accepted that the brand falls short of top-tier Danish handmade standards. Even so, good examples in wood can be found in the Knight grade and above within the Chess series; Celius's early experiments with lines that would later appear at other workshops lend the brand a certain historical weight.

r.x: Red Hat Pipes

is the brand Danish pipe maker Kjeld Sørensen uses in place of his own name. Sørensen, after spending twenty-five years in the corporate world as an economist, left that profession and began making pipes full-time from 2003 onward. His workshop is in Himmelev, near Roskilde, and production has never scaled beyond a one-man bench. The brand is counted among the later-generation representatives of the independent-maker tradition that has persisted in Denmark since the 1960s: there is neither mold production nor assistant labor at the workshop, and every pipe leaves the same hand from start to finish. That Sørensen came to the trade in mid-life and from a completely different field is a rare, though not unique, path in Danish pipe making.
Origin of the Name

The brand's name is taken from a tradition of the South Zealand pipe club Sørensen has long belonged to. The club takes part in slow-smoking competitions wearing red hats; this detail, which helps distinguish its members from one another in crowded halls, in time became the workshop's name as well. According to accounts, the pipes were first shown widely under this name at the annual pipe gathering in Chicago in 2005; the date has not been possible to confirm in an independent record.
Craftsmanship and Style

The decisive step in the move to the trade was the relationship built with Tom Eltang. Sørensen learned the fundamentals of the craft at Eltang's workshop, at the bench of an experienced maker; this period is considered the source of both his working discipline and the strict standard he holds in finishing. That the tie between the two workshops continued in later years is suggested by information that sandblasting is done with Eltang's equipment; however, this detail rests only on the maker's own promotional text.

The formal language of Red Hat pipes is described as sitting at the intersection of two traditions: the Danish school, known for balance and refinement of line, and the freer yet still measured Japanese maker's line. Sørensen's working method is built on leaving shape to the material rather than fixing it in advance; the grain flow of the briar largely determines how the chamber and shank will sit. His forays outside the classic patterns are cited as what sets the workshop apart from Denmark's more cautious names.
Material and Production

Blocks are said to come from Italy, Greece, and Algeria, and stems are said to be made mainly with German ebonite, with horn and acrylic occasionally used as well. The sole basis for this information is the workshop's own promotional material; there is no independent confirmation. Where shape allows, spacers of bamboo shank, horn, or boxwood come into play.

Annual output stands at roughly one hundred pipes, part of which is shaped individually according to sketches or ideas submitted by smokers. This scale allows every piece to be handled separately. Red Hat is thus counted among the Danish workshops known not for serial production but for a limited number of pieces completed entirely by hand.

r.x: Oppenheimer Pipe

is the name of the industrial group that grew out of an import-export house founded in 1860 by a London-based merchant family, and that formed the backbone of British pipe production in the first half of the twentieth century. It is known less for pipes bearing its own name than for the brands it purchased and the factories it established.
From Trading House to Factory

According to records, the firm was founded in 1860 by the Oppenheimer brothers and their partner Louis Adler; sources differ over which brother stood at the head of the founding, between the names Charles and Adolph. The company at first did not make pipes, but carried the output of continental European workshops to Britain and imperial markets. In subsequent decades, the division of labor among the partners changed and management consolidated into fewer hands; during this period the firm prepared the ground for the shift from trading to manufacturing.

In 1902 the company acquired the French maker Marechal, Ruchon & Cie, and with it the GBD brand. A year later, in 1903, it opened its own pipe factory in London. According to accounts, the plant only reached the capacity envisioned at its founding once the demand generated by the First World War arrived; it stood idle in the pre-war years.
Gathering of Brands

The real growth came after the war, through the acquisition of long-established London houses that had fallen into difficulty. Adolph Frankau & Co, founded in 1847 and maker of BBB pipes, passed into Oppenheimer's hands in the 1920s. In the interwar period, Loewe & Co. and Dr. Plumb's also came under the group's control; Comoy's of London joined the same roof at a later date. The years of joining are not given precisely in the records, but the outcome is clear: a single capital group came to hold, simultaneously, a series of well-known stamps that appeared to be rivals.

The group also put pipes on the market under its own name. Early production examples bear the mark "A. Oppenheimer & Co." and the name Keystone; on these pipes the mold stamp most often reads "Keystone — London England." This stamp is one of the few clues that ties a pipe directly to the group's own production, for collectors.
The Cadogan Umbrella

As acquisitions multiplied, management chose to gather them all under a single investment company. Cadogan Investments Ltd took its name, according to accounts, from Cadogan Square, where the company's London offices were located. Sources differ on the founding date, between the 1920s and 1930s; what is certain is that in the interwar period the brands attained a structure legally separate but commercially managed as one. Other English stamps, such as Orlik, were brought under this same umbrella in later years.

The Oppenheimer name gradually withdrew from commercial use, and the business's continuation ran through Cadogan. After the 1980s, production was consolidated into a single facility at Southend-on-Sea on the Essex coast; the stamps the group had acquired continued to live on at this factory even after their own workshops closed. The shape numbers and stamp arrangements of the old London houses were also largely preserved. Today, collectors trying to make sense of the stamp and shape-number systems of English factory pipes often trace their way back to this chain of mergers that Oppenheimer built a century ago.

r.x: Askwith Pipes

is a handmade pipe workshop run single-handedly by Chris Askwith in Plymouth, in southwest England. Producing since 2007, the brand is counted among the examples of the solo-maker workshops that regained strength in Britain in the late 2000s.
Shape Language

Askwith takes a flexible stance toward the shape tradition that dominates British pipemaking. Familiar patterns from the island school, such as the Billiard or the Bulldog, appear in the designs, but bowl height, shank thickness, and finish are usually shifted in measured ways. This approach is considered closer to the free interpretation of contemporary American makers than to English workshops. Sandblast and smooth polish are used in roughly equal measure across production.

The color choices on the mouthpieces are the brand's most quickly recognized trait. By the maker's own account, the vivid, even bold polyester colors were not a planned choice from the outset but the result of a broad color swatch that came into his hands as samples; over time it became the brand's signature.
From Silversmithing to the Pipe Bench

Askwith's first trade was silversmithing. By his own account, he took up pipe smoking in 2006, then moved into cleaning and restoring secondhand pipes, finding that the tools he had acquired for jewelry-making suited this work as well. Records indicate that his move from restoration to production came through attending South West Pipe Club meetings in 2007, where he met the Cornwall-based American maker Paul Hubartt. By his account, the first ten or so Askwith pipes were made at Hubartt's bench, on his machines, and the proceeds from their sale were spent on equipping his own workshop. The technical exchange with Hubartt's brand, Larrysson Pipes, continued in later years as well. The source of these details is the maker's own testimony; they are not backed by an independent document.
Materials and Construction

Alongside briar, the second body material worked regularly in the workshop is bog oak — oak that has spent thousands of years in a bog and become semi-fossilized. Askwith is presented as one of the few English makers who uses this material consistently rather than occasionally. According to the maker's own statements, bodies are also cut from strawberry wood and olive wood, and the smoke channel is bored to a 4-millimeter diameter; neither claim has been confirmed by an independent source.

Mouthpieces are hand-cut from polyester, lucite, ebonite, cumberland, and horn. The bore is kept generous and flattens out wider at the bite zone. The transition between body and mouthpiece is mostly built on a delrin tenon, a solution favored in contemporary workshops because it does not stress the briar during disassembly and reassembly. The thin decorative bands on the mouthpiece use exotic woods and various metals.

Pipes are stamped with the maker's surname. Again by the maker's account, a silver Askwith logo is inlaid into the mouthpiece — a detail that ties the brand directly back to its roots in silversmithing.

r.x: Ian Fisher

(b. 1965) is an American handmade pipe maker, based in New York, who carries on pipe making alongside his career in journalism. That he took up the craft as he neared fifty, without stepping away from writing, sets him apart from most makers of his generation. The pipes he produces are stamped with his own surname.
The Journalism Track

After graduating from Boston University in 1987, Fisher began his journalism career at The Lowell Sun in Massachusetts. He joined The New York Times in 1990, moved into reporting in 1992, and worked at the paper for a total of about twenty-seven years. A long stretch of that time was spent as a bureau chief: East Africa, based in Nairobi, from 1998 to 2001; Eastern Europe and the Balkans from 2001 to 2004; Rome from 2004 to 2008. Because many of his postings turned into conflict zones within a short time, war reporting was added to his beat as well. He left the paper in 2017; a stint at Bloomberg that began the following year ran through 2024, and he returned to the Times in 2026.
The Connection to Pipes

A cigarette smoker at first, and a cigar smoker during his years posted in Africa, Fisher switched to the pipe in his thirties and described it as a habit that kept him grounded under field conditions. For a long time he made do with cheap factory pipes bought from tobacconists' baskets. As the story is told, that habit changed when he came across a never-smoked Dunhill at a scrap dealer's in Baghdad during the Iraq War years; the difference between that pipe and what he had been using until then is counted as the start of his interest in the craft of making one.

Records show he finished his first pipe in 2016 from a hobby kit signed by Mark Tinsky. Once he left the paper, the time he devoted to it grew: he taught himself by following home-scale pipe-making guides, step-by-step videos, and pipe-maker forums, and gradually built up his bench equipment. For a while the pursuit carried no aim of income; requests to buy from people around him then brought in the idea of putting the work up to someone else's judgment.

He then sought direct instruction. As the account goes, he worked at Grant Batson's workshop in Indiana, learning freehand carving and various stages of the craft, and in later years attended classes with Jeff Gracik, maker of the J. Alan pipe. Through these two names he is counted as connected to the teaching line running back to Sixten Ivarsson and Poul Rasmussen, and from there to Tom Eltang and Teddy Knudsen — that is, to the American extension of the Danish School tradition.
Style and Materials

His main materials are briar and vulcanite; basing his mouthpieces on hard rubber is the usual preference of the tradition he belongs to. His design avoids showiness, favoring balanced proportions and a simplicity that sits well in the hand. By contrast, bamboo shank extensions, ferrules, and accents of horn, fossil ivory, or exotic hardwood appear frequently in his output; he has said he uses these both to push himself and because buyers favor them. In finishing, he offers both smooth polish and sandblasting.

The main direction of his style comes from the Scandinavian and Scandinavian-American line. His portfolio includes both well-known shapes of that tradition and less commonly worked examples: a quarter-bent egg, a strawberry, and, alongside Arne Jacobsen, Ib Loran's Pearl and Gert Holbek's Polonius can be counted among them. Italian pipes, particularly the work of Paolo Becker and his son Federico, are named among the makers that caught his interest early on; Gian Maria Gamboni, whom he met while posted in Rome, is another name from that period. English classics also find an occasional place in his repertoire.

Although his production stays at boutique scale, his pipes have reached a steady circle of buyers in America. According to the account, in 2024 he was asked to make the pipe of the year for the Sherlock Holmes Pipe Club of Boston. Fisher today continues to split his time between the workshop and journalism.

r.x: Heiner Nonnenbroich

is a pipemaker running a small-scale workshop in Germany's Lower Rhine region. Born in 1953, Nonnenbroich's actual profession was piano teaching; he pursued pipemaking as a second occupation while teaching at a music school. By his own account he began treating the work seriously and moved to regular production from 2002 onward; records indicate the workshop closed around 2016, though this date has not been confirmed by an independent record. In the roughly fifteen years that passed, the pipes that emerged, though few in number, became a signature recognized in German collecting circles. The workshop's address is given in sources sometimes as Krefeld, sometimes as Kerken; the year of the move between the two locations is unclear.
Workshop and Method

Every piece Nonnenbroich produced was hand-shaped, that is, of freehand character, designed without adherence to a ready mold. The briar he used, by his own account, was sourced as plateaux-cut blocks from the Mediterranean basin; this preference is explained by the ability to see the grain pattern in its entirety. It must also be added that sources do not agree on exactly where the briar came from: the description on his site cites Italy and Spain, while José Manuel Lopes's compilation adds Algeria and Corsica alongside Italy. After shaping and staining, the stummel was oiled, left to dry for several days, then polished and finished with carnauba wax. This sequence of steps also explains the workshop's limited production speed; annual output is reported not to exceed a few dozen.

He cut his mouthpieces himself, from German-made vulcanite rod; his turn toward vulcanite is counted among the workshop's distinguishing habits among mouthpiece materials. On the matter of filters, sources plainly conflict: according to the explanation on the maker's own site, most of the pipes were filter-less, with a 9 mm filter chamber opened only on order; Lopes's compilation, by contrast, reports that the bulk of production was 9 mm filtered and that acrylic mouthpieces were used as well. These two records have not been reconciled to this day.
Stamp and Grading

Nonnenbroich classified his output using a letter-based grading system. For smooth-surfaced pipes the scale ran from E up through D, C, B, and A, rising to AA; for sandblasted pieces a separate series was used — ED, EC, EB, and EA. The form of the stamp also changed over time: records indicate that until May 2007 the stummel carried the abbreviation "HN" and the inscription "Handmade," after which the maker's full name began to be engraved. The grade letter was added next to the stamp; so a pipe bearing "HN Handmade" points to an earlier-period piece.
Visibility

The workshop presented its products both through German pipe shops and, from the early 2010s onward, directly through its own website. Nonnenbroich was also among the participants of the German pipemakers' gathering held in Rheinbach, and was noted as one of the figures sharing workshop knowledge with those new to pipemaking. Since production stopped, his name has lived on mostly in secondary-market collector circulation.

r.x: Old Pal

is a briar pipe brand made in France, known today only through surviving examples passed from hand to hand. Its production period is estimated not from documents but from the form of the stamp; the common view is that the brand belongs to the first half of the 20th century. The name is thought to have been less a workshop's own signature than one of the trade names a large factory used for retailers. For this reason, what is known about Old Pal comes not from catalogues but from the stamp on the shank.
The Stamp

On Old Pal pipes the brand name is struck on the left face of the shank in a slight arc. Just below the name is a bird figure with wings spread to both sides, and below that the words "Made in France." This bird is the brand's most distinctive mark and the first detail a collector trying to identify the maker looks at. Yet no record has ever surfaced matching the figure to any French firm's corporate emblem; rather than answering the question of identity, the bird keeps it open. Shape numbers are also stamped separately on the shank; surviving examples are mostly straight and slightly bent (bent) billiard shapes. The bodies are worked from briar blocks.
The Question of the Maker

Which workshop Old Pal came from is not known for certain today. There is one written basis: "Who Made That Pipe," the reference book matching brand names to manufacturers, gives two French manufacturer names for the entry — Marechal, Ruchon & Cie. and Rubinovich & Haskell Ltd. Neither name appears alongside Old Pal in any other source; both are therefore unconfirmed, cited only as an attribution.

Rubinovich & Haskell Ltd. does not appear elsewhere in pipe literature; there is no information on where the firm was founded or its production history. It is recorded here only because it is named in that source. Marechal, Ruchon & Cie., by contrast, is a well-documented company historically — but Old Pal appears in none of that documentation either. The preference weighted toward this second firm within the community rests not on evidence but on probability: a manufacturer of scale would be expected to put out numerous secondary brands.

The firm in question is the Paris house that held the GBD brand, tracing back to 1850 and the partnership founded by Ganneval, Bondier, and Donninger. Because partner Bondier outlived the other two by about thirty years, the company name changed repeatedly: first Bondier, Ulrich & Cie., then Bine, Marechal & Cie., and finally A. Marechal, Ruchon & Cie. The names of Auguste Marechal and Ferdinand Ruchon stayed in the company title for more than fifty years. In 1902 the firm merged with London's A. Oppenheimer & Co.; as GBD's ownership passed into British capital, production continued at workshops in Paris and Saint-Claude. A 1915 London directory of briar pipe manufacturers listing the two companies separately but at the same address shows that both names were used side by side for some time after the merger. This is exactly the kind of structure a secondary name like Old Pal could have emerged from — but no record has been found showing that it did.
Its Place Today

The brand has long been out of production. Surviving pipes are collected because they represent the understated but solid craftsmanship of the period when French factories moved to series production after the briar revolution. With no serial record available for dating, the only measures left are the form of the stamp and the mouthpiece material, and these give only a rough date range. In this respect, Old Pal is a typical example of the broad, undocumented lower stratum of 20th-century French pipe production.

r.x: Aldo Velani

is not the name of a real pipe maker but a brand name devised to offer Italian-made pipes to the American market. Most of the pipes have been made in Livorno, the port city in Tuscany, at the workshop of Cesare Barontini. The brand is associated with the same factory's other signatures — Cesare, L'Artigiana, Stuart, and Cortina — which is why Aldo Velani is regarded not as an independent workshop but as a line an established Italian factory set aside for export.
Origin of the Name

Records indicate the brand was born in the early 1970s at the initiative of the New York-based importer Mastercraft. Having up to then brought in mostly French and English pipes, the company wanted to add an Italian-made line to its catalogue and contacted Barontini in Livorno. According to the account, the name was assembled from two names picked from a phone directory during the meeting in Italy — meaning "Aldo Velani" was a fictional identity from the start. This was a common practice among importers of the era: a name that sounded Italian to American buyers signaled the product's origin at a glance.

The Barontini family's history reaches back much further than the brand itself. Turildo Barontini opened a briar mill in Livorno in 1890, where at first only pipe blanks (ebauchons) were processed. The move to finished-pipe production came in 1925 under Bruno Barontini's management; the business, shut down for roughly seven years during the Second World War, reopened in 1946 under Bruno and Illico Barontini. Bruno's son Cesare Barontini took over the factory in 1955 and in later years shared its management with his daughters Barbara and Silvia.
Changes of Ownership

Aldo Velani's later years bear the mark of consolidation in the American tobacco industry. The dates for this period rest largely on an account compiled by the brand's current owner. According to it, Dr. Grabow passed to United States Tobacco in 1969 and Mastercraft to the same company in 1974, and the two businesses were merged in the town of Sparta, North Carolina. Unlike the American brands manufactured in Sparta, Aldo Velani continued to be imported from Italy. When Sparta Industries, founded in the 1980s, was acquired by Lane Limited around 1997, the brand came under that company's distribution. In the restructuring that followed Lane's 1999 merger with R. J. Reynolds, many brands were sold off or discontinued; Aldo Velani, too, withdrew from the market for a time.

According to the account, the brand was taken over by Mitchell Thomas Trading Co. in 2008, production was brought back to the Barontini workshop that had made the original pipes and restarted, and the relaunch was held at the IPCPR trade show in July of that same year. No independent record has been found to corroborate these details; that the brand continues under Barontini production, however, can be confirmed from current maker promotional material.
Shape and Stamp

Aldo Velani pipes are considered Italian interpretations of classic molds, enlarged in volume and leaning toward visual flourish. Established shapes such as the billiard and the bulldog are rendered with thicker walls and fuller bowl proportions; the result diverges noticeably from the restrained silhouette of the English school. Alongside smooth, rusticated, and sandblasted surfaces, the use of ornamental bands, connecting pieces joining briar stummels to acrylic mouthpieces, and colored mouthpiece treatments appear frequently across the lines.

The brand name appears clearly on the stamps. The mark most often cited by collectors is the combined logo in which the front stroke of the "A" in "Aldo" forms the silhouette of a pipe, with the letter's back stroke linking into the "V" of "Velani." Stamp details vary by line and period, so no single stamp form can be taken as a benchmark for the entire output.

r.x: Alden Pipes

is a small pipe workshop Ryan Alden runs alone in Texas. The brand is known less for flashy handmade experiments than for an approach that produces well-working classic shapes with plain, durable craftsmanship. Nearly all of the output is sandblasted, a choice that has largely defined the workshop's visual identity.
The Maker and the Workshop's Founding

Ryan Alden's path to pipe making did not run through formal craft training but through long-haul truck driving. By the maker's own account, during the years spent mostly driving, he would sit at the bench in the weeks he was home, adapting earlier hands-on experience ranging from ceramics to wood turning into pipe making. In 2013 he left driving to become a full-time maker.

The workshop's address in the mid-2010s was Rowlett, east of Dallas. In later years, at a date that cannot be precisely established, Alden settled in the sparsely populated countryside of East Texas. By his own estimate, annual output runs to around two hundred pipes; since the maker says he does not keep count, this figure should not be taken as a firm production statistic. In any case, the scale is one that allows working piece by piece rather than in batches, and it keeps the brand relatively uncommon on the market.
Material and Craft

Stummels are made from Italian and Algerian briar. Alongside this, alternative woods such as bog oak, olive wood, and strawberry-tree wood are also worked. According to the workshop's own promotional text, horn, antler, ivory, and various native or exotic woods have also been used for accent bands; there is no independent breakdown of these accessory materials.

Mouthpieces are, as a rule, hand-cut vulcanite; other mouthpiece materials such as acrylic and bakelite can also be used on special request. It is considered a deliberate choice that Alden builds his briar stock from well-grained blocks that do not reach the very top price tiers: the emphasis is placed on producing a pipe that is sound and works properly rather than on flawless grain. Sandblasting is said to suit this approach well, bringing out the grain texture on the surface while also absorbing minor flaws. Roughly one-twentieth of production has a smooth-polished finish; rusticated examples are rarer still.
Shape Repertoire

The workshop's center of gravity is proven classic shapes. From the round-bowled family, the apple and the billiard; from the slender-shanked long-bodied group, the lovat and the lumberman; and from the paneled-and-banded family, the rhodesian recur regularly; the thick-stemmed author is also a constant in the repertoire. Freehand and more open designs appear occasionally but do not form the main thrust of production. Alden's pipes are considered an example of the contemporary American workshop sensibility that preserves classic silhouettes while paying careful attention to details such as bore alignment, balance, and mouthpiece workmanship.

r.x: Biltor

is a British brand founded in London at the end of the nineteenth century, remembered in pipe history not as an ordinary manufacturer but as the commercial trial of an early filter patent. The brand as a whole was built entirely around a single invention Swiss-born Emil Alexander Wüterich patented in 1889.
Patent and Invention

Wüterich was a Swiss-national entrepreneur listed in London records of the period as a "medical agent." On February 22, 1889, he took out British patent no. 3199 for a device meant to keep nicotine from reaching the smoker's mouth in pipes and mouthpieces. The corresponding US patent, no. 415,690, was approved on November 19 of the same year; this document also confirms the inventor was a Swiss national living in London.

The invention itself is extremely simple. A small tube, closed at one end, is fitted into the shank's inner channel; the tube is made of an absorbent, porous material. Because smoke cannot pass through the closed end, it is forced to seep through the tube's side surfaces, and part of the condensation and residue is trapped during this passage. The patent text gives blotting paper, felt, and woven fabric as example materials, and also allows for the tube to be treated with substances such as tannic acid or scented. This detail shows how the late-nineteenth-century filter idea was intertwined with the period's discourse on hygiene and health; the approach can be seen as an early forerunner of today's discussion of pipe filters and systems.
The Company's Rise

The commercial thread traceable in sources shows Wüterich selling pipes under the Biltor name from an address in London's Holborn district by 1893; the same year the business is said to have moved to Oxford Street, and to have opened a second sales point on Cheapside before 1896. Since this address information rests on a single archival compilation, it should be read with caution. The company's registration as a limited company, however, only came in 1897. According to patent-case records, the founder transferred his invention to Biltor Limited for £5,000 and 15,000 one-pound shares. Names lending the business money include Marian Charlotte Vibart and Anna Wüterich; the information that Vibart was a member of the secret society the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn appears only in an amateur archival compilation and has not been independently confirmed.

On the promotional side the brand was quite active. It is said to have won a medal at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago and to have taken part in the 1900 Exposition Universelle in Paris; neither claim could be confirmed by independent sources. It is known to have advertised in the British, American, and Australian press, using not only major fairs but also smaller exhibitions in the pharmaceutical and chemical sectors. In this respect the brand is a typical example of the patent race British pipe making saw in its age of industrialization.
Loss of the Patent and the End

In February 1903, Wüterich and Vibart applied to have the term of the 1889 patent extended. The accounts submitted to the judicial committee of the Privy Council showed the business had made a loss overall, while the patented product's own profit could not be separated from other sales such as tobacco. The application was rejected; the invention passed into the public domain, and the brand's only competitive edge was gone.

From this point the Biltor name grows increasingly scarce in the press; records give one of the last references as 1909. It is reported that Wüterich went on to work on other inventions that brought no fortune, filed a patent application in an entirely different field in 1919, and died in November 1927 without leaving a will; this last piece of information has not been independently confirmed. According to company records, Biltor Limited was dissolved in 1934. Today the brand is of interest chiefly to researchers who date pipes via pipe patents and to collectors seeking the "EW" stamp on silver-ferruled examples.

r.x: Steinhart

is a short-lived signature that emerged in New Jersey in the 1970s, in the years American handmade pipe making was just taking root. Behind it is Vic Steinhart, nephew of Jack H. Weinberger, owner of the JHW Pipes brand. Pipes bearing his own stamp can today be found only in collections; by contrast, the names that passed through the workshops Steinhart worked at and helped set up went on, in the following decades, to become among the country's well-known manufacturers.
Trained at Weinberger's Workshop

As JHW's order volume grew, young people from the surrounding neighborhood began to be taken on at the workshop; Steinhart, who lived next door, was one of them. It is said he made quick progress on freehand bodies, which demand skill and are shaped without relying on a ready template. Most of those working at the workshop's benches in those years were of high-school age; some of those who joined were friends who already knew each other. Mark Tinsky and Curt Rollar, who began working at the same place, would go on to found the workshop later known as American Smoking Pipe Co.
SK Pipes and Briar Originals

Steinhart's first independent venture was SK Pipes, which he founded with a friend after finishing high school. The workshop operated out of a rented house in the same neighborhood as JHW. According to the account, the partner was a schoolmate given as Mitch Kaufman; since this detail rests solely on the testimony of contemporaries, it leaves no trace in independent records. One of the employees who had run the polishing work at JHW also moved over to the new workshop; two benches in a small neighborhood sharing the same pool of labor is a typical example of the fluidity among independent workshops of the period. The venture, even so, was short-lived.

Steinhart then founded the Briar Originals brand under his own name; the pipes were stamped with the abbreviation BOI. It is reported that the brand appeared at the era's tobacconists' trade show, RTDA, but production did not last beyond a few years. According to records, the total number of pipes produced is between four hundred and five hundred. This figure, small even for an independent workshop working in briar, explains why the BOI stamp is so rarely seen today.
The Workshop Changes Hands

Marrying young, Steinhart moved into a job offering steady income and left pipe making, going to work at a lumber business. The last unfinished BOI bodies left on the bench were completed by Curt Rollar and Mark Tinsky; with the money raised from selling these pipes, Steinhart's remaining briar stock and equipment were acquired. The remaining material of a small brand that had closed thus became the starting capital for one of the East Coast's long-lived workshops.

Steinhart's story as a maker ends here; by contrast, the generation that trained at the same benches built a line lasting more than forty years. For this reason the Steinhart name is remembered not for the number of pipes it left behind but for being a connecting point in the founding years of American handmade pipe making. A BOI-stamped pipe today is regarded by collectors less as an example of a brand than as a document of a particular workshop circle.

r.x: Sparta Industries

is a pipe factory operating in the town of Sparta, in the foothills of the Appalachians in North Carolina. The bulk of American factory pipe production has come out of this facility for more than eighty years; although the company has changed hands several times, production has always stayed in the same town. It is best known today for the Dr. Grabow brand.
An Industry Moves to Town

Sparta's introduction to pipes is tied to the supply shortages of the Second World War. When shipments of briar from the Mediterranean basin were cut off, American manufacturers set out to find usable wood domestically, and the search led to Alleghany County, whose slopes were covered with mountain laurel. The Lavietes family opened the finishing workshop of the business it founded under the name D&P Pipe Works just outside town in the spring of 1944. According to the local press of the time, the facility, with sixty-five employees, was turning out more than ten thousand pipes a week, and the workforce was expected to double before long.

The Spartan pipes made from the local wood were plain, thick-bodied pieces, finished with maple mouthpieces and military mount fittings. Most of these pipes went not to the civilian market but into the field rations of troops in Europe. It is also said that the laurel root was boiled in a boric acid solution to make it more heat-resistant; this detail appears only in records compiled by the pipe community. The material itself, meanwhile, was troublesome: roots pulled from the rocky slope cracked easily. Once briar began arriving again, the factory returned to its usual material; the local-wood experiment lasted only a few years and remains one of the known examples of the alternative woods resorted to during the war years.
Changes of Ownership and Today's Structure

The Dr. Grabow brand, which had been born in Chicago in the hands of the Linkman family, also had its production moved to Sparta in these same years and became the plant's main line; sources differ on the exact date of the move, giving anywhere between 1943 and the 1950s. Sparta's manufacturing and the operations of the Mastercraft group were brought together under the Sparta Industries umbrella in the 1980s; even before this, by the late 1970s, the plant had already become one of the country's largest pipe manufacturers. In the 1990s the company passed to Lane Ltd., one of the major names in North American distribution; ownership later changed again, this time landing with International Pipes & Accessories.

The factory manufactured for outside brands as well as its own; Mastercraft and Aldo Velani are known examples. Sources differ on annual output: pipe-community compilations cite figures exceeding a million, while the manufacturer's own statement points to around two hundred thousand pipes. The process is described as fifty-two separate stages, from the selection of the wood to the final polish. The plant employs a few dozen people today, and most of these craftsmen are said to have more than forty years at the bench — a picture that shows the same trade continuing across generations in the town.

r.x: The Czech Republic Pipe Brands Directory

gathers, in alphabetical order, pipe brands founded in the country or run by Czech makers. Czech pipe-making has two branches: on one side the factory tradition rooted in the Proseč region, and on the other, one-person workshops. Most of the entries below belong to the second group; brands for which no detailed information exists have still been included by name.
Brands
Adam pipes

— Carries the signature of Adam Schorcht, who works in Prague. The only quality recorded for the workshop is that its output is handmade; the founding year, shape preferences, and production volume are undocumented.
Biftek

— The brand's name comes from the nickname maker Jiří Maczko (b. 1991) uses in the community. Maczko trained in art, then worked for seven years as a carpenter building wooden houses. His interest in pipe tobacco first led him to carve pipes as a hobby, and in 2017 he took it up full-time. He learned the craft without a master, and set out to try shapes outside the accepted patterns.
Demirev Pipes

— Kolyo Demirev was born in Bulgaria, though his workshop is in Prague. Years spent working in electrics were what drew Demirev toward pipes, in search of a pursuit closer to nature and to handwork. His first attempts date to 2012; in the same period he shared a small workshop in Prague with a friend. He learned by working out, from photographs and videos, how a piece of briar turns into a pipe, and has continued his production by hand ever since.
Háp

— Behind this workshop, founded in Proseč u Skutče, stands Pavel Háp (1954-2011). Háp worked for a quarter of a century at the BPK factory, which carries the region's pipe-making tradition, learning the craft there under Jan Buben. In 1999 he left the factory and turned part of his house into a workshop; his catalog came to include more than a hundred pipes, both classic shapes and his own designs, alongside numerous accessories. For material he favored Italian plateau briar. He died suddenly in his workshop on 5 March 2011.
Hodula

— The Dýmky Hodula workshop in Opava is run by Pavel Hodula. The bulk of production consists of large-bodied freehand pipes. Hodula carves bodies from plateau-cut or top-grade briar blocks; he uses ebonite and acrylic for mouthpieces, and bores most of his pipes for a 9mm filter.
Kroupa

— Hanz Kroupa, whose workshop is in Nový Jičín, is among the craftsmen who treat the pipe as a sculptural object (Dýmky Hanz Kroupa). Records indicate he is not confined to briar; he works other wood species, and even stone, into his pieces.
Kucera

— The pipes of Prague-born Petr Kučera are known under the name Pipkin Pipes. Kučera took up pipe smoking at seventeen, but did not sit down at the bench until his mid-forties; he was guided there by Jan Gloucek and Tomáš Mahovský. In the workshop he opened in Voznice in 2003 he built up his own shapes and developed intricate rustication patterns; one of these is known as "honeycomb," while another draws on symbols from Aboriginal art. He uses Italian briar and applies smooth, sandblasted, and rusticated surfaces alike. For shanks and bands he turns to colored acrylic, horn, chestnut, and exotic woods such as gombeira and areca; for mouthpieces, ebonite and acrylic.
Machek

— Jiří Machek, who runs a small operation in Radešínská Svratka, first encountered pipes at fifteen. He says he feels an affinity for the wood quality of Charatan and Dunhill classics, and for the shapes of Tom Spanu. For Machek, what defines a pipe is not the model drawn but the grain of the wood. The brand's emblem is a bent pipe whose shank curves into the letter M.
Pearl Bee

— The brand is run by Radka Hofmannová, a woman pipe-maker living in Prague. At the time she was recorded, she had only recently entered the craft and was a member of an international pipe-makers' forum.
Swoboda

— Named after Czech craftsman Wincenty Swoboda. Swoboda settled in Przemyśl, Poland, in 1908, where he founded one of the era's leading pipe factories. It is said that many of today's well-known Polish makers began their careers at this factory's benches. The business continued operating until 1945.
Zapletal ART
— The brand of Jiří Zapletal. Records contain no information beyond the brand and maker's name.

r.x: Eells

is the name given to handmade pipes bearing the signature of pipe maker John H. Eells, who worked in Richmond, Virginia, in the USA. In the years when freehand shapes were in vogue at American workshops, Eells remained committed to classic English forms; his distinguishing trait was interpreting these familiar shapes at larger-than-usual scale. He is also known for the support he gave his surroundings alongside his own bench: the Doctor of Pipes title, given to only two people each year, was awarded to Eells in 2011, and the award record cites him both for his mastery of shape and for his frequently being sought out as a guide by American makers. The master is no longer living.
Learning the Craft at Mincer's Shop

Eells's introduction to the craft came at Mincer's Pipe Shop, across from the University of Virginia campus. The shop's owner, Robert Mincer, was the brother of Custom-Bilt founder Tracy Mincer, and had settled in Charlottesville in the mid-1940s to start his own business. As a student, Eells bought his first quality pipe here in 1961: a small, fully bent Comoy's Tradition, chosen by Mincer himself. In 1968, returning to his studies, he took a part-time job at the same shop; he began with repair work and within a few years moved to carving under Mincer's supervision.

He did not come to this apprenticeship unprepared. Eells, who spent his childhood in the town of Walton in Delaware County, New York, began working as a jeweler's watch repairman at sixteen after his family moved to Charlottesville in 1958; these years spent with fine mechanisms laid the foundation for his manual precision. He studied at the University of Virginia from 1961 to 1963, took a break for three years of military service, and returned to Charlottesville in October 1966.
The Richmond Years and the CORPS Circle

After graduating in 1972, Eells began working at the Philip Morris facility in Richmond; over the following twenty-six years, access to machine shops there helped him develop his bench skills. His continued involvement in pipe making owes much to the Conclave of Richmond Pipe Smokers (CORPS) club, one of whose founders was Linwood Hines, and to the club's annual show, which brought him together with collectors and new makers — a debt Eells acknowledged himself. American makers such as Paul Bonaquisti and Michael Lindner cite Eells's guidance, in their own accounts, among the turning points early in their careers. Eells is also counted among the American makers noted for sandblast finishes.
Stamp and Code System

Eells marked his pipes using both a stamp and pantograph engraving. On first-line pipes, the shank carries the "EELLS U.S.A." stamp along with the handwritten "JH Eells" signature, while size, year, and shape information is engraved. The signature on the mouthpiece is also engraved: it is cut roughly 0.8 millimeters deep with a fine-pointed chisel and filled with white enamel.

The code engraved on the shank, in the pattern of "2 DCU H*," consists of a number, three letters, and a single letter, with an optional star at the end. The components carry the following information:
The leading number
indicates size, not quality. Records show the largest pipe the master made, exceeding thirty centimeters in length and ten centimeters in bowl height, falls into group 14.
The first letter of the three-letter block
gives the production year; the system begins with "A" for 1998 and the letters advance in order, so that "F" corresponds to 2003.
The last two letters of the block
indicate bowl and mouthpiece shape; "CU" denotes a standard billiard with a tapered mouthpiece. By 2004, the number of recorded shapes exceeded eighty.
The standalone letter
describes the surface; "H" corresponds to a black sandblast with red highlights.
A star
, if present, indicates the mouthpiece is made from a material other than black vulcanite; without a star, the mouthpiece is vulcanite.
The Poplar Ridge Line and the Ardor Connection

Because briar is a natural material, not every block comes out flawless: sand pits, fine cracks, or small drilling deviations are inherent to the work. Rather than discard pieces carrying such flaws — ones that do not affect the pipe's smoke or lifespan — Eells set them aside under the name "Poplar Ridge." Pipes in this line are made from the same briar as the first line; the shank is engraved "Poplar Ridge" and stamped with the "JH Eells" signature, while the mouthpiece carries the line's initials, "PRSP." The size, year, and shape information along with the "EELLS U.S.A." stamp do not appear on these pipes.

The master's name is also associated with "The John Eells Giant" shape, introduced by Monjure International, the US distributor for Italy's Ardor. According to reports, Eells's interest in large sizes influenced Ardor's production of oversized series, and a frequently requested large shape interpretation was subsequently offered under his name.
