r.x: Montgomery Handmade Pipes

is a small-scale American pipe bench founded by American Jeremiah W. Montgomery in Pennsylvania in the mid-2000s. The brand is remembered in collector sources not so much for the number of pipes it produced as for its two-stage development line, recorded in the maker's own account, and its consistent marking system. Like many American benches of its era, this one too was born out of a basement workshop; a similar origin story appears in the article on J.L. Thompson.
From the Southmont Period to Montgomery

By the maker's own account, the venture's beginning goes back to years spent in Southmont, part of Johnstown. Montgomery, who had been smoking a pipe for about two years, tried his hand at making his own pipes together with a friend; this enthusiasm grew into a small venture called Southmont Pipe Company. This first workshop, set up in the garage of the basement floor of a house, is said to have operated until the beginning of 2006. Pipes from this period carry a stylized mark combining the letters "S" and "P."

Later the same year, having moved to Hollidaysburg, Montgomery chose to give the brand his own surname, since he was now working alone. He states that he also reviewed his production methods along with the new workshop; however, what these changes covered is not detailed in the sources. For a broader picture of the American handmade pipe scene during these years, see the Go West article.
Marking System

The brand's most easily recognized feature is its plain, legible marking system. Pipes from the Hollidaysburg period carry a four-digit code following the letters "MHP." The first two digits of the code give the year of manufacture, and the last two give the pipe's sequence number for that year. A collector looking at the mark can thus tell at a glance which year a given pipe belongs to and how many pieces preceded it that year. Such personal numbering systems are common among one-person American benches and make dating pipes easier; as with Denny Souers, the mark is often the only document a brand leaves behind.
What Remains Unknown

Nearly everything known about Montgomery rests on the maker's own promotional text. The total number produced, the briar sources used, stem material preferences, and how long the bench remained active are not documented in independent sources. The only available promotional text dates to the second half of the 2000s, and since no record exists for later years, when and how the brand ended remains unknown. For this reason, Montgomery counts among the many short-lived American benches of the period as one that can at least be traced through its mark. For efforts to compile maker names, see the Rex Poggenpohl article.

r.x: Ben Wade

is an English pipe brand founded in Leeds in 1860; yet the name is now most associated with a production period that has nothing to do with its country of origin — the freehand pipes made in Denmark in the 1970s. Having passed through three different owners and three different production setups over a century and a half, two pipes bearing the same name may not resemble each other at all. For this reason Ben Wade should be read not through a single description but through its eras.
A Century in Yorkshire

Benjamin Wade began in the pipe trade and opened his own briar workshop in Leeds sometime in the 1860s. The workshop remained in the same city for more than a century. Pipes from this period were made in classic English shapes, mostly of modest size and from unfilled wood; the brand is therefore counted among the top-tier English producers of its day. Before the war, products were divided into three grades: the top tier was stamped "Ben Wade," the middle line "BW," and the lower line "BWL." The factory was destroyed in air raids on Leeds during the Second World War; the family rebuilt the plant shortly after the war and resumed production where it had left off.
An American Owner and the London Stamp

In 1962 the family sold the business to Herman G. Lane, head of New York-based Lane Limited. Lane had also bought Charatan that same year and focused his attention there; Ben Wade's production was scaled back, and the Leeds factory closed in 1965. This marked the end of pipes stamped "Made in Leeds England."

The machinery moved to London, to Charatan's Prescott Street plant, and from then on the name was used entirely for machine-made mass-production pipes. Products of these years bear the stamp "Made in London England" or simply "London"; with their ready-molded stems and conspicuous fills, the brand is considered to have dropped to a second-tier line in this period. Lane's heirs sold both Charatan and Ben Wade to Dunhill in 1978. Since Dunhill's Walthamstow plant already covered second-tier pipes, the name was shelved once again.
The Danish Era Signed by Preben Holm

The collaboration that built the brand's present-day reputation was born right in the middle of this confusion. Preben Holm was a Copenhagener who, at twenty-two, had risen fast enough to run a workshop of forty-five people; but at the end of 1970, when his American distributor stopped paying him, he fell into serious cash trouble. In February 1971 he met Herman G. Lane in New York, and the resulting agreement was built not on mass production but on hand-carved freehand pipes. Because the old distributor still held unsold Preben Holm stock, releasing the pipes under the maker's own name was seen as risky; the Ben Wade name held by Lane filled this gap.

Pipes carved in Denmark were stamped "Hand Made in Denmark" and distinguished by series names such as Golden Walnut, Golden Tan, Royal Grain, Danish Pride, and Majestic. Lane promoted the brand with full-page ads in major magazines; volumes soon exceeded both sides' expectations. Holm fell into financial trouble again in 1986 and had to let go of most of his staff; production shrank and stopped entirely with the maker's early death in June 1989.
The Name's Latest Chapter

The Ben Wade stamp sat unused for a long time in Dunhill's hands. Records show that in 1998 Peter Wilson, who had worked at the established English workshop Duncan Briars, bought the brand rights and returned the name to the market. These new pipes are made at the Walthamstow plant in London, and are mostly large-bowled, dark-colored, and sandblasted. Even so, what defines the brand's value among collectors remains the Preben Holm-signed Danish-era pipes still circulating in the estate market.

r.x: Penkov

is the handmade pipe bench that Russian pipe maker Aleksandr Penkov signs under his own name. The brand is not a factory or a workshop partnership, but the pursuit of a single person that has, over time, turned into mastery. According to records based on the maker's own account, Penkov was born in Omsk in 1981, studied mathematics at first at Omsk State University, then switched to psychology a few years later.
From Experiment to Bench

The first pipe was made in 2005 and was entirely an experiment: the body was carved from a birch burl, and the mouthpiece (stem) was taken from another pipe. After this first attempt, Penkov tried every material within reach, working even with clay among other materials. As his technique advanced, his choice of material also narrowed, and production settled on briar. Today the maker uses German and Japanese ebonite alongside Italian briar, and occasionally turns to rarer materials as well. The preference for ebonite is a common standard among contemporary handmade pipe benches: hardened rubber is considered more suitable than acrylic for hand-working and for thin mouthpiece cross-sections. In the same way, Italian briar, thanks to the ease of finding long-cured blocks, is the primary source for single-maker benches.

Pipe making remained for a long time a pursuit carried on alongside his main job. Records indicate that the maker has said he once considered moving to full-time pipe making; whether this idea was ever carried out afterward cannot be traced through independent sources.
Benches That Influenced Him

The list of makers Penkov names clearly shows which tradition he stands within. From Japan, Hiroyuki Tokutomi; from Denmark, Poul Ilsted Bech, Tom Eltang, and Former; and from Italy, the DOC (Doctor's Pipes) bench all appear on this list. A name he once took a close interest in is also the Russian-born maker Alex Florov.

The list itself is instructive: Penkov belongs to a generation fed not by an established factory tradition in Russia, but by the contemporary handmade pipe line centered on Denmark and Japan. In this generation, the shape decision is made not against a series mold but block by block; proportion, balance, and how a piece sits in the hand come before ornament. That annual production stays limited on a bench where a single maker works is likewise a natural consequence of the same order.
Standing and State of Sources

Penkov is, more than a brand widely known in the international pipe community, a maker's signature followed for its limited output. A significant part of the information about the brand rests on the maker's own promotional texts and on compilations that repeat them; independent archival records are next to nonexistent. His birth year, educational background, and the 2005 date are therefore given with the qualifier "according to records." No reliable source could be found on stamp form, model series, or production volume, and these headings have been left blank in the entry.

r.x: Gubbels

is a pipe maker that arose in Roermond in the southern Netherlands, best known worldwide under the name Big Ben. The family firm moved from a shop selling pipes and smoking accessories into wholesale trading, then into manufacturing after the Second World War, establishing the country's first factory to make pipes from briar.
From Shop Counter to Workbench

The story begins with a small retail shop that Elbert Gubbels Sr.'s father ran in Roermond. Sources differ on the shop's opening year, giving dates between 1870 and 1873; the company's own promotional materials use 1870. In 1924 the business shifted from retail to wholesale trading in tobacco accessories. Since no factory in the Netherlands made briar pipes at the time, goods were brought in mainly from France and England.

The German occupation of May 1940 shut down import channels, and trade nearly ground to a halt. These years pushed Elbert Gubbels toward building a setup that would not depend on outside supply. As soon as the war ended, he began production in Roermond in 1946 with a handful of machines and a small crew that included French craftsmen; according to the record, the first pipes bore the name EGRO (Elbert Gubbels Roermond). When the cramped workshop soon proved too small, production moved, warehouse and all, into a larger building.
Big Ben and the Royal Title

As the firm looked to expand abroad, it became clear that introducing a new Dutch name would take a long time. Rather than build a brand from scratch, records indicate that in the 1950s the company bought a small Amsterdam trading firm that held the rights to the Big Ben name. The ready-made name made it easier to distribute products across Europe as well as to North America and more distant markets.

The opening of the modern factory in Roermond in December 1972 was attended by the governor of Limburg, and at the same ceremony the firm was granted the "Koninklijk" (Royal) title in Queen Juliana's name. The official name thus became Elbert Gubbels & Zonen – Koninklijke Fabriek van Tabakspijpen. The Royal Dutch brand, launched to mark the title, also helped counter the perception that Big Ben was a British product.
The Last Factory Left in the Benelux

By the late 1970s, Hillen in the Belgian town of Bree was the only briar pipe factory left standing in the region besides Gubbels. This financially struggling firm was acquired in 1980, bringing along the Hilson brand, which was stronger than Big Ben in the German market. After the Bree plant closed, Gubbels remained the sole factory-scale briar pipe producer in the Benelux. In later years, licensed design series produced in collaboration with car brands were also added to the production line.

With the shrinking market of the late 2000s, the company downsized and moved to a more modest facility in Herten. It filed for bankruptcy in March 2012; records indicate the business was restructured and returned to operation within the same year. In Dutch pipe-making, Gubbels is regarded as the representative of mass production, standing in contrast to solo craftsmen such as Martin Romijn.

r.x: Amadeus Pipes

, formally Achaiki Amadeus S.A., is a briar business founded in Demenika, near Patras in western Greece. In the pipe world the brand is known under two identities: it produced pipes under its own name, while also selling worked briar blocks to factories and individual makers around the world. Over time the second line of business overshadowed the first, and the company name came to mean, for most pipe enthusiasts, simply "where the material comes from."
Founding and Family Tradition

The core of the business was eight masters with decades of experience cutting briar root. According to the company's own materials, these masters carried three generations of accumulated briar-production knowledge behind them. Sources disagree on the founding date: some records say the family opened its own sawmill in the 1970s, while Greek trade-press files give the corporate entity's registration as 1995. The safest reading is that the family entered the cutting business in the 1970s, with the corporate structure formalized later. The business is associated with the Minetos family; its public face was Makis Minetos, who handled contact with the international pipe community and occasionally gave interviews.
Briar Supply

Amadeus's main weight fell on the raw material side. A vertically integrated facility was set up, carrying every stage under one roof, from root extraction to block, and from block to finished pipe. Greek briar enjoys an international reputation for its grain texture and even curing behavior, and Amadeus was one of the carriers of that reputation. Its client list included well-known names such as Stanwell, Vauen, Tsuge, and the Danish Bjarne. Community records also note that Vauen's Kansas line used Greek-sourced blocks. As a result, many pipes carrying no Amadeus stamp were nonetheless cut from wood processed at this workshop.
Own-Brand Pipes

Alongside block sales, the company also produced pipes under its own name. These pipes were made from Mediterranean briar worked by traditional methods, following a repertoire close to classic English and Danish shapes. Being a business that cut its own raw material also meant the workshop could select directly, for its own products, the blocks it set aside. Amadeus-stamped examples turn up today on the secondhand market and are regarded as unpretentious, workmanlike series-production pipes. Restorers' write-ups usually note their sturdy stummels and plain craftsmanship.
Closure

In the mid-2010s the company was squeezed both by a shrinking pipe market and by declining demand from foreign clients. According to financial reports carried in the Greek press, turnover fell noticeably in these years, and accumulated losses and debt grew. Accounts say the partners decided on liquidation in autumn 2016, and production was set to stop by the end of that year. Amadeus's closure is cited as one of the examples showing how few businesses the briar supply chain actually rests on.

r.x: J&J Pipes

is the name two Californian masters, John Klose and Jared Coles, gave to the pipes they made in their shared workshop. What distinguished the brand was not a family of models or a technical innovation but the working system they adopted: a pipe was not considered finished until both of them had approved the result. The two letters in the brand name likewise stood for the founders' names, and so for this dual check.
The Two Masters' Paths

Klose spent part of his childhood in New Mexico before moving with his family to the foothills between Yosemite and Sequoia national parks. During his college years he worked at a camp near Yosemite; hand skills such as woodworking, leatherwork, and repair developed during this period. Coles, meanwhile, grew up among the orange groves of the San Joaquin Valley, was homeschooled through high school, and studied economics. According to records, his first attempts at pipe making also date to these college years.

The pair's path took clearer shape when they met Jeff Gracik, a master working in Southern California. Coles got the chance to see firsthand how a top-tier pipe is made, and shared what he learned with Klose once he returned to the Central Sierra. According to sources, the two began learning together in 2009, set up their own workshop in 2011, and continued production under the J&J name. Gracik's guidance is considered the foundation of the technical discipline visible in both masters' later independent work.
Approach to Shape

The workshop's shape language claimed to melt three distinct traditions into a single pot. The Danish school brought its fluid lines and technical refinement, early-twentieth-century English pipes their measured proportion and classic silhouette discipline, and Japanese craft sensibility the idea of not being bound to symmetry. This combination produced a broad framework that left room for freehand pieces alongside classic shapes.

Another habit of the brand was documentation. Every pipe leaving the workshop came with a card bearing both founders' signature, stamp, and the date; the details of that particular pipe were noted by hand on the back of the card. This is considered a simple but functional way of providing identity and traceability for pipes made one at a time.
The End of the Partnership

The joint brand gained recognition among collectors within a few years. But the two masters' pursuits of form began to diverge. Records vary on the exact date of the split, giving anywhere between 2015 and early 2016; what is certain is that after continuing to share the same workshop for a time, the two began producing their pipes separately, and the J&J name fell out of use. Today both masters work under their own names.

Coles's work after the partnership is known for using accent materials such as orange wood, bamboo, or precious-metal foil on briar bodies. The J&J period, meanwhile, is regarded as a formative stage for both masters. The interview with Coles on the radio program hosted by Brian Levine is among the records where this period is told firsthand.

r.x: Anima Pipes
is the brand name for the pipes American maker Brian McNulty shaped one at a time by hand; the workshop is associated in the records with Culver City, California. The name comes from the Latin word
anima

, meaning "soul," and refers directly to the red point on the mouthpiece that is the brand's most distinctive mark. Production was carried out at workshop scale without adherence to serial molds; every bowl was cut according to the grain direction of the briar block used.
The Catlinite Point

The brand's signature is the red clay piece inlaid in the mouthpiece. This material is catlinite, the red stone North American Indigenous communities have used for centuries in ceremonial pipes. The inlay is described not merely as decoration but as a mark that gives physical form to the idea of the pipe's "soul." McNulty is stated to be of Cherokee descent, and the choice of catlinite is linked to this connection as well. The surface where the inlay is set is worked according to the hardness of the mouthpiece material.
Stamps and Grading

Two types of information appear on the shank of Anima pipes. The first is a single-letter code showing the region the briar came from: according to the records, S denotes Spain, M Morocco, and C Calabria briar. The second is the production date, struck as a month-year pair of numbers. For example, the "04 03" stamp seen on the shank of an estate pipe means the bowl was finished in April of 2003. This dating habit indicates that the brand was actively producing pipes in the early 2000s.

In addition, a single cross enclosed in a circle is struck on the underside of the bowl; restoration writings refer to this mark as the "medicine circle" and consider it the brand's distinguishing seal. Because the stamps are struck in small type on the shank and heel, they can be hard to read on used examples. No quality grading based on the number of these marks has been documented in the records; caution is warranted when secondhand listings refer to such a scale.
Surface Finishes and Shape Language

The brand offered a range spanning both smooth polished surfaces and bowls finished with sandblasting and rustication. On the shape side, McNulty draws primarily from classic skeletons; he takes established molds such as the billiard and pot and adds his own interpretation at the level of proportion, line, and shank length. Some examples, where the shank extends forward past the bowl, evoke the North American Indigenous ceremonial calumet when viewed in profile — a fit with the brand's catlinite emphasis. Symmetry, clean edge lines, and detail work are the qualities collectors most often cite when describing the brand. It is also noted that a matching tobacco tamper was sometimes provided alongside the pipe.

The brand is not widely represented today, and a current production flow cannot be documented. Anima-signed pipes largely appear in secondhand collector circulation, identified through their stamp and catlinite inlay.

r.x: Piet Binsbergen

is a craftsman working in Pretoria, South Africa, who specializes in repairing and restoring damaged pipes. He did not come to the craft through a classical apprenticeship, but from a background in visual arts — a foundation that shapes both the technical and formal sides of his work.
Painter and Teacher

Pieter Binsbergen's primary profession is painting. He is said to have studied fine arts at the University of Pretoria, earned a master's degree in painting, and spent many years teaching art. According to his Pipedia biography, he headed the visual arts department at Pretoria Boys High School in 1993 and took on the role of art education course coordinator at the same university's faculty of education in 2007; neither date has been confirmed by an independent source. As a painter he is said to have held solo exhibitions, won competition placings, and to have works in collections abroad.
Turning to Repair

Binsbergen's interest in pipes goes back to his years in the painting studio; repair only became an occupation later, after he made contact with pipe circles in the United States. As the story goes, he spent roughly two years working on old pipes gathered from family, acquaintances, and antique markets, testing what he had read and learned with his own hands.

He is reported to have learned the technical side of the craft from South African master Jean du Toit, who signs his pipes "Jan Pietenpauw." It was within this relationship that he also picked up turning briar and shaping stems on a lathe. It should be noted that these details rest on a single account. With the acquisition of a Myford ML7 metal lathe, what had been a scattered curiosity turned into a regular repair workshop.
Approach to Repair and "Hot Rods"

Binsbergen holds that the goal of an ordinary restoration is to bring a pipe as close as possible to its original state. For pieces too damaged to be salvaged, however, he takes a different path: rather than discarding pipes with a broken shank, a lost stem, or repairs that no longer make economic sense, he reinterprets them. He calls these pieces "Hot Rods," and is said to keep most of them in his own collection.

Methods he uses on pieces in the series include sandblasting, making new stems, layering leather dyes for color, and fitting bands onto the shank. He is reported to have turned to unusual band materials such as olive wood, hippopotamus bone, and buckeye burl, and to have used brass repairs on broken sections. The bodies he reworks are mostly old English and American pipes gathered from South African antique markets; among these, examples built on GBD stummels have been documented.
Standing

Binsbergen's name is counted among the few visible figures in South Africa's pipe craft, which is not widely known on an international scale. His output is not mass-produced; the weight of his work falls on repair and maintenance commissions. His reinterpreted pieces, meanwhile, are regarded by collectors less as products of a classic brand than as individual art objects. According to records, he has done repair work for some of the country's leading collectors.

r.x: Hasso Baudis

was a German master who became known in northern Germany in the late 1970s and who abandoned the craft entirely after sustaining full-time pipe making for only around five years. Despite the brevity of his career, his name is still cited when describing the young generation of masters taking shape in West Germany in those years.
The Workshop's Short Life

Production is thought to have begun in 1977, while Baudis was still a university student. His pipes are said to have first gone on sale at a Hamburg tobacconist; this detail rests solely on the pipe community's own accounts. As his renown grew, he is said to have established a working relationship with the firm Tuxedo, which handled German distribution for brands such as Dunhill and Stanwell; this collaboration, along with a feature said to have appeared in a 1981 German pipe magazine, has not been confirmed by independent sources.

The workshop closed in 1983. Baudis left his Oldenburg bench to architect and designer Robert Mewis, who had learned pipe making from him, and returned himself to his original profession of architecture. Mewis continued production until the late 1980s before making the same choice and also moving into architecture. Why Baudis stepped away so early was never explained.
Shape and Craftsmanship

Baudis is regarded as a master who, rather than repeating established molds, ventured into a fresh shape experiment with each piece. The briar burls he used were chosen for high grain quality, and the surface was finished in tones ranging from light to dark red. Mouthpiece work was also considered good by the standards of the period. Being mentioned alongside German masters working in the same years, such as Rainer Barbi, helped cement this perception of quality.

He also had experiments that departed from the classic pipe line: he is known to have made pipes approaching object design, built from acrylic tubing and large metal parts. The most talked-about of these experiments is described as a swan-shaped pipe with wings worked in white gold; the only account of this piece appears in pipe encyclopedias, with no independent record found.
Stamps

Total production is unknown; the pipe community estimates a figure between one thousand and twelve hundred, though this number is unconfirmed. Early pieces bear the "Hasso Baudis" stamp. At some point before 1981 the stamp was shortened to read simply "Hasso"; on the most carefully finished examples, the "o" in this word is replaced with a small diamond. This change in stamp style still serves today as a benchmark for roughly dating pipes changing hands.
Because the production period was so short and the number of pieces so few, Hasso Baudis-signed pipes are rarely encountered in secondhand circulation.

r.x: Roger Wallenstein

is the signature of a handmade pipe maker working in western Germany. The name is a pseudonym: registries give the maker's name as Ruprecht — Rupert in some sources — Wagner. It is said he adopted this name long before pipe making, to keep his circle from knowing whose paintings were whose. In the community he is known simply as "Walle."
A Late Start in the Craft

Wallenstein is a lawyer by profession, with neither technical nor artistic training. According to records he was born on 29 November 1950 in Offenbach am Main and did not take up the bench until the summer of 2004, at fifty-three. He learned not from books but at the side of experienced German makers; the name cited most often as his teacher is Peter Klein, with some sources also naming Gerhard Wilhelm. This apprenticeship did not last long: within a year, every pipe he brought to the Chicago pipe show had found a buyer. He and his jeweler friend Peter "Pit" Rohrbach then set up an umbrella to promote the work; the resulting name,
Blue Lobster Pipes

, is still associated with the maker today. Fittingly for the name, the early years' stamp also drew on the sea: alongside Wallenstein's logo and serial number, marine-creature symbols indicated quality, with a lobster marking the top tier.
Shape Language and Technical Signatures

The guiding principle of his early period was to look beyond the familiar shape repertoire for every piece of briar he received; this is why the bulk of the output falls into the freehand category. Over time this search produced the maker's own repertoire: "Cheeky Girl," "Longford," "The Pyg," "Lugalla," and the "Bonefish" and "Wartfish" variants are regularly reinterpreted. Most of the names refer to Ireland; the maker is attached enough to the island to visit several times a year. In recent years, classic and Scandinavian shapes have taken up a larger share; Wallenstein names Sixten Ivarsson as the pipe designer he considers most important. Mouthpieces have for some time been machined from rod stock and carry, at the tip, a thickening known as "Kussmaul lips"; this detail has nothing to do with smoking comfort and functions purely as a mark of recognition. The maker's "Jackbone" mouthpiece, dated to 2009, addresses a different problem: it is lengthened to rest against the jaw so that larger pipes do not hang from the teeth.
Driftwood

A search for a less laborious alternative to sandblasting produced the maker's most talked-about contribution. Perfected in 2009, Driftwood is based on subjecting briar to a light chemical treatment in an immersion bath. The result is a kind of weathering: the harder parts of the grain remain on the surface, and the wood takes on the look of driftwood that has spent years in water and washed ashore. The bath leaving the wood bleached provides an unexpected bonus, since it allows coloring in unusual hues. The method is said to work best on very old briar, and since such wood is rarely flawlessly grained, smooth finishes are seldom seen on Wallenstein pipes.
Collaborations and Jolly Roger

Having learned the shortcuts to learning at other makers' benches himself, Wallenstein has made room for collaboration from the start; Paolo Becker and Brad Pohlmann are among the names with whom he has produced joint pipes. One of the first such ventures in Germany ran with Axel Glasner and Oliver Camphausen; some thirty pipes bearing the stamp B.R.O.S., an abbreviation of "Bonny Rebels Of the Shape," survive from this partnership. The workshop first gathered at Uwe Maier's home in the Swabian Alb during carnival days in 2014 and, on Christian Wolfsteiner's suggestion, took the name "Grainstorm," becoming a recurring meet-up.

The maker's name also entered series production through a 2008 collaboration with the German wholesaler Kopp. Kopp handled the promotion of single-piece pipes, while Wallenstein designed a new series line for the wholesaler, resulting in the models known under the name
Jolly Roger

. Machine-made in France, these pipes came in three qualities, bored for a 9 mm filter; each was presented in a white tin box with two acrylic mouthpieces, one black and one white. On the "Tortuga" model, the cone joining the body and mouthpiece was replaced by a magnetic connection; this idea is recorded as having received a utility-model protection valid within Germany. The partnership with Kopp ended amicably after 2015.

r.x: Denny Souers

is a name that emerged from the generation of American pipe makers who worked alone. In the community, he is known for the three-letter DCS signature, which is carved rather than stamped under the shank of his pipes. His workshop is known to have been in the state of Ohio; according to accounts, it was in the state capital of Columbus, though the location has not been confirmed by an independent record.
Style and Material

Souers's work belongs largely to the freehand family: the line of the bowl and shank is determined not by a ready-made mold but by the block's own grain. Behind this approach lies the postwar Danish school, which popularized free-form pipes. Still, the maker has not confined himself solely to free form; he has also tried his hand at classic shapes.

His preferred material is plateau briar blocks sourced from Greece. Plateau blocks are cut so that the top surface of the root is left in its barked state, allowing the natural texture of the crown to be preserved in freehand pipes. According to the maker's own account, the decisive criterion in selecting a block is the direction of the grain, and the final form emerges to the extent the grain allows. In his own promotional writing, he has stated he has carved pipes for about forty years.
Construction Choices

A number of technical details the maker has described summarize what is distinctive about his work. Cutting the hole where the smoke channel opens into the bowl floor in a teardrop shape is aimed at easing draw. Leaving the bowl wall thicker than a quarter inch, on the other hand, is meant to keep the smoke cooler. At the same time, he is careful not to make the pipe heavy; his targeted finished weight is around two ounces, seeking a balance that is not tiring in hand or teeth.

He uses carnauba wax for the surface finish. Leaving the inside of the bowl uncarbonized beforehand is also a deliberate choice, meant to let the buyer see the wood's own texture directly. While there is wide variety in mouthpiece shapes, the material is mostly acrylic.
Recognition

Souers's work circulated for a time through a channel called Lion Crest; after that channel closed, his pipes have mostly become visible through secondhand circulation. The maker also attended a juried art fair held in Louisville, Kentucky for years regularly with his wife, promoting his work directly at such events. In later years, he is said to have spent much of his time in Florida.

Most of the records about Souers rest on discussion-group archives and the maker's own promotional writing. For this reason, details such as his date of birth, the year he set up his bench, and total production have not been verified by independent sources.

r.x: Poul Ilsted Bech

(d. 2017) is a Danish pipe maker who stamped his pipes simply with the name "Ilsted." He was known for a technique of working the chamber and shank into a series of intersecting flat planes; among collectors he is called "The Facet Master." Having learned the trade at the country's founding workshops ties him to the second generation of the Danish school tradition. Sources give his birth year as 1946.
From Apprenticeship to His Own Bench

Ilsted entered the trade not through formal training but through his own experimentation; he picked up knowledge of molds and proportion by reading whatever pipe publications came his way and drawing shapes. His starting point was Erik Nørding: Nørding sold him a few briar blocks and explained the path to follow at the finishing stage. When the resulting pieces convinced the master, Ilsted decided to take up the trade and worked for a time in Nørding's workshop.

According to the reported work history, his next stop was the newly established pipe factory in Svendborg, on the island of Fyn, where he worked with Jens "Tao" Nielsen for about two years. After a brief return to Nørding, he moved to the W.Ø. Larsen workshop in Copenhagen. At Larsen, production was based on a weekly quota, and a maker who completed his quota early could devote the remaining time to his own pipes; this arrangement is considered to have fueled the working pace common among Larsen's makers of the period.
From Bulldog to the Faceted Chamber

When he started working under his own name, his first fame came from bulldog interpretations. Because his experiments pushed the mold well beyond its usual proportions, he was long known in German collector circles as "Mr. Bulldog." The sharp ridge around the chamber that defines the bulldog family is also considered a forerunner of his later work.

What brought him international recognition, though, was his multi-faceted chambers. On these pipes, the chamber and shank are divided into a series of intersecting flat planes; the difficulty of the work lies in keeping the ridges where the planes meet the same width and unbroken from end to end. Ilsted carried out most of the surface work on a flexible-belt sander, and he was known for his mastery of this tool. Keeping alignment on a curved body is much harder than on a straight one; since a small irregularity could require sandblasting the piece, faceted work stayed limited in number.
Material and Style

He explained his use of Corsican-sourced briar by its tight grain and low flaw rate, according to his own account. He shaped his mouthpieces by hand, favoring black ebonite and Cumberland. For shank rings, spacers, and ornamentation, he used gold, silver, ebony, rosewood, and horn; in later years he began experimenting with materials such as lapis lazuli. Records indicate his annual output was around 170 pipes, of which fewer than a tenth were finished with a sandblasted surface.

Ilsted died in 2017. Thanks to figures who passed through his workshop, such as Manduela Ruger-Kusk, who continues to work under her own name, the faceted-chamber approach has remained a traceable line in contemporary artisan production.

r.x: Jim DeSchaine

is an American pipe maker working around the town of Auburn in the foothills of California's Sierra Nevada. Rather than a large-scale brand, the name belongs to a one-person bench: DeSchaine makes his pipes in a small workshop, in limited numbers, by hand. By his own account he has more than thirty years of woodworking background, having made furniture, jewelry boxes, and cigar cabinets together with his father. His move into pipes is described as a natural extension of that background.
The Bench's Founding

By the maker's own account, he began pipe production in 2013; this date has not been confirmed by an independent record. As the story goes, the turning point was a trip to Montana that gave him the chance to work at the same bench as experienced maker Mark Tinsky. In the period that followed he is said to have worked with California maker Chris Morgan, gaining ground in engineering, shaping, sandblasting, and surface finishing around the Morgan Pipes circle. Information about these two relationships rests mainly on the maker's own promotional material. The bench can be seen as one of the more recent links in an American handmade pipe scene that has grown through apprenticeship-like transmission.

The workshop is described as a family business. According to the single source available, the father does not make the pipes himself; he is involved only in the hand-carving and finishing of joint-signed pieces, and also makes tampers and leather pipe pouches.
Material and Craftsmanship

Bowls use Italian and Algerian briar; both plateau and ebauchon blocks are used. Plateau blocks are favored because they retain the natural texture of the root's outer surface, left as rough patches on the rim and shank face. Stems are mostly hand-cut from German-sourced vulcanite or Cumberland rod; acrylic has also been used on joint-signed pieces and on request. This preference among stem materials reflects a traditional approach in terms of hardness and mouthfeel. Beyond pipes, the workshop also makes accessory items such as ashtrays, pipe stands, and tampers from various exotic woods.
Stamp

Pipes are stamped in a script form reading "J. Deschaine," with "USA" and the production year added alongside. According to trademark records, the mark J.D.S.P. was registered in 2016 with the United States Patent and Trademark Office, used together with a circled deer-head drawing. Because the registration was not renewed in subsequent years, it has since administratively lapsed. Such a lapse concerns only the trademark registration; there is no independent information on whether the workshop continues production today.

r.x: Eike Hallmann

is a German pipe maker who produces his pipes under the signature Halunke Pipes. He was born on January 27, 1988, in Wilhelmshaven; the brand profile lists his address as the municipality of Wurster Nordseeküste on the North Sea coast of Lower Saxony. Production is at small-workshop scale, with every stage handled by one person; that is, there is no factory involved, but a studio where the maker takes on both design and bench work himself. "Halunke" in the brand name is an everyday German word meaning "rascal" or "scoundrel."
Founding the Brand

Halunke Pipes was founded in 2023. The threshold for the decision goes back a year earlier: at the end of 2022, Hallmann chose to stop making pipes only for his own use and turn the work into regular production. What made this step easier was seeing, over several pipes completed one after another, that he could carry every stage of production through without outside help.

The maker's path into this work is indirect. After finishing school he trained as an apprentice electronics technician, a trade he still practices today; pipe making is not his main livelihood but a pursuit that runs alongside it. His relationship with wood goes back much further, to childhood years spent in his father's hobby workshop. A pre-drilled briar burl given as a family gift proved decisive: when his father set out to make his own pipe from this burl, the son worked alongside him and learned the basic steps of the process. The pursuit fell into the background for a time amid other priorities; Hallmann returned to it years later.
Material and Shape

Ebonite is used predominantly for mouthpieces. Being a hardened-rubber-based material that lends itself to hand-shaping and individual fine-tuning, it is a common choice among small workshops; the feel it gives in the mouth and its maintenance needs are covered in the entry on mouthpiece materials. On many models, decorative rings of fine wood or horn are added where the shank meets the bowl; this detail is one of the brand's visible signatures.

On the shape side, the workshop's center of gravity is modern freehand production, an approach in which the maker is not bound to fixed dimensions from an established shape repertoire. Hallmann does not start by choosing a ready mold but by reading the grain flow of the block in hand; the final line of the body is largely determined by this reading. It naturally follows that making two pipes of the same size becomes difficult. Classic families such as dublin and bulldog variants appear often in the repertoire.

Every step from block selection to final polish is done by hand. This covers not just the outward shape but technical aspects as well — drilling the chamber and smoke channel, adjusting draw, and getting the balance right when the pipe is in the mouth. The brand has been active since its founding; production has remained limited by the capacity of a single master.

r.x: Sara Pipes
is the second brand Danish pipe maker Tom Eltang built alongside his own top-tier signature line. In the market it is mostly referred to as
Sara Eltang

, and it takes its name from the maker's youngest daughter. The brand preserves the structural logic of a hand-shaped Danish pipe while relying on a steady production flow that reduces the hours devoted to individually shaping each piece.
Origins

The person the brand is named after is the youngest child of Tom and Pia Eltang. Sara is said to have helped with the work in her father's workshop; the brand's emblem is also traced to a detail from this period, the girl's habit of working barefoot.

The line's actual founding, meanwhile, is tied to a bench changing hands: following the death in 2004 of another Danish master, Karl Erik, his lathe passed to the Eltang workshop. Eltang built a small-scale workshop arrangement around this bench and designed a shape list suited to it. The aim was to sustain a build quality comparable to the top-tier pipes with a much more modest budget of labor and material. The brand thus emerged as an arm sharing the same design thinking as pipes signed Eltang, but with more flexibility in grain selection. The master states that this arm gives him the chance to test new designs, materials and construction ideas at relatively low risk.
Production Arrangement

All shapes are designed by Tom Eltang. Rough turning and the early stages are carried out by hands assisting in the workshop; records show Eltang's fellow masters have taken on this work for many years, with the contribution of other Danish carvers noted more recently. Final inspection and finishing work pass through the master's own hands. Although production proceeds in batches, the numbers are limited; the brand's occasionally being unavailable on the market at all is a natural result of this arrangement.

Pipes are produced from briar block. Surface options proceed along two main lines, smooth finish and sandblasted. Stems are made of acrylic and hand-finished. Although the shape list leans toward classic lines, more experimental forms are also seen across the series. The grain quality accepted is a wider range than in the signature series; this flexibility is counted among the main factors that make the line's modest labor budget possible.
Stamp and Recognition

Pipes are recognized by the bare footprint emblem stamped on the bowl. Bowls that stand out for their grain are noted as also carrying an additional "Foot" stamp, said to mark an upper tier within the series.

Sara Pipes is regarded as a continuation of the Danish school line carried forward with classic shapes. For collectors, the brand's defining feature is that the design and internal construction are shared with the signature series, with the distinction concentrated largely in surface choice and the amount of hand labor invested.

r.x: Dunhill

is a business shaped, despite being known by its founder's name, not by a single person but by three successive generations. The brand's technical story on the pipe side is covered in the entry on Dunhill (White Spot); what concerns us here is the family and corporate decision-making that steered that story.
Alfred Dunhill

The founder was born on 30 September 1872 in a neighborhood in Hornsey, north London; he was among the children of Henry Dunhill (1842-1901) and Jane Styles (1843-1922). The apprenticeship he entered at sixteen was, in most sources, described as harness-making, the family trade; other descriptions of his father's profession also appear in sources. In 1893, at twenty-one, he took over the business and turned the workshop from horse-carriage equipment toward motor-vehicle accessories. The best-known product of this period is the pipe he filed a patent for in 1904, designed with a windshield so it could be smoked in an open automobile against the wind. To bring the legal side of his inventions under a separate roof, he founded a patent company in 1905; this company was not long-lived and was set aside at the end of 1906 as the tobacco business grew. The tobacconist's shop on Duke Street opened the following year.

The product of the truly productive years leading up to his retirement is two books. The Pipe Book, devoted to pipe history, came out in 1924; the same year saw the fifth edition of his earlier compilation, About Smoke. The interest the book aroused resulted in Royal Society of Arts membership the following year. His departure from management came in 1928, at fifty-six, for health reasons; he spent his remaining years on the Sussex coast and died in Worthing on 2 January 1959, at eighty-six.
Alfred Henry and Herbert Behind the Scenes

Born in 1896, Alfred Henry was the founder's eldest son and, like his father, began work as an apprentice in 1912, at sixteen. His apprenticeship was interrupted by the First World War: he went to war as a private, received the Military Cross in 1918 for his conduct in the assault at Frégicourt, and returned from the front with the rank of captain. Returning to his post at the company in 1919, Alfred Henry took over the chairmanship when his father stepped down in 1928, and held this seat for thirty-three years.

How much authority the chairmanship carried, however, is debated. According to his sister Mary's memoirs, the reins of day-to-day decisions lay with their uncle Herbert Dunhill, who lived abroad: turnover figures were reported to him by telegram, and every matter requiring a signature was submitted for his approval through a stream of mail and courier traffic. This family account has no third-party confirmation. Whatever the arrangement was until Herbert's death in 1950, the company reached an international scale during those same years. Part of the legacy Alfred Henry left is also his pen: The Gentle Art of Smoking (1954) is his book, and he also wrote the foreword to the revised edition of The Pipe Book.
Mary Dunhill and After

The founder's daughter, Mary Dunhill, born in 1906, joined the board in 1943, took over general management after Herbert's death, and became chairman in 1961. The Queen's Award to Industry given in 1966 and 1969 for export success falls within her tenure. Our Family Business, which she published in 1979, is the most-cited first-hand source on the brand's internal workings; it is also the sole witness for most of the family details in this entry. The family's ties to the company weakened in the following decades; one of the final links in this process is the Richard Dunhill generation.

r.x: Gamboni

is the brand under which Italian pipe maker Gian Maria Gamboni makes handmade pipes under his own name. Born in 1970 in Florence, Gamboni has spent most of his working life in Rome. He is a typical example of the one-person workshops that turn out a limited number of pieces a year: shape, size, and color are decided separately for each piece, and no two pipes are copies of one another.
Moving into Pipe Making

Gamboni's acquaintance with pipes goes back to the 1990s; he was first a smoker, then a collector. His move into production began in the mid-2000s, with the contact he established with the Becker & Musicò workshop, then operating in Rome. He made his first pipe in 2007. The shape sense of the Paolo Becker line can be traced in Gamboni's early work; in this respect, the brand ties into the master-apprentice tradition of the Italian handmade pipe.

According to records, Gamboni left the engineering profession he had carried on until then in 2010 and moved into full-time pipe making. Sources do not agree on where he worked after this date: some records speak of an arrangement rotating between several Italian cities, others of engineering work continued abroad. For this reason the workshop is known not by a fixed address but directly by the maker's name.
Material and Construction

The briar blocks the workshop uses come from the Liguria and Tuscany regions; Gamboni states that he selects the logs himself, in person. The blocks are bought in aged raw form, and shaping is done entirely by hand from start to finish; no series mold or ready pre-form is used.

Mouthpieces are cut from raw vulcanite rod brought from Germany. The tenon is not fitted as a separate piece; it is turned out of the rod itself. This is a labor-intensive method, but it is considered superior in terms of alignment and airtightness between the shank and the mouthpiece. For a comparison of materials, see the entry on mouthpiece materials.

In surface finishing, the emphasis is on a smooth, glossy finish. If a flaw appears in the wood during work, the piece is directed toward sandblasting or rustication; in the brand's repertoire, these two treatments serve as distinct finishing options in their own right, beyond simply concealing a flaw.
Golf-Term Quality Stamps

The brand's best-known feature is its grading system, introduced in 2011 and revised in 2013. Rather than the letter or star arrangement customary in the pipe community, the tier names are drawn from golf terminology:

rows: Individual pieces the maker considers his best

r.x: Because the names in the first three rows correspond directly to a surface treatment, the stamp tells whoever picks up a pipe both the finish type and the maker's own assessment at once; the practicality of the system is noted among collectors for this reason. "Hole In One," at the top of the list, does not indicate a surface type but the separate value the maker places on that particular piece, and is known as a rarely used stamp.

r.x: Directory of Russian Pipe Brands

brings together, in alphabetical order, pipe names made in Russia or recorded as Russian-made. Pipemaking in the country relies largely not on factory production but on small workshops clustered around a handful of masters; Saint Petersburg is considered the hub of this network, and the master-apprentice relationship has been decisive across generations. The entries below summarize only recorded facts, and points where the sources are silent are stated openly.
Brands
Boris Starkov
— Records contain only the brand name and a collection of images of his pipes. No information about the maker's working period, workshop, or production method has been documented.
Fyodorov
— Records mention only the name; there is no information about the brand's maker, location, or period.
Grigoriev

— Andrey Grigoriev (b. 1982), working in Saint Petersburg, took up pipemaking as a hobby alongside an engineering career in 2004. The decisive turning point came two years later, when he met Viktor Yashtylov, known for his high-grade pipes; from 2010 he worked as an apprentice at the master's workshop and absorbed his methods and approach to form. His own signed pipes appeared after this apprenticeship.
Java

— Java is a pipe brand produced for the tobacco company of the same name, known in Russia as Yava; it is therefore a name tied to the tobacco industry rather than to a master's workshop. The company's origin traces to a tobacco factory founded in Moscow in 1856. Pipe production was interrupted for a period. The Pipedia entry states the company was referred to after 1894 as the Russian arm of British American Tobacco, but this date is inconsistent: BAT was founded in 1902 and acquired a controlling stake in the Yava factory in 1991.
Kharlamov

— Aleksey Harlamov (Kharlamov) is recognized as the winner of the first pipemaking competition held in Russia. Also a sculptor and wood-carver, Harlamov produces freehand forms alongside traditional shapes. His pipes, densely carved with motifs such as crocodiles, iguanas, pangolins and bamboo, are made only to order.
Kiselyov
— No detail beyond the brand name has been documented.
Looshin

— The brand carries the signature of Russian master Yevgeni Lushin (Евгений Лушин). Sources contain no detail about the master's working period, workshop, or production approach; only images of his pipes and the name remain.
Mr. Pipes

— Mr. Pipes is the brand of Russian master Mikhail (Misha) Revyagin. The master's name first became known in the pipe community through a work video that circulated online, and later through forums where pipemakers gather. Sources lack information on the master's training and workshop history; on the other hand, his pipes' craftsmanship is spoken of with praise.
PS Studio

— P. S. Studio pipes are designed under the signature of Vladimir Grechukhin; production is carried out by two masters working under his supervision. At the Saint Petersburg workshop, Grechukhin began pipemaking in the 1970s, at a time when briar was hard to obtain, by working with other wood species, and quickly became counted among the country's leading masters. Pipes are carved by hand and finished either smooth or sandblasted; stems are cut from rod stock and finished with fine decorative pieces such as horn, boxwood, or black palm. On some examples, horn-look acrylic bands and hand-cut vulcanite stems are seen.
Sergey Cherepanov

— Sergey Cherepanov began pipemaking at a relatively advanced age, learning the craft as Mikhail Revyagin and Viktor Yashtylov shared their experience with him. At his workshop outside the city he produces around a hundred pipes a year and shows a preference for freehand shapes. He uses Mimmo and Mino briar as material, more rarely Jaume Houm briar, and German and Japanese vulcanite for stems. In his own smoking he is known to favor small, hand-comfortable pipes and plain Virginia tobacco.
Shaydullin

— Fidel Shaydullin's benchmark is internal engineering: a pipe cleaner must be able to pass from the stem tip to the bottom of the bowl without the pipe being disassembled. He favors working with bog oak alongside Greek and Algerian briar; for stems he uses German and Japanese vulcanite and Cumberland. By his own account, pipemaking is for him not a livelihood but a pursuit taken seriously, and he has made around 250 pipes to date.

r.x: Elliott Pipes

is the brand under which Alabama tobacconist Skip Elliott produces handmade American pipes under his own name. Because Elliott's main occupation is retail, production has never scaled up to workshop level, remaining a one-man, low-volume pursuit. For this reason, the brand is known within the American artisan pipe tradition more for its individually handled, low-volume examples.
From Tobacconist to Pipe Maker

Skip Elliott founded the tobacconist shop The Briary with his family in 1974. The shop spent its early years on the upper floor of Brookwood Mall in Birmingham; after twenty-six years at that address, it moved in November 2000 to a restored old farmhouse in Homewood. According to reports, Elliott, who handled hundreds of pipes daily, did not begin making pipes with his own hands until 1989; this date rests on a single account in pipe literature and is not backed by independent record. Production takes place not in the shop but in a small workshop attached to his home. Sources diverge on the workshop's location: some say Maylene in Shelby County, others the neighboring town of Alabaster.

Elliott positions himself not as a pipe maker but as a retailer who feeds his love of pipes through making them. This shows in his working pace: by his own account, a good month yields only two finished pipes, and a single pipe demands more than thirty hours of work.
Material and Craftsmanship

Elliott's material of choice is Greek briar burls. He mostly uses acrylic for mouthpieces, cutting them himself rather than buying ready-made ones; see the entry on mouthpiece craftsmanship for details. Brand promotional material also shows one-off use of alternative materials such as bog oak, horn, bakelite, and osage orange.

For surface finish, the maker's priority is the sandblasting method; rustication, the raised-texture surface treatment, is applied more rarely. One of the core principles Elliott states himself is that briar flaws are not covered with putty: a flawed burl is either set aside from the start or the shape is designed to route around the flaw.
Design Approach

Elliott's design approach stands out for taking the burl itself as the starting point. What determines the shape is not a pre-drawn mold but the grain direction and growth rings in the burl. For this reason the maker avoids committing to a specific model on commission; the requested shape is noted and brought to life once suitable briar turns up. The pipes that result accordingly move between classic forms and free (freehand) interpretations.
The brand's reach beyond its narrow circle came through a feature article published in
Pipe & Tobacco

magazine in spring 2006 and through radio interviews aimed at the pipe community. Even so, since production volume has never grown, Elliott-signed pipes are considered examples that circulate individually rather than being widely available.

r.x: Rainer Barbi

is considered one of the founding names of the master-made pipe tradition in Germany. Born in 1948, Barbi began making pipes in 1974 and carried on his working life, spanning more than thirty years, at his own workshop. Without apprenticing at any factory, he became a maker who learned by trial, which places him as an elder of the German freehand school.
Workshop and Style

Barbi's work rested on a way of working in which every piece leaving his hands was unique. Selecting the block, letting the shape follow the grain flow across the block, and leaving the surface open until the last moment were the basic elements of his style. The idea that grain structure should guide shape was widespread in Northern Europe; Barbi applied it in a more measured, more closed-lined interpretation suited to German taste. The resulting pipes carry a recognizable signature, which is why they are easily picked out among collectors.

Stem work was the most talked-about aspect of the maker's craft; his early pieces are reported to have frequently favored Cumberland stems. Barbi was also among the advocates of chamber lining, a thin protective coating applied to the tobacco chamber. Both bright-polished and sandblasted pieces came out of the workshop; the same care is known to have been maintained in both surface finishes. Records also mention meerschaum pipes stamped with his name.
Stamps and Grades

Barbi pipes carry different stamps depending on their year of production. Early pieces bear the grade-neutral "Styled by Barbi" stamp and a gold-colored signature on the stem. In the later period the body carries "r. barbi - handarbeit," while the stem bears a small embossed "r.b." mark; how this embossing was achieved was one of the details the maker never explained.

From the 1980s Barbi adopted a letter-based grading system. According to records this system started from the bottom with the sequence CC, CB, CA, BC, BB, BA, AC, AB, AA, with single-letter C, B, and A grades at the top tiers, and their numbered upper levels (A1, A2) above those. The letter largely reflected the grain quality of the briar; it did not mean the workmanship was weaker on lower-tier pipes.
The German Market and Afterward

Despite drawing international interest, Barbi did not overlook the habits of his own country. He kept producing pipes suited to the 9 mm filter standard in Germany; pieces drilled for a 6 mm filter are also known from the early period. It is noted that filtered models did not differ from the others in workmanship.

Rainer Barbi died on 23 May 2011, after a brief illness. Under an agreement made earlier, in 2014 a serial production line based on his designs, using rough blocks he had selected himself, was launched by Holmer Knudsen; these pipes entered distribution through Germany. The work Barbi left behind is considered important for showing that an independent German line existed that was not overshadowed by the Danish school.

r.x: Syring

is a one-man pipe signature bearing the name of Karl-Heinz Syring, from the northern German port city of Flensburg on the Danish border. The brand never became a factory, nor even a workshop with a regular schedule; the pipes it produced came out of the free hours found by a craftsman whose main occupation was repair work. For this reason the Syring name is remembered in German pipe history not through large series, but through a body of individually reworked bowls of known number.
From Police Officer to the Bench

Records indicate Syring was born in Kiel in 1933 and started as a police officer in the same city in 1950; he retired in 1993 after forty-three years of service. His interest in pipes appeared in the middle of this career, in the early 1960s. In other words, Syring pursued pipes as a secondary occupation for most of his life and was only able to move into full-time craftsmanship after retirement.

His shop in Flensburg was both a small sales section and a repair workshop. His daily workload consisted of repair jobs such as stem replacement, crack repair and general maintenance; independent sources also describe Syring primarily as a Flensburg-based pipe repairman and maker. The pipes he carved himself waited for enthusiasts in a small section next to the shop's tobacco shelf. Records show total production at a minimum of 1,611 pipes, and these bowls have spread beyond Germany over time.
Form and Influences

Syring's bowls were not shaped from a mold but as free forms drawn out by reading the grain of the block; in this respect they belong to the freehand tradition. The main influence shaping his direction came not from the south, but from the north — from the Danish school workshops on the other side of the border. He is considered to have stayed close to the form language of classic Danish masters in the line of Sixten Ivarsson and Poul Rasmussen. About half of his output was made with a filter socket and half without; this ratio can be seen as a practical balance struck between the German market's filter habit and the classic Danish approach.
Transmission and Closure

Syring's bench is known as a place open to those who wanted to try their hand at pipemaking. The best known of those who passed through this door is Tom Richard Mehret: he obtained his first unworked briar blocks and stems from Syring, is recorded as having completed his first pipes in 2003, and later became a maker known under his own name. This handover shows that the small shop in Flensburg was not only a repair workshop but also an informal apprenticeship venue. The master also hosted a monthly tobacco discussion circle at his home for years.

Records indicate Karl-Heinz Syring set aside the bench in 2004 and died in Flensburg in 2006. Since the brand ended with him, Syring pipes today can only be found in secondhand circulation. Being limited in number, mold-free and made entirely by one hand, they are also considered in German pipe history not so much as a production brand but as a signature identified with a particular city and a single bench.

r.x: Kapp & Peterson's move to a new factory

refers to Ireland's most established pipe workshop leaving the production building it had used for fifty years. Effective 23 May 2022, the Sallynoggin facility in County Dublin was closed, and production began being carried on in the same general area, in a new building in the neighboring district of Deansgrange. The Peterson brand thus moved to only its third production address in its entire history.
Address History

The workshop's first location was St. Stephen's Green in central Dublin. According to the record, the building was vacated in 1972 and production moved to Sallynoggin; the Irish press's account also holds that the workshop left the city center in the 1970s. The 2022 move is therefore only the brand's second relocation.

The fifty years spent at Sallynoggin correspond to the period in which the workshop placed greater emphasis on limited collector-oriented series rather than mass production. Series built on island identity such as Erin Go Bragh, and commemorative collections such as Mark Twain, took shape in this building.
Background to the Decision

According to the company's public account, the decision to relocate rested on practical rather than sentimental grounds. It is reported that a four-year lease was signed for the building after Kapp & Peterson passed to the US-based Laudisi Enterprises in 2018, and that needs were reassessed once that term ended; this detail rests solely on the company's announcement and is not confirmed in independent records. The two shortcomings that stood out were insufficient space for production and storage, and infrastructure in need of renewal. According to the same announcement, the building's electrical system had reached the limit of its capacity, and adding new equipment to the workshop was no longer possible without a comprehensive overhaul.
The Setup at Deansgrange

The move was planned to disrupt production as little as possible. Lathes, hand tools, and raw briar stock were moved to the new building within three days with the participation of the staff; the workshop left Sallynoggin on a Wednesday and returned to production in Deansgrange the following Monday.

The most notable change the new building brought was the ability to reorganize the workflow by function group. The lathes handling drilling work — bowl, mortise, and mouthpiece drilling — were gathered on a single line. Having makers doing similar work side by side is considered an arrangement that makes both monitoring production and the exchange of knowledge between benches easier. The facility also has open space allowing for future expansion of production and storage capacity.

Although from the outside it may look like nothing more than an address change, the event is considered a marker of continuity for Irish pipe production: the country's oldest and largest-scale pipe workshop has kept its production going without interruption.

r.x: Rivendell Pipes

is the name of a small pipe workshop run single-handedly by American Levi Zurcher in the early 2000s. The brand rested on neither a factory nor a corporate structure, and the pipes it produced never entered a wide distribution network. For this reason, Rivendell is counted not among the main names of the American handmade pipe scene but among the many independent workshops that briefly appeared and disappeared around its edges. What is known about the brand today amounts to little more than a few lines in a maker registry and a single promotional page the maker himself prepared; even the founding year has not been established with certainty.
The Maker

Zurcher graduated with honors from the zoology program at Northern Arizona University. In the fall of 2004, the only period in which the workshop's trace can be found, he was twenty-three — a notable detail in a craft where the average age tends to run quite high. Pipe making was never a full-time profession for him; it remained a pursuit fitted alongside his student years and the period following graduation.

In Rex Poggenpohl's compiled list of North American pipe makers, Zurcher appears under the name "Rivendell Pipes" with an address in Flagstaff, Arizona. This record shows that the workshop's name was known, if only narrowly, within the community. On Zurcher's own promotional page, dated to the fall of 2004, the address appears instead as Medford, in the state of Oregon. According to the same page, the maker was at that time in the process of applying to the optometry program at Pacific University and expected to move to Forest Grove near Portland. The discrepancy between the two addresses can be explained by the records belonging to successive periods; which was valid in which year, however, is not documented.
Production and Fate

There is no reliable account of Rivendell pipes' shape repertoire, the source of the briar used, or the stamping pattern. Neither a model series nor an annual production figure appears in the records. It might be assumed that a one-man, part-time operation would turn out a limited number of pipes, but there is no document to confirm this. In workshops of this scale it is common for every stage to pass through the same hands; for the general outline of the process, see the entry on how a pipe is made.

There is no publicly available trace of Zurcher continuing pipe making after 2004; the Pipedia entry itself was opened in 2009 with a call for current information. It is not known when the workshop closed, nor is there any record indicating it remains active. In this respect, Rivendell is placed in the same category as other hard-to-document American workshops such as Schoonmaker or Ozark Mountain Briars. That its name was recorded at all is owed largely to the maker registry compiled by Rex Poggenpohl.

r.x: Vauen

is Germany's oldest pipe factory still in production. The brand's origin traces to the business founded in Nuremberg in 1848 by Karl Ellenberger and Carl August Ziener, regarded as Germany's first pipe factory; production continues in the same city today. Vauen's true fame in the pipe world, however, rests on having developed the world's first 9 mm activated-charcoal pipe filter, thereby laying the foundation for the filtered-smoking tradition known as the "German school."
History

The factory founded by Ellenberger and Ziener merged in 1901 with the Gebhard Ott pipe factory, which had been operating in Nuremberg since 1866, and the company took the name "Vereinigte Pfeifenfabriken Nürnberg" (United Pipe Factories of Nuremberg). Today's brand name was born in 1909: Adolf Eckert derived a memorable name from the initials of this long title. Since the letter V is pronounced "fau" and N is pronounced "en" in German, combining the pronunciation of the two letters produced the spelling VAUEN.

Ernst Eckert, from the Ott family, took the helm of the company born from the merger; the period in which the brand established its place in European and overseas markets began under his leadership. Adolf Eckert, who coined the name, represents the generation after him. The person who rebuilt the factory after the devastation World War II left behind in Nuremberg was Adolf Eckert's son, Ernst Eckert, who shared his grandfather's name; with this recovery the company regained its international standing.

The company has remained in the Eckert family for generations; company sources emphasize that it has stayed a family firm since its founding. From 1982 Alexander Eckert, of the fifth generation, ran the firm. Martin Ramsauer, who joined the company in 2016, became co-managing director in 2018; that same year Julia Eckert, of the sixth generation, also began working on the marketing side. On 1 June 2026, Florian Eckert took over as managing director, joining his wife Julia Eckert in representing the family's sixth generation. This family continuity is regarded as a rare example of stability in the European pipe industry.
The Dr. Perl Filter and the German School

The two decades following World War I saw an international race in pipe filters and system pipes; in the advertising language of the era, these solutions were marketed under the heading "healthy pipe." Vauen joined this race early, and records show it released a simple paper filter around 1921. The turning point in today's sense, however, came after these early attempts.

The innovation that wrote Vauen's name into pipe history is the world's first 9 mm activated-charcoal pipe filter, introduced in 1934 under the name "Dr. Perl junior." Placed between the bowl and the mouthpiece (stem), this filter aims to provide a drier smoke by trapping the moisture and condensation products in the smoke. Over time this solution became the defining feature of German pipe-making; today it is accepted that the great majority of pipes sold in Germany — according to company sources, more than ninety percent — have a 9 mm filter socket. The working principles of the different filter types and their effect on the smoke are discussed in detail in the entry on pipe filters and systems.

A detail as important as the filter itself is how it seats. In 1968 Vauen made standard, in most of its models, the solution it called Conex: the tip of the filter socket inside the mouthpiece is narrowed into a cone shape, so the filter seats perfectly and the smoke is forced to pass through the filter rather than around it. Not every Vauen pipe after 1968 has this mechanism, but the system spread beyond the brand over time; several European makers, Stanwell foremost among them, used a similar conical socket in their own filtered models. Improved versions of the Dr. Perl junior are still made today, and it remains the first name mentioned when a 9 mm activated-charcoal filter comes up.
Series and Brand Identity

Vauen pipes are predominantly made from briar, and the mouthpieces on the upper-tier models carry a round dot, recognizable from a distance. Alongside the classic-shape series, themed collections also occupy an important place in the brand's production range. The best known of these is the Auenland series, inspired by Tolkien's Shire (translated into German as "Auenland"), made up of long-shanked models reminiscent of the churchwarden style. Bringing fantasy-literature readers' attention into the pipe world, this series is cited as an example of a long-established factory's connection with contemporary culture.
The Dot Mark and the Dunhill Case

The dot on the mouthpiece is Vauen's most discussed mark. According to the company's official history, the white dot began being used as a quality indicator in 1911. Records show that in the 1920s Vauen registered this mark for Germany and Austria; in those same years Dunhill had also registered the white dot for the international market. The two companies went to court, and the outcome determined today's picture: international use of the white dot went to Dunhill, while Vauen was left able to use the white dot only in Germany and Austria. Vauen pipes headed to other markets have since been marked with a gray or light-blue dot.

This distinction is a practical clue for an enthusiast trying to identify a pipe. The color of the dot points to the market the pipe was made for; the complete absence of a dot, meanwhile, is not a quality defect but a grade difference: lower-tier pipes carry only the VAUEN stamp on the mouthpiece instead of the dot. The Nuremberg factory has also handled distribution of labels other than its own; the best known is the Kansas brand, made at the Amadeus workshop in Greece.
Running production from design to final finishing under its own roof at its Nuremberg plant, Vauen continues today to stand as the symbol of the filtered-smoking culture.
