r.x: Ascot

is a pipe name whose origins trace back to France's pipemaking capital, Saint-Claude. Today the brand is remembered less as a workshop in its own right than as a name a long-established manufacturer used for different markets in different periods. The fact that the same name was also used outside France is the aspect of this entry that most rewards a collector's caution.
The La Bruyère Period

The earliest records of Ascot point to the La Bruyère structure at Saint-Claude. After the 1929 crash shook the pipe industry of the Jura region, Chapuis-Comoy & Cie merged with another company in 1932 to begin operating under the name La Bruyère. According to the manufacturer's own history, this merger produced the largest pipe concern of its day, with more than four hundred fifty workers. The partnership ended in 1957 as the commercial weight of the Chacom brand became decisive, and the company reverted to its old name. From that point on, Ascot was carried forward not as an independent concern but as a sub-brand of Chacom.

The main obstacle to dating the brand is its stamping: older Ascot pipes carry no mark pointing to a manufacturer, so placing a pipe in the La Bruyère years is usually a matter of reading shape and workmanship. Recent examples are unambiguous, however, bearing Chacom's "CC" mark on the mouthpiece. These later series are recognized by a trio of features: an army-style push-bit joint between shank and mouthpiece with no screw thread, a horn-look acrylic mouthpiece, and a 9 mm filter chamber. This choice of fittings was no accident — these series were made primarily for the German market, which was accustomed to filtered pipes.
Other Pipes Bearing the Same Name

The Ascot name was not confined to France. According to records, H. Perkins & Sons — a long-established London silversmith operating since 1901, incorporated in 1922 as Henry Perkins & Sons Ltd., and later known for elegant silver lighters — marketed pipes under the Ascot name over a period stretching from the 1960s into the 1980s. These pipes are said to have been produced as a private label for Dunhill; the same records also note that the firm later joined Beney Ltd. Neither claim is backed by an independent document, so both should be treated with caution, and a pipe should not be taken as Dunhill-made on this account alone.

A third branch appears in the United States. Here, modestly made, rustic-finished pipes of Italian origin circulated under the Ascot name; some also bear the name "Barracini." Which Italian workshop made this group is not clear from the record. What is certain is that this series has no production connection to the French or English Ascots.
A Note on Telling Them Apart

According to collector records, Royal Ascot, stamped with the addition "Algerian Briar," is also of French origin but is a name distinct from Ascot; since this distinction rests on a single record it should not be treated as certain, but the two names should not be confused with one another. When assessing an Ascot pipe, the full reading of the stamp, the mark on the mouthpiece, and the joint style should all be weighed together — determining origin from the name alone is misleading.

r.x: Bjarne

is a pipe brand Danish maker Bjarne Nielsen (1941-2008) founded in Copenhagen in 1973. The brand was less the signature of a single bench than a system for gathering and distributing: the work of Danish carvers Nielsen selected was brought together under a shared stamp and sent out from there to foreign markets. For this reason, Nielsen's name is remembered less as one of the makers behind Danish School pipes and more as one of the agents who put those pipes into international circulation.
From a Ministry to the Pipe Business

Records indicate Nielsen's relationship with the pipe began at sixteen, when he also made his first pipes for his own use. The first part of his career, though, was spent far from the bench: after studying business administration in Copenhagen, he was assigned at the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs to build overseas connections for exporting firms. This work put him directly face to face with the demand for freehand pipes in the 1960s; the capacity of Danish workshops was not enough to meet the demand coming in. Nielsen tried to fill the gap with pipes he made himself, and the orders he received soon reached a volume that could not be carried on alongside a civil-service post. In 1973 he left the ministry to take up the business full-time.
Workshop Arrangement and Makers

Once it became clear that sales, production, and collections could not all be run by one person, Nielsen began taking on carvers. Part of the first team was made up of names who had left Preben Holm's workshop, which employed a large crew in those years; by the early 1990s seven carvers are reported to have been working there. Because the carver's name is not stamped on Bjarne pipes, whose work belongs to which piece can only be guessed at from grade and style. Among the names working with high-grade briar blocks are Tonni Nielsen and Ph. Vigen; Ole Bandholm is also mentioned in records. Most of the plentifully produced budget line came from the hand of Mogens Johansen, known by the signature "Johs."
Stamps and Grades

The distinction between lines is read from how the brand name is written: standard production carries only the "Bjarne" stamp, while the upper grades are stamped "Bjarne Nielsen" and graded with letters. Sources do not agree on the scope of the letter scale; some stamp compilations give a short sequence running from A to D, while others give a longer ranking topped by AX and descending in the alphabet as far as J. The Viking mark is also recorded in sources as a secondary name for the brand.
Markets and the Brand's End

In the early years, the whole output was sent to the United States. Attending the pipe fair in Frankfurt at the end of the 1970s opened Germany as a second market; German buyers' preference, however, leaned not toward freehand but toward classic shapes, so a separate line made up of traditional forms was set up. This line caught on, and Germany remained the brand's top-selling market for a long time. By the 1990s the pipes were found in more than thirty countries, and Nielsen spent more than half of each year on the road, meeting with retailers and smokers. The catalogue also included a series called "Giant," made well above usual measurements.

According to records, Nielsen died in February 2008, at sixty-six, following a heart attack. Since no one stepped forward to take over the business, the brand ended together with its founder; no new pipes were made under the Bjarne name. A few pipe-tobacco blends bearing his name are reported to still be made by a manufacturer in Germany.

r.x: Loewe & Co.

is an English pipe brand that grew out of the shop and workshop the French-born Emil Loewe opened on Haymarket in London in 1856. Counted among the established nineteenth-century London pipe houses, the firm is known for silver-banded spigot fittings and shape names drawn from British place names.
The Haymarket Years

The Loewe name is regularly cited in pipe literature as the first English house to work briar on a consistent basis. No independent record documents this claim; similar founding narratives also circulate around Comoy's of London and Charatan, which set up business in London in the same years, so impartial sources do not award the title to any one brand definitively. What is certain is that Loewe was among the early London workshops to switch to briar.

The brand's signature is the spigot fitting. A silver band at the end of the shank, into which the stem's tenon seats, turns the stem into a removable part. According to sources, the fitting was originally adopted with overseas customers in mind: if a stem broke, a replacement could be made and shipped as a separate piece. London assay marks on the bands remain today the most reliable basis for dating the brand.
Stamps and Shape Names

The classic-period stamp is spread across three faces of the shank: "LOEWE" and "LONDON W." on the right side, the "L&Co" logo in an oval frame on the left, and the shape name on the underside. Most of the names are drawn from the map of Britain; Albury, Banbury, Kendal, Liverpool, Sheffield, and Woodstock are familiar entries on the list. The names do not directly reveal the shape: Larne is a canadian, while Boston corresponds to a billiard.

Quality designations came later. According to catalogues, at some point between 1956 and 1964 the names Centurion, Original, and Old English began being stamped beneath the oval logo, while marks such as Mounted, Spigot, Standard, and Straight Grain belong to a later period. Pipes dated before 1920 carry no quality stamp. Shape names were replaced, at some point before 1968, by three-digit numbers beginning with nine; this numbering ran until the early 1980s. Because numbering was reset from scratch during the Cadogan era, old and new numbers do not indicate the same shape.
From Civic to Cadogan

The firm passed, after generations following its founder, to the owners of the Civic brand. The exact year of the change of hands is unknown; sources hold that the transfer was completed well before 1960, at which point the business was run by Civic. Through the 1960s the original Haymarket building was lost to redevelopment plans, and production was dispersed to different addresses within London, one of which is cited as Hammersmith. The brand became the property of the Cadogan group, which also gathered names such as BBB, Comoy's, GBD, and Orlik, around 1979. The acquisition of Orlik in 1980 allowed the group to consolidate all its production at the factory in Southend-on-Sea. From this period, when production was not yet centralized, Loewe pipes are also known bearing a "St Claude - France" stamp on the shank side. Loewe's dissolution as a company is said to have come toward the end of the 1980s; the name survives today as one Cadogan uses only sparingly.
Standing in Collecting

In the estate market, interest concentrates on pipes made before production moved to Southend; the Haymarket period and the early Civic years are the most sought-after span. Dating the brand is not easy, because the stamp dies stayed largely unchanged across successive owners, unlike the frequently updated stamp calendars of Dunhill or Charatan. This makes silver-banded examples serve as the yardstick: the assay mark gives the pipe's year directly. That Cadogan kept using the "London" stamp even on its Southend production is one of the factors that adds to the confusion.

r.x: Dunhill Curiosities

is a heading gathering a number of records that do not fit into the known history of the Alfred Dunhill brand. It brings together patent files, workshop practice, a manufacturing license granted abroad, and the fate of the founder's private collection — independent details from one another. The brand's main story is in the entry on Dunhill (White Spot); the items here can be considered marginal notes to that story.
Cartridge Filling and the Vernon Connection

One of the inventions registered under Alfred Dunhill's name is a ready-made tobacco cartridge designed to speed up filling the pipe. The application in the United States was filed on 19 September 1921; the document numbered 1,490,808, titled "Means for Charging Smoking Pipes," was issued on 15 April 1924. The idea was simple: cylindrically compacted tobacco was wrapped in an easily torn paper or similar wrapping, and pulling a strip attached to the wrapping opened the packaging, seating the tobacco mass directly into the chamber. The cartridges were promoted in the tobacco section of the firm's "About Smoke" catalogue.

The second file is registered under Vernon Dunhill and concerns the spring-loaded push (spigot) mechanism connecting the mouthpiece to the shank. A longitudinally split metal tang holds the mouthpiece in place by pressing against the opposing band; it releases when pulled and re-grips when pushed. Two versions of the mechanism are known, one mounted on the shank and the other on the mouthpiece, and both are reported to have been used from the early 1930s to mid-1936. It appears in pipe literature that provisional protection was obtained in Britain in April 1931, and that the patent was finalized under number 363582 at the end of the same year; this has not been confirmed from the official registration record. The American counterpart was granted under number 1,861,910 in 1932. The role of stamps from this period in dating is the subject of the entry on Dunhill Patent Stamps and Dating.
Silver Bands and Factory Repairs

Band-fitting work was carried out in a separate department at the factory, with a small team of just a few people. The silver used was 925 sterling, and the gold was 9, 14, and 18 carat; original bands bear at minimum the "AD" stamp within a diamond-shaped frame, along with a hallmark. Since silver pieces below a certain weight are exempt from the full hallmark requirement under British regulations, a missing set of hallmarks on some bands is an expected occurrence. Leslie "Les" John Wood, a long-serving name in the department, joined in 1963 and rose over time to master silversmith; his departure date varies in sources between the late 1970s and early 1980s. Wood later founded his own brand with his wife Dolly, and for a while continued the work at his own workshop when band production was outsourced. Among former Dunhill employees who founded their own brands are also counted the founders of Sasieni and Ashton.

On the repair side, the firm used a seal certifying that the work had been done at the factory. In structural interventions such as replacing a broken mouthpiece or repairing a cracked shank, the pipe's original stamps were re-worked, without an additional service stamp being applied to separately record the procedure.
The Tobacco License Granted to Germany

It is reported that negotiations beginning in 1926 resulted in a licensing agreement in 1938, and that some Dunhill blends began to be manufactured at the Hamburg-based firm Joh. Wilh. von Eicken; the phrase "Hergestellt in Deutschland" appears on the bottom of these tins. Local production is said to have been aimed at avoiding the import tax burden. According to the firm's own history, Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed first the factory in Mülheim, then, four weeks later, the head office in Hamburg; von Eicken did not regain its license to produce tobacco until 1948. When manufacturing of Dunhill blends in Germany ended entirely is unclear: one account says production closed with the 1943 bombing, another says it continued until sometime before 1976. Details are in the entry on Vintage Dunhill Tobaccos Made in Germany.
The Founder's Collection

The antique pipes, tobacco jars, and tobacco books Alfred Dunhill gathered over the years went to auction at Christie's South Kensington on 12 May 2004. Among the one hundred twenty lots were a meerschaum bowl dated 1880, a pair of Delft tobacco jars from the late 18th century, and a tobacco-book catalogue printed in 1874; the company archive kept a few pieces out of the sale. For the founder's interest in tobacco and pipe literature, see the entry on Alfred Dunhill's The Pipe Book (1924).

r.x: Gabos Pipes

is the brand under which Romanian master Costin Gabos makes pipes under his own name. The workshop is located in eastern Transylvania, in the town of Miercurea Ciuc at the foot of the Harghita mountains. The brand is counted among Romania's examples of the generation of one-person pipe workshops that became visible across Eastern Europe in the 2000s, and is known chiefly for freehand work not bound to a mold.
Geography and Craft Setting

Miercurea Ciuc is the seat of Harghita County; it is built in a high basin surrounded by coniferous forest, in an area heavily populated by Romania's Hungarian-speaking Székely community. Wood carving is known in the region as a craft that has continued for centuries. The ornamented surface work and off-mold silhouettes seen in Gabos's pieces are, in the pipe community, most often considered an extension of this local carving heritage.
The Master's Background

According to the Lopés compilation, the only detailed source available, Gabos was born in 1971, graduated from the wood-industry faculty of Transilvania University in Brașov, and began making pipes in 2004. This information could not be confirmed by an independent record, so it should be read as reported rather than established fact. According to the same source, the master's field of training expertise is interior and furniture design. Such a background would explain why his shape decisions lean more on a design and ornamentation tradition than on classic English molds.
Production and Material

The brand's defining trait is that the lines of the bowl and body are built not to a predetermined mold but according to the flow of the grain in the block; dimensions and silhouette vary from piece to piece. This is a direct result of a workshop philosophy that treats the briar block's own texture as the starting point of the design.

The same source reports that, besides briar, the master also works with woods such as apple, wild cherry, sour cherry, and aged oak; this list of woods likewise rests on a single record. For the place of hardwoods other than briar in pipe making, see pipes in woods other than briar.
Its Standing, and What Is Unknown

Gabos Pipes is one of Romania's few signatures within the artisan pipe scene, unconnected to series production, that has spread worldwide. Nearly all the information circulating about the brand rests on pipe archives and records of the Romanian pipe community; the website the workshop used for a long time is no longer accessible today. There is no confirmed accounting of total production volume, stamp forms, or series. Whether the workshop is still actively producing is also an open question; no up-to-date record from recent years could be found.

r.x: Benner

is the name Danish maker Bent Nielsen (b. 1944) has signed onto his pipes since childhood, using a nickname from his youth. Nielsen, known today for his measured, classically proportioned shapes, actually started from a very different place — the flamboyant freehand shapes of the 1970s. Born in North Jutland, he moved with his family to the Roskilde area as a child and has lived in this region ever since; his workshop is in the village of Tune, south of the city.
The Move to Classic Shapes

Nielsen's first trade was carpentry. His change of bench came when he joined the workshop of Karl Erik Ottendahl in the early 1970s: American demand for fantasy pipes was so great that the workshop was looking for extra hands. He worked there for seven years, and most of the freehand pipes that went to the United States in that period passed through his hands. Some sources say he also drew model sketches for Stanwell in the same years; this detail has not been independently confirmed.

What actually changed his path came after he left. According to the account, while working at a workshop called Zetterwig, S. Bang asked him for support on pipes bound for the German market. Nielsen, working in the style he was used to, put together a set of fantasy shapes and presented it to the importer; but what Germany wanted was classic molds. This misunderstanding forced him to work in an area he had never tried. His skill with classic shapes eventually eclipsed his earlier work, and the Benner name is now associated mainly with this line. It is also said that the German distributor did not find the nickname Danish-sounding enough, which is why a portion of the pipes were stamped with the name Bent Nielsen.
A Thirty-Year Gap

After making pipes for Germany for a few years, he began working for the tobacconist Pipe-Dan; his acquaintance with a very young Tom Eltang dates to this period. A personal upheaval in the late 1970s — sources mention a divorce — led him to take a long break from pipe making. He sold off his machines and returned to carpentry, a trade he worked for thirty years.

He never fully severed the connection, however: in his spare time he kept making pipes at Karl Erik's workshop. When he decided to set up on his own again, he bought his first lathe from Eltang and gathered the rest of his tools over time, repairing most of them himself. Because his main job was full-time, his output stayed low; the few pipes he made mostly found buyers close to home.
Material and Signature

When he retired from carpentry in early 2011, the time he could devote to the bench increased, and his pipes became visible outside Denmark as well. His use of olive wood alongside briar is one of the features that sets him apart; he is said to bring these logs back from Crete, where he vacations every year. A significant portion of his briar stock, meanwhile, comes from material he took over after Ottendahl's death in 2004. For stems, he works with acrylic, Cumberland, vulcanite, and imitation amber; a small "B" is said to be worked into the stem on some examples. Production remains irregular and limited rather than a steady series.

r.x: Butz-Choquin

is a pipe brand founded in 1858 in the city of Metz in northeastern France, taking its name from the surnames of its two founders, Jean-Baptiste Choquin and Gustave Butz. With a history spanning more than a hundred and sixty years, it is counted among the oldest brands in the French pipe industry, and today continues production in Saint-Claude, the town at the center of the country's pipe tradition.
A Design Born from a Shop

Butz-Choquin's origins lie not in a pipe workshop but in a retail tobacco business. Jean-Baptiste Choquin's shop in Metz was busy enough by the mid-nineteenth century to employ several people, and Gustave Butz was among that staff. The pair's relationship turned into kinship in 1858, when Butz married Choquin's daughter, Marie.

The "Choquin pipe," which appeared that same year, is considered the brand's founding product. The distinguishing feature of this bent-shaped model was its flattened bowl base, which allowed the pipe to stand upright on a surface. Records note that the model's mouthpiece was made of albatross bone and attached to the bowl with silver bands — a detail that rests on the brand's own history and the collector sources that draw on it. To take the design beyond individual commissions, Butz opened a workshop in Metz that same year, 1858; the business came to be known by its present name, formed from the combination of the two surnames.
The Move to Saint-Claude

The brand's second life began in 1951. That year, the Berrod-Regad company, which had acquired the Butz-Choquin brand, moved production from Metz to Saint-Claude in the Jura mountains. Following the mid-nineteenth-century adoption of heath root (briar) as a pipe material, the town was regarded as the world's pipe capital; this transformation is discussed in detail in the entry on the Briar Revolution and Saint-Claude. Butz-Choquin thus became a neighbor of established Saint-Claude firms such as Chacom.

The new management's first task was overhauling the distribution system; after the agent network was renewed, the brand turned to export in 1960. That these years are also remembered for various awards and a "golden cup" symbolizing French taste is information that rests largely on the company's own history and has not been confirmed by independent records. The expansion of the catalog, however, can be traced more concretely: production, which started with around ten lines, grew over time to more than seventy. This variety gave the brand the ability to offer both classic English shapes and its own French interpretations at once.
Changes of Ownership and Current Status

The Berrod family, keen for production to remain in Saint-Claude, handed the company over to a local entrepreneur in 2002; this person's name appears in sources as Fabien Guichon, and in some places as Gichon. The transfer proved short-lived: in 2006 ownership of the business passed to Denis Blanc, and the brand has continued production under this management.

Butz-Choquin pipes are recognized by the "BC" letter combination on their stamps and the Saint-Claude marking. Although it works at factory scale rather than as a single-piece artisan operation, its broad shape catalog and unbroken history make it one of the load-bearing brands of the French pipe tradition.

r.x: The
Danish School

is the design and craft movement born in Copenhagen in the middle of the twentieth century that changed the course of handmade pipes worldwide. Carrying into pipes the functionalist (funktionalisme) sensibility that dominated Danish architecture and furniture design in the 1930s and 40s, the school is known for lines stripped of ornament, a rigor that puts smoking mechanics ahead of aesthetics, and a master-apprentice tradition passed down through generations. Today a significant share of the world's independent pipe makers, wherever they work, are considered heirs of this school, directly or indirectly.
Origins: The Copenhagen Workshops

The movement's founding figure is generally held to be Sixten Ivarsson, who began working during the Second World War years at Suhr's pipe repair workshop (Suhr's Pibereparation) in Copenhagen. Work that began as repair turned in time into design; in Ivarsson's hands, the pipe was rethought according to the era's Danish design principle that "form follows function."

After Ivarsson, the workshop's foreman role passed to Poul Rasmussen, who later set up his own workshop and died in 1967. Known for fine-lined classic shapes and a coloring technique referred to as "laboratory staining," this workshop trained figures such as Emil Chonowitsch, Björn Bengtsson and Tom Eltang; after Rasmussen's death, his wife Anne Julie carried the workshop on. Copenhagen's long-established pipe and tobacco shop W.Ø. Larsen also opened its own workshop in the early 1960s; Else Larsen, known as Denmark's first female pipe maker, along with Poul Ilsted and Hans "Former" Nielsen, worked there. This workshop closed in the mid-1970s.
Design Approach
The school's technical legacy can be summed up in a few principles:
The path of the smoke comes first:
The air channel running from bowl to stem is placed at the center of the design; the drilling work takes priority over aesthetic concerns.
Hand-cut stem:
Rather than a ready-made mold stem, a stem shaped individually for each pipe is the essential principle.
Following the grain:
Shape is determined not by classic molds but by the grain pattern of the briar; the wood's own structure is the design's starting point.

The result of this approach spilling beyond symmetrical molds was the freeform freehand pipe. The style's flamboyant second branch, "fancy freehand," became fashionable in the 1960s and 70s in the hands of Preben Holm and Karl Erik, especially in the United States.
Spread and Legacy

From the early 1950s Sixten Ivarsson designed models for the Stanwell factory; the handmade aesthetic thus spread around the world through mass production, and the concept of "Danish Design" became a mark of quality in the pipe world. In the 1960s, Denmark's pipe exports saw a major rise, particularly in the American market. From the mid-1970s onward, as the large workshops closed, the field was left to independent makers working alone; today's framework for distinguishing handmade (artisan) pipes from factory pipes took shape largely during this period.

One of the features that makes the school unique in the world is a master-apprentice chain spanning three generations. Among those Sixten Ivarsson trained are his son Lars Ivarsson, the Swedish maker Bo Nordh, Jess Chonowitsch, Jørn Micke and the Japanese maker Hiroyuki Tokutomi; the chain extends through Nanna Ivarsson to a third generation and today's global artisan generation. Ivarsson's culture of openness, summed up in his own words that "a bad teacher is one who does not let his student surpass him," is seen as the main reason the school spread so widely. The classic-elegant branch of the tradition was carried into the 2000s by the S. Bang brand, founded in Copenhagen in 1968, and by Tom Eltang's workshop.

r.x: Canaan Pipes

is a pipe workshop run single-handedly by Abi Natur in the Adriatic coastal city of Bar, Montenegro. The workshop's founding year does not appear in the records; what makes the brand recognizable is not its history but its way of working. Production is one-person and small-scale: pieces are taken up one at a time, and the maker does not move to the next until one is finished. According to the maker's own account, he lived for a long time in Europe and around the Mediterranean basin before opening the workshop, and traces of the places he saw later found their way into the shapes he works.
Approach to Making

No molds are used for Canaan pipes. Although a few classic shapes recur in the workshop, since every bowl is shaped individually no two pieces are identical; in this respect the brand is assessed within the freehand tradition.

The workshop sets itself two technical standards. The first is that the freehand-drilled smoke channel must enter the tobacco chamber exactly at its base; the second is that a pipe cleaner must be able to pass from the tip of the stem to the bottom of the chamber without any part being disassembled. A bowl that does not meet both conditions is not offered for sale. The chamber opens as a cone that narrows downward and is finished with hand sanding.
Stems are not bought as ready-made parts; they are hand-cut from rod stock, with the tenon cut from the same piece. The stem materials used are German ebonite alongside cumberland and lucite.
Materials: Briar and Olive Wood
Most bowls come from plateau-cut briar blocks. Some blocks are bought wholesale, others are selected by the maker himself; regardless of how they arrive, all are individually inspected before use.

What sets the brand apart from others, however, is olive wood. The area around Bar is known for a variety of olive that grows very slowly in the harsh climate between sea and mountain; records refer to this variety as "Barska žutica" (
Olea europaea

). Slow growth increases the wood's density, and the most sought-after pieces come from trees that have taken hold on almost bare rock: this centuries-long struggle leaves a tight grain texture resembling marble. The maker collects the wood himself from trees over three hundred and fifty years old, sometimes as old as eight hundred years, and cures it by traditional methods for several more years. This curing stage is considered necessary to reduce the risk of cracking in a wood that is oily and difficult to work.

Using olive wood for pipes is not a new pursuit; it is considered one of the most established options among woods other than briar. The Stara Maslina ("Old Olive"), the region's emblematic tree, estimated at around two thousand years old, is often cited to convey just how far back this tree's history in the Bar area goes.
Recognition

Because the number of pieces it produces is limited, the brand is known more within collector circles than through a broad distribution network. The names the maker gives his pipes are chosen from associations drawn from literature, seafaring, painting, and sculpture; this naming habit is considered an extension of his tendency to present each piece as a separate design idea.

r.x: Pohlmann Pipes

is the brand of handmade briar pipes American master Brad Pohlmann produces under his own name. Pohlmann's story is a clear example of a pattern often seen in American pipe making: workshop training in youth, a long career gap, and a return made in maturity.
From Apprenticeship to Workshop

Pohlmann, born in California, saw his interest in pipes turn into a professional pursuit in the mid-1970s; records say he toured England and Scotland's established pipe firms in 1975, and the following year researched the addresses of small American benches to find a place to apprentice. In 1976 he entered The Briar Workshop in Stowe, Vermont. The workshop, run by Elliott Nachwalter and Jorg Jemelka, was a place well regarded among the young American benches of the era.

Pohlmann stayed there for roughly five years and became one of the few able to carry out every stage of the work on his own. During this time the team moved from Stowe and Hyde Park to Coral Springs, Florida; the master's first technical foundation formed during these years.
A Long Gap and Return

Pohlmann returned to California in 1980. There he completed a four-year apprenticeship in tool and die making, training that later proved decisive in the interior work of his pipes. A sixteen-year career in the computer industry followed, and pipe making was reduced to the occasional piece for friends and small repairs. His return to production under his own name came, as the account goes, when that period closed in the early 2000s.

The moment that set the direction of his return is described as his meeting, at the 2004 Chicago pipe show, with new-generation American makers such as Todd Johnson and Jody Davis. Following this meeting Pohlmann changed his method: instead of drilling the body first and then shaping it, he began roughing out the shape first and drilling afterward. This sequence made it possible to follow the grain direction more freely and to try shapes less bound to the workshop mold of his early years.
Style and Current Status

Pohlmann's early work is regarded as a derivative of the Briar Workshop line; in the later period, a language stands out that combines classic English shapes with touches of the Danish school in his own measure. His tool-and-die background is read as a pursuit of tolerance beyond the ordinary in the working of the airway and the mortise. Production, as would be expected of one-person workshops, remains limited in number.

The master works today in rural Oregon, in a workshop he shares with his partner Silver Gray, herself also a pipe maker. Pohlmann's career is cited as an example of how the knowledge of small American benches founded in the late 1970s carried across a generational gap into the American handmade pipe scene.

r.x: Orlik

is the brand founded in London in 1899 by Louis Orlik, one of the familiar names in British pipe production for much of the twentieth century. The firm's address is recorded as Old Bond Street, a street that in those same years was also one of the centers of London's pipe and tobacco trade. Orlik followed a path somewhat different from the luxury Mayfair brands of its day: rather than a high price, it aimed to combine good craftsmanship with a reasonable price and solid after-sales service.
Development of the Company

Shortly after founding, the business became a family firm. Around 1907 the company's name took the form L & A Orlik; this change is explained by the joining of Louis's brother Alfred to the firm. In the first quarter of the century, a second base was established in Birmingham; this base's existence can be traced not only through records in industrial archives such as Grace's Guide but also through the stamps on silver rings. Archive records give the London address as 17-18 Old Bond Street. Looking at the catalogs, the company made not only briar pipes but also tobacco pouches, cigarette holders, cases, and lighters.

The brand's most enduring visual mark is the bewigged judge portrait used in its promotions. The accompanying slogan carries the same joke further, implying that those who choose the pipe are sensible, knowledgeable people.

The company was purchased by the Cadogan group, which brought London pipe firms together under one roof; most records give the year 1980 for this takeover, while some industrial archives note only the 1980s in general. In the same period, production moved along with other group brands such as Comoy's to the new factory established at Southend-on-Sea. From then on the brand name continued not as an independent workshop but as a branch of group production.
Stamps and Series

When dating an Orlik, the first place to look is the mouthpiece: on early pipes a round brass "O" inlay is set into it. On the shank stamp, the name is struck in capital letters, ORLIK, on a straight line; the origin mark likewise sits in the same arrangement, MADE IN ENGLAND. Examples stamped in serif letters are also known, though the years to which this variant belongs have not been determined. After the group's acquisition, this arrangement was dropped in favor of the group's shared Cadogan-brand stamp: MADE IN LONDON in a circle, with ENGLAND below on a straight line.

Early-period qualities were distinguished by letter codes. Pipes without a letter belonged to the Virgin series; the code A corresponded to Old Bond Street, T to Supreme, C to Corona, R to Old Root, L to De Luxe, and P to Prince Regent. An X appended at the end indicated the sandblasted version of the same series. Pipes coded M were meerschaum-lined; the code W belonged to the double-bore Double Bore model. Some lines, such as Clubman and Black Prince, carry number codes rather than letters.
The Name's Continuation in Denmark

From the mid-twentieth century onward, the Orlik name also began to be used on the tobacco side, and this branch moved to Denmark. The Orlik Tobacco Company, which today produces in Assens, is part of the Scandinavian Tobacco Group; the brand's best-known product is Golden Sliced, a Virginia-based flake. The judge portrait continues to appear on these tins as well.

r.x: Il Ciocco

is a one-man Italian pipe workshop that has been producing since 2011 in the city of Pescara, in the Abruzzo region. The workshop's owner is Antimo Parolise, born in 1963 and known in the community as "Mimmo." The brand name means a log or block of wood in Italian, pointing to a way of working centered on the raw material.
Materials

The main material for the bodies is Italian briar plateau. Alongside it, strawberry tree (corbezzolo), olive wood, and morta are used; Parolise is also open to trying other wood species. Mouthpieces are made from methacrylate or vulcanite, depending on what the piece calls for. The properties of these two materials are compared in the mouthpiece materials entry.
Shape and Finishing

The area the workshop emphasizes is freehand work. According to Parolise, briar's grain pattern already suggests a direction; the maker's job is simply to read that direction. Classic molds are not left out of production either, but they are most often taken up in reinterpreted form.

The finishing method that stands out is contrast staining: bringing dark and light tones together to make the flame grain more distinct. This approach, which emphasizes grain quality, goes hand in hand with carrying every stage, from selecting the body to polishing, through a single pair of hands.
Star Grading
Il Ciocco pipes are classified according to grain quality in a five-tier star system:

rows: Dense flame grain or pronounced bird's-eye

r.x: This scale is the maker's own definition; it has no shared equivalent across the industry. Similar star or letter systems are valid within many workshops individually and are not suited to direct comparison between brands.
The Workshop's Background

Parolise's first encounter with the pipe was as a smoker; he moved into making later. His woodworking goes back further: he worked on repairing antique furniture dating to the late nineteenth century, and it was there that he gained his manual skill. He learned pipe making not at a master's bench but from books and online sources, working out the stages of drilling, sanding, coloring, and polishing through his own trial and error. Records show his first pipe was completed on 6 January 2011.

One habit of the workshop is not to discard bodies that come out flawed; these pieces are kept and turned into small objects such as pipe stands or mallets. This measured use of raw material places Il Ciocco among the small Italian workshops defined not by production volume but by the labor spent per piece.

r.x: Directory of Pipe Brands of Uncertain Country

gathers together brands whose country of manufacture is not explicitly stated in the records, or cannot be reliably determined from available documents. The list points not to a single production tradition but to widely varying origins: sub-brands of large factories whose names have been forgotten, private series that tobacconist shops had stamped with their own name, one-person workshops that made only a few hundred pipes, and mysterious signatures known only from a single stamp. Since the records for most of these ninety-three entries run no longer than a few sentences, the brands have not been given dedicated entries but are presented briefly and factually within the directory; names for which no information exists are also kept in the list for completeness of scope.
Brands
AA Pipes

— A workshop that shapes its bowls from briar plateau or from pre-cut blocks. Two approaches are followed on the stem side: some pipes have hand-worked German ebonite or acrylic rod, while others use ready-cut stems.
Alberti Pipes
— The brand of a maker working in St. Louis, Missouri. He sold his pipes at the St. Louis pipe show; the absence of a maker's stamp on his products makes identification difficult.
Andreas Heinzer

— Andreas Heinzer began a toolmaking apprenticeship at Victorinox in Ibach in 1977, and after changing careers in 1997, turned to pipe making out of a longing for handwork. To revive the discontinued Yps pipes, he set up a family-scale workshop with his brother Paul and his sister-in-law Silvia, a jeweler. Alongside Yps, he makes traditional Swiss models from rosewood, mountain ash, boxwood, and horn; most of these pipes are metal-clad. See also Innerschwyzer Pfeifen.
B.B. Best Briar
— One of the sub-brands of the Comoy's house. Despite the similar name, it has no connection to BBB, known for the abbreviation "Britain's Best Briar"; the two brands are frequently confused.
BAMBOO * BRIAR
— A brand produced in Spain that uses bamboo-plant carvings on its pipes. Products are made of briar and offered in various shapes; documented examples include shape number 611.
Ben Rodgers

— Ben Rodgers (1904-1991) ran a small pipe and tobacco shop right next to Times Square in Manhattan, at 1083 Avenue of the Americas. The shop stayed open from 1930 to 1960, selling a wide selection of pipes at every price point along with its own brands. That he sold by mail order nationwide is among the information his son Howard Rodgers relayed to a news group in 2012.
Birkdale
— Long assumed to be a Wolsdorff brand, Birkdale may actually be a Comoy's brand, as argued by pipe-restoration writer Steve Laug. Known examples include London-made Canadian shapes.
Bolas De Fuego
— No record exists beyond a short announcement written by the maker himself; no factual information about the brand has been documented.
Bonato

— The brand of a craftsman named Sergio, who works daily at his workshop in Asti, Italy. He produces pipes individually hand-shaped using only high-quality material, and states that he follows a style loyal to tradition yet open to innovation.
Bonnie Brier

— A registered trademark of Finsbury Products, Inc., based in Elmsford, New York. The registration was filed in November 1976 and expired in August 1997. The pipes carry a script "Bonnie Briar" stamp, with the model name and the phrase "Imported Briar" beneath it; there are several model lines with distinct maker marks: Matterhorn (a crown), Standard, Highlands (a script "H"), Interlude (a stylized "JB" within an oval), and Willow Ridge (a script "W R").
Briars by Barnes
— A brand stamped as made in England. Box information carries the name S. R. Barnes & Coy, based in Saint Neots near Huntingdon, along with the phrase "Super Selected Grain."
Bushee

— George Bushee is the last pipe maker of the Ehrlich's house. In the 1970s and early 1980s, he found and completed a series of bowls turned and forgotten by Boston's Ehrlich's roughly between 1903 and 1913. He finished these bowls faithfully to the features of the period, fitting them with appropriate stems and bands; because the bodies were made by someone else, he did not stamp his own "GB" initials on them.
Cafe Artin

— A Farsi-language pipe and tobacco reference source and retailer founded in Tehran, Iran, in 2005. It has three branches; besides designing new pipe shapes, it produces balsa filters, pipe cleaning fluid, tobacco refreshers, and tampers. Pinocchio is Cafe Artin's registered sub-brand.
Caiden

— A brand reported to have been offered exclusively to Sears catalogs and stores. Quality lines were offered in order as Standard, Golden-Grain, Glow-Grain, and Vertagrain, all made in London and stamped accordingly.
Carey
— For detailed information, see the Carey Magic Inch entry; this name is the United States counterpart of the same brand.
Carey Magic Inch

— Takes its name from the "Magic Inch" air chamber placed between the briar bowl and the ventilated stem. In this chamber, cool air entering from outside mixes with the hot smoke coming from the bowl; the separated tar, oil, and moisture are caught by an absorbent liner called Papyrate at the bottom of the chamber. The pipes are recognized by a framed "C" on the stem, a triple row of ventilation slots, and the brand stamp on the side of the bowl.
Carl Weis Meerschaum Pipes

— An organization that produced meerschaum pipes and smoking implements in the late nineteenth century. Its retail store was at 399 Broadway in New York, with factories at 69 Walker Street, also in New York, and in Vienna. An advertisement in an 1880 official publication states it won first prize at the 1873 Vienna exposition.
Carmette Pipes
— The brand of pipes made by Adam Sheehan in Winona, Minnesota. Sheehan produces about forty pipes a year, most of them commissions. He also attends the Chicago pipe show.
Champion
— A brand known to be of Swiss and French origin, also carrying an "Algerian Briar" stamp. Documented examples show three white dots arranged horizontally, or a "-C-" stamp.
Cole Pipes
— A pipe business registered at an address in the town of Thayne, Wyoming. No documentation exists regarding its manner of production or history.
Consolidated Pipe Factory

— This name actually corresponds to the Colossus Pipe Factory organization. The information comes from Bill Feuerbach, an executive at S. M. Frank & Co., which absorbed Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy decades ago.
Correll

— The brand of pipes Tom Correll produced in Peru, Indiana, between 2014 and 2024. The pipes carry a hand-carved "T C" mark; documented shapes include freehand, nosewarmer, cherrywood, and pot billiard.
Cragmoor

— Long considered the second-quality brand of the Barling house, its rugby-ball-shaped "MADE IN ENGLAND" stamp actually points to Sasieni manufacture. The box lid of a seven-day Cragmoor set names a tobacconist called Au Sultan at 9 bis Boulevard Poissonnière in Paris, suggesting the brand may have been a shop name commissioned from various manufacturers for that store. One example examined has been identified as matching a GBD shape.
Curtis Draper

— W. Curtis Draper Tobacconist was founded in 1887 by William Curtis Draper. It is considered the oldest full-service tobacconist in the District of Columbia and the third oldest in the United States. It offers cigars, pipes, pipe tobacco, and smoking accessories.
Delacour Brothers
— Records contain nothing beyond the brand name; the place, period, and maker are unknown.
Di Franco

— Charles Di Franco opened his own pipe and tobacco shop in the 1960s at 797 Route 33 in Trenton, New Jersey. He was recognized as a skilled pipe maker; very few pipes made by his own hand exist. The shop carried on under his name after his death.
Double Thumb

— The brand of a pipe shop that operated for many years on Central Avenue in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Records indicate the shop owner appeared for a time in the Keystone Kops cast of silent film comedies. In the late 1970s the business moved into one of the bank buildings in Little Rock.
DUMONT
— One of the early sub-brands of the Comoy's house. Known examples carry a "MADE IN ENGLAND" origin stamp dated roughly between the 1920s and 1940s.
Dunhill Carved Heads

— This heading is not a brand but a catalog record signed by John C. Loring, bringing together carved human-head pipes made by the Dunhill house. The list arranges examples compiled from the Dunhill archive and several private collections by date and surface finish. Documented pieces span from 1928 to 1978; most are finished as Bruyère or Root Briar.
Eldritch Pipes
— The pipe brand Chris Kelly founded under his own name. The humorous tone the maker adopts when presenting the brand has been noted; no information exists on production scale.
Elenpipe

— The pipe brand of the company of the same name. Its first fifteen shapes were introduced in August 2009, with briar used for the bowls. By the company's own account, it has been the authorized supplier of pipes and stems made in Polish factories since 2001; the catalog includes more than one hundred twenty items.
Eppers Pipes
— The brand of Sean Eppers, a pastor living in Austin, Texas. He describes pipe making as the process of bringing an orderly, beautiful object out of a raw material.
Esterd

— An early sub-brand of the Tsuge house in Japan; thought to date to before 1970. In one documented example, the hand-carved billiard bowl and silver band come from Tsuge, while the ivory stem comes from the Hakusui Ivory Company, known for netsuke and jewelry. The estimated date given for this pipe is the 1960s.
Finn Skytte

— A maker little known outside Denmark. As the story goes, Viggo Nielsen stored part of his equipment in Finn's father's building, and in exchange offered to teach Finn to use the equipment and to make pipes. The information rests on William Krogh Lundsgaard.
Ford

— Between 1930 and 1960, Ford Motor Company had many respected pipe makers produce promotional pipes for the company. Among those who made these pipes, distributed at auto shows and similar events, are BBB, Kriswill, Georg Jensen, and Comoy's.
Germaine
— No factual information about the brand appears in the record; only an off-topic reader's note is present.
Giardina

— The brand of Joe Giardina, who worked in Edwardsville, Illinois. His emblem consists of a pipe-shaped curved "J" with a "G" in the middle and a dot on either side. He made very few pipes and was known primarily for pipe repair and repair materials. The sale of his business laid the foundation for the Pipe Makers Emporium in Arizona; between 1980 and 2000 he was the sole importer of many Italian brands, with Colorific as his best-selling product.
Goff
— Larry Goff works in the town of Buchanan, Tennessee. Aside from the maker's name and address, the record contains no information on his production or style.
Golden Sunset
— A French brand made from Algerian briar. Examples seen carry a twelve-karat gold-plated band and a large sunset emblem beside the stem; the stem connection is threaded.
Gordon Bilchik Pipes

— Founded by Mark Greene in 2002. Idaho-born Greene continues to hand-work his pipes at his workshop in Boise. His distinctive emblem, stamped into the wood near the stem, is the brand's identifying mark.
Grande Morez
— According to Pipephil records, a sub-line of the ROPP brand. Besides the house's well-known cherrywood pipes, it also produced other models; the documented example is French-made.
Gregorio Briarfection

— The brand of Joseph M. Gregorio (died 1985), who worked in the Bronx, New York. His pipes are noted for their designs and dry, cool smoke; Rob Denholtz of Fine Olde Briars in Poughkeepsie is reported to have said he used very good wood.
Herrera

— The brand of Leonardo Herrera, who works in the San Miguel district of Santiago, Chile's capital. The maker highlights, among his own work, a pipe he made inspired by the famous Nautilus shape signed by Bo Nordh.
Irish Briar Pipeworks
— A brand with no details documented beyond its name; kept in the list for completeness of scope.
J. M.

— An early brand about whose maker almost nothing is known. The emblem consists of the letters "J. M." within an oval cartouche. The documented example has a silver "olive" cap on the stem carrying the same letters and the word "STERLING"; no known maker's stamp corresponding to these letters has been identified.
Jameson's

— A sub-brand of the GBD house named after Horry Jameson, one of its leading designers. He made GBD pipes almost entirely from Algerian or Grecian briar. The "Collector" and "Unique" lines, introduced from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, came largely from Jameson's hand; he also carved for Barling for many years and mastered freehand design.
Jim Lilley
— A collector who has worked on Peterson pipes. The source contains nothing beyond a short biography and the titles of pieces he has written.
John B. Hayes
— A tobacconist operating since 1981. It offers pipes, pipe tobacco, and cigars; the record contains no information indicating it manufactures.
John Cotton

— A name that has become legendary in tobacco history. Advertisements place the brand's origin in 1770, in Edinburgh; but since no documents survive from that period, this date is disputed. It is also possible the shop was opened by George Cotton in 1773. John, after whom the brand is named, was George's youngest child, born in 1801; he opened his own shop in 1826, and after his father's death absorbed his business as well, establishing the John Cotton tobacco shop as it is known. The founding date may thus be 1770, 1773, or 1826.
John Dengler
— A maker who worked in St. Charles, Missouri. The record contains nothing beyond his name and location.
John Harvey

— A pipe maker employed by Philip Redman, owner and manager of the John Redman business. Harvey headed production on Whitecross Street until the late 1980s; it is likely this name refers to a brand or line he produced.
Ken Barnes

— English pipe maker Ken Barnes (1955-2021) began the trade at thirteen, during school holidays, at the Charatan factory in London, and at sixteen worked at the house's shop on Jermyn Street. Between 1973 and 1977 he trained in pipe making under Barry Jones and Joan Nicholson, who had worked alongside Reuben Charatan in the 1950s. Two years after Dunhill took over Charatan, in 1978, he founded The Tilshead Pipe Co. with Barry Jones, which made James Upshall pipes; he sold his stake in the company he ran for eleven years in 1989. After a twenty-seven-year gap, he returned to pipe making in 2016.
Kevin Arthur Pipes
— The record consists only of the brand name; there is no documentation of the maker, location, or production scale.
Lamb Pipes
— The brand of Ken Lamb. Lamb primarily produces tools, bench equipment, and pipe cabinets for other pipe makers; he occasionally makes his own pipes as well.
Manno

— The Italian brand of Manno S.r.l., owned by Rosanna Martino. The company was founded in Calabria and later moved to Tuscany. It began as a briar supplier before moving into bowl and semi-finished pipe production; it also produces series-manufactured pipes under its own name. The information is drawn from José Manuel Lopes's book on brands.
Marco Poltronieri
— The brand of Italian maker Marco Poltronieri, who works under the name Pipe MP. The record mentions only a few pipe examples; no information exists on production scale.
Markus Nielsen

— A Danish pipe maker born October 23, 1949. He worked in the past for W.Ø. Larsen and other Danish makers, then began producing independently, both in Denmark and in the Sicily region of Italy. He has a limited output of about a hundred fifty pipes a year; the pipes carry the VOLKAN stamp and are distributed by Alberto Paronelli.
Minoru Nagata

— A Japanese maker born in Hashimoto, Wakayama, who has spent most of his life in Nishinomiya, Hyōgo. He has been making pipes for more than thirty years, and has sold his work to tobacconists for the past decade. He uses only Mimmo briar in his pipes; he builds his designs around old Asian aesthetics based on the shin, gyō, and sō triad.
Mistella

— An Italian brand known in the 1960s for one-piece carved calabash-shaped briar pipes, which also offered a Gem series in traditional shapes. It is reported to have been counted among the best Italian pipes of its era, and to be rarely seen in the United States because it was never imported there; the accuracy of these claims has not been established.
Moorgate

— Cited among Comoy's sub-brands; even so, its right-side stamp reads "LONDON PIPE CO LTD, MADE IN ENGLAND." Its shape numbers are three-digit numbers beginning with nine and do not match Comoy's shape chart; however, the numerals' typeface matches early Comoy's. Documented numbers include 913 for the Prince, 912 for the Belgian shape, and 914 for the billiard. A Mansion House model bearing the same London stamp and considered a Comoy's product is also known.
Mullins & Westley
— A tobacconist at 27A The Piazza, Covent Garden, London. Today it is best known for its snuff tobaccos. It has had pipes bearing its own name made by various European brands.
Norwood

— Floyd Norwood's pipes are offered under the FLN brand through his pipe repair business. Norwood states his main occupation is repair, with pipe making as a pursuit; as a result, the models offered change constantly. FLN pipes are made entirely by hand and are sorted into three grades based on the wood's grain and whether small fills were needed.
Old Chum

— Old Chum tobacco was originally produced by the D. Ritchie Tobacco Company in Montreal. The company was founded in 1884 and was bought around 1889 by a predecessor of Imperial Tobacco. The Imperial Tobacco Company of Canada itself arose in 1908 from the merger of American Tobacco Company's Canadian holdings with the B. Houde Co. of Quebec City.
Orton
— Brian Orton works in Grants Pass, Oregon, and is known for his distinctive freehand shapes.
Ove Lindall
— Carved for Karl Erik in the 1980s before moving to independent work. Even after going independent, he continued to produce a significant share of his work for other brands.
Perry

— The brand of a craftsman who has made and repaired pipes for more than thirty years. The maker states he carved his first pipe from a persimmon tree in 1974; today, alongside briar, he uses mountain laurel, olive ash, kingwood, tulipwood, and hard maple. He learned pipe repair in 1976 under Joe Giardina.
Pipas Cassano

— Founded in Argentina by Italian immigrants. The pipes were initially handmade before machines were brought in. The briar used is sourced from Italy, Greece, France, and North Africa. The Cassano family has managed to keep a pipe factory running for roughly a hundred years in a country far from the main markets.
Pipas Elfo

— The brand of Uruguayan craftsman Helios Guidotti. Guidotti works, in his pipes, with a small type of gourd similar to those used for drinking mate in the southern part of South America, building an arrangement similar to that of calabash pipes. Since each gourd differs slightly from the next, no two pipes are exactly alike.
Pipas Elo

— A brand founded on the observation that no handmade pipes existed in Mexico. Production takes place at a workshop in Juriquilla, part of Querétaro, with each piece coming from a single craftsman's hand. Since briar does not grow in Mexico, the wood is imported; the pipes are finished with carnauba wax.
Pipas Ovejanegra
— The brand of Carlos Toro Urrutia, who lives in Santiago. His pipes are handmade from fine woods such as walnut, hawthorn, chestnut, and hybrid varieties; each piece is a one-off.
Pipe Articles

— This heading is not a brand but a compilation record bringing together writings on pipes by various authors. It includes pieces devoted to topics such as briar quality, grain, drying, and sandblasting.
Pipsan Pipes
— A pipe organization located on Uzunçarşı Street in Mercan, Eminönü, Istanbul. The record contains no details beyond address and contact information.
Planta Tabak-Manufaktur

— A family business that has worked with tobacco for four generations. Founder Dr. Manfred Obermann's family ran a tobacco factory in Bünde, Westphalia; Obermann moved to Berlin in 1956 and founded his own company there with his wife Rosemarie and ten employees. The company today employs more than a hundred twenty people and ships its products to forty countries; production takes place only in Germany. Planta was later taken over by Mac Baren.
Presti
— No recorded information exists; only the brand name and a few pipe images are documented.
Rettke

— A pipe produced by J. Rettke in Washington, Missouri, based on a patent dated June 12, 1962. The briar body consists of a lower chamber with a metal condenser and an upper chamber holding a filter; smoke passes from the bowl first into the lower chamber, then the upper chamber, and from there into the stem. Unscrewing the silver-colored wing screw under the stem removes a roughly 6-centimeter corkscrew-like piece. The business was later bought by Missouri Meerschaum and ceased to exist.
Rocky Briar

— A model produced by Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy, carrying the stamp "REG. U.S. PAT No298978." The company's early stamp was KB&B, changing to KBB from the early 1930s onward; both appear within a clover outline. A 1933 dealer catalog describes the model as a standard briar pipe sold for fifty cents, with a hard vulcanite stem hardened by a new heat treatment. It is thought to have come from the same hand as early Kaywoodie pipes of the same period.
Rose

— Fran Rose is a craftsman considered skilled in both woodworking and pipe making; he worked at the Santa Monica, California, branch of Tinder Box. His pipes carry a script "Francis A Rose" stamp and a dark or light oval wood inlay on the stem.
Rowhill
— The brand of pipes generally made from Algerian briar and produced by hand. No information exists about its maker.
Royal Meerschaum Pipe Co.

— An organization owned and operated by the Korn family. The family has brought hand-carved meerschaum pipes directly from Türkiye for more than forty years. According to the organization's own materials, the family is among the pioneering names in bringing meerschaum pipes to the United States; it states that its frequent trips to Türkiye allow it to work directly with carvers, without intermediaries.
Schoppe

— The brand of Colja Schoppe, a trained model maker and machinist. He took up pipe repair under the influence of his father, an avid pipe smoker, first reworking his friends' pipes, then repairing and selling pipes given to him to found the business Coljas-Pipecollection.
SDB Pipes
— No documented detail exists beyond the brand name; its maker has not been identified.
Shimizu
— The record documents only the maker's name, Kanji Shimizu; no other information exists.
Silverking
— Most likely not an independent brand but a line name of an unidentified French factory. Other lines of the same factory include Big Ben Reputation and Gold King.
Slazansky

— Patrick Slazansky is a pipe maker working in Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia. He has made only a hundred twenty pipes to date; while his work is still considered "amateur," it is noted to be steadily maturing.
Some 1979 Dunhill

— This heading is not a brand but a study record written by John C. Loring. According to the piece, Dunhill tried for a decade starting in the mid-1970s to work through its stock of roughly cut, unfinished bowls, an effort that resulted in the unfortunate 1979 "Sale" pipes. These pipes mostly consisted of shapeless Group 6 bowls and stems, were finished as Bruyere, carried only the "DUNHILL / LONDON" and "(6)" stamps, and were sold off at fifty dollars apiece.
SORN

— A brand written about only sparsely; it has been suggested the pipes are second-quality Stanwell or Nørding product. Against this, it has been argued Stanwell can be ruled out based on shape catalog, sub-brand practice, and stamp usage, with the strongest evidence being the origin stamp: the typeface and capital-letter arrangement of the "made in Denmark" stamp used on Georg Jensen pipes is highly distinctive and matches the one on SORN pipes.
Straus
— A tobacconist located in Cincinnati, Ohio. The record contains no information on its founding date or production.
Sunway DE LUXE

— A brand carrying a "Made in Denmark" stamp; the name is also read as Lunway. Nothing is known of its maker; the presence of an "L" at the center of the emblem in the Pipephil example has led to the interpretation that the name may be Lunway.
Surbrug

— Appears primarily as a pipe tobacco brand known by the name Golden Sceptre Smoking Tobacco, with an address at 159 Fulton Street, New York. It also has pipes bearing its own name; the documented example carries a crown-shaped emblem flanked by the letters "V" and "R."
Thorburn Clark Ltd.

— According to available information, a tobacconist shop in Manchester, England. It had pipes stamped with its own name, possibly carved on the premises. The documented example is a large bent billiard with the "STANDARD" stamp struck diagonally on the side; its underside carries the name Ronnie Forster, thought to have been the shop's carver. The shop is believed to have been closed since the 1970s.
Titan

— An English-made, unusual system pipe: the screw is part of the bowl, and the shank has a threaded nut. The stem is stainless steel, and only cleaning the metal part by dipping it in boiling water is recommended. Two examples have been identified with a "TITAN PATS PEND" stamp under the stem, another with "CITY PATS PEND." The stem is offered in three forms — straight, curved, and dental — with an easily interchangeable snap-fit connection. There are six bowl shapes, and their naming is explained by comparison to Falcon models.
Trail Blazer

— A system pipe with several variants. The inner shank consists of a filtering mechanism integrated with the stem; the outer sleeve was produced in different designs. Turning the perforated outer shank changes the flow of the smoke-and-air mixture. Documented examples were offered under the Bing Crosby name; a variant was also released under the name Trailblazer by Pipes by Lee Inc.
TRG Handcrafted Pipes

— The brand of Tim George, who runs a small ranch called "The Rafter G" near Waxahachie, Texas; TRG is both his own initials and an abbreviation of the ranch's name. Bowls are cut and shaped by hand from start to finish; George states he does not use filler putty. For stems he hand-works German ebonite, Cumberland rod, or acrylic. The bore is drilled so a pipe cleaner can pass from stem to bowl in a single stroke.

r.x: Laxey Pipes Ltd.

is an unusually large production venture for its scale, founded on the Isle of Man in the middle of the Irish Sea. Born at a time when pipe manufacture was concentrated in centers such as Saint-Claude, London, and Copenhagen, the factory was set up to bring work to the island economy, and is counted among Britain's few meerschaum workshops.
Founding and the Factory Building

The company began operating in the mid-1960s in a four-story stone building on the quay in Old Laxey. The building had not originally been designed for pipe making: archive records show it was built in 1866 by Richard Rowe, manager of the Laxey mines, as an additional grain store for the town's flour mill. After changing hands several times it passed into island government ownership in the 1960s, and from there was leased to the pipe factory. Production was spread across the building's four floors, with the stages from turning to polishing divided among them. How many people the factory employed at its busiest is not clear from archive records; accounts point to a workforce of a few dozen.

The factory's raw material came from East Africa. Laxey processed block meerschaum mined by the Tanganyika Meerschaum Corporation in the Amboseli basin into bowls; this material, distinct from the classic Eskişehir stone of the Mediterranean basin, supplied a significant share of the world market in the postwar period.
Brands and Stamps

The company used several trade names associated with itself: Manxpipe, Manxman, and Manxland were the principal ones. Names like "White Knight" (unfinished) and "Domino" (black or lined) were not separate brands but color and shape variants of the same line. Mouthpieces mostly bore one of two marks: a symbol combining a circle and an arrow, or the Isle of Man's coat-of-arms motif of three legs within a circle. A significant share of sales came through the factory's own shop in Laxey, sold to visitors coming to the island; the rest was distributed through pipe retailers off the island.

Names tied to the island, such as "Manx Pipes Ltd." or "Man Pipe Co.," are sometimes mistaken for separate manufacturers; in fact there is no record of any pipe factory on the Isle of Man other than Laxey. These names are seen as labels the same workshop's pipes acquired through different sales channels; it is also reported within the pipe community that Man Pipe was distributed through Comoy's of London.
Contract Manufacturing and Closure

Laxey's real significance comes less from its own brands than from the bowls it made for others. From the late 1960s until 2001, the meerschaum bowls of firms such as Peterson, Barling, and Nørding were turned here. The name of the commissioning party generally does not appear on these bowls; most often only a mark indicating the material was block meerschaum was worked in, and the same bowl could appear in different brands' catalogs with different mouthpieces. For this reason the origin of British and Irish meerschaum pipes of the era can often only be guessed at through shape and workmanship.

The depletion of the East African source sealed the business's end: the mines' yield had fallen, and alternative deposits had become inaccessible. The last Laxey meerschaum stones were released to market in May 2001. The company tried to stay afloat by turning largely toward briar pipes in the Danish school line, but the attempt did not take, and the factory closed in the summer of 2002. The building has been preserved; the company's order books, production notes, and promotional materials are kept in the island's archives.

r.x: RC Sands

is the signature American pipe maker Raymond "Chuck" Sands (d. 28 September 2022) used on his pipes. Living in the Columbus area of Ohio, Sands learned the craft from the region's well-known maker Tim West; by the records he began producing under his own name in 1998. He lived in Reynoldsburg and carried on his work at his farm in Pickerington.
Workshop and Method

The workshop was converted from an old dairy building on the land where he kept his horses, and its equipment was out of the ordinary: a significant share of the benches and fixtures came from the maker's own hands.

The core choice that set Sands's method apart was that he did not use a lathe. Nor did he turn to templates or ready molds; he settled on shape on the spot, reading the grain direction of each briar block. He used a large grinding wheel of his own making for rough shaping, leaving the finer details to smaller, softer wheels. The final stage of smooth surfaces, however, went entirely by hand; it is known that he would hand-sand a single pipe for days, sometimes weeks. Nor did he have a fixed recipe for sandblasting; he judged the result by eye and by hand, according to the character of the block.
Material and Approach to Shape

Exotic wood, precious-metal bands, or ornamentation had no place in this signature's vocabulary. Bodies were of Grecian briar, and stems were hand-finished pieces shaped with durability and comfort in the mouth in mind. The bulk of the effort went into mechanical details such as bore alignment, the smoke channel, and the fit of body to stem; over time the maker developed his own particular system of drilling and joining in this area. By his own description, this was an "old-school" way of working.

The result is a thick-walled, large, unpretentious American proportion. Sands described his work as a craft addressed not to a collector's display case but to the everyday smoker. Surviving examples range across a spectrum from classic shapes to freehand; given the grain-reading method, no two pipes are exact copies of one another.
Stamp and Legacy
The pipes carry no date, series code, or size mark; the only mark is the "Lazy S" stamp, an S drawn on its side. This simplicity is consistent with a brand that never moved toward numbered series.

RC Sands is counted among the quiet names of the American handmade pipe scene that gained visibility in the 2000s. No production carrying the signature forward is known following the maker's death in 2022; pipes bearing his name are today seen in limited numbers, mostly circulating secondhand.

r.x: Pre-war Dunhill Bruyere DRs

are pipes carrying the DR stamp that Dunhill applied to straight-grain bodies in the period stretching from the 1910s to the early 1930s. On nearly all of these examples, a small, square-shaped mark appears around the shank writing. What this mark meant remained unclear for a long time; once position data compiled from collections was set alongside the era's catalog grading tiers, the idea arose that the square could be tied to a grading scheme.
The Years When Bruyere Was the Only Option

Alfred Dunhill's tobacco shop opened in 1907 on Duke Street in London's St James's district; the brand is accepted as having begun making its own pipes in 1910. Until the light-colored Root finish was introduced in the early 1930s, Dunhill's only smooth-surfaced finish was Bruyere. For this reason all pre-war DRs are Bruyere-finished; in later generations, the finish that comes to mind with DR will instead be Root. The shank writing reads DUNHILL over DUKE ST SW on the very earliest examples, and DUNHILL over LONDON in later years. For the stamp itself and the selection criteria behind it, see the Dunhill Dead Root entry.

According to the record, the distinction between the two finishes was not just about color. Bruyere bowls were turned, until the 1960s, from hard Calabrian briar, which, though considered well-figured, was not especially suited to straight grain; the Root finish, on the other hand, relied on Corsican briar, more inclined to yield straight grain. The same account states that the source regions changed in the 1960s, with the emphasis shifting to Greek briar. That early smooth-surfaced Dunhills lag behind later ones in grain is mostly explained by this distinction.
How Many Tiers Were in the Catalogs

According to the source, the first trace of a formal grading appears in the 1912 catalog: DR pipes are listed in three tiers. This three-tier arrangement continues until 1923-1924, with the correspondences of the tiers updated a few times in between. Around 1925 a fourth tier is added on top of the existing ones; the large 1928 catalog also shows a four-tier arrangement. These dates and numbers are the only documentary basis making it possible to compare against the positions of the square stamp.
Positions Compiled from Collections

The only bulk data on the stamp's position rests on reports John C. Loring gathered from collectors owning pre-war Bruyere DRs. For sixteen pipes spanning the Duke Street period to 1933, the reported positions break down as follows:

rows: Beside the D at the start of DUNHILL

r.x: The single example without a square dates to 1920. Because the compilation was carried out by a single person and limited to sixteen pipes, these numbers show no more than a tendency.
What Can and Cannot Be Said

Even with a small sample, the mark does not appear to have been applied at random: the square recurs at a few specific points on the shank from the early 1910s to the early 1930s. Positions around LONDON are taken to correspond to lower tiers, those around DUNHILL to higher ones. The idea that the positions form a four-step sequence from lowest to highest remains at the level of a hypothesis, and is not presented as a firm conclusion in the source either. It is reported that the mark continues on Root-finished DRs after the 1930s, but that both the positions and the tiers change. Similar squares seen beside the letter A, or an A enclosed in a circle, on ordinary non-DR Bruyeres have no corresponding tier in the catalogs; these are thought to relate to a production or distribution arrangement. For other secondary marks found on the shank, see the Dunhill's supplementary stamps entry, and for reading the year codes, see Dunhill patent stamps and dating.

r.x: J.L. Thompson

is a one-man pipe workshop operating in the town of Parkville, Maryland, in a suburb just north of Baltimore, in the United States. The name behind the brand is Jason Thompson; he makes his pipes at a small bench set up in his home's basement, and earns his living not from pipe making but from a landscape architecture job at a firm in the area.
Founding the Bench

The workshop was not originally set up for pipes. When Thompson got a small lathe for his bench, his intention was to make wooden ornaments and similar gift items; the pipe is a change of direction that emerged from within that lathe pursuit. His first attempt is dated 2013, carved not from briar but from a piece of osage orange he had on hand. This was followed by a self-taught period spanning years and many pipes; the technical knowledge circulating in the online forums where makers gather, along with critiques of his early work, were the defining factors of this period. For the basic steps of the craft, see the pipe making entry.
The BriarLab Years and Recognition

From 2015 to early 2017, Thompson was a member of the BriarLab team run by Nate King. This connection is considered the brand's turning point both for settling his technique and for introducing the small-scale production he ran alone to the pipe community; the name "J.L. Thompson" becoming a signature also dates to these years. Records indicate that in 2016 one of the maker's pipes was among the winners of the carving competition held at the Kansas City pipe show; sources disagree on whether this placement was one of seven individual winners or part of a joint team of seven pipes. His work also became visible in the estate market during the same period. In estate records the pipes are identified by stamps reading "JL Thompson" and the abbreviation "JLT."
Style and Production

Since it runs alongside a full-time job and a household with three children, production is deliberately kept narrow: roughly twenty to thirty pipes a year. For this reason he rarely takes orders. This scale places the brand within the American workshop tradition that treats every piece individually rather than in series production; the general framework of this tradition is discussed in the American handmade pipe scene entry. The main material is briar, and the weight of the work goes toward bringing out the wood's own texture: making the grain pattern visible is, in the maker's own description, among the top standards. Both smooth-polished and sandblasted surfaces are used; the shapes are trim, restrained interpretations drawing on the classic English-American repertoire.

Thompson is also recorded to have appeared as a guest on the radio program hosted by Brian Levine, where he spoke about his workshop; which episode the interview aired in has not been independently confirmed.
