r.x: Yunas Edge
is a form encountered in international pipe sources, taken to be a garbled spelling of the name of Eskişehir meerschaum carver
Yunus Ege

. That both refer to the same person is understood from the overlap of facts on both sides: in each, there is an Eskişehir-born son of a meerschaum-quarry worker, an apprenticeship beginning in 1965, and a master with the surname Yanık. Since no document directly establishes the match, this should be regarded as an inference drawn from the records.
From the Mine to the Bench

Ege's father was a worker in the meerschaum mines around Eskişehir, and his son's turn toward carving came through the acquaintances this work created. In the region, the distance between the one who brings the stone out of the ground and the one who shapes it on the bench has never been great. The sources agree on the year he entered the craft: 1965. They diverge on his birth year. José Manuel Lopes's compendium of makers gives 1941, while two separate profiles of the maker agree on 1948. As there is no independent record resolving the difference, both dates are noted here without being settled.
Three Years at Yanık's Bench

According to the account, the father, Ege, supplied block stone to the well-known carver of the period, Hüseyin Yanık; his son's acceptance as an apprentice came about through this relationship and the father's insistence. In foreign records the master's name appears in garbled forms such as "Huseyn Yankik." The apprenticeship is said to have covered 1965–1968. What was passed on over these three years was not just carving technique: the whole process was taught, from selecting the block to opening the bowl, from finishing to wax polishing. This is also the measure of mastery in Eskişehir meerschaum carving; only years spent at the bench teach one to sense in which vein the stone will crack.

The chain changed direction a generation later. With Hüseyin Yanık leaving the bench in the late 1980s, Yunus Ege's role in training his son, Sadık Yanık, is noted both in dealer profiles and in the Yanık family's own account. So the master's apprentice, some time later, came to teach the master's son. It is one of the examples showing that in Eskişehir, knowledge is passed on through people rather than institutions.
His Work and Its Circulation

Ege's repertoire leans heavily toward figural bowls rather than classic pipe shapes: the entire bowl turns into a human head or an animal, with historical and literary figures prominent. Lopes's compendium states annual production at around three hundred pipes; this figure has no independent breakdown. Since pieces are shaped individually rather than tied to a serial mold, the production falls within the definition of artisan pipe.

Some of his work has entered circulation through SMS, which carried Turkish meerschaum to the United States; the company lists Ege under a separate maker heading in its own catalogue. Care is needed when attributing work: the surname "Ege" appears with more than one carver, and catalogues also contain pipes signed Erdoğan Ege and H. Ege. Before attributing a piece to Yunus Ege, one must look at the full signature, not just the surname. At what stage the name was garbled in foreign written records remains undocumented.

r.x: Ahmet Buyukcopur

is the name of a small-scale meerschaum pipe workshop operating in Eskişehir, and of the signature carried by the pipes that come out of it. Because the products are announced under the heading "White Pipe" via a promotional website launched in 2000, the brand is mostly known abroad under both names. The spelling of the name varies from source to source: the product label reads "Büyükcopur," while international records drop the Turkish letters and use "Buyukcopur." Since the exact Turkish spelling of the surname cannot be confirmed from the available documents, only the forms found in the sources are used here.
Workshop and Team

Records indicate the workshop employs two master carvers and an assistant, with a fixed division of labor between the masters: one handles smooth-surfaced pipes, the other takes on the carved work. The workshop's own promotional material describes production along this same split, calling the carved group "artwork" and making it up largely of figural head carvings. Some of the model pages name Adnan Biçer as the master carver; the rest of the team goes unnamed. Production runs on order rather than on stock, and each piece is carved individually. This arrangement is typical of workshops operating at artisan scale. Pipes leaving the workshop come with a product tag reading "Hand Made – Büyükcopur – In Turkey"; this is the main mark the community relies on to identify the brand.
Material and Flaw Correction

The workshop states that it works only with block meerschaum, not the material produced by pressing meerschaum dust with a binder. Natural stains, spots, and sand grains that appear during carving or after polishing block stone are, according to the workshop's own description, taken as evidence of the stone's authenticity. Two different approaches are used to address these: on carved pipes, the flaw is removed during the already-deep cutting process; on smooth-surfaced pipes, the stummel is reworked. This second process can result in a classically shaped piece being turned into a lattice pattern. This removes the stain and gives the pipe a new shape. The workshop illustrates this practice with its models numbered 540, 550, and 900, adding that not every classic model is reworked this way — the decision depends on the structure of the stone.
Model Lines

Alongside classic shapes, the catalogue includes a few special solutions. In the line called "Reverse," a second chamber is opened inside the shank; because of this chamber the stummel sits short and stout, and the mouthpiece is made of black acrylic. Another special line carries a 9 mm filter; here the filter housing is drilled not in the shank as usual but inside the mouthpiece, and the two pieces join with a push-and-pull connection. Wood-bodied calabash models, examples with a silver band fitted where the shank meets the mouthpiece, and custom carvings such as portraits and club crests are also made.
State of the Sources

The information base on the brand is thin. The Pipedia entry consists of a few sentences and has not been updated since 2015; part of the detail comes from a German pipe site's brand listing. The only independently verifiable date is that the promotional website's domain was registered on August 30, 2000; the site's copyright line also spans 2000-2019. The model pages remain accessible, but parts of the site are filled with clusters of unrelated links, suggesting the domain has not been maintained for years. No reliable record exists of the workshop's founding year or whether production continues today. The brand is nonetheless counted among the examples that have managed to reach beyond the small-workshop layer of Eskişehir meerschaum carving; its name first appearing in foreign sources coincides with this promotional site's launch in the early 2000s.

r.x: Mincer

is the bench known by the name of American pipe maker Tracy Mincer. Mincer's real fame comes from the Custom-Bilt brand he founded in 1934; with their thick walls and deeply carved surfaces, these pipes presented a look diametrically opposed to the slim, polished English style of the period. According to records, the workshop operated in Indianapolis from 1938 to 1946, with Chicago cited for the period before that.
The Custom-Bilt Years

The brand's name changed in 1946, following Mincer's partnership with Eugene J. Rich, Inc., from the hyphenated spelling to a single word, Custombilt. The expansion of the distribution network and the brand's advertising line — "as personal as a thumbprint," long remembered — date to the same years. Among collectors, the hyphenated mark is taken to indicate the Mincer period, while the unhyphenated spelling points to later years; alongside this, the heavy body and coarse rustic texture are also considered marks distinguishing examples from Mincer's own hand.

In the early 1950s Mincer's financial troubles worsened, and he was unable to sustain Custombilt production, eventually losing his rights to the brand name as well. The brand's subsequent path is a separate matter and is covered in the Custom-Bilt article.
Doodler

After losing the name, Mincer released a new model in 1952: the Doodler. In this pipe, a series of holes runs down the side of the bowl and a channel runs around the rim; the aim is to keep the bowl cool by allowing air circulation from the wall. For the hole series to sit properly the bowl had to stay cylindrical, so the Doodler was made predominantly in three sizes of billiard shape. In the early 1950s, the turning of the bowls for Mincer was undertaken by the National Briar Pipe Co. Sources diverge on when the model passed to this firm: one account puts the transfer around 1960, while another documentation holds that Mincer continued production until the mid-1960s.
Later Owners of the Name

Tracy Mincer died in 1964. The company was later bought by Claude Stuart, who continued production under the Tracy Mincer mark. Most of the pipes from the Stuart period consist of carved or textured bowls; smooth-grain examples are also seen here and there. This period achieved a measure of commercial success, but following Stuart's illness the Tracy Mincer Pipe Company closed in 1990. The name later changed hands again, passing according to records to Jim Tedesco's ownership.

The mark Mincer left behind is considered to be less a single model than an approach: a large-bodied bowl felt by the hand as substantial, one that foregrounds the surface of the briar as it is rather than hiding it under a polish. Custom-Bilt bowls are counted among the early examples of this line whenever American-made rustic-surfaced pipes are discussed.

r.x: R. Ubben Pipes

is a small American pipe bench run by Randolph J. Ubben in the town of New Milford, Connecticut. What sets the bench apart from its peers is that the pipes it produces are shaped not to contemporary taste but to a specific historical moment: 1860s America. In this respect the workshop speaks less to the pipe community than to the living-history reenactment circle.
The Standard: Period Accuracy

A single question governs all of the bench's production decisions: does this detail have a counterpart in the 1860s? A shape is put into production only once it can be traced in period records; the sources cited are photographic archives, reference books, and examinations carried out in museum and private collections.

The same standard applies even to the least conspicuous part. Because the airway shape of ready-made stems does not match the period, none are used; the stem is either hand-carved from rod stock or turned from wood or horn. Such distinctions at the level of stem materials are considered details that determine whether a pipe is accepted within reenactment circles.
Workshop and Materials

The list of materials used follows the same logic: Grecian plateau briar, vulcanite, various woods, and horn and bone — that is, the materials found on a mid-19th-century pipe bench. Every pipe is finished by hand, piece by piece; tools of the kind available to a maker of the period are preferred for finishing. Completing a pipe can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks, depending on the complexity of the shape and the carving.

Ubben's own route into this work also explains the bench's character. By his own account he has taken part in reenactments as a living historian since 1974, and has researched period pipe and tobacco gear within that interest. He came to pipe making as a pursuit in itself, gradually drawn both to the technical side of building a smokable pipe and to the formal freedom that carving offers. Where the two strands meet, production has become an object whose "accuracy" is debated much as period clothing or equipment would be.
Scope and Position

The promotional text mentions an intention to eventually add Central European shapes that would round out German immigrant reenactments; whether this intention was realized is not known. Considered alongside the period's widespread clay pipe tradition, the bench can be said to represent the briar-and-wood wing of the mid-19th-century pipe world. Within reenactment circles, Ubben is counted among the few names producing Civil War-era pipes with period materials and techniques. In this respect the bench occupies a documentary lane apart from the mainstream of the American handmade pipe scene, which leans toward the art object. Whether the bench continues production today is unclear; the website where its products were promoted cannot be reached, and reenactment forums have periodically raised the question of whether it is still active.

r.x: Bertram Safferling

is a German designer and pipe maker who has devoted his entire career to hand-shaping single briar blocks. His name is known in the German pipe community as one of the most consistent advocates of "freehand": pipes that are not bound to a serial mold but take shape according to each block's own grain pattern. His bench worked first in Stuttgart, then, after 2005, in northern Italy.
The Stuttgart Years

The maker's bench was set up in Stuttgart following his studies at an applied arts college. From the start the workshop was not a space devoted solely to pipes: records note it was a shared production space used by an industrial designer along with craftsmen who made puppets and mechanical street organs. This multi-craft arrangement was decisive in Safferling positioning his own work as a craft. The Stuttgart period lasted more than twenty-five years; the maker's style, as well as his habit of teaching in the workshop, took root during these years.
The Move to South Tyrol

In December 2005, Safferling opened a second workshop in northern Italy, in the village of Termeno (German name Tramin) on the South Tyrolean Wine Road. Production started there the following year. The pipe-making seminars he had long held in Stuttgart also moved to the new workshop from this date on. Thus a German-rooted bench continued working in a region where the Italian pipe tradition runs strong; this is why Safferling pipes are sometimes listed on the secondhand market under a German heading and sometimes an Italian one.
The Freehand Approach

Safferling uses the word "freehand" not as a loose style label but as a narrow definition with two criteria. One criterion is the hand's share: the plateau briar block is worked predominantly by hand, without being fixed into a machine mold. The other is the wood's share: the grain pattern and flaws in the block determine not only how the shape turns out but also the angle of the drilling axis, the pipe's size, and its proportions. In other words, the shape does not come from the maker alone but from the negotiation between maker and wood.

This stance is a philosophy of pipe making that reverses the usual relationship between block and mold, and is kin to the freehand tradition that spread across Northern Europe. Safferling pipes are reported to carry large, dynamic forms noted for their proportions, with mouthpieces hand-cut from rod material. In surface treatments, the emphasis falls on smooth finishes; here too the choice is left to the condition of the block.
Recognition

The Safferling name is counted among Europe's recognized artisan signatures, and his workshop is one of the regularly visited addresses within the German pipe community. That Safferling has not confined his work to production alone is a separate factor in his recognition: the pipe-making seminars held at his workshop carry on the tradition of passing knowledge on at the bench, positioning Safferling as a teacher beyond his own pipes.

r.x: Whidbey Islander Pipes

is the name of a small-scale pipemaking operation run out of the town of Langley, on Whidbey Island in Washington State in the northwestern United States. Because the pipes were sold one at a time from the back counter of a shop, they never entered a wide distribution network; the brand is known mainly through the limited number of examples that have reached collectors.
The Shop and Its Founder

At the center of the operation was a tobacco and pipe shop that opened in Langley in 1972 and is recorded as the "Virginia Tobacco and Pipe Shoppe." Travers LaRue carved the pipes himself on the premises and sold them from the same location. The shop's operation ended in 1983. The maker's year of death is inconsistent across sources: pipe literature gives 1983, while accounts based on a local newspaper record point to 1982.

Total production thus spans a little over a decade. This brevity explains why the brand is seen so rarely; the number of examples in circulation is nowhere near comparable to the factory brands of the same period. Today the brand is known more by the name of the series it produced than by the maker's own name.
Pipes and Stamps
LaRue worked both classic shapes and freehand bodies not tied to any mold. His own single pieces are said to have been marked with a silver dot set into the shank and his signature.

The maker taught the craft to his son-in-law, Charles "Chuck" Whitmore, who in time came to carve pipes on his own. The shop's hand-cut series, known as "Whidbey Islander," is largely Whitmore's work, and customers could have their name carved into the shank on request. Examples that have come up for restoration are said to carry the hand-engraved words "Whidbey / Hand Cut" on the shank, alongside the maker's initials and the year of production. Among the known pieces, freehand bodies with the plateau surface preserved stand out.

Sources mention that the briar used came from blocks said to originate in Sardinia, Greece, and Italy, described as being very old. Such age claims are a familiar promotional convention in pipe history and cannot be independently verified; the subject is also addressed in the hundred-year briar entry. The main quality that stands out in these examples is that the grain pattern was chosen to read in harmony with the shape of the body.
Tobacco Blends and What It Left Behind

The shop was known not only for its pipes but for the blends it prepared behind the counter. The best known of these mixes, which combined domestic and imported leaf, carries the name "Brown Crock"; the recipe is said to have stayed in the family.

Because of its short life and narrow distribution, the brand never entered the main narrative of American pipe history. It is nonetheless counted among the examples of the small-scale handmade workshop tradition seen in Washington State in the 1970s; today its name comes up mostly in restoration and collecting circles.

r.x: Semus

is a brand name classified under Türkiye in pipe reference sources, though the documents behind it trace not to a workshop but to an import business operating in Bremen, Germany. The available records consistently link the name to the same outfit, SEMUS-SHOP, which deals in the import and export of Turkish handicrafts; German trade directories list Mustafa Nuroglu as the business's owner. There is no publicly available document indicating which bench actually made the pipes carrying this label.
What the Records Show

The Semus entry in pipe archives amounts to little more than a short catalog record compiled in the late 2000s: the brand name, the Bremen business, and the other brands offered under the same roof. According to that record, alongside the Semus name, Pipsan pipes and their briar line Dapper were also brought to Europe through the same business. In the same record, the brand name appears together with the German word
Holzpfeife

, meaning wooden pipe; this points to Semus-labeled products being wood-bodied rather than meerschaum. Since no other supporting material exists, the material information cannot be considered settled: the wood species, chamber dimensions, model names, and stamp form appear in no source.

Both the business's own presentation and independent trade directories describe SEMUS-SHOP not as a manufacturer but as an import-export company. In that description, pipes appear not as a specialty in their own right but as one small branch of a wide product range running from ceramics to copperware and handmade musical instruments.
A Label, Not a Maker

The archive's classification places the brand on the "pipe makers by nationality" list; the documents do not fully support that. What exists is not a workshop with documented production but a distributor marketing a Turkish-origin product under its own name. This is not an unusual situation in Turkish pipe making. In both Eskişehir's meerschaum workshops and wooden-pipe workshops, a significant share of production reaches the shelf under a name set by the foreign importer, with the maker's own name often never appearing on the box at all. Because of this, where such a label falls on the line between single-maker signed work and factory production also remains unclear.
What Remains Unknown

According to the records, the business is still active today; but its current offering focuses on oriental game sets, musical instruments, and handmade household goods, with pipes no longer a prominent line. When the Semus name began being used, how many models were released, and whether the label is still in use cannot be confirmed by independent sources.

The practical takeaway for a collector is this: the Semus name should be read as a distribution label rather than a maker's signature. An example separated from its box cannot be reliably dated on the strength of this name alone; in assessment, the workmanship of the bowl, the fit of the mouthpiece, and the cut of the chamber are considered more reliable guides than the stamp.

r.x: Del Grano

is a small-scale brand founded in the northern Italian city of Parma that treats pipes and smoking accessories together with jewelry-making craftsmanship. Behind the brand stands Alberto Del Grano, trained as an engineer. The firm is not a mass-production pipe factory; alongside numbered, limited-quantity pipes it also makes cigar cases, shellac-varnished tobacco boxes, humidors, ashtrays and cigar-gauge tools. No independent record of the founding year has been found; the brand name becomes visible in publications from the early 2000s onward.
Working Method

Del Grano's work is not the product of a single bench. The craft each piece requires is farmed out to separate specialists, whom the founder gathers around his own design. As a result, techniques kept alive today in only a handful of workshops — shellac polishing, marble carving, precious-metal casting — sit side by side in the same catalogue; carved marble and metal casting are combined together in the ashtrays.

The briar blocks used in the pipes are selected from Tuscany. Finished bodies carry yellow or white gold bands, and on some models diamonds set in a gold mount; a model with a black-lacquered body inlaid with white gold and diamonds is a frequently cited example of this approach. The same material scheme extends to accessories beyond pipes as well: cigar cases, ranging from single-cigar tubes to box-shaped holders, are also made of briar and encircled with a gold band.
The Verdi Pipe

The brand's most cited work is the pipe prepared in memory of the composer Giuseppe Verdi. Verdi died on January 27, 1901; his birthplace, the village of Roncole, also lies within the boundaries of Busseto, in the province of Parma. Both date and geography thus form a direct link for a Parma workshop. Introduced in 2001, the hundredth anniversary of his death, the pipe was announced as a numbered series of 999. The composer's portrait was worked in relief, yellow gold applied over white gold; the pipe was presented with a wooden case fastened with leather straps. How many pieces of the series were actually completed cannot be traced through independent records.
Position and Fate

The known centers of gravity in Italian pipemaking cluster around the Pesaro and Como schools; Parma is not counted among these centers. Del Grano, too, is considered a separate branch closer to jewelry and luxury-goods craftsmanship than to these main currents. The criterion emphasized in the firm's own promotional text is not the classic pipe grading based on grain pattern, but ornamentation and finishing craftsmanship.

The same texts also give a family tree: the Parma painter Giorgio Gandini del Grano, who died in 1538, and the painter Riccardo Fainardi, who likewise worked around Parma, are cited as evidence of an artistic streak running in the family. That both painters actually lived can be confirmed by independent sources; the claim of kinship, however, rests solely on the firm's own statement. No independent record documenting the brand's regular production beyond the mid-2000s has been found either; the firm's former domain name today redirects to a page unrelated to the brand.

r.x: Don Warren Pipes

is the name of a one-man handmade-pipe bench operating in the city of Albuquerque, New Mexico. Behind it stands not a factory but a single maker working to order. The brand name does not carry the maker's surname; pipe sources sometimes record the bench's owner under the name Donald W. Gillmore as well, though the two names describe the same workshop.
From Woodworking to the Pipe Bench

By the maker's own account, pipe making sits atop a woodworking background spanning years. When he returned to pipe smoking after a hiatus and found that his pipe did not meet expectations, this led him to make his own pipe. It is said that his first attempts were made with the native hardwoods he was accustomed to in carpentry, with briar and bog oak entering the picture later. Encouragement from the region's pipe-enthusiast circle, and pipe gatherings where the work of various makers could be seen together, are considered to have played a role in the pursuit moving beyond a personal experiment. These details rest on the bench's own promotional material and have not been verified in independent records.
Shape Philosophy and Materials

The bench's best-known work consists of freehand bodies following the Danish school line that runs from the mid- to late twentieth century: pieces shaped not to a mold but to the wood's own grain. Alongside these, semi-classic shapes such as bulldog, poker, pot, prince, brandy, and author are also produced.

The material range is not confined to a single wood. Alongside briar, bog oak, darkened after long immersion in a bog, and non-briar hardwoods such as walnut, hickory, maple, oak, and pecan are also used. Surfaces are sometimes left smooth-polished, sometimes carved rustic or sandblasted. Ebonite and acrylic are preferred for mouthpieces. Since the work is carried out at a one-man bench, each piece is shaped individually; even two pipes bearing the same name are not identical in measure and surface.

The bench's most distinctive choice, however, is deer antler. Antler most often appears in the band between the shank and the mouthpiece or in small details added to the body. Combining a natural material with man-made materials such as ebonite and acrylic in the same pipe is counted among the brand's familiar signatures.
Recognition

Don Warren Pipes is a bench known not for series production but for a limited number of mostly one-off pieces; for this reason, its name circulates in the collector community more through secondhand records and pipe gatherings. According to the bench's own promotional material, the maker is a member of the North American Society of Pipe Collectors; this connection has contributed to sustaining the bench's visibility within the American handmade pipe community. When the bench was founded, however, is unclear: no definite year appears in the records, and the available information indicates only that production has continued uninterrupted for some time.

r.x: James Upshall

is a briar (briar) workshop founded in 1978 in the village of Tilshead in England's Wiltshire county, known for its hand-turned, straight-grain pipes. From its founding, it followed a small-scale path built on individual carving rather than molds or mass production, placing it among the late representatives of the English handmade pipe tradition.
From the Charatan School to Wiltshire

All three founders of the workshop came from London's storied pipe house Charatan. The firm's then-general manager Kenneth Barnes, his son Kennedy (Ken) Barnes, and Barry Jones — who had been carving pipes in London since the age of fifteen — left the company after Charatan came under the Dunhill umbrella and settled in Wiltshire. According to the company's own account, the brand's name comes from James Archelaus Upshall, a pipe-loving ancestor of the Barnes family.

Jones is said to have turned a substantial share of the brand's best-known shapes during his years at Charatan. Upshall's shape repertoire draws on that same body of knowledge and largely reinterprets classic English shapes.
How the Workshop Works

Production made no use of a copy-milling lathe or pre-set machinery; shaping was done on a single engine lathe, by hand with a chisel. The natural consequence of this method is that even two pipes bearing the same shape number differ from one another in the details.

The choice of raw material follows the same line. According to the workshop's own promotional material, rather than kiln-dried ebauchon blocks, it used naturally dried, aged plateau briar sourced from Greece; lightness and mature grain texture were cited as the reasoning behind this preference. The brand's most repeated promise was that pipes bearing its name contained no putty or fill.
Grade Letters and Series

The letter stamp on an Upshall shank describes both the quality of the grain and the surface color together. Root-quality pipes, whose grain may be cross, flame, or straight, are divided into three by color tone: mahogany-red S, chestnut A, walnut P. Only the straight-grain top grades are stamped B, G, E, X, and XX in ascending order. Since XX requires unbroken straight grain across the entire bowl and shank, this top grade is achieved in only a very small share of production and is considered the rarest mark.

Pipes outside the letter system are identified by their surface finish; sandblasting, a bark-like crust texture called "bark," and a black finish are the main ones. Because large briar blocks were scarce, the limited number of oversized pieces was grouped into a separate series called Empire. The brand's second line, Tilshead, was reserved for pipes with a minor briar flaw; since the workmanship was done in the same workshop by the same methods, these pipes too draw interest among enthusiasts.
The Brand Today

The difficulty of finding good-quality plateau briar and the time hand-turning demanded kept production small-scale throughout. According to records, Ken Barnes settled in Cornwall in his later years and made a limited number of pipes, passing away in 2021. Today the brand lives more in the secondhand and collector market than in regular production; the grade letters on the stamp, along with shape numbers, remain the main clues for assessing the quality of an Upshall pipe.

r.x: Lars Ivarsson

(c. 1944 – 11 February 2018) was a Danish pipe maker, son of Sixten Ivarsson, and the second-generation representative of the handmade pipe tradition. Within the line known as the Danish school, his name is remembered for tightening the methods he inherited from his father down to the level of measurement and proportion; a number of details that look ordinary today — the shank's cross-section, the turn of the chamber rim, the continuity of the air channel — are in part traced back to him.
Growing Up at the Bench

His birth year is not clearly recorded; being seventy-three at his death, and being shown as fifty-one in 1996, together point to 1944-45. His childhood passed alongside his father's bench in Copenhagen, and he earned his pocket money there doing small tasks. Accounts differ on the age at which this work began: one account gives eight, while another, based on Ivarsson's own words, gives twelve. In 1969 he finished a business degree at the University of Copenhagen, but he did not leave the bench. By the late 1960s three people worked at the workshop: Sixten, Lars, and Jess Chonowitsch, who had joined Sixten around then. This arrangement broke up when Chonowitsch left in 1970 to set up his own workshop.

In later years Lars preferred rural living. In the mid-1990s he bought a coastal house about a hundred kilometers from Copenhagen and set up his workshop next to it; records listing Danish makers give his address as Nykøbing. Annual output in the same period is given as around seventy pipes.
Measure, Proportion, and Shape

His influence shows less in individual pipes than in decisions about measurement. Moving the shank's cross-section from round to teardrop became a widely used solution in later generations. The blowfish shape, known for its bulging, asymmetrical body, is also credited to him; this attribution rests on a single secondhand account saying the idea came to him while watching a fish in an aquarium. The shape's difficulty lies in requiring the direction of the briar's grain and the body's bulging surfaces to be reconciled within the same block.

On the technical side, he focused on the air channel's measurement: he argued that the channel should run at the same cross-section, without narrowing, from the bottom of the bowl to the tip of the mouthpiece. This cross-section is reported to have been kept at 4 millimeters throughout; since the figure comes secondhand, it should not be taken as certain. He cut his mouthpieces by hand from hard rubber (ebonite) he had shipped in from Germany. He rejected the common belief about the age of briar, openly dismissing the hundred-year-old-wood rumor; he said most of the blocks he used had been seasoned for one to five years, and that overly dried wood made working harder. He also did his own sandblasting at the workshop, in an oven he acquired solely for that purpose.
Stamps

On Ivarsson pipes, the stamp reads "an Ivarsson product," arranged in a ring. By Lars's own account, the right to strike this inscription belonged only to his father, himself, and Chonowitsch. To distinguish the maker, Lars's pipes were stamped with an "L," Sixten's with a sun mark. Most pipes also carry the production year and that year's sequence number; the stamp 24/1970 marks the twenty-fourth pipe made in 1970. Beyond these, he struck a separate fish stamp on pipes he judged flawless by his own standards; the number of pipes carrying this stamp is reported to have stayed around thirty-five through the mid-1990s. Chonowitsch used a bird stamp for the same purpose.
Circle, Family, and Influence

The Copenhagen workshop of the 1960s was a gathering place for Scandinavian pipe making; Swedish maker Bo Nordh came here to learn method, and the resulting friendship lasted for years. Jørn Micke, who also passed through the same circle, is better known in Japan. Ivarsson pipes reached American collectors almost not at all after the 1970s; the bulk of production is said to have gone to Japan. The younger of his two daughters, Nanna Ivarsson (b. 5 April 1974), went to Copenhagen at eighteen to work alongside her grandfather Sixten, and after design training returned to her father's bench, becoming the family's third-generation maker.

Lars Ivarsson died on 11 February 2018 at seventy-three, after a long period battling cancer; he left behind his wife Annette and daughters Nanna and Camilla. His name is remembered today as one of the few that set the measurement and surface habits now established in artisan pipe making.

r.x: Gray Mountain Pipes

was a pipe bench Mark Gradberg ran single-handedly in Kankakee, Illinois. The bench never moved into series production; it made only one-of-a-kind freehand shapes and closed with its founder's death in 2018. Though its name never spread much beyond a small circle, the brand is a typical example of the single-maker benches that multiplied in America in the late 1990s: limited in number, unmoldable, and coming off the same hand from start to finish.
A Craft Begun Late

Gradberg was born in 1950 in Harvey, Illinois, and spent most of his working life outside the pipe bench; according to his obituary, he finished his career at the Dow Chemical plant in Channahon. His relationship with wood, however, ran independently of his working life: for years he built miniature wooden structures for HO-scale model railroads. The hand discipline learned from working at millimeter scale was the real foundation he later carried over to briar.

He carved his first pipe for himself in 1995. Requests that followed from the few examples he made for those close to him grew the pursuit; the bench turned into a full-time occupation with his retirement in the late 1990s. This transition's year shifts across sources: Pipedia gives 1999, while some secondhand catalogue listings give 1998.
Origin of the Name

The brand name is derived from a Swedish reading of the founder's surname. According to the account, this reading was brought into the family by Gradberg's grandfather, and the grandson kept the same rendering when he set up his bench. It is not linguistically certain; it has also been suggested that the second element of the surname,
berg
, denotes a settlement name rather than a mountain. What matters for the brand is that the name ties into a hand-craft tradition carried across generations of the Gradberg family.
Style and Legacy

Gray Mountain pipes sit close to the free line American benches inherited from Danish modernism; the obituary itself describes the output as "freehand and Danish-style" pipes. The unworked plateau surface left at the rim, body lines that follow the grain of the briar block, and the uniqueness of every piece are the style's clearest markers. Because blocks with readable flame grain were favored, pipes are most often recorded with a smooth finish in secondhand listings. Body sizes span a wide range; secondhand records show large-volume examples alongside more measured, comfortable-in-hand shapes. It is also the trade's established practice to mention the bench alongside American makers who embraced the same free approach, such as Tim West; the common thread is following the shape the block itself offers rather than a mold.

Gradberg showed his work at national pipe and tobacco shows, and his pieces reached beyond America as well. Even so, the bench never grew beyond one-man scale. This limited total output places the brand's pipes among today's less commonly encountered pieces. No new pipes have been made under the Gray Mountain name since 2018.

r.x: Ranz Freehands

is the brand name American pipe maker Ron Smith uses for his own work. Production is carried out single-handedly at a home workshop near Dandridge in East Tennessee. The name was not derived from the maker's own; Smith says he preferred a word with a pleasant ring, one that leaves his identity a little in the background, over direct options like "Ron's Pipes" or "Smith Freehands." By the records, he made his first pipes in 2015.
A Late Start in the Craft

Smith came to pipe making after finishing his working career. By his own account, the free classes Tennessee offers older state residents drew him to the art courses at Walters State Community College in Morristown; an interest that began with photography gradually shifted to sculpture, and it was there that the affinity between carving stone and carving a pipe took hold. His first attempts were made with purchased briar blocks, ready-made stems, and a handful of simple hand tools; his workshop equipment and technical knowledge expanded slowly in the years that followed.
Visits and Seminars as a Path to Learning

Smith's education did not proceed under a single master but through scattered contacts. A day spent working with Tim West, two rounds of attendance at the Chicago pipe-making seminar, and a separate session with two makers ahead of the Raleigh show are the chief among these. To this are added days of observation spent at noted workshops in America and Germany. This is a typical route for the American handmade pipe scene: knowledge transfer spreading not through a closed master-apprentice chain but through shows, seminars, and mutual workshop visits.
Material and Making Choices

The bodies of Ranz pipes are cut from briar bought wholesale as ebauchon — that is, from blocks cut from the interior of the root rather than its outer plateau surface. Stems are sourced ready-molded and fitted to the pipe; the joint with the body is most often made with a Delrin tenon. Smith speaks openly about these choices, makes no claim to top-tier work, and considers himself a hobbyist still developing his skills. He says the smoking quality of his pipes has been shaped by feedback from colleagues and buyers.
Surface and Shape

When the grain turns out well, the briar is left smooth and polished. On blocks where the grain is weak, sandblasting, rustication, or other surface treatments come into play. Among these, by Smith's account, a "driftwood" finish developed by Roger Wallenstein holds a special place: it leaves a texture reminiscent of sandblasting, though the outcome cannot be predicted in advance, and it lends itself to light colors and stone-like appearances. As the color fades over time, the pattern beneath is said to become even more pronounced. In terms of shape, freehand interpretations outweigh classic proportions; most of his work falls into the freehand family. Alongside traditional black, brown, and tobacco tones, vivid colors are also used.

r.x: Michel

is the name not of a pipe workshop but of a tobacco shop. Maison Michel, run by Michel J. Mitchell in North Carolina, followed a practice common at the time: rather than carving its own pipes, it had ready-made factory production stamped with its own name. For this reason, the Michel mark does not correspond to a single workshop, a single country, or a single approach to craftsmanship.
The Private-Label System

In the mid-twentieth century, large tobacconists commissioned well-known factories to produce batches under their own names in order to expand their product range. Michel-marked pipes are a product of this same system. Surviving examples do not agree with one another in their marks: some show "Made in England," others France, and still others Denmark as their origin. This inconsistency points to the shop having worked with more than one supplier over the years. According to records, most of the pipes date to the 1960s and 1970s. When the shop itself opened, however, remains unknown.

Two separate marks are known: MICHEL and MICHEL DELUXE. On part of the Deluxe line, the Charatan logo appears together with the origin stamp "made in London England"; these examples are accepted as having been prepared for the shop at the English factory. Which workshops the remaining marks belong to has largely not been clarified. As a result, both examples of high briar craftsmanship and ordinary mass-produced pieces can be found under the same name; the difference between two pipes can sometimes be seen even within a single display case.
Stock Left in Storage

After Michel Mitchell died in 1980, his sister sold the shop to a bank, and the unsold inventory, rather than vanishing, waited in storage for nearly forty years. When this stock came onto the market via a bulk auction in the early 2020s, hundreds of never-used Michel pipes spread into the secondhand market within a short span, sparking lengthy debates about the brand's identity. Because they had never been smoked despite the decades that had passed, these pipes are rare examples showing the period's factory craftsmanship and finishing standards in unspoiled condition. The same body shape appearing with different origin marks is also one of the clues supporting the idea that the shop did not stay tied to a single supplier.
Assessment

For the collector, the Michel mark is not the trace of a manufacturer but of a point of sale. Identifying a Michel pipe means looking not at the name but at the shape, the stem structure, the bowl proportions, and the origin mark; only these details give away the actual manufacturer. For this reason, the entry is regarded less as a single brand's history and more as a window onto the mid-twentieth-century private-label system. The same cautious reading applies to Danish-marked examples: the origin mark indicates the country where production took place, not the name of the workshop.

r.x: Sergey Dyomin

is a Russian pipe maker working in Saint Petersburg. He both produces pipes under his own name and is considered the senior maker of the joint workshop PS Studio. His name is associated with his insistence on working briar on the lathe, and with his stocky, voluminous bodies.
Pushing the Lathe's Limits

What sets Dyomin apart in the community is a choice of method. In pipe making, complex bodies are usually shaped freehand or with hand tools; Dyomin, by contrast, is known for seeking ways to produce those same shapes on the lathe. Presentation texts about him cite, as examples of this pursuit, a spherical four-sided body and a diamond-cross-section shank worked on the lathe — since these examples rest on a single maker's page, they should not be taken as a verified production record. The general thrust of the approach is clear, though: lathe shaping is being extended into work usually considered the domain of freehand craftsmanship.

His work reads with the line of his master, drawn from industrial and automotive design. He also has a manner of his own: keeping bodies voluminous while still holding their balance is counted as his signature. Precision of measurement is especially highlighted in the mouthpiece materials and the fit of the joint, a rigor that matches the shared manner of the Saint Petersburg school.
Apprentice Years

Dyomin came to the bench late in life. Records state he spent his youth in the military, serving at the Baikonur Cosmodrome during the Soviet period; this period of service has not been confirmed by an independent source. His birth year is likewise not known for certain; age information about him rests only on maker profiles.

His turning point back into the trade came in 2002. That year, at an event held by the Saint Petersburg Pipe Club, he met Vladimir Grechukhin and became the apprentice the master was looking for at the time. The two worked together for years; the division of labor was clear from the start — design was Grechukhin's domain, and Dyomin acquired his production and bench skills over the course of this period.
PS Studio

The partnership took institutional shape in 2008. Grechukhin, Dyomin, and Aleksandr Tupitsyn — said in records to have been twenty-five at the time — founded the workshop they called "The Project" among themselves, PS Studio. The arrangement was an extension of the apprenticeship years: design belonged to Grechukhin, and craftsmanship was left to the other two makers. Over time the brand became identified with the phrase "Grechukhin's student," and Dyomin became the most senior hand in this structure. His continuing to produce work under his own stamp alongside his workshop duties means that both signatures draw on the same workshop culture.

This structure makes Dyomin's name legible in two separate places: in work bearing the PS Studio stamp, he is a workshop hand, while in work bearing his own stamp, he is the maker who takes on every shape decision himself. In the apprenticeship chain that took institutional form in Russian pipe making during the 2000s, the line running from Grechukhin to Dyomin, and from there to the workshop's younger names, is counted as one of the frequently cited forms of transmission from this period. Since most of what is known about the maker rests on dealer profiles and community compilations, no reliable record exists regarding production volume or line names.

r.x: Trebor

is a British pipe brand that emerged in London at the start of the twentieth century and is today known less for its name than for the patent number it carries. The 6518/12 stamp seen on the shank marks a registration taken out in the name of Baron Cohen, owner of Baron & Co., which advertised itself in Piccadilly as a "cigarette specialist." The application was filed on March 16, 1912, and the registration was published on December 12, 1912. What year the brand itself was founded is not known; the earliest firm date we have is this patent itself.
The Solution the Patent Brought

The subject of the registration is a cooling chamber opened into the shank. The extended end of the stem enters this chamber; instead of a single channel between chamber and bowl, there are two or more parallel holes. One opening at the tip of the stem draws in smoke, while a second opening lets condensed moisture drain into the chamber; the end of the chamber is closed with a screw plug, so that accumulated moisture can be cleaned out. The specification states the same mechanism could also be applied to cigar and cigarette holders. The purpose is twofold: to cool the smoke by lengthening the path it travels, and to keep moisture from reaching the mouth. Other British patents from the same period explored the idea of a multi-channel smoke path as well; the best known of these is the Falk patent. Stamping the patent number onto the pipe was common practice in those years, and it is considered today a clue useful for dating purposes.
Chain of Ownership

Who held the Trebor name is surprisingly unsettled across trade directories. The only detailed account on this subject is a list shared by a collector in a forum post that cannot be confirmed elsewhere; the sequence below should therefore be taken as a sketch drawn from the records, not a certainty. As the account goes, the brand appears under Cohen & Co. in 1921; by the late 1920s, Trebor Ltd and Cyril Arnold Ltd are cited together, and by the 1930s Baron & Co. joins them. After the gap opened by the Second World War, the name pairs with L. Hill & Co. alone at the end of the forties, then with Trebor Products & Agencies in the fifties, dropping out of the listings entirely after 1957.

Some of these companies are noted as directly connected to Baron Cohen, while the rest appear for a few years and then vanish; Cyril Arnold Ltd, for instance, appears in London telephone directories only through the second half of the 1920s. Researchers wanting to trace such short-lived companies turn, alongside trade directories and company registers, to archival projects compiling British industry. A frequently cited reference book on brand-to-manufacturer matching is also reported to link Trebor to Cyril Arnold Ltd and Baron & Co.
Not to Be Confused With

The much better-known Trebor of today, sharing the same name, is a confectionery company founded on January 4, 1907, in Forest Gate, east London; its name comes from reading "Robert" — the surname of one of its founders — backward. There is no known connection between the two Treborys; the resemblance is simply two separate businesses searching for a brand name arriving at the same wordplay.

The pipe-world Trebor today is a name encountered only in secondhand collections. It is said the brand was occasionally presented alongside John Cotton products in American tobacco publications, and that some surviving examples are recorded with silver bands; neither detail has been confirmed by independent sources. The one certainty is that the number on the shank provides a solid basis for dating these pipes to a specific year.

r.x: Prohibition Pipes

(formally Prohibition Co.) is a small-scale pipe workshop run by American wood craftsman Jonathan Lavezzo in the state of Virginia, USA. Work leaving the bench is announced in batches, and the maker reports that a significant share of it remains one-off. The brand is not a continuation of Moonshine Pipe Company, which the same maker had earlier founded and built up, but a separate chapter opened after that business changed hands.
A Background in Wood and the Moonshine Years

Lavezzo came to pipe making after more than twenty years of work in wood and burl. As a student he ran a small business in his home town of Fairfax, Virginia, building fences and cages; he later founded a renovation company focused on restoring old houses and hardwood flooring. Records indicate he turned to pipe making in the early 2010s, after meeting a briar pipe maker.

This interest soon grew into the business known as Moonshine Pipe Company. Accounts describe the brand as founded in Charlottesville, in a hut roughly two and a half by three meters. When demand outgrew the workshop's capacity, Lavezzo moved part of production to BriarWorks in Tennessee, and eventually handed the brand over to that firm entirely. The Moonshine name still continues today as a product line in the BriarWorks catalog. In writing on Virginia pipe making, Lavezzo is counted among the names who influenced the state's newer generation of makers.
Prohibition Co.

The workshop the maker now runs under his own name carries the name Prohibition Co. Both the brand name and the series known as Speakeasy allude to the period of alcohol prohibition in the United States between 1920 and 1933 and the hidden bars of those years; the maker has not separately explained the reasoning behind the name.

Briar is the essential material in production. Featured work includes sandblast-finished apple and dublin bodies and the rhodesian shape; for these names see classic pipe shapes, and for the distinction between smooth and sandblasted surfaces see surface finishes. The workshop sits closer to the artisan pipe world made up of single-person benches than to high-volume American manufacturers.
The Lathe's Other Domain

Alongside pipes, Lavezzo also runs Moonshine Rod Company, a fishing rod business he founded with his brother Nick Lavezzo. That brand's rods use reel seats turned from burl and hand-shaped cork grips. Prohibition Co.'s work is, by the maker's own account, a second line pursued in the time left over from the fishing rod business; the workshop's small scale is also linked to this.

Much of the information about the brand rests on the maker's own account; details such as the founding year are not clearly documented in independent records. The workshop's current level of activity likewise has not been confirmed by an up-to-date, independent source.

r.x: US Pipe Brands Directory

is an attempt to gather the scattered record of American pipe production in one place; this first installment of the three-part directory covers ninety-one entries running from Admiral to Gerrard. Pipe making in America followed two tracks: on one side, factories and house brands concentrated around Brooklyn and New York turning out hundreds of thousands of pipes a year, and on the other, mostly one-person workshops that multiplied rapidly after the 1960s. The entries below are short and factual; brands for which only a name is on record are kept in the list with the gap clearly noted.
Brands
Admiral
— recorded as one of the Anglo-American joint brands; its production is tied to the names E. Deguingand & Son and L&H Stern. No documentation exists on the brand beyond these two names.
Aero Kool

— dated to around 1946, this pipe was designed as a simplified take on the Kirsten and Bryson-type metal-bodied pipe. The bowl is briar, the body aluminum; the spiral pattern on the shank is the same as on the Kool Twist pipe.
Albert-John

— Albert-John Briars, Ltd. was founded in 1976 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, by Evan C. Schwemer. The firm appears to have stopped work in or shortly after 1987, and the remaining Albert-John line appears to consist of pipes in the Danish freehand style fashionable at the time. Because the company carried the name Uhle Tobacco Corporation until August 22, 1977, the line is thought to have been a private line made for Uhle's.
Alexander
— the brand of David D. Alexander. Not to be confused with Alexander Pipes, which carries the same name and forms a separate record.
Allen, George
— a now-deceased pipe maker from Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania. Whether pipes stamped ALLEN and HANDMADE belong to him or to John Allen has not been settled.
Alpine Briars
— the brand of Stephen Johnson, working in the Los Angeles area of California. No documentation exists beyond the maker's name and the region he worked in.
Ambassador

— a brand produced by Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy in the early twentieth century. Since the Italian brand Ambassador by Gasparini carries the same name, the two can be confused; the American Ambassador's record sits under KB&B.
Americana
— referred to as an Anglo-American brand and considered a GBD second line. Records associate it with the names L&H Stern, Pioneer, and Appleby.
Anderson, P. A.
— the brand of Phil A. Anderson. The last pipes appearing on his own site are dated 2006, leading to the assumption that he stopped pipe making.
Andre Mermet

— a French master who emigrated to America. The son of a craftsman, he came to New York at fifteen and set up a pipe manufactory here employing six people. He made pipes for numerous American brands without his name being mentioned, chief among them Barclay Rex, and there is a record that he made all of the Wilke brand's pipes. He also made pipes for the army, later settled in California, and his son carried on the business.
Andrew Staples Pipes
— Andrew Staples's workshop in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho. He works with quality briar, vulcanite, and selected decorative materials, and makes his pipes to order.
Ansell's
— the brand of a pipe and tobacco shop on 14th Street in Washington D.C. It is one of three Washington brands whose city name appears in the stamp; the others are Bertram and A. Garfinkel.
Antony André Pipes
— a workshop registered under the name Antony André in White House, Tennessee. Records give no more than the maker's name and the workshop's location.
Arista

— a pipe line produced by VanRoy, on the market by 1944 at the latest. It continued after the firm was bought by Henry Leonard & Thomas Inc. in 1953 and was made with the Ajustomatic fitting that became widespread on Dr. Grabow pipes.
ASB Pipes

— Aaron Berwick's handmade briar pipes in Taylorsville, North Carolina. The pipes carry a burned-in "ASB" mark and are individually numbered; the maker has stated he does not do this work full-time and that production stays limited.
Asselta
— Asselta Briar Pipe Co. was located in the old train station building in Bellmore, on New York's Long Island. The best-documented item on the firm is a period matchbook cover.
Atilano Pipes
— handmade pipes produced in his free time by Emmanuel "Manny" Atilano. The maker says he works starting from raw material and that his priority is a good smoke.
Balkovec Pipes
— a workshop registered under the name Mark Balkovec in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Nothing beyond the maker's name and city has been documented.
Barnaby Briar
— the brand of Barnaby Briars, a pipe dealer on Powell Street in Brooklyn. Known for briar-stemmed pipes; the same dealer also had a brand called Yorkshire Courtesy.
Beck

— Aaron Beck is one of the first American makers to turn to freehand pipes in the modern sense. Starting in the mid-1950s he worked in the Queens borough of New York, later retired to Florida, and is said to have died in 1984. What set his work apart was layering different woods and other materials in the stem and shank; he is counted among the first to try acrylic inlay on stems. He is suggested as a possible designer of the DC (Double Comfort) stem developed for Charatan.
Benjamin Pipe Co.
— a pipe manufacturer based in Brooklyn. It appears to have been active in the 1930s, with pipes made in New York distributed through Scholler Brothers of Philadelphia.
Big Casino Pipes

— the handmade pipes of Harry Crisman, who lives in Sarver, Pennsylvania, about forty kilometers north of Pittsburgh. Crisman has worked at a steel mill since 1995 and as a blacksmith since 1999; he makes his pipes on weekends and in his spare time.
Birnbaum

— William Birnbaum was a maker of meerschaum and briar pipes in the late 19th century. A meerschaum pipe's box label shows it was sold at his shop on Cortlandt Street in New York. The business, seen at that address in 1881, had moved to Nassau Street by 1890; the exact date of the move is unknown.
Blue Ridge
— Blue Ridge Pipes, based in Asheville, North Carolina. No record exists beyond the brand name and the city.
Bosi Pipes

— the workshop of Italian-born Kirk Bosi in Manhattan, Illinois. He produces a small number of pipes a year, drawing a range from freehand to classics out of blocks shaped according to the grain. His work is noted for conically opening the smoke channel and leaving the bowl walls thick.
Bowl Dry
— a system pipe produced by the Hollman Pipe Company of Toledo, Ohio. Nothing survives beyond a period display device demonstrating how the pipe worked.
BP Jum

— a brand of uncertain origin. Because its design resembles Custom-Bilt pipes, it has been suggested it may be the work of Tracy Mincer, though no direct link has been established. Another possibility is that the name comes from an abbreviation of the Jumbo line of Biltmore Pipes; this too remains at the level of conjecture for now.
Braddock

— the workshop Bill Braddock runs in Oklahoma City under the name "Art That Smokes." He uses Italian and Algerian plateau briar, reworking classic shapes in his own interpretation; he shapes stems by hand and lines bowls before smoking with a pre-smoke coating mixture.
Brancher

— a venture that began in Georgia on February 20, 2012. The first series was made from locally gathered hickory wood; the maker particularly uses the section of trunk where branches emerge, as this cut is more durable. The brand's mark is a large letter B with a leaf added to its base.
Breezewood

— a brand that appeared by 1942 at the latest. During World War II, when Mediterranean and European briar became hard to reach, American manufacturers turned to native alternatives; the most common of these was mountain laurel, a distant relative of briar. Breezewood advertisements built a narrative tying this wood to the untouched forests of the Great Smoky Mountains. The debate over the material's toxicity has no basis beyond the fact that animals eat it.
Briar Bird Pipes
— the brand of Jason Cochey in Bellevue, Ohio. Known for colorful stems and stout shapes. He first learned pipe making from internet forums, then worked alongside Premal Chheda.
Briarbilt
— appears to have been the house brand of the L. Bamberger & Co. store. This large store, founded in 1893, was bought by Macy's in 1929, and the name was retained until around 1986.
Briarlee
— a sub-brand of Lee, likely a second line. It appears in at least one Pipes by Lee catalog.
Brick

— Max Brick ran a pipe and tobacco shop in Trenton, New Jersey; in a workshop attached to the shop he did repairs and made freehands drawing mostly on the Danish style. He was the third generation of a family of Lithuanian immigrant descent.
Brissett

— the hand-carved pipes of Mike Brissett. He works with air-dried briar, opens the smoke channel to 4 mm and polishes it with a conical taper inside; he coats bowls with a thin layer of activated carbon using a natural binder, arguing this protects the wood during the break-in period and lays the foundation for an even cake.
Bryson

— a screw-fitted pipe with a wooden bowl and aluminum body. Like Kirsten, it was designed to trap moisture and tar and cool the smoke to prevent tongue bite. It was distributed in 1947 by Bennett Brothers, Inc., based in Chicago and New York.
Busa

— the brand of North American maker A. Dana Busa. The author of Pipe and Tobacco Register, Busa won first place in the International Pipe Carving Competition and placed in the top ten of the competition Pipes and Tobaccos magazine ran in partnership with Butz-Choquin.
C.B. Perkins

— a chain that opened its first shop in Boston in the early 1900s, considered New England's leading tobacconist for more than seventy-five years. In 1986 management handed the Pennsylvania and New Jersey branches to DES Tobacco Corporation, a subsidiary of S. Frieder and Sons. S. Frieder, a cigar maker since 1920, had sold its manufacturing arm to United States Tobacco in 1978 to focus on retail.
Carroll

— Charles Carroll made pipes at his home in Traverse City, Michigan. Though not widely known beyond his own state and the Midwest, he is considered a skilled maker. He stamped his pipes "Charles Carroll"; his real name was Chuck Holiday.
Cazzetta
— no recorded information exists; only the brand name is documented.
Charles Tulsa
— a now-deceased maker who had a workshop in Florida. He is the creator of the Old Reliable brand and also worked for The Briar Workshop.
CHP-X

— one of the earliest American freehand pipe ventures. Founded in the early 1970s by Jay Rostov, former owner of Jay's Smoke Shop, together with Chuck Holiday. Shortly after founding, Rostov hired his relative Michael Kabik, and Holiday left the partnership; for what followed, see the Kabik entry.
Chris Best
— a maker who has made pipes since the 1970s. His mark is a circular C surrounding the letter B.
Cipolla
— the brand of Robert Cipolla. His pipes are said to draw on the Lee von Erck line; they are known for containing no filler and coming with a plug alongside them.
Clark
— Chris Clark, a pipe maker from Toledo, Ohio. Nothing is known about him beyond his name and the city he worked in.
Clark Briar Originals

— the pipes of Bob Clark in Warren, Rhode Island. Clark spent twenty-five years as an offshore fisherman; drawing on influence from past and present English masters, he reworks classic shapes with an eye to smoking performance and cures his pipes with oil in the English tradition. He also runs a fully equipped repair workshop.
Clewell
— a brand registered under the name R. A. Clewell. The name is the only data kept in the directory; neither location, date, nor production information is available.
Collins

— Bill Collins, working in St. Louis, Missouri. Two accounts stand side by side in the source: one holds that the maker produced his pipes under the name Jost, the other that Jost is a pipe and tobacco shop in St. Louis where Collins worked as a repairman and maker.
Comeaux

— the brand of Tennessee maker Larry E. Comeaux II. Born October 24, 1943, died November 16, 2015. Known as "The Pipe Doctor," Comeaux got into the trade through the encouragement of two master friends from Knoxville, M. O. Vickers and Robert Blackwell; he produced numerous freehand, exotic, and sculptural pipes and was also respected as a repairman. He won the freehand competition at the 1986 PCI members' meeting and was honored by the Saint-Claude guild of pipe masters. He worked with Greek briar and vulcanite and lucite stems.
Connoisseur

— the shop Ed Burak opened in New York in 1968, run first on 46th Street then on 6th Avenue. It closed in February 2009 after forty years. Burak was a designer rather than a carver; his pipes were made by Tony Pesante of New Jersey and Joe Cortegiano of New York. The shop is also remembered for its own blends. For more, see the Ed Burak entry.
Continental Briar Pipe Co.
— a briar pipe manufacturer based at the intersection of York and Adams streets in Brooklyn. The address comes from the firm's letterhead dated July 28, 1941.
Conway Jr.
— pipe maker C. E. Conway Jr. of Orlando, Florida. Only this name and address remain.
Cook, Tom

— a carver from Amarillo, Texas, often confused with J. T. Cooke. His freehands were at times as flamboyant as to recall Preben Holm's carving style. He stamped his pipes "T. Cook"; he is now retired.
Cooke, Charles Patrick

— an England-born, well-known pipe maker in southern California; not to be confused with his namesake J. T. Cooke. He did not live long enough for his craftsmanship to gain international recognition. He specialized in combining sitter-shaped bowls with other shapes; he signed his pipes "Cooke" with an engraving tool.
Cortegiano

— Joseph "Joe" Cortegiano was one of New York's most frequently cited pipe masters, known for the precision and exactness of his work. He was known in particular for his very large-scale freehands, said to be in high demand. His pipes were carried by well-known shops such as E. Wilke on Madison Avenue; he also worked for Barclay Rex. His grandson Scott Parfumi made pipes under Jack H. Weinberger before returning to New York to work at the family shop.
Courtley

— a sub-brand or second line of Custom-Bilt, positioned at the cheap end. A 1957 wholesale catalog presents Courtley as the economy version of Custombilt: walnut-toned polish, vulcanite stem, and sold by the dozen in a display box. That same year, an even cheaper Custom-Bilt sub-brand called His Nibs was also sold.
Creator's Design Pipes & Blades
— the workshop Dan and Amy Sanford run together in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The brand name rests on the couple's belief that creativity is a gift.
Crisman, Harry

— founder of Big Casino Pipes. He lives in Sarver, north of Pittsburgh; he began pipe making in 2012. Because he works days at a steel mill and evenings as a blacksmith, he makes his pipes in his spare time; he says he comes from a family of craftsmen.
Cristiano

— Thomas Cristiano entered the pipe trade at the S. M. Frank factory on Long Island just weeks after emigrating from Italy to America at sixteen in 1968. After ten years at this factory, which also made Kaywoodie pipes, he left and founded his own company, Cristom Imports and Exports, in Tampa, Florida. Alongside the Cristiano Signature Series and Calabresi lines, Cristiano is thought to have made Kaywoodie pipes in Tampa from the mid-1980s to around 1992. He was one of the country's most respected humidor makers; he died in Italy on November 7, 2005.
Crosby

— John Crosby began making pipes after meeting carvers at the Chicago Pipe Show; his work, which started with ready-made kits, developed step by step. Today he works with Italian briar and stems he cuts by hand from German vulcanite rod. He trained in painting, earning a bachelor's degree at Jackson State University and a master's at Purdue.
Dagner Pipes

— born when a father and son who first evaluated pipes and tobacco on a video channel decided to make their own pipes. Their plain pipes, of their own design, are made to order in Italy by a manufacturer and produced by hand from rested briar.
DANA 31

— a promotional pipe accompanying a two-pack purchase of Edgeworth tobacco in 1949; advertisements state the offer ended on October 31, 1949. Its design is close to Kirsten: an aluminum body, a screw-fitted briar bowl, a plastic stem with an aluminum tube extending into the body, and a screw-on cap. Fiber gaskets are used at both the bowl and the cap.
Danco

— sources tie the brand to both Denmark and America without giving a specific maker's name. Period ads show the firm was located on Hudson Street in New York. Some pipes carry the stamp "Imported Briar," which points to American manufacture; examples stamped "Italy" suggest the American distributor had part of the run made in Italy. Danish-made examples would be expected to carry a "Denmark" stamp.
Darby
— the brand of the Darby Pipe Shop in Illinois. The shop was founded in 1945 by maker Royal Aten and later passed to other owners.
David Jones

— David Jones began making pipes in 1986, and by 1988 the number of pipes he had sold had passed two thousand. Having bought a large briar stock early on, he knows the origin of his wood; he lets the burls rest for years in a controlled environment before curing them a further five to seven years at the workshop. He tapers the holes in the shank and stem at the bit and mouthpiece. His stem mark is a mother-of-pearl dot; pipes are stamped with his signature, "handmade," "USA," and a grade.
Delta Pipes

— the brand of Michael Fauscette. Fauscette came to pipe making after years as a collector and smoker; he describes his interest, which began with Italian and English pipes, gradually shifting to the handmade work of Danish and American makers. A friendship with a freehand maker gave him a chance to closely observe workshop practice.
Diebel

— pipes thought to have been made under the name Diebel by George Becker, the house carver at Diebel's Sportsmans Gallery (originally Fred Diebel, Pipemaker, Tobacconist) in Kansas City, Missouri. Becker also made pipes under his own stamp for a period.
Doerr
— Diane Doerr, who worked under Jack H. Weinberger in the 1970s. For more, see the JHW Pipes entry.
Donald Kayne

— cited in one sales record as a well-known pipe master active in the 1970s. According to scattered online information he was based in the Long Island area of New York in those years; his name appears together with the Germaine record.
Dr. Kernel

— Dr. Joseph E. Kernel was an ophthalmologist in Indianapolis, Indiana; his office was in the city's Traction Terminal building in 1951. Bernard Batty, also of Indianapolis, received patent number 2,614,568 in May 1950. Tracy Mincer, also of the same city, is known besides his other pipes for The Doodler. What relationship connects these three names has not been clarified.
Dr. Shotton's

— a system pipe distributed by Foster Products, Inc. of Cleveland, Ohio; a second address in New York is also on record. Removing the plug at the bottom of the bowl lets a pipe cleaner pass straight through, meant to remove the need to disassemble the stem. The open slit on the top of the tube running under the bowl is meant to ensure full airflow. Promotional material states that the briar is left unvarnished so that it can breathe, letting the wood color naturally with tar.
Drysmoke

— Drysmoke Silvertone pipes, produced by National Briar Pipe Co., were made, in the marketing language of the day, from DuPont nylon "light as a feather." Because the pipes carry only a "nylon" stamp, they are most often referred to by that name.
Duke of Dundee

— a model marketed under the slogan "the pipe science built." It had two notable features: an air-adjustment hole set into the outer lower edge of the bowl, and a shank with a replaceable filter. The firm called these two parts the "unclogging filter" and the "coordinated air regulator"; the filter arrangement is close to that of Medico and similar brands. The pipe was made by Continental Briar Pipe Co. in Brooklyn, most likely in the 1940s.
DuPont Explosives promotional pipes

— pipes given out as souvenirs by du Pont's explosives division between 1912 and 1933. The maker is unknown. The shape is thought to recall an 18th- or early-19th-century powder keg; poker and bent examples exist, some with a band. One face carries the du Pont logo with the word "explosives," the other the stamp "Genuine French Briar"; stems are vulcanite or a similar material.
Eastman Pipe
— a pipe signed Eastman Scientific. How long it was produced and its details are unknown; the only surviving document is a period promotional brochure.
Emperor

— the brand of Empire Briar Pipe Company Inc. of New York. Advertisements from 1945 call it "the pipe without equal," claiming every example is a piece of craftsmanship in the bespoke tradition. The firm was a subsidiary of Continental Briar Pipe Co. Inc., located on York Street in Brooklyn. It had three grades: Standard, De Luxe, and Supreme.
Ensslen
— pipe maker Bob Ensslen of Cresco, Pennsylvania. Nothing beyond his name and town has been documented.
F.L.N.

— F. L. Norwood's bespoke briar pipes in Clifton, Tennessee. The maker says his main occupation is pipe repair, and pipe making is his pursuit. He uses the FLN stamp only for three grades: AX (flawless grain, no fills or flaws), A (good grain, no fills or flaws), and B (good grain, a few small fills). His son Kenneth Norwood marks his pipes with the KN stamp.
Fairchild, Don
— recorded as a pipe maker from Bellaire, Texas. This record is quite likely to have been confused with pipe maker Ron Fairchild.
Ferdinand Feuerbach

— began work at William Demuth Company in 1897 and was responsible for launching brands such as Royal DeMuth and Hesson Guard. He moved to S. M. Frank in 1919 and was made vice president of the company in 1943.
Fillenwarth

— Tony Fillenwarth of Mazon, Illinois, began pipe making as a hobby and became known for original, exotic-shaped freehands. Records give his annual output as around a hundred, while the maker's own account puts the figure under seventy-five; some of his pipes are made of olive wood. He works Greek and Algerian briar with acrylic, vulcanite, and Cumberland stems. His stamp reads "Fillenwarth / USA." He says he made his first pipe from a purchased kit, and once that pipe was finished he knew he would carry on the work for life.
Filto

— dated to around 1965, a design recalling the Kirsten and Bryson pipes: an aluminum body and a screw-fitted briar bowl. It was produced in many colors and color combinations. It was made in Burgaw, North Carolina.
FloggleWerks
— the pipes of James Millar. Made from native wood species with no glue used at all.
Forecaster
— a pipe produced by National Briar Pipe Co. of Jersey City, New Jersey. It was marketed with an "aluminum coil" placed in the airway, claimed to clean and cool the smoke.
Frey

— Michael J. Frey made pipes in Lockport, New York from at least the early 1980s. He is a student of Michael Butera and, like his teacher, kept his production low and his standard of quality high. His work is considered superior in craftsmanship, proportion, and interior dimensions; his mark is in ivory and silver, and his shapes follow a classic line. Once PCI shows turned into an environment where makers sold directly, he tried full-time carving but is said to have found it impossible to make a living in such a narrow field and given up the work.
Galehouse
— pipe maker Joseph Galehouse, working in Wooster, Ohio. Records consist only of the maker's name and city.
Gardner
— Russ Gardner began the trade in his grandfather's lumber workshop. A pipe smoker himself, the maker works alone; he makes mostly freehands and produces pipes to customers' sketches or suggestions.
Genna

— Frank Genna makes mostly freeform, sculptural pipes. The son of a woodworker father, he had worked with wood since childhood, though he did not make his first pipes until after 1993. He accepts bespoke work based on customer designs.
George Becker
— the staff pipe carver at Diebel's Sportsmans Gallery in Kansas City; he also appears in the directory under the Diebel heading. It is known that he also made pipes under his own stamp.
Georgopulo

— G. A. Georgopulo & Company was founded by George Georgopulo and his brothers Basil and Theodore. In the early twentieth century it produced quality cigarettes from Turkish and Egyptian tobaccos and was the sole American importer of these tobaccos. George B. Georgopulo joined the business in the 1940s, followed later by Panos Georgopulo. The firm issued the Andron, Ramses II, and Duo-Blend brands; it was based on Stone Street in New York for many years and is credited as the inventor of the unbranded cigarette. It is known to have also sold pipes, some of which were made and stamped for them by Saville. The company was dissolved in 1995.
Gerrard
— bespoke pipes made by E. E. Lushbaugh of Hagerstown, Maryland. Lushbaugh referred to his product as the "Gerrard Three-way pipe."
