r.x: Jacono

is a small pipe workshop Tonino Jacono runs alone in Jesi, in Italy's Marche region. Pipes bearing his stamp have been made in limited numbers since 1983; the brand is best known in the community for its unusual system of naming its quality grades after chess pieces.
The Road to the Workshop

Tonino Jacono's start in the trade was not the result of a planned career. Good briar was already close at hand within the family: his father-in-law ran a timber mill that cut block and plateau for major Italian pipe factories, and could pick out the best pieces from the tons of blocks passing through it. When his brother-in-law, who had an interest in pipe making, bought the necessary machinery, a three-person venture was set up in 1981 aiming at freehand pipes. The claim that the venture was founded in Calabria rests on a single account. Each had a defined role: preparing and drilling the wood fell to the father-in-law, rough shaping and sanding to the brother-in-law, and finishing and marketing to Jacono.

This partnership did not last long; after about a year and a half, Jacono decided to strike out on his own and returned to Marche in 1983. In October of that same year, the first pipes stamped "JACONO" emerged from his small workshop in Jesi. Records show he buys his briar from the same supplier used by established workshops such as Cavicchi, and seasons it a few more years himself in his own storage.
Chess Grades

Jacono stamps every pipe with the name of a chess piece based on its surface treatment and grain quality. Fully rusticated bodies are called Knight, partly rusticated ones Bishop; Rook, Jack, Queen, and King are the smooth grades, differing from each other in the beauty of the grain. Sources diverge on the details: some retailer records add a Pawn grade set aside for sandblasting and note that Bishop was previously stamped "Jack." Since the arrangement is understood to have changed over the years, the order should not be read as a fixed hierarchy. The letter "E" at the end of the stamp marks an in-between step between two grades, while the inscription "Checkmate" indicates an exceptionally large body.

The logic of the system is that it ties surface treatment directly to quality: if a flaw appears in the wood during carving, the body is rusticated and drops a grade. For this reason, a Jacono's surface treatment is not merely an aesthetic choice but a report card on the wood.
Style and Production

The workshop has stayed small-scale since its founding; pipes are finished by hand one at a time. Acrylic (lucite) is used for mouthpieces; silver and fine woods are preferred for bands and inlays. Examples made from olive wood alongside briar are also known. A significant share of production goes to the United States, with the rest spread across Europe, Russia, China, and the Japanese market.

r.x: Artisan pipes and factory pipes

name two different approaches to pipe-making. In a handmade (artisan) pipe, a single craftsman carries every stage through by hand, from selecting the block of briar to hand-cutting the stem; in a factory pipe, each worker specializes in a single stage and the pipe takes shape along a production line. The difference lies not just in who makes the pipe, but in the entire approach, from design through finishing.
Two Production Philosophies

Factories produce a standard range drawn from a shape chart, with the same dimensions year after year, so a smoker can find nearly the same model they liked years later. In artisan production, by contrast, each pipe is usually one of a kind: rather than following a pre-drawn template, the maker designs the shape around the grain of the block in hand. As a result, output volumes are low in handmade work; some makers produce no more than a few dozen pipes a year, and even the most productive workshops rarely exceed a few hundred.
Technical Differences
The main technical differences between the two approaches can be summarized as follows:

rows: Drilling axis, mortise depth, and tenon fit are each measured individually
Usually pre-molded, in ebonite or acrylic
Spray lacquer and varnish that can mask flaws are common
One of a kind, following the block's grain

r.x: The airway is considered the most critical difference: the maker checks the axis of every hole and the fit of every part individually, so smoke flows uninterrupted from chamber to stem. Stem work also takes up a large share of the effort; according to some makers, a hand-cut stem alone can account for thirty to fifty percent of the total labor time. That said, the generalization that "factory pipes use lower-quality briar" doesn't hold up; top-tier makers such as Dunhill and Castello are known for careful material selection despite producing at scale.
Hybrid Models and Historical Interplay

The line between the two worlds isn't always sharp. US-based workshops like BriarWorks take a "handcrafted factory" approach, producing standard shapes with small teams. Castello, meanwhile, is cited as an example of a semi-artisan maker that works from catalog shapes but finishes its pipes by hand. The best-known example of this historical interplay comes from Denmark: in the 1950s and 1960s, the Stanwell factory brought designs by makers such as Sixten Ivarsson into series production, bringing handmade aesthetics to a wide audience.
The Terms "Artisan" and "High-Grade"

The word "artisan" in its current sense is a relatively recent addition; it's said to have become widespread after the 1990s, before which the same pipes were described as "handmade," "freehand," or "high-grade." In collecting circles, high-quality handmade pipes are still classified as "high-grade" today; the term is especially associated with the Danish School generation of makers such as Ivarsson, Nordh, and Chonowitsch. Whichever term is used, the essence of the distinction stays the same: the factory pipe represents consistency, the artisan pipe the labor of a single maker's hand.

r.x: Kybele

is a Turkish brand producing pipes from meerschaum. The available records state that the brand was founded in 2002, that a craftsman named İsmail Özdamar stood behind it, and that a company called Kıraç is associated with the brand. It appears under the Türkiye heading in international pipe reference sources; yet the documented information that has survived about the brand amounts to no more than these few lines.
Its Place in the Records

Everything known about Kybele rests on a single record: founding year 2002, the name running the brand as İsmail Özdamar, and the registered company as Kıraç. This record has passed from a reference book compiling world pipe brands into pipe encyclopedias, and from there into collector forums; a Spanish-language collector forum repeated the same information in 2022. No official brand page, catalog, or independent trade record has been identified. Which city the workshop operated in, which shapes it produced, how it stamped its pipes, and whether it is active today all remain unknown.

Such gaps are not uncommon in Turkish pipe making. The meerschaum trade runs mostly in small workshops, often within a family; a brand is born with the name of a craftsman or a company, and when the bench closes, the name disappears without leaving a record behind. At this scale, the line between the work of a single craftsman and series production often blurs as well.
Where the Name Comes From

The brand takes its name from one of Anatolia's oldest goddesses. Kybele — commonly written Kibele in Turkish — is the mother goddess held to rule over fertility and the wild; her worship was organized into a structured cult in the Phrygian period, and her depictions were most often flanked by lions. The region where open-air shrines and lion reliefs dedicated to her are most densely found stretches between Eskişehir and Afyonkarahisar.

Eskişehir, at the center of that same region, is where meerschaum is extracted: nearly all commercially workable deposits lie within that province's borders, and the carving of the stone has continued in the same area for centuries. So the name the brand chose and the source of the material it works both trace back to the same region. Whether the name was a deliberate reference is not stated in the sources.
What Remains Undocumented

The founding year given, 2002, falls in a period when brand-building accelerated in Turkish meerschaum production. After the export of raw meerschaum was banned in 1980, processing the stone stayed entirely within the country, and the Eskişehir area became the world center for this field; in the 2000s, many small brands reaching foreign buyers directly emerged on this ground. Exactly where Kybele stands in this picture cannot be determined.

Practices common to almost every Turkish workshop — carving the block stone by hand, a wax bath after carving, coloring that progresses from white to yellow and amber tones as the pipe is smoked, and the frequent use of amber-look acrylic in mouthpieces — may well apply to this brand's work too. None of it, however, is documented under the Kybele name. Until new documents surface, the brand will remain among Turkish brands whose name is known but whose work has not been recorded.

r.x: Nachwalter

is the brand under which American maker Elliott Nachwalter signs his handmade pipes under his own name. Trained in art history and photography, Nachwalter turned his profession into a craft and set up his workshop in Vermont. Though the brand runs today as a one-person studio, its name is still linked with the Briar Workshop, which served as a training ground in American handmade pipe history.
A Bench Set Up in Vermont

Nachwalter's first workshop was a small wooden structure fitted with a few basic tools in the town of Stowe in the late 1970s; sources give the founding year not as a fixed date but in relative terms such as "about twenty-five years ago." In these early years he briefly shared a shop in Stowe with Andrew Marks.

In the same period, the Briar Workshop was founded jointly with Jorg Jemelka, and the bench stopped being a solo pursuit. The involvement of Danish designer-maker Finn Meyan Andersen brought the workshop's freehand leanings into direct contact with the Danish School approach. Over the years, Brad Pohlmann, J. T. Cooke, and Carole Burns — craftspeople who would later become known under their own names — all worked there; in this sense the Briar Workshop is counted among the training benches of the American handmade pipe scene. Records show that some pipes from the workshop's period in Florida bear the "The Briar Workshop" stamp. It should be noted that the names Cooke and Burns also appear in sources as "Jim Cooke" and "Carol Burns."
The New York Years and a Hiatus

In 1980 Nachwalter opened a shop in New York; he designed and made pipes in the back of the shop, selling them straight to customers. Sources bracket this shop period as 1980–1983. What follows is a stretch when the maker set his craft aside, not making pipes for about three years. Pieces from these years carry "Pipeworks / New York City / USA" on one side of the shank and a personal stamp indicating handmade work on the other.
The Studio on the Battenkill

In the autumn of 1996 Nachwalter set up a small studio in southern Vermont, on the banks of the Battenkill River, ringed by the Taconic and Green Mountains. Known as Pipestudio, this workshop is where the brand still produces today. The briar blocks used come from Italy and Greece; vulcanite, acrylic, and cumberland are the preferred mouthpiece materials. The maker notes that working with well-rested blocks shortens the break-in period.

Scale is not what defines the output — individuality is: since the grain comes out differently in every block, the design is determined by the block itself; this is why the brand is known for pieces that are never identical to one another. Nachwalter describes his own work as making a sculptural object that never loses its function. The pipes' distinguishing mark is a small emblem resembling a six-pointed star set on the mouthpiece; collectors weigh this mark together with the shank stamps, which change over time, when dating a piece.

r.x: Rex Walden Pipes

is the product of a one-man bench, signed under his own name by American pipe maker Rex Walden. Since Walden is not a full-time craftsman, output is low; pipes are completed not in batches but one after another, individually. Trade records show the bench to be located in Texas; an exact founding year does not appear in publicly available sources. The bench's name is counted among the makers who, working alone in the American handmade pipe scene of the 2010s, were known within collector circles without ever building a wide distribution network.
Formal Language and Influences

By Walden's own account, two main currents shape his style. The first is the makers of the Danish school, whose shapes have become a signature in their own right; the second is the Japanese pipe-making tradition he came to know through his long time in the Far East. Where these two sources meet, freehand bowls stand out, full-bodied while the shank and stem taper thin. Walden says he also follows the work of American makers of his own generation closely.

Trade records cite surface finishes as the bench's chief distinguishing feature: unconventional finishing methods and heavily textured sandblast surfaces. This preference is considered consistent with an inclination to foreground body proportions over any display of grain.
A Self-Taught Craft

Walden has not gone through a workshop apprenticeship; he says he learned the craft in a small work corner of his home, with ready-made kits and technical tutorials circulating online. Adapting the general-purpose hand tools he had on hand to pipe making, and beginning to source briar blocks regularly, marked the stage that let the bench stand on its own. This route can be counted among the typical examples of the generation of globally scattered briar craftsmen that emerged after the 2000s, relying less on workshop tradition than on knowledge shared over the network. Slow progress at a bench not worked full-time allows separate time to be devoted to each individually completed pipe, but also keeps the number of documented examples limited.
Distribution and Current Status

The bench's products have reached buyers as far as Asia and Australia through connections built directly online; Walden states that he also works with buyers by corresponding over shape. The brand's own website cannot currently be reached, and no verifiable information exists about its current level of production. Examples signed by Walden continue to appear from time to time in secondhand pipe records.

r.x: BPK

is a factory operating in the town of Proseč in the Pardubice region of the Czech Republic, tracing its roots to a local pipemaking craft dating from the mid-nineteenth century. The start of production in the town is traditionally dated to 1842; although today's company was founded in 1993, it is considered a continuation of this lineage. About 150 kilometres east of Prague, this small settlement has for nearly two centuries been counted among Central Europe's most concentrated pipe-production centres.
From Town Craft to Factory

According to local tradition, the craft arrived in Proseč when two men from the neighbouring village of Paseky went to the Kladsko region behind the army and learned pipemaking there. The first pipes were carved from local woods such as alder, maple, and pear; briar root entered the picture much later. By the end of the nineteenth century, some two hundred people in the town and surrounding villages were making a living from this trade.

The turning point came after 1880, when merchant Bernard Kopperle set up a workshop employing around thirty workers. The workshop became a steam-powered factory in 1905. From 1910, following the example of French manufacturers, Kopperle began working briar himself, importing the block and also selling it to other manufacturers in Proseč. In this way the town became an extension of the period in which briar spread across Europe. After 1919, French milling equipment enabled a shift to short-pipe production, and by the end of the 1930s more than six hundred people in the town were producing around five hundred pipe models.
The State Enterprise Era

After the Second World War, production was consolidated at a single centre: with the nationalisation of private workshops in 1950, all pipe production in Czechoslovakia moved to Proseč. The newly established state enterprise took over not only the confiscated machine park but also Italian briar stocks and semi-finished goods. The factory was managed successively under Koh-i-noor and TOFA. In the 1970s production reached a level of one million pipes a year; roughly ninety percent of this output was exported, mostly to Western countries. This scale points to a production philosophy in which the distinction between mass-produced and workshop pipes became pronounced.
After 1993

Following the political changes of 1989, the factory passed into private hands, partly through restitution and partly through privatisation. B P K, spol. s r.o. was registered in the commercial register in 1993 at the Proseč address. Records indicate the brand name comes from the initials of the surnames of the three partners who privatised the company. The firm today reports exporting to more than forty countries; the 175th anniversary of pipe production in Proseč was celebrated in 2017.

Production follows the customary factory stages, from working the briar block through to polishing; heavily handworked finishing is one of the points the brand highlights. The town also has a pipe museum recounting the history of the craft.

r.x: Sèvres

is the porcelain manufactory established under French royal patronage. Although its name is mostly associated with tableware, vases, and figurines, the workshop's eighteenth-century output also included a small group of porcelain pipe bowls. The number of these bowls was never large; today Sèvres is remembered in pipe history less as a brand than as a name representing the French branch of the porcelain pipe tradition.
The Birth of the Royal Manufactory

The workshop's core was established in 1740 in Vincennes near Paris, in a tower of the old royal château. After lengthy trials, soft-paste porcelain was successfully achieved, and a royal privilege was granted in 1745; this privilege covered the right to produce porcelain painted and gilded in the Saxon manner, that is, in the style of Meissen. The monopoly granted in 1752 for polychrome pieces reinforced this position. The business moved to Sèvres in 1756, and was bought outright by Louis XV in 1759. The long-standing support of the king's mistress, Madame de Pompadour, is considered decisive in the workshop rising to a trend-setting position in Europe.

The move to hard-paste porcelain came later. The discovery of kaolin deposits at Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche near Limoges in 1768 opened the way for this technique, and hard-paste production began in 1770; according to accounts, the workshop had bought the secret of the formula earlier, around 1761. The two pastes were used side by side for a time, and soft-paste production was discontinued in 1804.
Pipe Bowls and the Problem of Identification

The bowls were side products that emerged within the workshop's ordinary division of labor. At Sèvres, a single craftsman did not finish a piece from start to end; paste preparation, shaping, painting, and gilding were distributed among separate specialties. Within this arrangement, the pipe never became a regular line item. There is only one estimate for total production: in the view of a Paris antique-pipe specialist, the number of bowls made by the close of the century did not exceed three hundred. This figure has not been confirmed by an independent count.

Their small numbers do not make the pieces easy to identify today. On the contrary, because most early porcelain bowls carry no factory stamp, it is often impossible to distinguish a French-made bowl from its contemporary German counterparts. The only remaining basis is shape. In Peckus and Rapaport's study of porcelain pipes, the polygonal-faceted "à pans" bowl is considered the main criterion for attribution to Sèvres; how well this criterion corresponds to primary documents, however, is not clear. Gilt traces on metal rings and rococo ornament serve as secondary clues supporting dating.
Current Position

The manufactory continues to exist under the name Manufacture nationale de Sèvres. In 2010 it merged with the National Ceramics Museum to form "Sèvres – Cité de la céramique," and since 2012 it has been part of a larger institution that also includes Limoges. Pipes have no place in the institution's current output; Sèvres bowls today document, purely as museum and collection objects alongside examples of meerschaum and clay pipes, a brief but notable chapter of porcelain in pipe history.

r.x: Jørn Larsen

(b. March 25, 1949) is a Danish pipemaker. Born in a small village roughly fifty kilometers south of Copenhagen, he began the craft not at a pipe bench but at a locksmith's bench. This background gives him an unusual place among Danish workshops: he has not only made pipes but has also drawn up and built the machines he uses to make them.
From Locksmithing to Pipes

His connection to pipes began at age sixteen, in a pipe club he joined with a friend; the two carved pipes for themselves from briar blocks bought in Copenhagen. He left school at seventeen and turned to mechanics, entering a locksmithing apprenticeship, which he completed in 1970 at the age of twenty-one. Following his military service he worked in this trade for many years, during which pipemaking all but stopped. A briar block that came into his hands in his thirties turned him back to carving; this time he had a mature background in metalwork behind him.
The Chonowitsch Circle and Stanwell

A trip organized by his pipe club had once taken Larsen to Emil Chonowitsch's workshop. Around 1985, he went a second time, this time to show his own pipes, and met the master's son Jess there. What began with him producing the specialized tools Jess needed turned into a collaboration lasting years; this acquaintance was also the link connecting Larsen to the Danish school circle. In the same years he prepared semi-finished parts for Stanwell, taking on silver band, bamboo, and horn mountings.
Machines of His Own Making

Larsen had already begun producing tools specific to pipemaking during his apprenticeship, and had designed and built a lathe for the purpose. The machines that followed served to lighten the heavy work; the finishing stage remained by hand on every pipe. When he was going to produce the same shape several times, he used the copying rig he had built himself; when working on a single piece, he would shape the pipe on the lathe or freehand. Records indicate a similar lathe later served other Danish workshops as well; which workshops used it has not been confirmed by independent sources.
Materials, Production, and Stamp

He sourced his briar from Greece and Corsica. For mouthpieces he mostly used black vulcanite, occasionally Cumberland and cultured amber; for bands he turned to silver, boxwood, horn, and amber. He turned out roughly four hundred pipes a year; most were plain-polished, with a significant portion brown or black sandblasted. Most of the output went to Japan, Switzerland, and the United States; an attempt to open the German market brought 9 mm filtered models along with it. His workshop was set up in a room of the house he and his family moved to on the island of Lolland. His pipes generally carry a three-line "JORN / LARSEN / DENMARK" stamp; this signature is found today mainly on examples in secondary-market circulation.

r.x: Pollner

, in full Carl Pollner & Sohn, is a wood-turning and tobacconist business that has stayed in the hands of the same family in the Westphalian town of Bünde since October 9, 1878. Founded as a small turning shop producing stair treads, table legs, and furniture parts, the business began selling umbrellas, canes, and pipes as well once a small shop opened in 1881; in later generations the emphasis shifted entirely to pipes and tobacco.
Founding and Generations

The workshop's founders were Carl and Elise Pollner. Otto Pollner, born in 1883 and representing the second generation, learned the wood-turning trade in the pipe branch in Münster and completed his training around 1900; the direction of the business became clear in this period. The firm was registered under the name "Carl Pollner & Sohn" in 1920 and that same year moved into its own building housing both the workshop and the sales section together; the second generation's management continued until 1957.

The name at the head of the third generation is Otto Pollner II, who took over management in 1958. According to Pipedia, he ran the business during this period together with his wife Wanda, and later with Christel Pollner; the tobacco side became notably prominent. In 1990 management passed to the fourth generation's Otto-Karl Pollner. The fifth generation is represented by Julian Gronau, who took charge of the business in 2015.
Otto Pollner II and OP-Studio Pipes

The best-known name in the family is Otto Pollner II (1925–2004) of the third generation. He is considered Germany's last certified master pipe turner. Alongside the pipes he finished individually by hand, he published numerous articles in specialist magazines and wrote several books on pipes. Among these are
Pfeiferauchen leicht gemacht
, which explains pipe smoking to beginners;
Tabakpfeifen aus zwei Jahrhunderten
, covering the turners of the Westphalia and Lippe region; and the 1997
Die Pfeifenmacher zwischen Rennsteig und Rhön
, examining the pipe makers between Rennsteig and Rhön across a three-century span. The last book is regarded as one of the reference texts of regional pipe historiography.

He also developed the workshop's signature product, OP-Studio pipes. These hand-finished briar pipes continued to be known under the brand name even after the maker's death. Records indicate Otto Pollner II was, from 1992, a member of the pipe makers' guild in Saint-Claude (Confrérie des maîtres-pipiers); this tie to the French tradition also points to German wood-turning's place on a European scale.
Today

The business is still active in Bünde today; alongside pipes and tobacco, its range also includes other products such as cigars, wine, and Erzgebirge-region woodwork. The pipe retains its place in the business's emblem, and the OP-Studio name continues. Since Bünde is one of the historic centers of the German tobacco industry, Pollner's story counts as a record not just of a single workshop but of a town's relationship with tobacco.

r.x: James Gilliam

is a craftsman who settled in Germany after retiring from the United States Navy and signs his pipes with the JSEC stamp. Though American-born, his workshop is based in Germany, so he is listed among both American and German makers — a dual affiliation that has led his name to appear in the brand directories of both countries at once.
From Repair to Making

Gilliam's introduction to the craft came not through making but through repair. After retiring, he began reconditioning worn briar pipes he owned using whatever tools he had on hand, and the results encouraged him to try carving pipes from scratch. This is the story passed down in trade listings and collector write-ups: restoration first, then his own designs. This period spent on repair also explains why his stem work is so often singled out for praise — the shaping of the bit and the tooth chamber receives particular care in his pipes.
Materials and Stamp

Mediterranean briar is used for the bowls, and German-made ebonite rod for the stems. Various exotic woods, horn, and pre-ban ivory are also used as band material in his designs. Bamboo-shanked freehands and billiards are among the maker's best-known work; the clean transition between bamboo shank and briar is what sets these pipes apart.

Gilliam does not use a letter-based grading system; each pipe is treated as a one-off. The JSEC stamp is said to be formed from the initials of family members' names. According to information passed down from the maker's now-defunct personal site, the stamp is applied in two distinct forms: one for bowls where the plateaux surface is preserved, another for bowls cut from an ebauchon block. The anchor figure that accompanies the stamp is a nod to the maker's Navy background; this anchored stamp is favored for nautically themed pipes.
The Grainstorm Circle

Through the ties he built with craftsmen working in Germany, Gilliam is counted among the founders of the group known as Grainstorm, formed in 2014. This circle of seven includes names such as Roger Wallenstein, Uwe Maier, Steffen Mueller, and Manfred Hortig. The group gathers every year at Maier's workshop in Balingen to produce pipes around a shared theme. These gatherings have become a tradition that keeps the technical exchange between members alive.

That the maker's workshop was located near Stuttgart in 2015 rests on the notes of a collector who visited him that year; no independent record of his whereabouts in later years has been found. Likewise, the current volume of production is not precisely known; records point to a small, made-to-order operation.

r.x: Koncak

is a brand that works meerschaum in block form in Eskişehir and is counted among the country's oldest makers of finished pipes. According to records in the pipe literature, the business was founded in 1934 by Ekrem Konçak. The family name is written on pipes and boxes in the Latinized form "Koncak," dropping the Turkish diacritic. What sets the brand apart from the city's other workshops is that, at the end of the twentieth century, it took over the rights to a Vienna-based European brand.
Founding and Family Generations

In the years the factory was founded, Eskişehir meerschaum carving relied largely on small workshops, with a significant share of the extracted stone sent raw to Europe. The business founded by the Konçak family became one of the select firms that processed the stone domestically and sold it abroad as a finished product; over time it came to be regarded among the regular suppliers to the German tobacco trade.

Management stayed within the family across generations. According to the same records, Ekrem Konçak's son Sedat Konçak took over in 1974, and the company's day-to-day management passed to the founder's daughter in 1980; her name is given in sources as "Nurham." Since both dates rest on a single compilation, they cannot be considered confirmed against official commercial records.
Taking Over the Andreas Bauer Brand

In the early 1970s Türkiye banned the export of raw meerschaum abroad; the aim was to keep carving and its added value within the country. This decision left European workshops working with block stone without raw material. The Andreas Bauer brand, founded in Vienna in 1906 by Andreas Bauer and run from 1942 by the founder's son Ernst Bauer, could not overcome this shortage either. The brand rights passed first to Otto & Kopp, which distributed meerschaum pipes to German tobacconists, and then to Sedat Konçak in 1990. So pipes carrying the Vienna name began to be carved in Eskişehir.

Collector sources state that the "Made in Austria" mark was retained on boxes prepared after the transfer. To distinguish Vienna-era examples from later ones, collectors look less at the stamp than at construction details: early pipes used a genuine amber stem and a bone screw fitting, while the later period used amberoid or acrylic stems with a delrin push fitting. The differences between these materials are covered in the entry on stem materials.
Pipes and Distinguishing Features

Koncak's output was not confined to classic pipe shapes; the brand is also known for non-standard, figural shapes. One example examined in restoration write-ups shows leaf reliefs running along the bowl and shank, a reclining Pegasus figure on the front, a twisted-pattern silver band, and a box with the brand's crest sewn onto the interior lining. These details rest not on manufacturer catalogs but on observations drawn from individually examined pipes.

There is no verifiable current information about the company's present activity. Even so, the brand continues to be recognized in the estate market as one of the known names of twentieth-century Turkish meerschaum production.

r.x: Spanu

is an Italian pipe workshop founded in 1979 by Sardinian master Tommaso "Tom" Spanu and carried on today by his son. The trading name of the company set up to market the pipes is Novarte S.N.C. di Spanu Tommaso, though the products are commonly known as "Tom Spanu." The work that has done the most to promote the brand is briar pipes with bodies clad in cork oak bark.
From Chiaramonti to Varese

Spanu was born in 1944 in Chiaramonti, in northern Sardinia. Sources agree that while still young he left the island and, in the early 1960s, went to Gavirate, in the province of Varese in northern Italy, where pipe workshops were then concentrated; the job had been arranged by a relative. His years there brought him into the circle of Alberto Paronelli, one of the most influential pipe designers and dealers of the period. Paronelli both got him trained alongside experienced carvers and personally worked with him on shape and design.

The result was that he took part in making Paronelli's distributed premium Clairmont line. It is reported that the brand name is a Frenchified form of Spanu's home town, and that according to records he was able to strike his own name on some of these pipes as well. Over the more than fifteen years he spent in the north, he shared the same milieu as names like Giuseppe Ascorti and Luigi Radice, who would go on to found the Caminetto brand. This generation is the one that drove the leap forward in Italian handmade pipe making in the 1960s and 1970s.
Return to the Island and the Workshop

In 1979, with support from his brothers, he returned to Sardinia and set up his own workshop in Laerru; the business moved to Sassari in 1999. The reason for the return was raw material: Sardinian briar holds a place apart among Italian makers for its heat resistance and its color leaning toward red. It is known that during the Laerru years he harvested and dried his own briar, carrying out the cutting and curing stages of the burls at the workshop. Hand tools dominate the working method; shape is often decided not by prior sketching but by following the burl's grain, so that no two pipes are the same.
Cork Cladding and Other Woods

The workshop's distinctive work is what is called "sughero" in Italian — cork cladding. The briar body is clad in bark from the island's extensive cork oak (Quercus suber) forests; the resulting pipe is lighter than an ordinary briar body and leaves a rough texture in the hand. The technique is also considered a link to Sardinia's long-standing cork craft.

Spanu did not stop at briar. He also worked with other woods such as wild olive, cherry, myrtle, juniper, oak, beech, and boxwood, sometimes combining more than one wood in a single pipe. Among these, the rarest are lemonwood pipes, distinguished by their white-to-pale-yellow color; these examples also carry the additional stamp "LIMONE."
Afterward

Tom Spanu died on 26 August 2015 at the age of 71. Some of his work is exhibited at the Italian pipe museum in Gavirate, where he spent his apprenticeship years. The workshop is carried on in Sassari by his son Massimiliano Spanu, who worked alongside his father for many years.

r.x: D'Capo

is the brand of handmade pipes Argentine maker Pablo Minotti carves one at a time at his bench in Buenos Aires. The name recalls the musical term "da capo," marking a return to the start of a passage; the family behind the brand does in fact come from musical-instrument and furniture craftsmanship. As production has never been large in scale, D'Capo-stamped pipes are considered uncommon pieces today.
Family Background

The Minotti family comes from the town of Cabiate, in the Como region of northern Italy. Records indicate the family has been known since the late 19th century for ebony furniture-making and lutherie (stringed-instrument making). The town lies within the woodworking basin of the region that gave rise to the Como school of Italian pipemaking; Minotti's later turn to pipes is thus not entirely disconnected from the family trade. The brand's own promotion has emphasized this dual belonging, describing its products as Italian-crafted pipes carved in Argentina.
From Bench to Market

Minotti is said to have carved his first pipes in 1994, in the period he took up pipe smoking, for himself. After keeping this up as a pursuit for a long time, he decided in 2003, at the urging of those around him, to sell what he made. That same year he presented his work at a slow-smoking competition held in Barcelona, and the reception there marked the start of the brand's move abroad. In the years that followed, D'Capo pipes reached, besides Argentina, Spain, Italy, Poland, Sweden, the United States, Colombia and Uruguay.

Minotti has also prepared special series for clubs: chief among these are the fifth-anniversary pipe for the Pipa Club Buenos Aires, founded in November 2000, and special pieces made for the pipe community in Mexico.
Approach to Making

D'Capo pipes are made from briar blocks, carved one at a time by hand rather than within a mold-based series-production system; the phrase the brand uses to describe itself is "hand-carved." There is no reliable record of where the briar used was sourced. Working this way, D'Capo represents the one-man workshop tradition against factory-scale operations in Argentina such as Luigi Pipes.

Argentina never built a briar-pipemaking tradition on a European scale, and production has remained largely limited to a handful of workshops and individual makers. D'Capo is remembered within this narrow circle as one of the few names that has managed to reach beyond it; the brand's name is generally mentioned in this context in writing on Argentine pipemaking.

Records indicate Minotti stopped making pipes in the early 2010s; since this date rests on secondary-market listings, it is not certain. The address dcapo.com.ar used for the brand has also been offline for a long time.

r.x: Ed's Hand Made

is the name given to pipes finished by hand by Edward August Kolpin Sr. in Santa Monica, California. Despite being one of the most recognized names in American pipe retail, Kolpin's real attachment was to the bench; after passing on the chain he founded, he returned to making pipes alone once again. For this reason Ed's Hand Made is considered less a factory brand than one person's signature.
From Pharmacy to Tobacco

That Kolpin was born in 1910 in Kenosha, Wisconsin, is the commonly cited information in pipe literature. He chose pharmacy as a profession, studied it at the University of Southern California, and worked for many years at his father's pharmacy. Yet his real interest did not lie in the prescriptions behind the counter. Records indicate that in 1927 he turned the pharmacy's soda-fountain section into a corner where tobacco could be smoked; at the same time he began studying blends on his own and selling them to pipe shops. When this second pursuit outpaced pharmacy in income, a change of profession became unavoidable, and around 1930 he opened the doors of Ed's Pipe Shop on Santa Monica Boulevard.

His 1947 divorce left him financially wiped out. The European trip he took while in debt, however, produced an unexpected outcome: the first pieces of a pipe collection that would grow to thousands of items over the years came from this trip. After returning to the country he built Tinder Box on his family's lot on Wilshire Boulevard, with a facade recalling an old English cottage. The business's founding year differs across sources: local historical records point to 1928, while pipe literature writes that the Wilshire shop opened in 1948. It is known that the store building standing today was built in 1951 and its well-known neon sign in 1953. The shop was one of the haunts of the Hollywood crowd of the period; for named customers, see the entry famous pipe smokers.
The Chain, the Split, and the Scratched Signature

The name Tinder Box was used in other cities as well starting from the late 1950s; records indicate the business primarily turned into a wide franchise network in the 1970s and reached a large number of stores across the country. Kolpin handed the company to his sons Karl and Ed Jr. in 1967; accounts state the brothers sold the chain a few years later to a Canadian investment group. The original shop in Santa Monica, however, split off from the chain.

After this split, Kolpin ran Ed's Original Tinder Box at the corner of Wilshire Boulevard and Harvard Street, and began making pipes with his own hands again. The briar pipes he produced in this period again carried the name Ed's Hand Made; but instead of a metal stamp, the name was scratched in by hand, often together with the year of manufacture and the name of the person who had commissioned the pipe worked into the body. This practice is considered a distinguishing mark for collectors, since it makes the pipes individually documentable; a similar tradition of personal signing is also seen at other benches within the American handmade pipe scene.
Aftermath

Edward Kolpin Sr. died in 2007 at his home in Santa Monica, aged ninety-seven. The shop was run by his family for a while longer and closed in May 2017, after a history of roughly ninety years. Ed's Hand Made pipes today circulate only in the secondary market; their scratched signatures and dates are among the concrete examples frequently cited in the debate over handmade versus machine-made, a definitional problem in pipes.

r.x: Tobey

is a name that does not fit the usual brand narratives of the briar world. Behind it is not a factory or a registered stamp, but a Northern Paiute master living at the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in Nevada: Hilman Tobey. The pipes Tobey makes are not objects produced for commercial smoking but stone-bowled pipes used in prayer and ceremony. In this respect, this entry describes not pipe collecting but a living link in the tradition of the sacred pipe of Native Americans.
The Maker and How the Craft Is Learned

The pieces made at Tobey's bench are not tied to a single material: alongside stone, he is reported to use hardwoods and various minerals as well. What he produces with them is not new designs but examples that follow the traditional forms of ceremonial pipes. The only information available on how long he has practiced this craft comes from secondary sources pointing to more than thirty years; the same sources also state that he graduated from the Stewart Indian School in Carson City. Neither piece of information has been confirmed by independent archives. Likewise, his participation in the annual Sun Dance (Sundance) ceremonies held in the Pine Ridge area of South Dakota rests solely on the same sources.
Material and Construction

In this tradition, the body of the bowl is carved not from briar but from carvable soft stones. Sources do not name which quarry Tobey's stone comes from; this general family of material is covered under the heading catlinite and related stones. After the bowl is roughly cut, it is shaped with hand tools, the channel and smoke hole are drilled, and the surface is smoothed by abrasion. The stem piece is prepared separately and fits into the bowl; joining the two pieces only during the ceremony is described as a practice belonging to the tradition as a whole rather than to individual makers. In the documentary, Tobey's account of materials and tools proceeds intertwined with the place of ceremonial pipes in prayer; here the pipe is positioned not as a smoking implement but as the carrier of the prayer. This distinction also explains why the term peace pipe, common in Western literature, is considered misleading.
Documentary and Transmission

Tobey's name entered pipe literature largely through a short documentary that began circulating in early 2015. Filmed with an apprenticeship grant from the Nevada Arts Council's folklife program and credited to Gabe Lopez Shaw,
Nevada Stories: Pipemakers of the Great Basin

documents the master passing on his construction techniques to his apprentice, Norman Zuniga; the production was completed with support from the National Endowment for the Arts. According to the film's promotional text, Tobey had just turned a hundred years old at the time; no record establishing his birth year appears in the sources. The documentary's real subject is not one master's skill but transmission itself: knowledge passes not from bench to bench but from hand to hand. Tobey's work represents a much older strand that lies outside the briar- and mass-production-centered narrative of pipe making in the United States.

r.x: Manger

is a pipe maker founded by Anton Manger in the village of Wollbach in Germany's Lower Franconia region. Production began in the autumn of 1957. The brand is known for making both understated series models and individually hand-shaped freehand pipes under the same roof.
Founding and Growth

The founder was a craftsman trained in wood carving and turning; he entered the trade not through pipe making but by repairing whatever came to hand during the shortages of the postwar years. Since sound pipes were hard to find in Germany at the time, the repair bench quickly turned into a map of demand. Manger built the cutting tools and lathes needed for production himself over many years, and only reached regular production in 1957.

The business did not remain a small village workshop. According to the record, at its peak in the 1970s it employed nineteen people, with daily output reaching several hundred pipes. This scale is also why the brand is counted among the last professional pipe makers in Germany to have grown "from scratch." In the following decades production contracted again, returning to a family scale.
Style and Product Range

The workshop's founding principle was simple from the start: to make useful, durable, unpretentious briar pipes. The product range was therefore kept broad; at one end sat plain series models in classic dimensions, at the other freehand examples hand-shaped to the grain flow.

Manger pipes give an impression of handwork that favors function over the polished elegance of the Danish school; among collectors they are known primarily for their smoking qualities. The brand first became widely known across Germany in the early 2000s, when the founder's son Arno Manger began promoting the pipes on online auction platforms.
Collection and Written Legacy

Anton Manger was not only a pipe maker but also a writer on pipe history. He authored three books devoted to the history of tobacco, the burl-wood pipes of Ulm, and the meerschaum tradition of Ruhla. For the Ulm tradition, see also the PipoWiki entry Ulmer Maserholzpfeifen.

The founder also built up a collection that began with two porcelain pipes he received from his grandfather at age fourteen. 1,630 pieces from this collection, amassed over thirty years, were sold off in 1984 and formed the core of the Erstes Deutsches Tabakpfeifenmuseum, which opened in 1996 in the historic school building in Oberelsbach. Spread across nine rooms on two floors, the exhibition covers pipe production and tobacco-culture artifacts from the German-speaking world from the 17th to the 20th century.
Anton Manger died in 2021 at the age of ninety-two. Today the brand is remembered as much for the documentation work he left behind as for the pipes it produced.

r.x: Fribourg & Treyer

was one of London's oldest tobacconist houses. Traditionally dated to 1720, the shop operated at its Haymarket address for two and a half centuries and earned its main reputation through snuff. Among pipe enthusiasts it is remembered for the blends and pipes it put on the market under its own name.
Founding and the Forming of the Name

The business traces back to the Fribourg family, said to be of Swiss origin. The founding date of 1720 rests on tradition rather than documentation: the oldest surviving account book from the shop is dated 1764. A firmer trace exists in a tax record from 1767, which shows Peter Fribourg paying tax on a property on the Haymarket. The second name comes from the German-born Gottlieb Treyer, who married Martha Evans of the Evans family, already partners in the business. Treyer's surname was added alongside the long-established Fribourg name, giving the firm the title it would carry until its closure.
Reputation as a Snuff House

The house's main trade for a long time was snuff. Around 1820, roughly nine-tenths of sales came from snuff, with smoking tobacco making up the small remainder. Cigarettes and cigars entered the shelves only from the mid-nineteenth century onward. The shop was also known for Turkish tobacco; these tobaccos have long been considered the backbone of fine blends in English pipe smoking and are still examined today under the heading of Oriental tobacco. Its customers included figures such as the actor David Garrick, King George IV, and Beau Brummell, the era's model of dress. The building at 34 Haymarket, its façade largely preserved, still holds listed-building status today.
Pipes and Closure

Fribourg & Treyer never had its own pipe workshop. Following a practice common in the trade, the shop had its pipes made by outside manufacturers and stamped only its own name; who actually produced these pipes went unrecorded in most cases. This approach marks the essential difference from firms such as Barling or Comoy's, which manufactured in their own factories: here the brand is a name for selection and retail rather than for manufacture. The collector interest the stamp attracts is therefore tied more to the shop's history than to any technical feature of the pipe.

Accounts of the firm's final period do not fully agree. It is said to have passed into the hands of Imperial Tobacco in the 1970s and to have moved to Regent Street when it could no longer cover the rent on Haymarket; these details have not been confirmed by independent sources. What can be confirmed is that the shop closed in 1981 and that the snuff and tobacco recipes changed hands. The brand name is carried on today by Wilsons of Sharrow, the long-established Sheffield snuff maker. The house's old blends remain a subject of curiosity among enthusiasts tracing the English blend tradition.

r.x: Sesa

is the pipe brand carrying the name of Branko Sesa (b. 1962), who works in Turin. Born in Croatia, Sesa settled in Turin in 1994 and began making pipes in 2000. His workshop remains one-man to this day: both new pipes and repair work come from the same hand. This dual mode of working is the main factor that defines the brand's identity.
An Apprenticeship in Turin

Before taking up the bench, his profession was teaching philosophy; woodworking was a leisure pursuit. He learned the finer points of the craft, shortly after starting with pipes, from Italian maker Mauro Gilli. His time with Gilli built his technical foundation; aesthetic decisions, by contrast, were left to Sesa himself. Although he holds both Croatian and Italian citizenship, he considers himself an Italian pipe maker, on the grounds that he learned the craft in that country. To understand the brand's place, see the entry on the short history of the Italian handmade pipe.
Material and Surface

On the body side, Sesa has experimented with briar, olive wood, lemon wood, and morta — oak semi-fossilized after thousands of years in a bog; on the mouthpiece side, with acrylic, ebonite, and amber. The goal was not simply a good-smoking pipe but a style of his own. Morta is today the brand's most recognizable side; part of the pipes he has produced in this wood carry a nautical theme inspired by boat and ship forms.
On the surface, he uses all three of smooth, rustic, and sandblasted treatments; there are examples where he combines them on the same body. For the distinction, see the entry on surface finishes.
Approach to Shape and Production

In the first decade, production consisted mainly of freehand and sculptural pieces; fossil-like carvings in briar date to this period. When the grain of the wood came out especially beautiful, he also turned to plain classic shapes. In the last decade, the emphasis has shifted to classic shapes; freehand production continues but has moved to second place, and he no longer returns to the figurative carvings in briar. Records indicate annual output stayed around fifty pieces for a long time; when he made the work full-time in 2017, that figure roughly doubled. Since the mid-2000s, the maker has also taken part in pipe gatherings in Italy, chief among them the Smoke Style fair held in Bologna and the Cagli Pipe Festival.

Alongside pipes, he also makes mouthpieces (bocchino) for Toscano cigars and small parts called pigini, in which he can be seen combining different materials. Repair work has also served as a separate school for him: taking apart and gathering pipes made by the hands of other makers has given him close familiarity with technical details.
Stamping

Sesa pipes are stamped with the maker's name; stars struck beside the name indicate grade. As the number of stars increases, the pipe moves to a higher tier. Sesa is a member of the Bugianen Pipa Club in Turin; the club chose him to make its 2019 pipe of the year.

r.x: Royal Copenhagen

, officially Den Kongelige Porcelænsfabrik, is a porcelain factory founded in Copenhagen on May 1, 1775, by the chemist Frantz Heinrich Müller. Known for its tableware and blue-patterned figurines, the institution's mention in pipe literature concerns a small slice of its two-and-a-half-century history: a run of porcelain pipe production that began around 1970 and lasted roughly fifteen years. This brief venture is remembered for bringing together, in a single project, the bulk of the masters who defined Danish pipe design during those same years.
A Porcelain Experiment

Behind the decision to enter the pipe business is a story often told within the pipe community: a pair of porcelain pipes and a tobacco jar the factory prepared for King Frederik IX (1899-1972). According to the account, this gift marked the king's seventieth year, meaning it falls around 1969; and its favorable reception is said to have prompted the move to mass production. Neither the gift itself nor the king's supposed fondness for pipes has been confirmed by an independent record outside pipe literature; the story should therefore be regarded as a founding narrative.

What can be confirmed is the product itself. In 1970 a series of eight models was introduced; these were porcelain adaptations of established shapes such as the billiard, the zulu, and the bent billiard. The model that drew the most attention from the series was Golf Ball, named for its nearly spherical bowl. For the material's earlier use, see the entry porcelain pipe.
The Design Panel Formed in 1971

To expand the series, a design competition was held in the autumn of 1971. Those invited included Anne Julie, Emil Chonowitsch, Jess Chonowitsch, Poul Hansen, Gert Holbek, Lars Ivarsson, Sixten Ivarsson, Svend Knudsen, Ib Loran, Jørn Micke, and Karl Erik Ottendahl. The list covers nearly the whole of the generation known as the Danish school; the competition is therefore regarded as an unusual gathering in the history of the country's pipe design.

Details of the competition rest on a single chain of narrative, and secondary sources repeat the same account. According to this record, close to forty-nine shapes were proposed, the judging was carried out with designer names concealed, and first and third place went to Jørn Micke, second place to Ib Loran. The winning shapes, along with one design by Lars Ivarsson and a few more taken separately from Micke, went into production. Because Micke's name became identified with these pipes, the examples circulating in the collector market today are mostly attributed to him.
The Material's Limits and the End of Production

Although porcelain proved to be an unexpectedly durable material for the bowl, it caused difficulty at the joints. In the early models the tenon was machined in the traditional direction; it has been reported that the joint would loosen during smoking, allowing the bowl to separate. Pipe literature says the direction of the tenon was reversed around 1972 to fix the problem; since this detail too rests on a single source, it carries no claim to certainty.

Production ended in the mid-1980s, after a run of about fifteen years; no exact closing date appears in the records. The factory went through a series of ownership changes and mergers during these years, and today Royal Copenhagen continues as a porcelain brand with no remaining connection to pipes. The pipes of that period are today regarded less as objects for use than as a document of a short side branch of Danish design.

r.x: Dunhill Factory

is the name the community gives to the workshop where Dunhill (White Spot) pipes are made. It is not the name of a single building but of a production tradition spanning more than a century: the workshop that began behind the tobacconist's shop opened on Duke Street in 1907, out of dissatisfaction with the quality of externally purchased pipes, turned into its own workshop in 1910, and moved location several times within London in the following decades.
The Workshop's Journey Within London

According to records, with the company's reorganization in 1912, pipe manufacturing moved to Mason's Yard, and in 1916 another building was acquired at Notting Hill Gate for both office and manufacturing use. The Walthamstow branch in northeast London begins in the mid-1930s: the brand set up its own facility on Forest Road next to Hardcastle Pipes and took a minority stake in that company's capital in 1936. The move to full ownership of Hardcastle and the closure of pipe manufacturing at Notting Hill came in 1946. Today, White Spot pipes are made at Walthamstow; the same site also houses a separate department dedicated to leather-goods production. The workshop's relocations also roughly align with periods in the brand's stamp and grading system; details are in the entry on Dunhill's Additional Stamps.
Material Selection and Curing

Production begins with briar extracted from the root of the heath tree growing in the Mediterranean basin. These blocks, cut into a rough pipe shape, are called ebauchon. The most discussed stage at the workshop is curing: removing the sap and moisture from the wood. The aim of this process, whose details the brand kept undisclosed for years, is to eliminate the bitterness coming from wood residue when a new pipe is first smoked. The general framework of curing is covered in the entry on Briar Curing.

The narrowness of the selection criteria is another frequently cited feature of the workshop. According to an account based on a magazine interview, unconfirmed by independent sources, out of a sack of a hundred blocks, only one or two are judged fit for the brand's top tier; the rest are set aside for other pipes.
Shaping and Surface

The cured block takes its rough bowl and shank shape on the lathe. A hard-rubber (vulcanite) mouthpiece is paired with it; it is stated that mouthpieces were made by hand until 1976, after which the task was turned over to machines for labor-cost reasons. What follows is a long polishing sequence carried out with materials such as grindstone, sand, oil, and wax. The surface shine comes not from varnish but from repeatedly applying and removing layers of wax. According to the same interview-based account, a pipe goes through roughly ninety separate steps before it is finished.

The surface treatment cannot be decided on from the start, because the grain pattern only becomes readable as polishing advances; for this reason, a pipe can be steered during the process toward a finish different from what was initially envisioned. Grain-reading criteria are covered in the entry on Grain in Briar.
The Share of Handwork

Keeping mechanization limited leaves the bulk of the work to the maker's hand. It is therefore ordinary for pipes made by two different makers from the same briar not to match exactly in balance, weight, and color. Those who have visited the workshop in recent years report that production is carried out by small, specialized teams, and that the main difficulty for the continuity of the work is training apprentices.

r.x: Paronelli

is a family workshop that has been making handmade briar pipes since 1945 in the town of Gavirate, in northern Italy's Varese province. The brand is known in Italian pipe making not only for the pipes it produces but also for its founder's effort to document and institutionalize the country's pipe culture.
Founder and Early Years

The workshop's founder is Jean Marie Alberto Paronelli, born in Gavirate in 1914. Records say he went to London at eighteen, learned pipe making within the tobacconist circles there, and, after returning to Italy, worked on the wholesale, design, and production sides of the trade. He founded his own brand in 1945. This date coincides with the period when the Italian pipe industry was recovering after the war and the Italian handmade pipe tradition was beginning to gain ground in the international market.

Records indicate that in the workshop's early years, Alberto Paronelli did the design himself while having the bodies worked by outside craftsmen; a significant share of the pipes sold in this period was stamped with the name Clairmont. In pipes of these same years, it is reported that, alongside the "Italy" mark and a reference to Sardinian briar, a gold-colored "P" or, at times, an anchor-shaped emblem was used.
Museum, Magazine, and Academy

The undertaking that truly carried the Paronelli name beyond the workshop is the pipe museum the founder opened in Gavirate together with his sons; sources place the opening at dates ranging from 1970 to the late 1970s. Regarded as Italy's first museum in this field, the collection holds together the historic pipes the founder gathered over many years, along with production tools, ceramic and porcelain pieces, and printed documents; nearly thirty thousand pieces are said to be displayed today across thematic rooms spread over two floors. In the same period, a magazine devoted to the subject, called
La Pipa

, also began publication. In 1984 Alberto Paronelli led the founding of the International Pipe Academy in Gavirate, whose meeting hall was also housed within the museum. In this respect, the brand is considered to have added an archivist and publisher identity to its identity as a maker.
Approach to Production

The workshop is today run by the founder's grandchildren, with Ariberto Paronelli at its head. Production rests on hand craftsmanship, and the annual count is limited to a few hundred pieces; sources give figures ranging between six hundred and a thousand. The briar used comes from Calabria and Sardinia. Blocks are removed during the plant's dormant period, balanced by boiling, and rested for periods ranging between two and five years.

The shape repertoire draws largely on classic English and Italian molds; alongside billiard and reverse-bowl shapes, long-stemmed churchwarden examples are also said to be made. Smooth-polished, sandblasted, and rustic finishes are all used on the surface. Mouthpieces are generally shaped by hand. Made-to-order, one-off production is among the working methods the workshop continues to keep up.

Paronelli is regarded as a family brand that remains small next to larger-scale Italian producers such as Castello or Savinelli, but that has earned a distinct place in Italian pipe history through its continuity and archival work.

r.x: Directory of Brazilian Pipe Brands

gathers, in alphabetical order, pipe names either born in Brazil or run by Brazilian makers. Pipemaking in the country continues less as a deep-rooted factory tradition than at the benches of a small number of mutually acquainted craftspeople; at these benches, a European sense of shape sits alongside local materials such as wood and horn. The entries below summarise only what has been recorded.
Brands
Flávia Rodrigues

— A brand carrying the name of a Brazilian maker who works with briar. She first sat at the bench simply to try it, and it was the desire to make and a closeness to nature that kept her at it. Her pipes are mostly traditional shapes bearing the traces of the Danish school; horn, the Brazil-native jabuticaba wood, and precious metals are used as accent materials. She learned to use bench tools and to advance her briar technique from her life partner Gustavo Cunha, maker of MarTelo pipes. Tom Eltang, Hans "Former" Nielsen, Becker, and Chris Asteriou — whose work she follows for questions of shape and proportion — are the sources of inspiration she names. She also experiments with freehand pieces, believing she can express her own culture more freely in unmolded shapes.
Giulliano Spitaletti

— A brand carrying the name of a Brazilian-born maker who later became a British citizen. Trained in architecture, he has practised various crafts, including jewellery-making, at his own workshop since his university years, and intensified this pursuit after settling in London. Inspired by his pipe-smoking father, and after smoking pipes himself for a while, he began pipemaking in England; traces of Renaissance art and classic English pipe shapes can be seen in his work.
Ranieri

— A pipe line named after the Ranieri Tabacaria tobacconist shop in São Paulo's Jardins district. Who made these pipes sold by the shop is unknown, and the line is considered to have gone out of production. No other recorded information exists regarding the maker, period, or model.

r.x: Civic

, in full The Civic Company Ltd, is an English pipe and tobacco-accessory company founded in London in 1921. Rather than a long-lived brand in its own right, it is remembered as a turning point in the twentieth-century reorganization of the British pipe industry: the core of the Cadogan group, which brought Britain's best-known pipe brands under one roof, grew out of Civic.
From Imperial Tobacco to an Independent Company

The company's origin lies not directly in pipe workshops but in tobacco retail. Imperial Tobacco was founded in 1901 through the merger of domestic British tobacco firms, in response to American capital's entry into the British market. Within the Salmon & Gluckstein retail network Imperial acquired in 1902 was a unit that prepared briar pipes roughly shaped in France and finished in Britain. This unit, which in time turned into Imperial's "fancy goods" division, operated on Fulham Palace Road in Hammersmith, and in 1921 it was made a separate legal entity under the name The Civic Company Ltd.

The new company's earliest known commercial document is its 1921 price list. Both this and the one from the following year are preserved at the National Pipe Archive in Liverpool, and are the primary documents researchers turn to when dating Civic. The sixteen-page 1921 list includes photographs of the pipes, showing that the company launched with a broad model range from its very first year.
The Core of Cadogan

Civic's real importance emerged in 1928. That year, the merger of several manufacturers and retailers formed Cadogan Investments, and Civic became the backbone of the new structure. In the decades that followed, established brands such as Comoy's of London, GBD, and Loewe & Co. joined the same group; records show Loewe's first change of hands was to Civic. Following the acquisition of Orlik in 1980, records indicate the group's production was consolidated at its facility in Southend-on-Sea.

As a brand name, Civic remained in use — with its own catalogs still being published — from the 1950s into the early 1970s; lists dated 1956, the 1960s, and 1971-72 are among the documents collectors consult.
Stamps and Collecting

Collectors report that Civic pipes carry a "CIVIC" stamp on the body or shank, often together with a notation indicating London manufacture; on examples with a silver band, the hallmark set on the band can help pin down the production year. Pipes dated before 1928 are treated under a separate heading, since they represent the brief period before the group merger. It is also known that in the period when Civic took over Loewe production, some pipes from both brands used the same three-digit shape numbers; what these numbers mean for dating remains a matter of debate.

r.x: Edward's Pipes

is the brand under which Edward Czerny produces handmade pipes under his own name in the city of Villach, in Austria's southern Carinthia state. Behind it stands neither a factory nor a team; the brand is a typical example of workshops that work from a single person's bench, producing in limited numbers and largely to order.
Founding the Workshop

According to Czerny's own account, the venture began with a desire to make his own pipe after buying a handmade Danish one; the shape tradition of such pipes is discussed in the entry on the Danish School. By the same account, he sought guidance from an experienced maker in December 2002 and began building his bench around this time. As there is no independent trade registration or official website, the founding date is not certain.

Czerny has stated that in the foundations of the craft he saw support from Austrian maker Peter Matzhold, and from Raimund Holzer in sourcing tools. The most concrete difficulty for a small-scale workshop is finding a source that will sell material in small quantities. Reportedly, briar came from the Mediterranean basin, acrylic from London, Cumberland rod from Switzerland, and the carnauba wax used in polishing from Austria's Styria state. This shows that even a one-man bench relies on a supply network spanning several countries.
Way of Working

The workshop does not mass-produce; each pipe is handled individually and shaped to the buyer's wishes. Acrylic and Cumberland are known to be used for mouthpieces; the properties of these two materials are compared in the entry on mouthpiece materials. Czerny has also announced that he teaches beginners the fundamentals of pipe making. The brand's recognition rests on this teaching side more than on production volume, built through small-scale knowledge transfer rather than product output.
Source Status and Name Similarity

Nearly everything known about the brand relies on the maker's own promotional text. No independent catalog, archival document, or trade record has been found; for this reason there is no reliable information on production numbers, stamp styles, or whether the workshop is currently active. Nor is there a documented body of examples on which to base a stylistic assessment.

Name similarity is also a source of confusion. The "Edward's" brand founded in the United States, based in Tampa and known for producing with Algerian briar, shares the same name with this Villach workshop but is unrelated to it. There is no connection between the two brands in ownership, period, or production.

r.x: Ph. Vigen

is the signature name of Danish master Jes Phillip Vigen Gertsen. Within the Danish school, he is counted among the least-heard-of top-tier (high-grade) makers despite a bench career of nearly forty years. The reason is not that his craftsmanship was limited, but that most of what came off his hands went to sale under other brands' stamps. Born, according to records, in 1953, the master spent nearly his entire career in this kind of invisibility.
Apprenticeship and Early Years

He learned the trade within W.Ø. Larsen, one of Copenhagen's large workshops. His apprenticeship began in 1972, with his principal teacher being Former, the same workshop's chief designer. When the workshop closed at the end of the 1970s, Vigen had to look for a new bench. He worked briefly for S. Bang, which had taken him on to meet its growing orders, but according to accounts the two parted ways after about a year and a half.
The Pibe-Dan Workshop

His next stop was the workshop of Pibe-Dan, the Copenhagen shop founded in 1943 that brought together the pipes of Danish makers. Vigen's main job there was repair; in addition, he turned out around eight to ten new pipes a month. Under the shop's standard practice, these pipes were double-stamped: both the maker's name and the shop's name were struck. It is in these years that the Ph. Vigen signature was first used. The same workshop is known to have housed young makers of various periods, such as Tom Eltang and Preben Holm; Vigen stayed there until the shop closed in 1991.
Top-Tier Production for Bjarne

After Pibe-Dan closed, he tried working independently. The period was one in which demand for top-tier pipes was declining in many markets, and this venture was not long-lived. According to accounts, in 1993 he reached an agreement with Bjarne to produce the brand's top-tier line and carried on his work from his rural workshop in southern Denmark. Pipes from this line carried the "Bjarne Nielsen" stamp, had no brand logo on the mouthpiece, and were classified with a quality grading running from A to D. Other makers, such as Ole Bandholm and Tonni Nielsen, are known to have also worked on this same line; as a result, attributing a single Bjarne top-tier pipe to its maker is often not possible.

This arrangement ended with Bjarne Nielsen's death in 2008 and the closing of the business. Vigen did not return to pipe making after this date, nor did he move to set up a new brand under his own name. He is remembered as one of the last examples of the "workshop-to-workshop master" model that persisted for a generation in Denmark. What remains explains why his name is heard so little: the briar pipes carrying his own stamp are relatively few, and most of them date to the Pibe-Dan years; his mature-period craftsmanship, meanwhile, circulates under another brand's name.

r.x: Dunhill shape numbers

are codes struck on the shank of the brand's pipes to indicate which mould the body came from. The compilation the community calls, in short, the "Dunhill Shapes List" arose from collector Eric W. Boehm scanning the brand's published catalogues to gather these numbers into a single index. It is not an official document issued by the brand itself, but a compilation built through collector effort; its scope and precision are therefore limited to what can be found in the catalogues. For the brand's history, see the Dunhill (White Spot) entry.
Scope of the List

The compilation rests on Dunhill catalogues dated 1928, 1950, 1960, and 1969. The rows follow a fixed layout: first the shape number, then a short description of the body, the group size, the length in inches, and the catalogue years in which the shape appears. The digit at the end of the row indicates the shape family the body belongs to, and matches today's numbering. Grouping likewise follows these families: straight and bent billiards, apple and pot bodies, dublins and zulus, bulldogs and rhodesians, long-shanked canadians, liverpools and lovats, princes and pokers; a separate cluster is opened for singular bodies that fit none of these.

Dunhill's own shape numbers begin at 31 and run to two or three digits; records indicate that 1 through 30 were reserved for pipes the brand had made outside in its earliest years. There are also bodies coded with letters alongside the numbers. R for pot, K for apple, and LB and LBS for large billiards are the best known of these. The panelled, polygonal-shanked, and matching-carved-bit bodies gathered under the heading "Quaint Shape" in the 1928 catalogue make up the bulk of these letter codes.
Reading the Number

The brand overhauled its numbering in the mid-1970s. According to dating guides, the old numbers were dropped in 1976-77 and replaced by a new system in which three-, four-, and five-digit codes appeared together; the five-digit form settled in for stampings after 1978. The form most often encountered today is four digits, read as follows:
The first digit gives the group size; group 1 is the smallest body, group 6 the largest.
The second digit shows the bit type: 1 tapered, 2 saddle.
The last two digits indicate the shape family; per the list's key, 01 is apple, 03 billiard, 04 bulldog, 05 dublin, 09 canadian, 11 lovat.

Accordingly, the number 4103 means a group-4-sized, tapered-bit billiard. What the added digit means in the five-digit form is not certain; it has been suggested it distinguishes deviations from the standard body within the same family.
The ODA and 800 Series

A separate series was used for large bodies falling outside the usual group sizes. ODA-stamped pipes, begun in 1950, are numbered, with gaps, between 801 and 866. This series should not be confused with the brand's early Dunhill OD pipes, individually carved to a customer's request in the 1920s; the ODAs were made not to order but with fixed moulds. The compilation's ODA section rests on the notes of John C. Loring, who worked on the brand's records. The group values Loring gives for these shapes are mostly 4, occasionally 5; that is, the ODA stamp alone does not indicate the largest size, and some group-6 bodies are in fact larger than a typical ODA. The bit difference is also reflected in the number: the saddle-bit form is stamped by prefixing a 6 to the shape number. The list notes that 842, the saddle-bit counterpart of the tapered-bit 806 apple, later carried the stamp 6806, and that 843, the counterpart of the 835 billiard, carried the stamp 6835.
Using the List

The shape number alone gives no date; for the year of manufacture the stamps must be read together, and the method for this is covered in the entry Dunhill patent stamps and dating. The same number has also been given to different bodies at different times: 59 and 60 appear in the list as both straight and bamboo-shanked billiards, while 250, 251, and 635 appear a second time under the name "Windscreen." Group sizes do not map neatly onto shapes and overlap between them; since the group number is known to have first appeared on stamps in 1951, values assigned to older bodies are a retrospective approximation. The compilation itself also contains measurements left with a question mark and numbers of uncertain correspondence. The list is therefore used not as a definitive catalogue but as a reference index.
