r.x: JanPipes

is the stamp Czech pipe maker Jan Klouček has applied to his pipes since 1999. The workshop operates in Kostelec nad Černými lesy, a small town near Prague. What sets Klouček apart among Central Europe's contemporary workshops is that he runs a standard line of recurring classic shapes alongside a small number of individually designed pieces, all from the same bench.
Training and the Workshop's Founding

Klouček learned the craft in France, around Saint-Claude, considered the cradle of the pipe industry. As he transitioned into his own production, his most concrete support came from the established French manufacturer Chacom; the firm's owner, Yves Grenard, was his chief technical advisor in the workshop's early years. This is why JanPipes' approach to craftsmanship sits closer to French bench tradition than to the Danish school. As the story goes, the maker's first encounter with pipes began in a Prague pipe and tobacco shop; this detail has not been confirmed in independent sources.

The town where the workshop was founded has its own craft history: records indicate that in the nineteenth century, small workshops producing ceramic pipe bowls operated in Kostelec nad Černými lesy. Klouček's work is regarded as a contemporary continuation of this local tradition.
Production Program

Production splits into two branches. The standard line consists of a small number of classic, conservative shapes; the same bowls are repeated with varying surface finishes and color schemes. Aimed mainly at the Czech market, this line is considered the technical foundation that keeps the maker's hand in practice; the repeated production of classic shapes in high numbers over the years has built up the base the workshop draws on when moving into free design.

The second branch consists of custom designs made in limited numbers. These pieces are finished entirely by hand from start to finish; the shape idea comes from architecture, technical objects, and nature. The most-cited example of architectural inspiration is the "Gaudí Dreams" series, which emerged after a 2006 trip to Barcelona and references the buildings of Antoni Gaudí. In these works, the grain of the briar block is the determining factor in the design; the pieces are often finished with silver rings and fittings, and sometimes with exotic wood inlays. Since the shape emerges from the material rather than a mold, this approach is regarded as close to the freehand ethos.
Courses and Club Work

Another well-known side of the workshop is the amateur pipe-making courses it has run since 2006. Initially open to the Czech pipe community around Dýmka.net, these sessions have over time reached an international group of participants. Each participant gets to see every stage of production firsthand and finish a pipe of their own design; more than fifty sessions are reported to have been held over the years. Klouček has also prepared special pipes for clubs and events; club pipes made for the Barcelona Pipa Club and Dýmka.net, and the competition pipes for the 2006 world slow-smoking championship held in Mariánské Lázně, are among those cited.

r.x: Jönsson
is the workshop run single-handedly by Swedish carpenter Lars Jönsson (b. 1955). His pipes carry the
Lomma

stamp, named after the small town where the maker's family has lived for four generations. Working in this small settlement just north of Malmö, Jönsson learned the craft under two Danish masters, which is why his style is considered closer to the Danish school line than to a Swedish one.
What the Name Carries

The name Lomma carries more than a hometown marker. Sixten Ivarsson, regarded as the founding figure of the modern workshop pipe, was also born in this corner of southern Sweden in 1910, before settling in Copenhagen in the 1930s and laying the foundation of the Danish school. The stamp thus commemorates both the maker's own roots and the starting point of Scandinavian pipemaking. That a tradition founded in Denmark by a Swedish-born master should, generations later, continue through a maker again working in Lomma, is cited as a detail reinforcing the region's place in pipe history.
From Carpentry to Pipes

Jönsson has spent his entire working life with wood: furniture, ornaments, toys, and window restoration on old houses. His connection to pipes was established in 1998, during his devoted pursuit of sailing, when he met Tom Eltang. He first entered the workshop doing rustication work; as his assignments broadened over time he learned every stage of finishing a pipe from start to finish. His second mentor was Hans "Former" Nielsen. Drawing simultaneously from two different branches of the Danish school is regarded as the main factor explaining the workshop's present shape sensibility.

For a long time he worked on the Sara Eltang series, and later on the Former-Eltang series, which carries the joint signature of Eltang and Nielsen. His carpentry background also brought requests for work outside pipes: the case he made for one of Eltang's sets of seven, and the case he made in 2008 for the set assembled by members of the Swedish Pipe Club, stand at the head of these.
The Independent Workshop

2011 was the turning point. The Swedish Pipe Club approached Jönsson to design that year's club pipe; though hesitant at first, he accepted the offer, and the prototype he prepared was quickly approved by members. Records indicate an order of fifty-eight units resulted. This was the first pipe he designed entirely on his own, and it is regarded as the beginning of his independent pipemaking career. From that same year he turned to developing his own shapes.

Production runs single-handedly and on a small scale. Jönsson's work is built on briar and stays true to the Danish tradition's fluid line sensibility; he is known for shapes with rounded lines. Both plain polish and the rustication that opened the door to his craft appear among his surface finishes. The pipes are stamped "Lomma Sweden."

r.x: Roush

is the brand of handmade briar pipes American maker Larry Roush produces under his own name. Working alone in his Ohio workshop, Roush combined a background in jewelry-making with pipemaking; his craftsmanship, joining wood with silver and gold, makes him one of the recognized names of the American handmade pipe scene.
From Collecting to the Workshop

Roush came to pipemaking from jewelry-making. Knowing how to work silver and gold through his trade, he first fitted the pipes he collected with bands made by his own hand — not moulded rings but patterned pieces requiring jeweler's tools. This craftsmanship caught the attention of American maker Michael Butera, whom he met around the same years, and the relationship between the two first turned into a business partnership, then into something resembling an apprenticeship. The guidance Roush received from Butera in his early years is counted, both in the maker's own promotional material and in the pipe press of the time, among the factors that shaped his work.
Hiatus and Return

After the brand became known in the 1990s, it went quiet for a while when the maker withdrew from the market; during this interval Roush returned to jewelry-making and workshop work. It is said that by the end of the first period his numbering had approached four hundred, and when the maker returned to the bench in 2001 he continued the count from where he'd left off rather than resetting it. Production became far more regular after this return than in the first period. Erwin Van Hove's "Go West" review of American workshops, published in the French-language pipe press, is among the pieces that cover this return.
Material and Making

The workshop's briar supply comes mostly from Italy; in the maker's own account, that country is the only current source mentioned. Selecting the raw block, curing it and finishing the surface are stages Roush states he has refined over the years. Grain pattern is the first criterion determining whether a block becomes a smooth-surfaced pipe or a carved one. Only solid silver and 14-karat gold are used in the metalwork; bands are prepared individually for each pipe rather than cut from ready-made tubing. Fossil walrus and mammoth ivory from Alaska are also used as inlay material on some pieces.

Stems are hand-cut. The most commonly used material is vulcanite; alongside the black, there is also a blue-green streaked variety, and on some pipes Cumberland or Bakelite has been chosen. The tenon that seats the stem into the shank is machined from Delrin. Surface options include smooth, colored rustic carving and sandblasting; sandblasting is a finish the workshop adopted relatively late and which developed into a separate grade over time.
Grading and Stamps

The brand uses separate grades based on surface finish. For smooth pipes the criterion is the letters R, O, U, S and H; this sequence spells out the brand's name. Sandblasted pipes are numbered S1 through S5, and carved-surface ones 6 through 10. The L1-L6 range is reserved for pieces the maker considers "special," carrying unusual designs or out-of-the-ordinary features. Beyond these grades there are two more stamps: pipes with bowls far larger than usual are marked "297," and slim pipes made for women are marked "TIFFANY." Based on announcements on the workshop's official site, Roush was still producing new pieces as of early 2026.

r.x: Kharitonov

is the name Moscow-based maker Andrey Kharitonov carries on his handmade pipes. Kharitonov, who began working briar in 2019, turned this pursuit into a full-time occupation within two years; today he is counted among the most closely watched names in contemporary handmade production in Russia. What makes his pipes recognizable is the combination of textures carved into the bowl with dark-toned contrast staining.
A Long Preparation for Pipes

Records indicate he was born in Moscow in 1961 and spent his whole life in the city. His acquaintance with the pipe reaches back to his twentieth birthday, in 1981: that day he received a pipe carved from cherry wood as a gift from his brother, and for the following decades he was rarely without a pipe. During this long period of smoking he also took up repair work; he fitted new stems in place of broken ones and reinforced cracked shanks, working on worn stummels. Following the path his brother had opened, he also tried his hand at carving his own pipes from cherry wood. The real turning point came in 2019, when he noticed a shop in Moscow selling Italian briar; that same year, with blocks he acquired, he made his first pipes from briar.
Building Shape Without a Lathe

The years spent on repair had introduced him to hand tools but had not provided the equipment of pipemaking; at the outset he did not even have a separate workshop. Since classic European shapes were developed to be worked on a lathe, entering this repertoire without one was not possible for him. So his early work took a different turn from the start, toward freehand pieces — experimental shapes emerging from whatever the block allowed. The first pipes he shared on Russian pipe forums did not receive the attention he expected: critics' common point was that the shapes did not sit comfortably in the hand and appealed more to collectors than to smokers. Kharitonov then turned toward designs that put usability and grip first. This shift did not mean a return to twentieth-century shape catalogs; his measure came instead from the contemporary artisan line descending from the Danish school.
Texture, Stain, and Accent Materials

The most distinctive feature of his current work is his approach to surfaces. Instead of the customary surface finishes such as rustication and sandblasting, he places pronounced patterns carved into the briar side by side with smooth polished areas. Contrast staining built on walnut, copper, and plum tones is also considered part of his signature. He works bowls from Italian briar and stems from ebonite. For accent materials he uses silver, cupronickel, and exotic woods; his most frequent choice of ornament is fossilized mammoth ivory. He has a particular fondness for bamboo: he often achieves curves that are hard to obtain with briar and ebonite using this material instead.
Full-Time Making

Records indicate that by the close of 2020 he had completed fifty pipes; their proceeds funded his workshop equipment. In 2021 annual output reached one hundred and ten, and the volume of incoming orders was enough for him to leave his job and move to full-time making. Since then he has been seen to work more freely with design, returning to the unusual shapes of his early period. He himself says he is still searching for a style of his own; records cite Russian makers such as Viktor Yashtylov, Misha Revyagin, and Aleksey Kharmalov among the names he feels a kinship with. For an earlier generation's signature in Russia, see the entry on Grechukhin.

r.x: Old Nellie Pipes

is the name Joe Nelson gives to the pipes he makes by hand at his workshop in a farmhouse in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin, in the United States. Nelson came to pipes as a craftsman at the end of a long life spent with wood; for that reason his brand reads less as a factory tradition than as the story of a one-man bench.
From Carpentry to the Bench

Nelson's introduction to briar dates to 2005; at that point pipes became the latest addition to the list of pursuits of a craftsman with more than forty years of woodworking behind him. His attending the major pipe gathering in Chicago is cited as the turning point that turned this interest into ongoing production; over time Nelson made both instrument-making and pipe making his full-time work.

The experience built up in earlier years came from two directions. Nelson made custom cabinets and furniture semi-professionally, and renovated the 120-year-old farmhouse he lives in with his own hands. He turned to stringed-instrument making (luthiery) in 1995, and at the start of 1998 fitted out his workshop for this work and began building and repairing instruments. His focus on steel-string acoustic guitars is the source of the measurement-and-finish sensibility that later carried over into his pipes.
Craftsmanship and Signature

Old Nellie pipes are known, in trade records and estate listings, for their sharp lines, the precise transition between shank and mouthpiece, and clean finishes. This precision is traced to the millimeter-tight fit habits of guitar making. Nelson's most recognized detail is the iridescent mother-of-pearl (abalone) inlay he sets into the mouthpiece — another technique borrowed directly from instrument making. Among mouthpiece materials, such inlays carved into hard rubber count as both a signature and a mark of craftsmanship.

Production revolves around the classic English-American repertoire. Examples circulating on the market include billiard, lovat, dublin, brandy, and bulldog shapes. In terms of finish, smooth, sandblasted, and rustic surfaces have all been used; sandblasting, as with many American makers, has been one Nelson turns to often, in step with the rise of the American sandblasting school in the 2000s.
Stamps and Scope

Pipes are stamped "Old Nellie Pipes." Three-letter codes accompanying the pipes appear in dealer records; while these seem to indicate surface and grade distinctions, no complete grading table explained by the maker is known. Because production rests on a one-man workshop, annual numbers are limited, and the pipes have circulated mainly through American pipe gatherings and a handful of specialty dealers.

Old Nellie is less a brand that has achieved wide fame than a typical American example of the artisan pipe approach: small-scale production that emerged from a maker coming from another craft applying the hand discipline he acquired there to briar.

r.x: Pipe Tristan

is the name of the handmade pipe workshop that Tristan Lefebvre runs single-handedly in Saint-Étienne-de-Fontbellon, in the Ardèche department of southeastern France. The business entered the French commercial register on January 12, 2016; the registration remains active today, and the workshop has no employees. Lefebvre's relationship with pipes goes back well before he began making them: by his own account, he started smoking a pipe at sixteen and was a collector for a long time. He is said to have taught himself pipe making largely on his own, building on his background in woodworking. The same record shows the workshop's original Le Chambon address closed at the end of 2020, and the current Saint-Étienne-de-Fontbellon location opened in the autumn of 2022.
Two Production Lines

The workshop presents what it makes across two lines. In the line called Handmade, the pipe is shaped entirely by hand from start to finish, beginning with a raw briar block. In the Timeless line, the starting point is a pre-turned rough body; in pipe making this semi-finished piece is called a stummel. This division is a common arrangement among small workshops working in the transitional space between artisan and factory pipes: the buyer knows from the outset from which point the piece passed through the maker's hands.
Granite, Ammonite, and Other Finishes

What the brand is best known for is its surface finishes. Granite, as its name suggests, is a coarse-grained rustication that evokes a stony surface, with the texture spread evenly across the whole body in a single character. Ammonite has a much finer grain, with the main effect carried by curved grooves that wrap around the bowl. The name comes from fossil ammonites, whose shell cross-sections resemble this pattern of grooves. Alongside these two, the catalog also includes a finish called Bark, classic sandblasts, and smooth polished bodies.
Material, Shape, and Color

The workshop's material repertoire is not limited to briar: bog oak, olive wood, and the strawberry tree of the Mediterranean maquis (French: arbousier) have also been used. Some of the shapes come from the classic English-French repertoire; billiard, dublin, liverpool, poker, cutty, brandy, apple, and bullmoose are the main ones. Another recurring shape is the "55," known from the numbered shapes in the Castello catalog.

The workshop's one shape of its own is the Chestnut. Its essence is a full bowl that tapers toward the base and connects there to a thin, straight shank; the name is said to come from the chestnut trees of the region where the maker lives. Chestnut has been made not only in the Granite and Ammonite finishes but also in bog oak and olive wood bodies. Color use is another distinguishing feature of the brand: it departs from the common dark brown and black for stems, pairing amber-look acrylic or single-color resin stems with briar left with very little stain, or conversely with a deep black background. The resulting combinations are considered warm but understated.

r.x: Jobey

is a pipe brand that catered mainly to the North American market throughout the twentieth century, with its owner and manufacturer changing hands repeatedly. Today the name is most associated with two things: the screw-in "Jobey Link" fitting joining stem and shank, and its line of free-shaped pipes made in Denmark in the seventies. Because its early history is carried not by a tidy corporate archive but by scattered registration records and period publications, many points of the brand's past remain in dispute to this day.
The Origin Dispute

Pipe literature repeated for years that the brand was born in England around 1920 and later moved to the U.S. No document supporting this account has ever been produced, and it remains an unverified claim. The earliest trace that can be tied to a document is instead in the U.S.: Louis and Ulysse N. Jobey, living in Brooklyn, filed for a pipe design on 9 November 1914, and the design was registered as USD46998 on 23 February 1915. The same surname also appears in the management of another, separate pipe company incorporated in New Jersey, listed in a company directory from the twenties; as the account goes, Louis Jobey went bankrupt in the meantime, in 1918. These scattered records suggest the name may have been American from the start, but they are not enough to reach a firm conclusion; the matter is a typical example of the debate over how patent and registration records are read for dating.
A Name That Changed Hands

By one account, a 1941 trade magazine states that Norwalk Pipe Corporation made both Jobey and Shellmoor pipes; the article names Louis Jobey as head of the company. Over the following forty years the brand changed hands many times, at times separating maker from seller. Names appearing in records include George Yale Pipes & Tobacco and Norwalk Pipe Co. in New York, Arlington Briar Pipes Corp. in Brooklyn, Hollco International in 1969, and Weber Pipe Co. in Jersey City in the seventies; during these same years much of the distribution ran through the Tinder Box chain. The brand's market also stayed narrow throughout: it never went beyond North America and England, never catching on in continental Europe. Production continued mainly in classic shapes at a mass-manufacturing scale; within the community, Jobey is remembered less as a collector's item than as a sturdy pipe suited to everyday use.
The Jobey Link

The brand's most recognizable technical detail is the connecting piece joining stem and shank. The patent Brooklyn resident Peter V. Genna filed for on 25 February 1969, granted on 3 November 1970, is registered in the name of Wally Frank, Ltd. In this fitting a threaded connector is screwed into the shank's seat; the stem seats by friction onto that piece's smooth end. The aim is to reduce the thread wear and moisture seepage seen with tenons screwed directly into the shank. The "Jobey Link" stamp is therefore useful for dating: pipes carrying this fitting date from after 1969. Stamps mostly show a script "Jobey" name with a series name underneath, and on most examples a three-digit shape number as well; series names encountered on restored pipes include Shellmoor, Stromboli, Asti, and Sterling.
Jobey Dansk and the Later Period

While the brand was in Weber's hands, freehand pipes made at the workshop of Danish maker Karl Erik Ottendahl were offered under the name Jobey Dansk. Ottendahl was also producing for Wally Frank in these same years; this line became one of the routes carrying the Danish style, with its emphasis on the grain of briar, into the American market. According to the account, this line ended when Ottendahl stopped exporting to the U.S. in 1987. Secondary sources write that the Jobey name passed that same year to the Saint-Claude-based Butz-Choquin facility; since this is not supported by a primary document, the claim should be treated with caution. Production is reported to have stopped for a time, then the brand was relaunched in 2002 by F&K Cigar Co. of St. Louis, Missouri. Records indicate the name remains with the same company today.

r.x: Directory of Swedish Pipe Brands

gathers, in alphabetical order, pipe names founded in Sweden, run by Swedish makers, or mentioned in the country's brand records. What survives on record draws a two-sided picture: on one side, individual masters working the benches of 18th-century clay pipe workshops, and on the other, series-production factory brands of the 20th century. Stockholm's Museum of Tobacco and Matches is the principal place where pieces from both ends can be seen together. The entries below summarize only documented facts; details with no basis in the sources are not included.
Brands
Olaf Forsberg

— A clay pipe master. Records show him taking his place at a Stockholm workshop bench in 1739; his name is counted among the recognized figures of 18th-century Swedish clay pipe making. His pieces are scattered across the collections of various specialist museums, with the largest number found at the capital's Museum of Tobacco and Matches (Tobaks & Tändsticksmuseum).
Ratos

— A series-production brand present in the Swedish market for more than forty years, known for a broad range of shapes. It is stated that only aged briar is used for the bowl material, and in some models the bowl interior is lined with meerschaum. According to information from 2009, every pipe in the series was filtered, and production took place at what was then still the oldest active pipe factory in France. Some Ratos pipes have been distributed by the Borkum Riff tobacco brand at pipe-smoking competitions.
Skapi

— The shortened name of Skandinaviska Pipfabriken, based in Uddevalla; it stands for both the factory and the brand under which its pipes reached the market. The factory's founding in 1936 was the work of Max D. Schwab, who came from a family engaged in pipe craft in Germany. Production covered classic shapes as well as system pipes; the business closed in the late 1960s.

r.x: Bay Pipe

is the brand of a Turkish pipe workshop in Eskişehir that carves block meerschaum. The name appears in some records written as one word, "Baypipe," and on the brand's own older pages as "Emre Bay Pipe Meerschaum." Behind the workshop is master carver Emre Mangaltepe, who came to the craft from mine work. The founding year has not been disclosed; archive records show the brand's website was already online by 2013 at the latest.
The Master's Path

According to his published biography, Mangaltepe was born in 1986 in Eskişehir's Mihalıççık district, worked outside the craft between 2003 and 2007, and turned to meerschaum mining in 2007. He describes having learned carving afterward, going from workshop to workshop alongside masters, and traveling to Denmark to see how the craft was practiced elsewhere. He has served multiple terms as chairman of the Eskişehir Meerschaum Handicrafts Association, and spoke about the story of meerschaum at a TEDx event in 2019.
The Workshop's Output

Bay Pipe pipes are not made on a production line but shaped by hand one at a time. According to the master's own account, the raw stone passes through twelve separate stages from cleaning to final polish. The brand's old catalog groups its products roughly into five clusters: classic straight shapes (billiard, bulldog, rhodesian, canadian, poker), embellished pipes decorated with calligraphic and miniature motifs, figural carvings with human and animal heads, freeform freehand pieces that don't follow a set mold, and portrait pipes worked from photographs. Alongside these, the workshop also makes meerschaum cigarette and cigar holders, as well as decorative objects like busts and animal figures. Some pipes are said to use silver bands and bamboo inserts. Portrait commissions, per the master, take between three and ten days, and this likeness work is considered the most demanding part of the job.
Motifs and Markets

The workshop's output goes mostly abroad. According to information the master has given the press, the main buying countries are Denmark, Germany, Italy, China, and the United States. The same accounts note that taste in motifs shifts from market to market: Greek mythological scenes stand out in Europe, Bavarian-flavored models in Germany, zodiac animals and dragons in China, and bison along with Native American symbols in America. Such a practice — choosing motifs by the buyer's country — is common among meerschaum workshops.
The Stone and the Craft Today

Alongside the bench, Mangaltepe is also involved on the raw-material side: he chairs the board of a projected meerschaum quarry operation in the Karatepe neighborhood of Odunpazarı. In an interview in 2024 he said there had been no official mining in the area since 1993 and that they were bringing the illegal extraction under legal footing; the quarry project also drew opposition from surrounding neighborhoods. In the same interview he noted that the youngest of the workers digging the shafts were in their fifties and sixties, while export demand was rising. According to the association's figures, Eskişehir has 135 registered masters listed with the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, some eight hundred people work in the sector, and roughly ninety percent of workshop production is exported. Within this picture, Bay Pipe is one of the workshops carrying on the Eskişehir meerschaum carving tradition. The baypipe.net address given in the Pipedia record no longer works today; the domain had shifted to unrelated content by 2021 at the latest.

r.x: Siyahi

is a name that appears in international pipe brand compilations as a Turkish-origin meerschaum pipe brand. According to the record, the brand belonged to a meerschaum pipe company of the same name; the company's founding year, founder, the city where its workshop stood, and how long it operated remain unknown. In this respect, Siyahi is a typical example of brand names whose products have survived while their corporate trail has been erased.
Spelling of the Name and Details on Record

Information about the brand rests on a single chain: a few lines in a reference compilation on pipe makers and brands, and the encyclopedic sources that have carried this note forward. Although the entry's heading is Siyahi, in the body of the text both the brand and the company title are written as "Sihahi." The difference between the two spellings comes down to a single letter; "siyahi" is a word in use in Turkish, while "sihahi" has no such meaning. For this reason the form in the body is considered a transcription or typesetting error; however, no second document has survived to show which spelling actually appeared on the brand's stamp.

The only technical detail on record is that the pipes were finished with acrylic mouthpieces and synthetic amber parts. The combined use of these two materials points to the period when genuine amber was first replaced by early plastics and then by acrylic; for more detail see the mouthpiece materials entry. This material choice places the brand roughly in the second half of the twentieth century, without allowing for a more precise dating.
The Isle of Man Record

The same compilation reports that some of the pipes sold under the Siyahi name were made on the Isle of Man by "Manx Meerschaum," citing pipe writer Richard Carleton Hacker as the source. The island's place in meerschaum pipe production is documented: Laxey Pipes Ltd., working out of a four-story stone building at the pier head in Old Laxey, produced meerschaum bowls from the late 1960s until 2001 for houses such as Peterson, Barling, and Nørding, and also used names such as Manxpipe, Manxman, and Manxland for its own line. In restoration writing, these pipes are still often referred to simply as "Manx."

What stands out in the record is this: the stone Laxey worked was not from Eskişehir but meerschaum extracted from the Amboseli basin in East Africa by Tanganyika Meerschaum Corporation. Consequently, these pipes bearing the name of a Turkish-origin brand are not Turkish in either their body stone or their workmanship. When the African supply ran out, the workshop released its last meerschaum pipes in 2001, and after an attempt to switch to briar failed to take hold, it closed in 2002. There is no separate manufacturer record corresponding to the name "Manx Meerschaum"; since there is no indication of any other pipe maker on the island besides Laxey, this name is thought to point to the same workshop.
The Problem of Undocumentation

A Turkish-origin meerschaum brand would be expected to be linked to the Eskişehir area; almost all commercially workable meerschaum deposits are found in this province. Throughout the twentieth century, a great many small workshops operated in the region, some exporting under their own brand and others working under contract for foreign firms; most closed without leaving behind a catalogue, a registration record, or an archive. Given this scattered structure of Eskişehir meerschaum carving, it is not surprising that only a few lines have survived about Siyahi today. What is known about the brand will continue to rest on this single record until a stamped example or a period document comes to light.

r.x: Design by FRANZ

is the brand of the pipe workshop Swiss architect Franz von Matt founded in 1998. Over roughly a decade of production, the brand was known for treating the shape of the pipe as a design question rather than repeating established molds; von Matt's name is mentioned together with the period when pipe making briefly gained visibility in Switzerland.
An Architect's Second Career

Raised in Zurich, von Matt worked as a freelance architect holding a technical-college diploma (HTL). This profession, based on measurement and tolerance, later became the foundation for his work at the bench as well; repairing antique clocks with metal and wooden gears in his spare time had also accustomed his hand to fine work. A longtime pipe smoker, von Matt turned his hobby into his main occupation in 1998. He set up his workshop in an old house in the village of Teufenthal in the canton of Aargau, at the foot of the medieval Trostburg Castle; the workshop appears in records under the name Pipe-Factory 22, while products were signed with the label Design by FRANZ. According to records, only four people were making pipes in Switzerland at the time, and von Matt was the only one pursuing it full time.
Briar Selection and Grading

The workshop announced that it used only plateau briar individually selected from Tuscany and Corsica. The tobacco chamber was left without any paint or filler, smoothed only with fine sandpaper. According to the workshop's own account, once cracks, foreign matter, and grain flaws were culled, only about 60% of the blocks processed remained usable. The remaining material was sorted according to a five-tier scale: at the top sat AAA, from straight-grained and blemish-free blocks said to make up at most one percent of the total; AA2 and AA1 allowed for increasingly visible flaws, AAL was reserved for a glossy finish after multiple layers of staining, and AAS for a sandblasted matte surface.
Birds and Shape Experiments
The brand's first product to draw attention was
Timeless

, with a spherical bowl and unusually colored finishes; it is considered a contemporary interpretation of the traditional Appenzell pipe (Lindauerli) with its metal lid. Most of the later designs converged on a bird theme.
Coq de Bruyère
, released in 2000, referred to a species of grouse (Tetrao urogallus) declining in numbers in Switzerland; a long mouthpiece giving the impression of a tail completed the curved body.
Bluebird
, introduced the same year, and the 2002
Pelican
continued in this vein. The most talked-about series was
Schräge Vögel / Odd Birds

, a name that in German can be read both as "strange birds" and as "odd characters"; these short-bodied, sculptural pipes are said to have won the Form Forum Schweiz award in 2001, according to records. In shapes without bird names, such as Willy (2002) and Gina and George (2003), classic molds were developed in a measured way instead. In smoker discussions of the period, it is said that von Matt worked by varying roughly seven basic molds, not differing in method from other makers producing freehand pieces, but distinguished instead by his contrasting stains ranging from orange to anthracite.
The Bench Closes

von Matt regularly attended pipe fairs and craft events, and opened his workshop to visitors on certain days; he is known for regarding his fellow makers not as rivals but as a mutually nourishing community. According to records, from 2000 onward he also gave pipe-making courses at the Ballenberg center in the canton of Bern. In early 2005 he closed the Teufenthal workshop and moved to Zofingen, where he set up a new workshop, and in the same period returned part time to architecture. When he took charge of the planning and building-inspection unit for the municipality of Gränichen in spring 2006, the bench became a secondary concern; he disposed of most of his machinery, finished a few more pipes, and in summer 2007 stopped pipe making entirely. Design by FRANZ thus remains a short but distinct mark in the history of the artisan pipe.

r.x: Jud

is the pipe signature carrying the name of Daniel Jud, a physician working in the town of Erlen, in the canton of Thurgau in northeastern Switzerland. Born in 1958, Jud's actual profession is psychiatry and psychotherapy; pipemaking has remained a side pursuit for him from the start. That said, his interest in machinery and metalwork has turned his workshop into a well-equipped precision-machining space; sources indicate he regularly spends an hour or two there each day.
The Path to Mastery

When Jud began smoking a pipe at sixteen, his first pipes were of the Italian-made Lorenzo brand. During his years as a medical student in Basel he became acquainted with the work of German and Danish masters; Karlheinz Joura and Knudsen are among the makers named as acquaintances from this period. When he mentioned the idea of carving a pipe with his own hands to his tobacconist, he was directed to Hans "Former" Nielsen, who was making Bentley pipes at the time in Kleinlützel in the Swiss Jura. Nielsen both gave him guidance on making and supplied his first briar blocks.

Jud, who began regular production in 1990, later visited Jacques Craen, owner of the Genod workshop in Saint-Claude, several times; for a long time he obtained the bulk of his block supply from there. Still, since he built the main body of his technical knowledge through his own experimentation, he is considered a largely self-taught maker.
Production and Style

Jud only felt his output was ready for the market in 2000. His pipes first found interest within a narrow circle of collectors, and the same circle also gave him access to sources for horn, exotic woods, and surface-finishing materials. His acquaintance with German maker Cornelius Mänz dates from these years as well. Annual output, according to records, ranges between sixty and seventy pipes. The briar he uses is predominantly Moroccan, Algerian, and Spanish in origin.

His interest in pressed tobaccos is also reflected in shape: a significant portion of his pipes are made with large-capacity chambers where flake-type tobaccos can settle comfortably. A nine-millimeter filter chamber can be opened on request. Surface options include plain polish, sanded matte, and rustic; the sanding applied after rustication produces distinctive texture patterns (surface finishes).

Mouthpieces are mostly worked from vulcanite rod, with the multicolored Cumberland material tried from time to time. What truly sets Jud's work apart, however, is its metalwork: titanium, stainless steel, and brass bands have become the brand's signature. Over the years a handful of shapes have become established as the workshop's recurring repertoire.
Work Beyond Pipes

His facility with metalwork has also led Jud into making tools beyond pipes. He is said to have designed a plug cutter for producing clean slices from pressed tobacco plugs, along with a household-scale tobacco press; according to accounts, these tools have made his name known independently of his pipes within German-speaking pipe circles.

r.x: Steven Johnson
was an American master who worked in Philadelphia in the 1970s and 1980s and signed the pipes he made with the stamp
S. JOHNSON

. His name is usually mentioned not as a standalone brand but together with the Philadelphia branch of Wilke, the long-established New York bench. Since his total output remained limited, his pipes are seen only rarely today.
A Workshop Inside Wanamaker's

Wilke Pipe Shop was founded in New York in 1872 by Edwin Wilke, and worked for decades out of its shop on Madison Avenue. The second sales location the bench opened, at Philadelphia's landmark department store Wanamaker's, dates to the 1970s; according to records, the branch opened in 1977. Johnson took on two jobs there at once: he managed the branch, and he worked briar in a small room set up in the middle of the store. Letting customers watch the master at work was not a common arrangement in American retail of the period; it was also the most talked-about aspect of the branch.

Information about his personal background comes from a single newspaper article. According to this account, Johnson made his first pipe at age nine, was considered a master by his early twenties, and in later years worked six days a week, turning out three pipes a day. Though this figure falls well below mass-production scale, it is high for a bench worked by a single pair of hands. Johnson's way of working can be seen as an early example of the workshop approach that would become widespread in the American handmade pipe scene in the following decades.
Stamps and a Case of Confused Marks

Johnson's own work is simply stamped S. JOHNSON. The confusion arises because the same store's name also appears on a much older group of stamps. Pipes prepared for Wanamaker's tobacco counter in the 1930s and 1940s carry the wording
NO. 1 BROAD STREET

, the abbreviation (J.W), and the period's circular MADE IN ENGLAND country-of-origin stamp; these are reported to have been made by Comoy's of London. The history of this wording goes back to a US federal trademark application filed in the name of John Wanamaker in 1933. In short, this stamp belongs to a period some forty years before Johnson's own; it has nothing to do with the pipes that came from his hand.
Afterward

It is said that after leaving the Philadelphia branch, Johnson worked at Zino Davidoff's business; this stage has not been confirmed by independent records. The Wilke brand passed in 1983 to pipe maker Elliott Nachwalter and his wife Carole Burns, and the Madison Avenue shop closed in the early 1990s. The Wanamaker name was also removed entirely from stores in 1995, and the Philadelphia store reopened the same year under another chain's name. Johnson's rarely found pipes today stand as tangible remnants of a short-lived and unusual retail arrangement.

r.x: Enricoro

is the pipe brand of Enrico Marola, who works in the town of Vercelli in Italy's northern Piedmont region. The name is born of the fusion of the master's own name with "orologiaio," the Italian word for watchmaker: Marola's principal trade is watchmaking, and pipemaking has remained a second pursuit running alongside it for years. The brand's emblem reflects this dual identity too; a brass watch-movement bushing is used as the logo.
The Founding of the Bench

According to the record, Marola's acquaintance with briar began in 1998, following an encounter with Bruto Sordini, founder of the Don Carlos bench. In the early years production remained entirely at the hobby level; Sordini's guidance was also largely limited to recipes given over the phone. According to the same account, Marola completed his basic equipment and settled into more regular work in 2007, and formally registered his activity in 2010.

In the same interview a few masters' names are mentioned: help is said to have come from Vilma Armellini of the Armellini bench for disc shaping, and from the experienced maker Luigi Crugnola for bench work. A week spent in 2010 with Swedish maker Ronny Thunér is also said to have been one of the turning points where he pulled his technique together.
Workshop Setup

The Enricoro bench's equipment is considered modest: a column drill, various bits, a disc grinder, and a set of files. Since Marola does not use a lathe or a copying machine, measurements vary from piece to piece; the rough shape is taken on the disc, while proportion and line are established with the file and successive grades of pumice and sandpaper. Because this method is slow, annual output stays low.

The briar used comes from timber workshops the master selects himself. There is no pre-drawn list of shapes; the decision is made by looking at the block's grain and its condition on the day. The repertoire consists largely of classic shapes, and Marola says he chooses these molds for their functional simplicity while still leaving a small personal touch on each one.

Surface finishing follows the same restraint. Staining is kept light enough not to hide the grain, and natural-based mixtures are used for polishing rather than heavy synthetic coatings. In the master's own words, the aim is not an object for display but a pipe that smokes dry and trouble-free, built for everyday use.
Position

Enricoro belongs less to Italy's large workshops than to the tradition of one-man artisan benches. Its pipes have reached collector circles abroad as well as in Italy; sources mention the United States, Sweden, Denmark, Switzerland, France, and India among the countries reached.

r.x: Adam Davidson

is a handmade pipe maker working in the United States, producing only a few dozen pieces a year. His name is associated with rounded designs that reinterpret the classic shape repertoire, along with meticulous internal workmanship. Each pipe is individually hand-shaped; it is less a brand than a signature.
From Design to the Workbench

Davidson grew up in Monticello, Indiana; his interest in pipes traces back to childhood, to old black-and-white films and antique-shop window displays. He studied industrial design at Purdue University. This training is considered the main factor shaping how he later balanced form and function in his work. The Chicago pipe show he attended after graduation marked the turning point where he began to see the pipe as a design object.

He made his first briar pipe, according to records, in 2005: a bent Dublin finished with a three-node bamboo shank and a hand-cut mouthpiece. Around the same time, his path crossed with Todd Johnson, who was then looking for help with his Medici line. This led Davidson to move to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, where he learned pipe making at Johnson's side while also handling the appraisal and restoration of estate (secondhand) pipes. Within a few years he reportedly took over responsibility for that side of the business and became further known for his estate pipe restoration work.
Materials and Craft

The workshop has stayed small in scale from the start. Sources give annual output figures ranging from a few dozen to seventy-five pieces, varying by year. Briar blocks, according to records, are sourced from the Italian supplier Mimmo Romeo. For mouthpieces, German-made vulcanite is the preferred material; pieces are hand-cut from rod stock and the tenon is lathe-turned. Vintage stock bakelite is used only occasionally. The comfort of the bite profile is the most frequently discussed technical detail of his work.

Accent materials include bamboo, horn, silver, boxwood, and dark tropical woods. Surfaces are either left smooth and polished or sandblasted; the sandblasting approach, which removes a generous amount of wood, is akin to the approach taken by European workshops. Bamboo is cited as the maker's favorite material and appears sandblasted on some pieces.
Shapes and Influence

Davidson's repertoire ranges from early English classics to retro Danish freehands, but he is best known for the shapes he has named himself. The Fig, developed out of the Cutty, has become a shape widely reinterpreted by American workshops; BriarWorks is known to have adapted this design into a factory-production model. The flattened and deliberately asymmetric Amoeba, the Almond, the Figu, and the Lorraine, a nod to old French-English forms, are his other signature names. His detachable-stem Cavalier interpretations draw on the German hunting-pipe tradition.

Since the start of his career, the maker has continued to work with other workshops as well; accounts describe periods spent at the bench of Jeff Gracik in California, and of Hiroyuki Tokutomi and Kei-ichi Gotoh in Japan. He exhibits regularly at the Chicago and Richmond shows. He reportedly received the Master of Pipes title from the Chicagoland Pipe Collectors Club in 2019.

r.x: Grunewald Pipes

is a small handmade pipe bench American Paul Greenwood founded in Indiana in 2022. Rather than being a continuation of a classic workshop tradition, the brand was born to answer a specific imaginative world: Greenwood noticed at pipe shows that no examples resembled the pipes depicted in The Lord of the Rings, and decided to fill that gap at his own bench. The bench is presented as a father-and-son venture he runs together with his son, Chris.
Founding

By Greenwood's account, he returned to pipes in early 2022 after a long gap, and that same spring attended a pipemaking seminar held as part of the Chicago Pipe Show together with his son. This seminar was the pair's first experience of making a pipe. The brand was founded that same year, and its promotion has run largely through social media accounts. In trade records, the bench appears as a limited liability company at an address in Martinsville, Indiana; whether the workshop actually operates at this address has not been confirmed by independent records.
Series and Style

The brand's starting point is a group called the "Shire Series." These pipes are set apart by pairing a briar bowl with long stems carved from wood; the aim is to visually approach the long-stemmed pipe described in the literary source. Because a wooden stem requires different workmanship from acrylic, both in drilling and in shaping the bit, these pipes are made in limited numbers.

Greenwood has over time also turned to more conventional shapes, making classic models with short acrylic stems. According to brand records, a second series named "Emberling's" was introduced in 2025. The bench's output is thus split between thematic groups and traditional shapes.
Place in the Trade

Paul and Chris Greenwood are reported to be members of the Indiana Pipe Club and to attend pipe shows regularly in neighboring states. In this respect, Grunewald follows the typical path that has fed the American handmade pipe scene since the 2000s: individual benches that start out with seminars given at shows and promote their product through the club and show network. In working with shapes inspired by fantasy literature, it is also mentioned alongside American workshops in the same vein, such as Luna Pipes.

Because of the short time since its founding, the brand has not yet settled into a fixed stamping arrangement or built a wide secondary-market record; much of the available information rests on the founder's own account and observations from the show circuit.

r.x: Bertoldi

is a pipe maker founded in the town of Timbó, in the southern Brazilian state of Santa Catarina. What brothers Idelfonso and Valmor Bertoldi started as a small workshop in 1984 has run for decades and is considered the most visible name in the country's pipe production. The brand operates under the Só Cachimbos Comercial umbrella; of the founding brothers, Idelfonso Bertoldi is recorded as the business's sole owner.
Founding and Early Years

When founded, the business carried the name Bertoldi & Bertoldi, and its output was exceedingly modest: an average of ten pipes a day, and in only a single model at that. This first model, called "Elite," is recorded only as a straight-shanked shape; it appears to have been an undecorated design close to the billiard family. At the end of the first year the brothers decided to add bent-shank models to the catalogue as well; this step required both hiring their first employee and serious work on production technique. The goal was clear: to bring domestic production up to a standard comparable with the imported pipes then entering the Brazilian market.
A Correction in Mouthpiece Bore

One of the most lasting decisions the workshop made in its early period concerned mouthpiece design. Records indicate that Brazilian-made pipes of that era had a mouthpiece bore of 5-6 millimeters; this measurement both stiffened the draw and left a rough feel in the mouth. Bertoldi redesigned its mouthpieces, switching to the 4-millimeter bore already established on imported pipes. This change, seemingly a small detail, is remembered as the first concrete step in the brand's pursuit of quality in domestic production.
Series and Material

Over time the workshop added the Hobby, Maestro, and Montana series alongside Elite, plus a Bertoldi line bearing the family's surname. According to the company's own figures, the catalogue today holds around 150 models.
On the material side, the brand took a path that set it apart from Brazilian workshops working with native woods. It began importing
Erica arborea

— that is, briar — the root underlying traditional European production, and started making its Maestro series from this wood; the company states in its own promotional material that it is the only importer of
Erica arborea

in Brazil. This claim has not been independently confirmed. Series made with native woods still continue; that Brazilian workshops work with species other than briar is a good example within the broader picture of alternative woods.
Scale and Markets

According to figures the company gave in the early 2010s, the business had 22 direct employees, with monthly output running around 14,000 pipes; about 6,000 of these are classified as top-tier models. This scale makes Bertoldi unusually large in a field dominated by one-man workshops. The brand also states that it exports to Portugal, Spain, Argentina, and Uruguay. It cannot be said to have wide recognition among collectors outside Brazil; even so, it is counted among the few examples showing the continuity of domestic production in South America.

r.x: The Directory of Austrian Pipe Brands

brings together, in alphabetical order, pipe names founded in Austria, run by Austrian makers, or noted in the country's brand records. Austrian pipemaking has two distinct strands: meerschaum carving, which made Vienna one of Europe's leading centers in the nineteenth century, and handmade briar production, carried on today in one-person workshops across various regions of the country. The entries below summarize only documented facts; points on which the sources have nothing to say are noted explicitly, and makers who appear in the list despite having worked in other countries are flagged accordingly.
Brands
Andreas Bauer

— A name found among Austrian meerschaum makers. No further detail about the brand has made it into the record; the same records name the Vienna-based Strambach as the country's last meerschaum manufacturer.
Baff Tabakpfeifenunikate

— The workshop where pipemaker David Wagner produces one-off pipes to order. Wagner learned the craft under Franz von Matt in Switzerland, Rainer Barbi in Germany, and Josef Prammer in Austria. His workshop sits in the Salzkammergut region, near the shore of the Traunsee; he is recorded as hand-shaping roughly 100 to 120 pipes a year from briar.
Erste Ottakringer Pfeifenmanufaktur

— The workshop Patrick Rutka founded in Ottakring, Vienna's 16th district, from which it also takes its name. Born in 1977, Rutka is also a musician who plays the chromatic button accordion, a traditional instrument of Austrian folk music; together with guitarist Klaus P. Steurer he forms the duo "16er Buam," performing the classic Viennese song.
Fisher

— The brand of Austrian maker Paul Fisher, known for his meerschaum work. Fisher emigrated to New York to pursue his trade, worked in Lower Manhattan, and became an American citizen; he marked his pipes with the letter "F." One of the names who worked alongside him for six years in the 1960s was Ed Burak.
Guyot

— Takes its name from the French pipemaker Gilbert Guyot; its appearance in Austrian records is purely a matter of listing. Born in 1938, Guyot began making pipes in 1961 and later retired. His father, H. Guyot, also ran a brand under his own name and worked for GBD in Paris between 1921 and 1923. The son was awarded the title "Meilleur Ouvrier de France" in 1994, and also wrote a book on the history of French pipemaking.
GWS

— The English stamp used in the first half of the twentieth century by G. W. Sims, known as both a maker and a repairer; see the Sims entry for details. His shop in north London closed around 1980. Sims is reported to have possibly worked for Charatan and Barling as well.
H. Richmond
— A French pipemaker working from his own home workshop near Saint-Claude. His working period and scale of production are not on record.
H.A. Savinelli

— An Italian carver and wood pipemaker active in the nineteenth century, who worked in woods other than briar. A pipe from his hand, dated to around 1850, was exhibited at the Tobacco Art and History Museum in Nashville, USA, which has since closed.
Huml

— Emerged when Austrian Karl Huml began making pipes in 1993. Working mostly in classic shapes, his annual output ranged between five and thirty pipes. A note entered into the record in 2015 indicates Huml may have stopped working by that date.
J.N. Menhard

— An Austrian master active in the nineteenth century. Known for his skill in carving meerschaum and amber, he produced other carved works alongside meerschaum pipes, some set with precious stones. He won a "Medal of Merit" at the 1873 Vienna World's Fair. His pieces on display at the Austrian Tobacco Museum bear the signature "J.N. Menhard Wien."
Krenn

— Born when Hans Krenn, a passionate pipe smoker, began making pipes in 1991, first for himself and his friends. Despite growing demand, Krenn produces only a few dozen pipes a year, saying each piece takes ten to forty hours. He works with Corsican briar and generally fits his pipes with stems suited to a 9 mm filter, also preparing a standard, filterless stem on request.
Lenz

— The name for the pipes Josef Lenz makes within the Tischlerei Lenz carpentry workshop in Bad Gleichenberg, in Austria's Styria state. No record exists of the production method or the workshop's history.
Stiegler
— Bears the name of pipemaker Christoph Stiegler, working in Winklarn, Lower Austria. The only documented information is the maker's identity and place of work.

r.x: Vardry Pipes

is the name of a small-scale pipe workshop operating in the southeastern United States. According to the business's own promotion, every pipe made is a one-off, finished from start to finish by hand; the claim that no two pieces are copies of each other is the workshop's core proposition. Public sources on the brand are extremely limited, so the information below is kept within a verifiable frame.
Location and Scale

The only address given for the workshop, in its own promotional records, is the settlement of Cleveland in the state of South Carolina; no second independent source confirms this. Cleveland sits in the state's northwest corner, in a sparsely populated area at the foot of the Blue Ridge Mountains. In keeping with this scale, Vardry Pipes is described not as a factory but as a one- or a few-person workshop. No independent record has been found for the founding year, the founder's name, or total production volume; like many small American workshops that work briar, the brand is known more through its own promotional channels than through commercial records. At this scale, annual output stays limited to a small number of pieces, and the continuity of the work depends on a single person's working pace; tracking periods of activity from the outside is therefore difficult.
Its Place in the American Workshop Tradition

Vardry Pipes can be considered a typical example of the handmade pipe scene that has spread across America since the late twentieth century. In this scene, the maker gathers every stage, from block selection to mouthpiece turning, in their own hands; the resulting pieces are thus tied not to a numbered catalog of shapes but to that day's block grain and the maker's judgment. This distinction from factory production is covered in detail in the artisan pipe versus factory pipe comparison.
State of Sources

There is no reliable breakdown available on Vardry Pipes regarding stamp format, series names, the mouthpiece (stem) material used, or production periods by year. The Pipedia entry on the brand is likewise a short introduction; at the time this article was prepared, that page could not be accessed directly, so the information at hand has been limited to the business's own promotional records. Basic data such as the founder's name, the year the workshop opened, and the years in which it produced have therefore not been included in this article: leaving a fact uncertain has been preferred over filling it with an unsourced guess. The article has been kept short, to be expanded as new and verifiable records emerge. For general methods and terminology, see the pipe-making entry.

r.x: Martin Romijn

is a pipe maker working in Leerdam, on the river Linge in the Netherlands' Utrecht province, who comes from a background in stonework. Born in 1969, he first encountered pipes at twenty, in 1989; he did not begin making his own pipes until 2016. He carries on production alone in the workshop at his home; this scale is the customary arrangement for one-man workshops.
A Trade Born of Stone

After finishing school he served four years in the Dutch Marine Corps; after leaving the service he worked in security and at a motorcycle shop. When the shop went bankrupt he was forced to find a new trade and turned to stonecutting and carving; according to the record, this work remained his main livelihood for nearly thirty years. He produced work across a range running from gravestones to door and window sills, from kitchen counters to bathroom and fireplace cladding; alongside the old methods carried out with hammer and chisel, he also learned decorative carving. In choosing stone he favors Belgian hard stone and Jura stone, both of which he likes for their fossils and crystals. Marble, granite, onyx, and petrified wood have also passed through his bench.

Accessory production began after an injury: knee surgery following a torn cruciate ligament kept him out of work for about a year. In this gap he turned leftover stone scraps from the workshop into tobacco tampers, shared his first examples on the pipe newsgroups of the day, and set up his own website for these pieces in 2003. Production later expanded to ashtrays and magnetic pipe stands that create the illusion of the body floating in the air. By the time a progressive condition that made walking difficult rendered the physical burden of stonework impossible to bear, he had over a decade of accessory-making behind him.
Moving into Pipe Making

Romijn took up pipe making in 2016, largely self-taught. He first got to know the material by reshaping the bodies of estate pipes he already owned; according to the account, one of these experiments was done on an old Vauen. He then moved on to working with pre-drilled briar blocks; again according to the account, his first blocks were a gift from Belgian maker Nick Ramaekers. In the early years he received occasional guidance from German maker Dirk Heinemann; beyond that, what he learned rests on trial and error and online craft resources.

The workshop's defining tool is the wood lathe his parents gave him as an encouraging gift; Romijn credits this lathe with turning his production serious. His insistence on a wood lathe rather than a metal one is explained by the freedom of movement he finds when turning chambers. Alongside it he uses a band saw, a sanding disc, loose-belt sanding, a buffer, a Dremel, and hand tools. The briar he uses comes from Italy; he makes his mouthpieces from ebonite and acrylic.
Approach to Form

He describes his own work as "organic." He carries the attitude he adopted for carving stone over into briar as well: rather than sticking to a design drawn in advance, he lets the form be determined by the material's grain and flaws. This is why spending a long time on a single block and changing direction midway through the work are considered a normal part of freehand work.

His portfolio leans toward round bodies evoking eggs, apples, strawberries, and acorns, along with wide-chambered Dublin and brandy shapes. Workpony, Workhorse, and Buster are models he has named himself; bamboo-shanked variants of the first two are also produced. He openly expresses admiration for the masters of the Danish school; he particularly values Poul Winsløw's work and met the master in 2018.

r.x: Bowles & Son Ltd

was a Welsh tobacconist company based in Cardiff that operated from 1888 to 1979. It did not make pipes; it delivered pipes and tobacco to the user — retailing through its own shops on one hand, and supplying pubs, clubs, and small tobacconists across South East Wales wholesale on the other. Because the history of British pipes is usually told through manufacturers, this intermediate link, often overlooked, matters for showing the routes by which the product spread into the provinces.
Three Generations Within the Family

The company remained in the Bowles family's hands throughout its ninety-year existence, effectively bearing out the "& Son" in its name. In the 1950s the business was headed by Reginald Bowles and his brother Ivor Bowles. Management passed to the next generation, two cousins: Reginald's son Tom and Ivor's son William (Bill) Bowles; it was these two who made the decision to sell in 1979. With the sale, the Bowles name withdrew from Cardiff tobacconism.
A Network of Shops

The head office was at 9 James Street in Butetown, the district opening onto Cardiff's docks. The building's three floors were each dedicated to a different function of the business: the basement for storage, the ground floor for sales, the first floor for offices. The basement store also had a separate curing room where cigars were rested.

The retail arm spread across the city centre. The company's shops stood on Cardiff's busy streets — St. Mary's Street, Castle Street, Queen Street, and High Street — with a branch also in the neighbouring town of Pontypridd, on the road up to the railway station. Records indicate the number of branches reached eleven at one point. Some of these had been taken over from Percy Cadle, known from 1907 local newspaper reports to have run a tobacconist business in Cardiff; how many shops the takeover covered and in which year it occurred cannot be determined from the records. The shops were furnished similarly to one another, yet were not identical: two had a barber section at the back, and one had a confectionery counter.
Shelves of a Port District

Butetown was Cardiff's port district, which made its customer base unusually varied for Britain of the period. Alongside domestic blends, the shelves also carried foreign brands sought by the district's established Somali community and by sailors calling at the port. Since the pipe was still an everyday habit in the first half of the twentieth century, the range of pipes was wide, complemented by accessories such as matches, wicks, pipe cleaners, lighters, and ashtrays. At the time, lighters and ashtrays were not disposable items but pieces kept for years.

The wholesale arm, in turn, made the company a regional distribution point. In the era's English market, products from English manufacturers such as Barling and Comoy's of London also largely reached small retailers through this kind of regional wholesaler.
The Trace Left in the Archives

The company's commercial papers are today preserved at the Glamorgan Archives. These documents are counted among the few records that make it possible to trace, in detail, how the briar and clay pipe trade was carried on in a city outside the capital.

r.x: Dunhill mouthpieces

are treated in the brand's history not as a part independent of the bowl, but as one half of a whole shaped together with the pipe. This production habit has turned the mouthpiece into the most-discussed detail of Dunhill collecting: for most old examples, it cannot be said with certainty whether the mouthpiece sitting on a pipe left the factory together with that bowl.
Hand Cutting and Lip Shapes

In the early period, most pipes were sold with a screw or military-style push mouthpiece, with bowl and mouthpiece made separately and joined at the end of the process. At Dunhill, however, the push-style mouthpiece was fitted onto the roughly cut bowl from the very start, going through sanding and finishing together with the bowl. Mouthpieces were not molded but hand-cut from ebonite (vulcanite) rod or sheet, with the tenon end individually thinned to fit the shank.

The lip shape changed over time. The thick lip of the earliest examples became thinner and wider in the 1920s, and the fishtail shape was added to this in the 1930s. When machine cutting was tried in 1976 to cut labor costs, the lip thickened again; following complaints, the brand returned to hand craftsmanship. The detailed breakdown of this evolution is in the entry on Old Dunhill vs. New Dunhill.
The White Dot

Since which side of a hand-cut mouthpiece should face up could not be distinguished by eye, a small white marker was placed on the top face. Common consensus dates this practice to 1915; some sources cite 1912. The dot was initially a thin ivory cylinder; in later decades it was replaced by plastic and acrylic, and its diameter also grew. For mouthpieces made of materials other than ebonite, it is stated that the factory deliberately used a dot that was not white. The brand's general history is covered in the entry on Dunhill (White Spot).
What the Stamps Say and Do Not Say

A registration number was stamped on early mouthpieces; it is generally accepted in compilations that this practice ran from the mid-1910s to the early 1930s. The information the number carries is narrower than assumed: since the factory produced replacement mouthpieces with the same number, the stamp only shows that the piece is an early Dunhill mouthpiece, not that it belongs to that particular bowl. The stamp is also shallow and can wear away with repeated polishing. The patent numbers and year codes stamped on the shank, meanwhile, are information about the bowl, not the mouthpiece; their reading is the subject of the entry on Dunhill Patent Stamps and Dating.
The Difficulty of Measuring Authenticity

The remaining criteria, taken alone, are not proof either. Lip shape, the alignment between shank and mouthpiece, and the profile of the tenon end are affected by years of wear and repeated refinishing; on an over-polished mouthpiece the fit can degrade on its own, and a pipe with a thinned shank can look the same as one that has simply been heavily polished. For marks left by maintenance and repair, see the entry on Pipe Repair and Mouthpiece Care.

The final factor complicating the picture is that the brand was open to special order. Records state that amber, tortoiseshell, and ivory mouthpieces appeared in the catalogue, and that horn was used during the Second World War due to material shortages; the comparison of these materials is in the entry on Mouthpiece Materials. An unusual-looking mouthpiece is therefore more often not a later replacement but one of the era's ordering options. Taken together, the established approach for an old Dunhill is to weigh all the markers together rather than issue a definitive verdict of authenticity for the mouthpiece.

r.x: William Demuth Company

is a firm founded in New York in the second half of the nineteenth century that, within a generation, grew into one of America's most recognized pipe houses. The letters WDC, set inside an inverted equilateral triangle, appeared for decades on both carved meerschaum and mass-produced briar pipes, becoming a mark better known than the brand name itself.
Founder and the Company's Origins

Wilhelm C. Demuth, the man who gave the company its name, was born in Germany in 1835 and, according to records, emigrated to America alone at sixteen. After years of working for wages in New York's tobacco trade, he opened his own business in 1862 and remained at its head until his death in 1911. The product list of the founding years resembles a carving business more than today's pipe brands: alongside pipes, the same workshops produced smoker's accessories, canes, and life-size carved figures set outside cigar shop doors.
Meerschaum and the Presidents Series

The firm's most talked-about work today lies in meerschaum carving. Foremost among these is the figurative series of portraits of U.S. presidents. The series, running from John Adams to Herbert Hoover, comprises twenty-eight portrait pipes plus a bust of Washington; adding a pipe carrying the face of each newly elected president to the series long remained the firm's custom, a practice that ended with Hoover.

Accounts trace the series's origin to an acquaintance formed with President James A. Garfield, known to be a meerschaum enthusiast: at his 1881 inauguration, Garfield was presented two pipes, one bearing his own face and one his wife's. The place of such gifts in American politics is further discussed in the pipes presented to American presidents entry. Another example of the same carving tradition is the meerschaum composition titled "Columbus Landing in America," which took two years to complete and exceeds eighty centimeters in length; the piece was shown at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
Briar Lines and the Factory

As the twentieth century began, the emphasis shifted from hand carving to series production, and from meerschaum to briar. The center of this transformation was the large factory built in 1895 in Queens's Richmond Hill neighborhood, which operated for decades; thanks to this plant, WDC is counted among the country's largest pipe producers. Ferdinand Feuerbach, who joined the firm in 1897 and rose to production manager in 1903, played a decisive role in shaping the Royal Demuth and Milano Hesson Guard lines. The Hesson name comes from William Wallace Hesson, who held two patents for inventions related to the pipe's internal mechanism. Feuerbach left the firm in 1919 and took charge of his old friend Sam Frank's factory in the Bronx. The firm's Fifth Avenue proximity to, and intersection with, its English rival in these years is the subject of the Demuth and Dunhill connection entry.
The S. M. Frank Era and Closing

The paths of the two firms crossed in 1937 for an unexpected reason: New York's city government decided to condemn part of the land on which Frank's Bronx factory stood, for a street-widening project. Searching for a new production site, Frank began negotiations for the Richmond Hill plant; the resulting agreement turned the Demuth company into a subsidiary of S. M. Frank & Co., and the production of the two brands was gathered under a single roof.

Demuth pipes continued to be made at this factory through the last day of 1972; the company was formally dissolved through liquidation the same year. The brand was not wiped out entirely: its best-selling model, Wellington, continued to appear in the S. M. Frank catalogue until 1976, and records indicate it was briefly reintroduced in the mid-1980s. The factory building itself was not torn down; in later years it was repurposed as housing, remaining part of the neighborhood's fabric.

r.x: KW Pipes

is the name of the small workshop American pipe repairer and carver Kirk Walden founded in the early 2000s. The brand was short-lived and its output limited in number; even so, it stands as a tidy example of how one-man workshops rose and quietly closed in the years when the internet transformed pipe commerce.
From the Repair Bench to the Carving Bench

Walden's entry into the trade followed a familiar sequence in American workshop craft: first a tobacco shop, then a repair bench, and finally carving. By his account he learned repair work from a shop's repairman while employed at a tobacconist, taking over that repair work in 1998. This information rests on the maker's own promotional text; there is no independent record of it. He carved his first pipes of his own in the early 2000s, following a long stretch of repair work. Sources disagree on the starting year: one reference work states production has run part-time since 2002, while the workshop's own 2005 introduction places the first pipe two years earlier. Production never became a full-time trade, remaining a pursuit carried alongside family life. From the start, the pipes found buyers through an online auction site.
Style, Material, and Lines

Walden's work consists of freehand pipes shaped individually under the influence of the Danish school; it is emphasized that no two examples are alike. Greek briar was used for the blocks. Ebonite (vulcanite) was mostly preferred for mouthpieces, with acrylic (lucite) and cumberland occasionally worked as well. Pieces were mostly reshaped from pre-drawn rod to fit each pipe. Shank ornamentation used bamboo along with deer, elk, and caribou horn.
The workshop's 2005 introduction lists four lines:
Freehand Series
— the workshop's core freehand line
Deer Horn Series
— models with a shank split by a horn insert
Bamboo Series
— bamboo-shanked pipes, the workshop's best-known group
Blue Hawaii Series
— examples with a blue-painted bowl surface

These lines are not separate shape families but branches of the same freehand approach, distinguished by material and surface treatment. Pre-carbonizing the chamber on request was also among the options the workshop offered.
Stamp and Fate

The pipes were marked with the carver's name, i.e. the "Kirk Walden" stamp; the red, jewel-like dot on the mouthpiece is considered the brand's distinguishing mark. Pipe encyclopedias note that the workshop's website closed in 2007, with its online activity ending in the same period. Since secondary sources repeating this note trace back to the same reference, the date should not be taken as certain. No reliable record of Walden continuing pipe production after that date has been found. For this reason, KW Pipes is remembered today as a short-lived American workshop known through a limited number of examples in second-hand circulation.
