r.x: Paul Becker
is a German pipe maker running a one-man workshop in Pinneberg, about twenty kilometers northwest of Hamburg. He has signed his pipes for some time under the name
Paulpipes
, by his own account to avoid confusion. There are other makers in the pipe world who share his surname; he has no connection to Fritz Becker or Paolo Becker.
From Behind the Counter to the Lathe

Becker's life story rests largely on his own account and has no chronology backed by official records. According to this account, he was born in Pinneberg in January 1947; his family ran a tobacconist shop in the town. After finishing a two-year business school in Hamburg and completing an apprenticeship in trade, he entered the family business, and in 1970 took over the shop together with his wife, Erika. He had started smoking a pipe at sixteen; he says he had wanted to make his own pipes since youth, and that the names he took as examples were masters of the Danish School.

The turn came in 1982. The purpose of the first workshop he set up in his home's basement was not production but being able to repair, on the spot, broken mouthpieces and similar minor faults brought in by customers to the shop. Becker recounts that German master Rainer Barbi played a large part in equipping the workshop, and that the suggestion not to stop at repair but to try making himself a pipe also came from him; he says he learned the technique directly by watching at Barbi's bench. This mentoring relationship has not been confirmed by an independent source. His first freehand pipe dates from this period. Given the interest shown by shop customers, he kept his own pipes on the counter for eight years alongside the rest; in 1990 he closed the shop and moved to full-time pipe making.
Craftsmanship and Finishes

Every stage of a Paulpipes pipe passes through a single pair of hands: from freehand drilling in the block to coarse and fine sanding, from coloring to the bowl-coating layer and the hand-shaped mouthpiece, the maker does every job himself. There is no varnish on the surface; shine is given with carnauba wax. Mouthpieces are cut thin enough to sit comfortably against the teeth. The color range is limited to three tones, though the naming of these tones varies from source to source: tones referred to in older promotional texts as natural, orange, and warm brown appear in current material as light orange, dark, and warm brown.

Becker emphasizes that he uses no putty filler in his briar blocks. Small marks (spots) coming from the wood's own texture are not noticeable in use; they only determine which grade the pipe falls into. Both filtered and unfiltered pipes come out of the workshop. Filtered models have a removable insert machined to size, so that the same pipe can also be smoked without a filter.
Removable Shank Section

The maker's own best-known solution is the pipe whose shank has a removable middle section. With the spacer in place, the pipe is used like a long-stemmed churchwarden; once the piece is removed, it drops to the ordinary length. The bowl of this model is shaped either round or faceted; Becker states that he does not keep the design fixed, but tries to push it a little further each time.

Production scale is small, and the figure given varies by source: current information puts output at around a hundred pipes a year from the workshop, while older material gives the figure as two hundred fifty.

r.x: Henry Leonard & Thomas Inc.

, known as HLT, is one of the most defining companies of mid-twentieth-century American series-production pipemaking. It was founded on May 31, 1938, in the Ozone Park neighborhood of Queens, New York, by Henry J. Lavietes and two partners. Within fifteen years of its founding, the company had grown large enough to purchase a brand both older and far more famous than itself, Dr. Grabow.
The New York Years and Royalton

In its early years, the company's mainstay was patented small mechanisms. Records indicate that a mouthpiece (stem) arrangement developed by Henry Lavietes, used in both pipes and cigarette holders, was patent-protected on March 9, 1943. The innovation that truly made the brand's name, however, was the Royalton filter chamber; its patent is said to have been obtained in 1944. This cavity opened into the shank was meant to trap condensing moisture and tar before it reached the mouth, and was a typical example of the filter and moisture-trapping systems rapidly multiplying in the American market of the era. Although HLT's catalogue contained many other lines, the name that has lasted has been Royalton.
The Move to Sparta

The step that changed the company's geography came from within the family. Henry Lavietes's father, David Lavietes, went to the town of Sparta, North Carolina, in the early 1940s. Since wartime had disrupted the supply of Mediterranean-sourced briar, the aim was to gather laurel and mountain-laurel root from the region and ship it to production in New York. David Lavietes eventually chose to stay in the town; together with his son Paul he founded a fifteen-person workshop called D&P Pipe Works. The idea behind the Ajustomatic mechanism still found in Dr. Grabow pipes today is, records indicate, attributed to him.

Shortly after 1944, Henry Lavietes made a sudden decision to close the New York operation and move all production to Sparta. This small town in Alleghany County remained one of the centers of American pipe manufacturing for generations to come.
Growth, Acquisitions, and What Followed

In 1953, HLT purchased all the assets and machinery of the Chicago-based Dr. Grabow company; according to secondary sources, the deal also covered production within M. Linkman & Co. After the machinery was moved from Chicago, manufacture of the Grabow and Hollycourt lines continued in Sparta. In the same years, the Continental Briar Company, which held the Royal Duke, Duke of Dundee, and Honeydew brands, was also acquired. The word "Duke" still appearing in Grabow model names today is regarded as a holdover from this acquisition.

On October 21, 1969, United States Tobacco announced it had acquired HLT, which also owned the Mastercraft brand. The company was run for a time as a separate legal entity; in 1985, Sparta Pipes, Mastercraft, and HLT were merged under the name Sparta Industries, Inc. The HLT name passed in subsequent years first to Lane, then in 2006 to its current owner, International Pipes & Accessories. Royalton continues to be produced as part of the Dr. Grabow line, under the original HLT stamp.

r.x: Tanganyika Meerschaum Corporation

is the most notable industrial venture in meerschaum pipemaking established outside Eskişehir. The company's starting point was a meerschaum deposit found very close to the surface around Kilimanjaro; pipe literature places its founding in 1955 and its founders in Nairobi. Tanganyika in the name is the old name of today's Tanzania: the country gained independence in 1961, and in 1964 united with Zanzibar to take the name Tanzania. Even so, the old name continued to be used in trade for a long time, appearing in British catalogues as late as the mid-1970s.
African Meerschaum and the Sinya Mine

The raw material comes from the Amboseli basin, stretching along the western foot of Kilimanjaro. Known in the geological literature as the Sinya Beds, the formation consists of carbonate rocks and magnesium-rich clays deposited in a semi-arid lake basin; sepiolite, the mineral equivalent of meerschaum, also forms within these clays, in the voids and veins of the beds. The deposits spread across both sides of the Tanzania-Kenya border. The company's long-running principal operation, the Sinya mine, is located in the Arusha region, Longido district, of Tanzania.

The stone found here differs markedly from stone mined in Eskişehir: it has low porosity and high hardness, and its cost also fell below that of Anatolian stone. These properties made it well suited to mass production rather than delicate figurative carving. Indeed, African stone appears not in showpiece carved pieces but in plainly formed pipes made for everyday use; the surfaces are usually finished stained in shades of black, brown and yellow.
Brands and Stamps

Production was carried out not under a single name but as a broad family of brands. Records mention names such as Kiko, Kilimanjaro, Countryman, Sportsman, Townsman, Kudu, Twiga, Tembo, Merlin and Caveman. Some of these come from Swahili: kiko means "pipe," twiga "giraffe," and tembo "elephant." The emblems distinguishing the brands also reflect the same geography; Kiko and Countryman are reported to have used an elephant figure, and Kilimanjaro a rhinoceros. Not all of these names were the company's own property: the meerschaum bowls for some brands, such as Townsman and Merlin, were made under contract in East Africa for British firms.

Pipes are generally stamped "Genuine Block Meerschaum" along with a shape number; "Made in Tanganyika" is also seen as an origin stamp. Among collectors this stamp is treated as a rough dating marker, since the name Tanganyika fell out of official use after 1964. Alongside solid stone, the company also worked imported briar bowls, producing meerschaum-lined and leather-covered pipes. Its best-known collaboration was with GBD, from which that brand's block meerschaum series drew its stone and workmanship; models tied to the series such as Iringa and Jenga still appear in GBD's 1976 catalogue.
The End of the Mine and the Company

Pipe sources write that the company formed a partnership with a Belgian firm and closed a few years afterward; no exact closure date is given. Official mining statistics, however, show the operation still active in the 1970s: the Sinya mine's annual meerschaum output was around thirty tons in 1972, fell by half the following year, and the ratio of usable stone recovered from the ore dropped at the same pace. The mines were eventually abandoned, and the area now lies within a wildlife management zone.

Production using African stone continued after the company's end. In Britain, London Meerschaum, and on the Isle of Man, Laxey Pipes, worked with the same raw material; Laxey also prepared meerschaum bowls for recognized brands such as Peterson. This production too came to an end as the East African stone ran out, with Laxey making its last meerschaum pipes in 2001.

r.x: Briar Art

is the name of the one-man bench American pipe master Brian Ruthenberg ran in Michigan. Ruthenberg's original trade was machining and tool-and-die work; the habit of working to tight tolerances later carried over into his pipe craftsmanship as well. The number of pipes coming out of his workshop north of Detroit was never high, yet the brand nonetheless became one of the recognised names in the American handmade pipe community in the 2000s.
Founding the Bench

Ruthenberg's first contact with the craft came through a ready-made pipemaking kit he obtained from American maker Mark Tinsky. His move into regular production followed a trip to Michigan's Upper Peninsula; records indicate he obtained his first briar blocks there from Lee von Erck.

A significant portion of his technical knowledge came from an IRC chat channel that brought together pipemakers of the era; Ruthenberg has stated he received help in these years from Robert Vacher and Dale Adkins. He learned the hand-cut mouthpiece technique from Michael Lindner, and won second place in the amateur category of a carving competition at the pipe show held in Richmond. The bench was founded in 2001 as a part-time pursuit and turned into full-time work after 2005; until that date Ruthenberg made his living as a long-haul truck driver.
Craftsmanship

Briar Art pipes used plateau-cut briar, with blocks sourced from Italy and Morocco. Mouthpieces were not bought ready-made but cut by hand from vulcanite and cumberland rods. The smoke channel was drilled 4 millimetres along the shank, narrowing toward the tip within the mouthpiece; for pipes with a larger bowl diameter, the channel would also be widened. This wide channel, polished on the inside, forms the basis of the brand's approach to easy draw and a cool smoke. Annual production stayed between one hundred and one hundred fifty, with the brand's real reputation within the community earned through its sandblast craftsmanship.
Marks and Grades
Autumn 2002 marks a turning point in the marks. Records indicate that up until October 2002 the pipes carried the
BAR
mark, formed from the master's initials, after which the switch was made to the curved
RUTHENBERG

script; beneath the mark are lines indicating the country and that the piece is handmade. The pipes are also dated by the last two digits of the year of manufacture. The name of the top tier the master reserved for his favourite pieces is
Caliper
; this mark was used for select blocks with grain sitting evenly or in a ring pattern.
Current Status

The Briar Art bench has not produced for some time now. The brand can today be traced only through pipes returning to circulation from their former owners, and these pieces are counted among the examples of high-grade American craftsmanship.

r.x: Carsten Ringling

is a pipe maker working in Saarland, in southwestern Germany near the French border. With output not exceeding a few dozen pipes a year, it is a small workshop in scale; even so, its surface craftsmanship and distinctive shape interpretations have made its name known beyond Germany as well. Records indicate his first contact with the wood came not through production but through repair: in his twenties he reworked his father's old pipes, and this pursuit gradually turned into a desire to make his own.
Shape Language and Surface

Ringling's style is considered to have become distinct in recent years and is generally described by two elements. The first is the flattened interpretation he brings to the bulldog family: the bowl is lowered and widened, and in most examples tilted slightly forward relative to the body. The same approach appears in freer forms in his freehand pieces, whose proportions are not tied to a ready template.

The second element is finishing. Most of the maker's surfaces are closed with a deep, animated sandblast; this texture, in which the grain gaps are opened up, is regarded as the main factor shaping the impression his pipes leave in the hand. Decoration is almost nonexistent; horn appears only occasionally, for accent.
Workshop and Material

It is reported that Ringling finished his first pipe in 2008, and has since turned out between thirty and forty pipes a year. This scale stems from the fact that the work is carried alongside his main profession: per the same sources, Ringling works professionally as an occupational therapist and runs his own practice, with pipe making added as a second pursuit. The small number of pieces allows more time to be given to each.

Spanish and Italian briar is preferred for the bodies. Both smooth and sandblasted surfaces are seen in the finish, while the choice is singular on the side of bit material: the maker uses only vulcanite.
The Gnarly Series

The line known as "Gnarly" is kept separate from the workshop's ordinary production. The bodies here are old blocks left over from a closed pipe factory, aged for a long time. Since the pieces go through machine pre-shaping and are finished by hand, the series is considered semi-handmade. The shapes stay within the classic repertoire, while the sandblast retains the maker's usual texture. This time the bit uses acrylic, vulcanite, and horn together; examples with a 9 mm filter chamber are also encountered.

Ringling's ties to the German pipe community are a frequently mentioned detail. Accounts resting on his own statements say he keeps in regular touch with names such as Roger Wallenstein, Gerhard Wilhelm, Axel Glasner, Tobias Höse, and Marc Prokein; contacts of this kind are considered the main channel through which small workshops learn technique from one another.

r.x: Ascorti

is a pipe workshop founded in the town of Cucciago, in northern Italy's province of Como. The brand takes its name from Roberto Ascorti, who began producing under his own name in 1980 at just twenty-two. Ascorti is considered a direct heir to the workshop tradition concentrated around Como in Italian pipemaking, a tradition shaped along the line of Castello and Caminetto.
Family and Origins

The family's connection to pipes began a generation before Roberto. His father, Giuseppe Ascorti — known in the trade as "Peppino" — joined the Castello workshop in Cantù in 1959, left nine years later, and founded Caminetto in 1968. For Roberto, then ten years old, pipes became the trade discussed at home. While studying at art school, he also moved in and out of workshop tasks; in 1980, at twenty-two, he decided to make it his sole occupation. Since there was no room for him at his father's workshop, he began production directly under his own surname. The small early team included his brother Pierangelo and his then-fiancée, later his wife, Silvana. Roberto lost first his father and then his brother at a young age, and kept the workshop running together with Silvana.

The two brands' paths later crossed again. Caminetto had been shaken when partner Luigi Radice left in the late 1970s, and halted production in 1986. Records indicate that after the closure, part of the old team moved over to Ascorti, and the young brand found a wealth of skill accumulated over the years ready at hand. The Caminetto name was revived after a long gap in 2013 by Peppino's grandson, Tommaso Ascorti; the two brands are today regarded as two separate branches of the same family.
How the Workshop Works

Production at Ascorti rests on the logic of a single piece followed individually at the bench. For rough shaping, small machines that Peppino Ascorti built by hand in the 1970s are still in use. These are kept not to shrink the share of handwork, but so that each stage of the process can be carried out separately and under control.

Material selection is among the workshop's chief preoccupations. The briar blocks to be used are sorted by size, weight, and flaw; after the initial drying done in the region where the root is harvested, the material is, by the workshop's own account, left to rest roughly two more years. Once the chamber and shank are bored, the pipe enters a long sequence of steps carried out by hand for its weight; again by the workshop's account, a piece passes through some ninety stages, large and small, before it is considered finished. The mouthpieces are not bought ready-made either, but cut in-house from methacrylate (acrylic) sheet.
La Silvana

Silvana Ascorti learned briar craftsmanship within the Caminetto team from the mid-1970s onward. According to Pipedia, after more than thirty years of this experience, she created the "La Silvana" line under her own name in 2008. Built on a classic Italian line, the series was offered in two groups, smooth-polished and rusticated; it is set apart from the main production by its colored mouthpieces and separate logo.

r.x: Altınay

is a meerschaum pipe workshop that has operated in Eskişehir since 1964 and has been run by the same family for three generations. The brand is known for producing smoking pipes tied to the established forms of European pipe making rather than the figural decorative carving common in the region. In foreign catalogues the name is written "Altinay," dropping the Turkish letters; the business is known under the title Altınay Pipo Ltd. Şti.
Founder and Generations

The workshop was founded by Necdet Altınay (1941-2018). According to the firm's own history, he entered carving at fourteen and opened his own bench at twenty-three; the founding year given as 1964 is consistent with this account. The same source attributes the brand's recognition abroad to the founder's regular presence at international trade shows. This detail has not been cross-checked against independent documents, though the workshop can be seen listed as an exhibitor at European tobacco trade fairs.

Before Necdet Altınay's death in 2018, the business had already passed to his son Nedim Altınay (b. 1967) and grandson Said Altınay (b. 1990). The second and third generations now run the workshop together and report doing the carving with their own hands. Passing the craft down a father-to-son line is common enough in the Eskişehir meerschaum carving tradition to be considered close to a rule; production in this trade rests not on large factories but on family benches where a few masters work.
Material, Shape, and Models

The workshop works only with block meerschaum. This distinction is a benchmark in the craft: unlike material produced by pressing crushed stone with a binder, block stone is carved in the mass form it came out of the mine. Classic pipe shapes dominate the catalogue, alongside lines carried under their own names. On silver-mounted models, a metal band fitted at the end of the shank holds the mouthpiece in a joined fashion; when the joint is visible from outside it is called a spigot mount, and when the mouthpiece sits inside the metal ferrule it is called an army mount. In the bamboo line, a jointed bamboo piece is set between the stummel and the mouthpiece; in the pencil-shank models the shank is noticeably thinned. Translucent pieces, in which the stone is thinned after carving until it lets light through, form a separate line as well.

Acrylic is used for mouthpieces; see the mouthpiece materials entry for details. Some models are drilled to take a 9 mm filter. According to restorers' notes, a round brass-colored brand badge bearing two pipe motifs is set into the side face of the mouthpiece; this badge is the primary mark used to identify the workshop's work.
Production for Other Brands

Alongside the pipes it sells under its own stamp, Altınay has also produced for foreign pipe houses. According to the firm, these brands have in the past included Dunhill, Peterson, Savinelli, Chacom, Brebbia, and Butz-Choquin, and more recently Rattray's, Barling, and Andreas Bauer. This list has not been confirmed by independent archival documents, though European distributors repeat the same names. It is a known practice in the trade for established briar brands to have their meerschaum lines made at Eskişehir workshops and sell them under their own name.

r.x: Jørn Micke

(1937-2005) belongs to the second generation of Danish pipemaking, a master who left behind very few pipes despite a wide reputation attached to his name. He spent most of his life on Bornholm, the Danish island in the Baltic Sea, working in painting and sculpture alongside pipes.
From Medicine to the Workshop

Micke's first professional choice was medicine; in his youth he studied medicine in Copenhagen. According to the account given, this direction began to unravel after a trip to Bornholm in 1958, and turned into a lasting decision the following year on his second visit to the island. He had drawn since childhood; a pipe-smoking habit begun early on led him to carve a few pipes for his own use.

What turned this amateur pursuit into a profession was his friendship with Sixten Ivarsson, formed through a shared passion for fishing. After working roughly a year as an apprentice in Ivarsson's workshop, Micke settled permanently on Bornholm in 1963 and set up his own bench. From that point on the idea of medicine never resurfaced; he made his living through a threefold artistic output of painting, sculpture, and pipes.
Style and Production

Micke's name is linked with the generation that gathered around Sixten Ivarsson in Denmark in the 1960s — Lars Ivarsson, Jess Chonowitsch, and Bo Nordh. The strongest link in this connection was Lars Ivarsson; the closeness between the two masters is said to have lasted until Micke's death. Still, the life he led on the island kept Micke outside the everyday circulation of Denmark's pipe circles: most Danish makers never met him in person.

The workshop's output was extremely low; records indicate the annual total stood at around twenty pipes. The bulk of these pipes went directly to buyers, with a significant portion going to Japan. Micke's shape sensibility is considered a line that is hard to define but recognizable on sight, one that highlights the grain of the briar root and the balance of the mass. It is said that a Micke pipe appeared on the cover of a well-known Chicago-based tobacconist's catalogue in the late 1960s. The master is also reported to have made porcelain pipe designs for Royal Copenhagen.
Stamps

Micke's pipes are generally stamped with the name "Micke," the year of manufacture, and a number. Examples he judged the most successful by his own standard are said to have carried a zebra figure as well; this mark is considered an indicator of the workshop's own internal grading. "Denmark" may also appear in the stamps as the country name.

Jørn Micke died in 2005. The number of pipes he left behind is very small compared with the output of his contemporaries within the Danish school; for this reason his examples are seen today only rarely, on the secondary market.

r.x: TMpipes

is the name American artisan Thomas Martin used for his small-scale pipe bench, taken from his own initials. Based in Massachusetts, this bench emerged in the early 2000s and never grew beyond workshop scale; records indicate around fifty pipes a year in the early period. Before turning to pipe carving, Martin was known as a craftsman who made wooden flutes in the Native American tradition, and this background in woodworking was decisive in the bench basing itself on a small number of handcrafted pieces.
Material and Shape Choices

The bench's primary material, as with nearly all American artisans of the period, was briar. Martin also occasionally turned to white ash and olive wood, referring to his pieces made from olive as "Bethlehem Olive wood." These experiments with woods other than briar are part of a search seen at many small-scale benches in the US.

Two periods are noted on the shape side. The early work consisted of freehand examples guided by the wood grain; in later years the preference shifted from showcasing grain toward balanced proportions and lightly classic shapes. In this respect, TMpipes counts among the artisan benches shaped by a single hand rather than series production.
The distinguishing detail for collectors is the stamp: early pipes carry only the letters
TM
, while later production used the script-form
Thomas
stamp. Records date this change to the fall of 2007; since the date is not independently confirmed, it should be treated as a rough boundary.

The calabash question was also among Martin's interests. In a piece he wrote for the Sherlock Holmes Pipe Club of Boston, he explained that no one was left in the US making real gourd calabash pipes, and that finding a suitable gourd was even harder than finding quality briar.
Transition to The Pipe Cooperative

In June 2008, TMpipes turned into a joint venture called The Pipe Cooperative (TPC). Its base was in Beverly, Massachusetts, north of Boston. The idea behind the venture was for craftsmen, each specialized in a particular stage, to work on the same pipe in sequence, with the final hand belonging to Martin — an attempt to combine the experience of several makers with the capacity of a one-person bench.

Records indicate Martin was dealing with a long-term, painful health problem during this period; the hours spent at the bench had become increasingly taxing for him. The joint-venture format can also be read as a way of continuing production under these conditions. There is no record of the TMpipes name being used on new production after 2008; the brand today is known largely through collector interest.

r.x: Gezer

is the surname shared by three brothers — Şevket, Kudret, and Mesut Gezer — in meerschaum carving. It is not a single registered brand or factory, but describes a family of masters who shared a bench for a time before each went on to produce under his own name. The brothers' work is discussed separately in collector circles; what they share is figural bowls depicting people and animals and dense floral ornamentation.
From a Quarry Village to the Bench

The eldest of the brothers, Şevket Gezer, was born in 1955. According to records, he was born in the village of Kozlubel — formerly Margı — some thirty kilometers from Eskişehir, one of the few settlements in the region where meerschaum is quarried. The same records state that his father both worked at the quarry and carved the stone, meaning the craft entered the family directly through the quarry. Şevket took his place at the bench as an apprentice at fifteen and trained in the workshops of Eskişehir's masters of the day.

Kudret Gezer's introduction to the stone came in 1977, at age twelve. Sources report that he started under his older brother Şevket and was working at his own bench by the early 1980s. Mesut Gezer, the youngest of the brothers, likewise entered the craft at twelve, following his older brothers. Today, all three produce out of Eskişehir.
Partnership and Separation

That the brothers worked together for a time appears in every source; the exact dates of the partnership, however, do not fully agree across records. Retailer biographies say that Kudret and Mesut formed a roughly five-year partnership with their older brother Şevket starting in 1985. That Şevket Gezer has worked alone since 1992 is repeated in multiple sources. The same biographies also note that, besides his brothers, Şevket worked with other well-known masters of the region, such as Salim Şener.

After the separation, the brothers' paths took different shapes. Kudret Gezer is known for the works he signs under his own name, while Mesut Gezer is presented in foreign retailer profiles as the head master of the Servi workshop. Sources diverge, however, on who actually runs this workshop; the information has not been confirmed by an independent record.
Style and Signatures

All three brothers' repertoires include figural carving that turns the entire bowl into a single composition. Şevket is said to be known in particular for floral patterns; Kudret for subjects such as an eagle's talon grasping an egg, a bearded head, and floral-leaf arrangements; and Mesut for portraits and medallion carvings. None of these preferences amounts to a fixed specialty; the same subjects appear across all three men's work.

On signatures, the one clear detail known concerns Mesut Gezer: he is said to have signed his pieces first as "M.GEZER" and, in a later period, simply as "MESUT." How the other two brothers' stamps changed over the years has not been reliably documented.

The brothers' output represents the late-20th-century generation of the Eskişehir meerschaum carving tradition. Because their work rests on narrative figural composition rather than mass-produced molds, it sits close to the artisan pipe conception. The fact that three separate signatures carry the same surname occasionally causes confusion about which brother's hand produced a given piece.

r.x: Tsuge

is a brand founded in Tokyo in 1936, considered today Japan's largest pipe manufacturer. The company's story does not actually begin as a pipe story: founder Kyoichiro Tsuge entered the trade as an apprentice to a master who made ivory cigarette holders. This path — from ivory mouthpieces to cherry wood, then to briar, and finally to hand-shaped freehand pipes — also traces the main line of the brand's more than eighty years of production history.
From Ivory Mouthpiece to Pipe

Kyoichiro Tsuge, records indicate, was born in 1911 in the Ishikawa region of western Japan; what is told of his family background rests largely on the company's own catalog and has not been confirmed by independent records. Orphaned at a young age, he was brought to Tokyo by relatives and began learning to make ivory mouthpieces. In the language of the time, these thin mouthpieces were also called "pipes"; the brand's name was thus associated with a tobacco implement long before briar was ever worked.

He opened his own workshop in 1936. The Second World War, however, soon derailed the business; the benches were redirected at government demand to producing wooden rifle stocks. When the war ended, ivory supply was nearly impossible to come by, so Tsuge kept production going by sourcing cherry wood from the Tohoku region.
The Postwar Pipe Wave

The postwar years were a period when Western-style pipe habits took hold alongside traditional kiseru culture. Pipe tobacco released onto the market by the American military and photographs of Douglas MacArthur published with his corncob pipe visibly fed this curiosity. Tsuge, which had planned to return to mouthpiece production, saw where demand was heading and turned his course toward pipes: bringing craftsmen who worked umbrella handles onto his staff, he began series production of billiard and bent billiard pipes from cherry wood. The company is reported to have employed around a hundred and twenty craftsmen at its busiest period; this figure has not been confirmed by independent sources.

In the 1950s, once imported briar became accessible, the brand switched to briar pipes. During this period, pipes on which an ivory carver engraved traditional motifs such as Mount Fuji, the three monkeys, and geisha onto the bowl were offered as souvenirs to American servicemen in Japan. It is reported that a significant share of the cherry-wood pipes made in Japan in the 1960s were shipped to American units in Southeast Asia.
Apprenticeship in Europe and Ikebana

In the 1970s, the yen's rise in value and competition from cheap-producing Asian countries pushed Tsuge toward a new search. The company sent six of its craftsmen to workshops in Italy and Denmark to be able to make higher value-added pipes. Among them, Fukuda and Sato learned freehand pipe making alongside masters such as Sixten Ivarsson and Jørgen Larsen. The freehands they produced upon returning to Japan found favor first in America, then in Germany and Switzerland.

This accumulated knowledge turned into Ikebana, the brand's best-known top line. Run under Fukuda's supervision with a small number of craftsmen, the Ikebana workshop produces pipes with soft lines that clearly carry the influence of the Danish school. Tsuge has thus become one of the rare brands to sustain both large-scale factory production and a limited number of hand-shaped pipes under the same roof.

r.x: John Aylesbury

, despite what its name suggests, is not an English workshop but the joint brand of a tobacconists' association founded in Germany. Seven family businesses came together in Mülheim an der Ruhr in 1974, reasoning that their individually small shops would be stronger under a shared name. Among the founders are named Paul Bresser of Herne, Elfriede Bruck of Wuppertal, Georg Huber of Munich, Peter Linzbach of Düsseldorf, Alois Koster and Karl Bühl of Cologne, Walter Offermanns of Aachen, and Udo Schilde of Essen; since these names rest on a single source, minor spelling variants may also appear. The brand name is entirely invented: chosen to carry the stately connotation of English tobacco culture, it corresponds to no real person or workshop in England.
How the Association Works

John Aylesbury is not, in the classic sense, a factory but a shared brand and supply structure used jointly by member shops. The association has grown since its founding and is said to now cover more than fifty retailers across Germany; the one unchanging condition of membership is that the business be an independent, family-run tobacconist. Each shop stocks the joint brand's products on its shelves while also broadening its own range with other brands of its choosing. The group's parent company is registered in Munich, and marketing, supply, and brand management run through that office.

The brand umbrella is not limited to the pipe itself; cigars, pipe tobaccos, and various smoking accessories are gathered under the same name as well. The association is also said to play a role in distributing brands such as Peterson, Brebbia, Bartoli, and Big Ben in Germany; this list rests on a single source and may have changed over time.
Private-Label Pipes

The pipes bearing the association's own name are not made in a single place. Models spanning different price and craftsmanship tiers are commissioned from established pipe manufactories across various European countries, and stamped with the John Aylesbury mark. As a result, the brand encompasses both plain models that give the impression of mass production and examples that show notably more careful workmanship. A 9 mm filter chamber is a nationwide habit in pipes made for the German market; the extent to which this convention applies to the brand's models has not been verified catalogue by catalogue. For more on the filter question, see pipe filters and systems.

Among collectors, the products that draw the most interest are the limited "Pipe of the Year" series issued annually. A well-known workshop is generally brought in as a collaborator for these series. According to one account, the 2008 model was made at the Bentley workshop, with the silver band encircling the pipe crafted by Les Wood, founder of Ferndown; since this detail appears in only one source, it should be treated with caution. The fact that these annual series are produced in fixed, non-repeated numbers has made them sought-after pieces on the secondary market.

r.x: RJR coupon pipes

is the name given to the pipe lines that the R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company distributed via coupons inserted into its pipe-tobacco packages and had manufactured at the Dr. Grabow factory in the town of Sparta, North Carolina. These pipes never appeared on store shelves; they could only be obtained by collecting coupons and mailing them in.
The Life of the Campaign

The scheme is said to have gone into effect in the early 1950s; the exact starting year is not on record. Collector sources give a range of 1955-1985 for Westbrook, the best-known of the lines. The campaign closed in 1987, when Reynolds transferred its pipe-tobacco brands to John Middleton Inc.; the sale of Prince Albert that same year is also confirmed by independent sources. At its closing it was claimed to have been the longest-running mail-order campaign in the American market, though this claim has not been verified.
How the Coupons Worked

Reynolds's pipe-tobacco division included, alongside the country's best-known brand, Prince Albert, both Carter Hall and George Washington. According to records, the coupons were placed in the packages and tins of these latter two brands; once a buyer had collected enough coupons, they would mail them along with a small additional payment to the Sparta address and receive a pipe in return. Orders were boxed and shipped together with a promotional set that included a shape chart, so that anyone interested could choose among models and shapes.
Lines and Their Differences
The models given out for coupons were distinguished from one another by surface finish and filter mechanism:

Emperor was the top tier of the series and required notably more coupons. Sculptura, meanwhile, was added midway through the campaign in response to growing demand for a sandblasted surface. The metal fittings on the shanks of these models are among the condensation traps common in American factory pipes of the period; how such mechanisms work is discussed in the entry on pipe filters and systems. Collector reviews note that the orange spade mark on Westbrook mouthpieces makes the line easy to identify.
A Collector's View

The pipes bear the Dr. Grabow stamp, but the brand kept them outside its retail line; store products of the same years never shared a shelf with the coupon models. The widespread account that coupon pipes were made from more carefully selected blocks than shelf products rests on a single period testimony and has not been independently confirmed; for the brand's block selection, see the entry on the briar used in Dr. Grabow pipes. The metal-filter mechanism has long been out of production; the paper-filter models are said to have been less popular in their own day, which is why they are said to turn up rarely today.

Coupon pipes are considered an interesting offshoot of the factory pipe tradition that formed the everyday face of American pipe culture: the pipe circulated as an appendage of a tobacco brand, spreading via mailboxes for more than thirty years.

r.x: Erickson

is the name of the one-man workshop run by American pipemaker Ken Erickson (d. January 2003). Erickson started making pipes in the late 1960s and built a solid reputation among American collectors with his freehand pipes, while remaining almost entirely unknown outside the US. His name today is a signature known only by longtime pipe enthusiasts and estate-pipe followers.
From Minnesota to California

Erickson began the trade in Minnesota; shortly after, he moved his workshop to the town of Sunland in California and continued production there for the rest of his life. His way of working resembled that of the small American workshops of the era: bodies handled one at a time rather than by series mold, limited output, and a relationship built directly with a network of dealers.

The growth of his reputation owed much to the mail-order pipe newsletters of the pre-internet era. In the years when well-known dealers announced new arrivals to their customers via duplicated lists, Erickson-signed examples were, according to the account, among the names that disappeared quickly from the list. This mode of circulation, despite the small scale of production, allowed his name to reach collector circles across the country.
Style and Stamping

Erickson's work falls mostly within the freehand family: bodies that step outside mold shapes, developing by following the grain direction of the briar block, with freely established proportions. This approach places him within the Scandinavian-inspired freehand movement that spread in America from the 1960s onward.

The workshop had no known grading system; pipes left the bench without being sorted into quality tiers. This choice, common among one-man workshops, makes classification unnecessary when production is already limited and each body is considered individually. The stamping is extremely simple: a cursive "Erickson" signature and a two-digit number showing the production year. A "68" stamp, for example, indicates 1968 production. This plain arrangement is one of the rare practices that makes dating pipes easier in the secondary market.
A Break and the Final Years

According to the record, Erickson suffered a serious heart attack relatively early in his career and stayed away from the bench for a long time. He began making pipes again a few years before his death; the number of pieces he completed in this final period is limited. Following his death in January 2003, he was honored at the West Coast Pipe and Cigar Expo held that March with the title "Outstanding American Pipe Maker."

Since the workshop closed with the master, Erickson pipes are found only in the estate market; reading the signature together with the year stamp is the main way of determining which period an example belongs to. Where the stamp has worn faint, the body shape and mouthpiece work remain the only guide; for this reason Erickson pipes are treated as a limited body of work identified through examples with a legible stamp.

r.x: M. Linkman & Co.

is the company that made pipes in Chicago from 1898 to the early 1950s and brought to market one of the most talked-about inventions of American mass production: the pipe broken in at the factory before sale. The company's own name is little remembered today; by contrast, the Dr. Grabow brand it launched in the 1930s has survived long after the founding firm passed into history.
A Pipe Factory in Chicago

Records indicate the company was founded by Louis B. Linkman, who worked for a Midwestern pipe wholesaler, together with August Fisher, with a few hundred dollars they had saved; it began as a small workshop employing only a handful of people. When Anton Burger, who came from the same trade, joined as a partner, the staff grew; the business incorporated in 1907 and Linkman took the role of president. Within fifteen years, production had outgrown workshop scale: a three-story reinforced-concrete factory building was put up in 1922. The lathes worked both briar and meerschaum.

What the "M" in the company name stood for is not certain. The common account holds that the letter refers to Linkman's mother, Mary Linkman; no such explanation appears in the firm's own promotional materials. One of the early-period brands carried the name Alco.
The Pre-Break-In Idea and Dr. Grabow

What set Linkman's brand apart from its rivals was not a pipe shape or a coating but a process applied before sale. The aim was to prevent the harsh taste that arises during the breaking-in of a new pipe from putting the buyer off. When shortcuts such as treating the chamber with a chemical failed to catch on, the company chose the route of smoking the pipe with real tobacco at the factory instead. The setup built in the early 1930s slowly puffed pipes fitted onto tubes using alternating vacuum and compressed air, with the process running until the chamber had been filled and emptied several times. Period advertisements refer to the tobacco used by the name Edgeworth.

The brand name was registered as a trademark in 1932, and the first pre-smoked pipes went on sale in 1933; the phrase "Pre-Smoked" became a fixture of the advertising from 1937 on. The mechanism drew enough attention to make newspaper copy, and it sped up the brand's nationwide recognition. As for the source of the name, the story told is that Linkman got permission from a doctor he knew in Chicago, Dr. Paul E. Grabow, to use his name; that permission is said not to have rested on a written agreement.
From Chicago to Sparta

During the Second World War years, most of the factory's output was set aside for the military, and shortages began on the civilian market; the cutoff of briar shipments from the Mediterranean pushed American manufacturers to look for domestic woods. Though capacity was raised after the war, the company could not sustain this arrangement for long. Linkman is reported to have stepped down from the presidency in 1952; the following year, the company's business and the Dr. Grabow brand passed to Henry Leonard & Thomas, a firm based in Greensboro. Production continued in Chicago for a while longer before the lathes were moved to the firm's plant in Sparta, North Carolina. The town had been home to pipe production since 1943; the source of the blocks worked there is discussed in the entry the briar used in Dr. Grabow pipes.

The brand passed to US Tobacco along with the Sparta plant in 1969, to Lane Limited in 1992, and changed hands once more in the 2000s. The Chicago era thus came to a close. The M. Linkman & Co. name withdrew from production; the pre-break-in idea it introduced, though, remained a marketing asset that was repeated for years in the American pipe market.

r.x: Sir del Nobile

is an Italian pipe manufacturer based in the province of Livorno, Tuscany. The brand's origin lies in an American pipe company's decision to build its own logistics arm in Europe. New York-based S. M. Frank & Co. opened a subsidiary in Livorno in the early 1960s under the name KYM Europe Srl, from which it began shipping goods not only across Europe but also to Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. The name's initials brought together three of the parent company's brands: Kaywoodie, Yello-Bole, and Medico.
From Warehouse to Workshop

Conceived on paper as nothing more than a warehouse and distribution center, the facility soon began operating its own workbenches as well. In 1965, a pipe workshop opened under the same roof, and the pipes coming out of it were sold under the name Sir del Nobile. The American brands' European distribution hub thus turned into a production address.

For many years, the bulk of the workshop's day-to-day business consisted of Medico pipes and filters. These pipes were fitted with 6 and 9 millimeter filter chambers, both sizes corresponding to established filter standards in Europe. While the Medico name is better known in America for its disposable absorbent filter, the European production was shaped around these chamber sizes customary on the continent.
Within the Maremma Tradition

The region where the workshop is located is no accidental address for Italian pipe-making. Tuscany's Maremma coast is considered a center both for the workshops where briar burls are cut and cured and for a lathe-turning heritage passed down through generations. The claim that the craftsmen working at Sir del Nobile's benches come from this local tradition is highlighted in the brand's own promotional material; it has not been documented by an independent record. The idea that the mass-production discipline acquired on mid-range filtered pipes was gradually carried over into a more painstaking premium line is the core of the brand's own narrative.

The products generally remain within classic Italian shapes and are prepared using the usual Italian mass-production method, in which hand work and machine work are combined. The brand is counted among mid-sized manufacturers who work from a regular catalogue, rather than among workshops bearing the signature of individual craftsmen.
Later Period

According to the account circulating around S. M. Frank, the company closed its American production facility in the early 1980s and for a time based its brands entirely on pipes made in Italy. The same account states that this arrangement was not long-lived, and that the company, wanting to keep quality control in hand, returned to American production in 1992 by purchasing a manufacturer in Florida. These turning points have not been confirmed by an independent record. The Italian arm, meanwhile, continued its European distribution with Sir del Nobile and Medico pipes.

The company appears in records under the name Sir del Nobile Pipes Srl, based in Cecina. According to trade directory records, the firm has entered liquidation; since this information is based solely on the directory listing's heading, it is not certain. Nevertheless, the brand's pipes are still mentioned in the catalogues of tobacco and pipe retailers across Europe, and occasionally come up in secondhand collecting circles as well.

r.x: Jacobean

is the first brand name English pipe makers Leslie and Dolly Wood stamped on the pipes they made by hand after leaving Dunhill. Its run lasted only a few years, so its recognition is low; even so, the continuity between it and the couple's later, far better-known brand Ferndown makes Jacobean a starting point for collectors. Pipes bearing the stamp are regarded as the surviving handful from the workshop's not-yet-settled early period.
Founding the Workshop and Division of Labor

Leslie Wood had learned the trade at Dunhill, on the silversmithing side. Toward the end of the 1970s he founded a silversmithing company called L&J Silverware together with Jimmy Craig; the two letters in the name came from the partners' first names. By the years the Jacobean pipes appeared, Craig had long since left the partnership and the business rested entirely on the Wood couple. Wood was still doing contract silverwork for Dunhill and other manufacturers at the time; so Jacobean is the name of a production squeezed between two jobs rather than a full-time pipe brand.

The division of labor was clear: Leslie turned the bowl (stummel) from the briar block on the lathe by hand, the body went into oil curing, and polishing and final touches fell to Dolly. Most of the pipes bear a silver band that reveals Leslie's real specialty. The one clear difference from the Ferndown period is in the mouthpiece: Jacobean pipes were fitted with ready-cast ebonite mouthpieces, while in the later brand mouthpieces were cut and shaped by hand from rod.
Finishes
Because production fell in a transitional period, finish names were never settled and shifted within a few years. Three known finishes are:
Natural:
Light-colored smooth polish; later known as Root.
Original:
Dark brown smooth polish.
Reo:
Red smooth polish.

By what is reported, Leslie Wood initially hesitated to use the name "Root," thinking Dunhill might see it as an infringement; once the firm confirmed the name was free, the finish's name changed. Some of these names carried over to Ferndown as is, while others came to denote an entirely different look under the same name. For this reason, placing a secondhand pipe in time based on finish name alone is not considered a reliable method.
Dropping the Name

The Wood couple had leaned from the very start toward names drawn from English royal history; "Elizabethan" and "Tudor" were also options considered in the same years. Yet the name Jacobean did not find the expected response abroad: buyers unfamiliar with this period of history had trouble pronouncing it correctly. Added to this was a desire for a fresh start that came along with a change in the workshop's location and production method, and the brand was dropped. The Ferndown name that replaced it has come, over time, to represent the entire Wood couple's production history on its own.

r.x: Ehrlich's

, formally the David P. Ehrlich Company, is a tobacconist and pipe maker that operated in downtown Boston for more than a century. The business traces its roots to a cigar and tobacco shop Ferdinand Abraham opened in 1868 in the South End, on Washington Street; Abraham moved downtown in 1880, and the firm never left that neighborhood again. David P. Ehrlich joined the shop in 1881 at age twenty, later married his employer's daughter, and devoted the rest of his life to the business. The company took his name in 1916; management later passed to second-generation relatives, including Richard A. and William Ehrlich.
Addresses in the Heart of the City

The firm's addresses line up along Boston's historic core. The 25 Court Street location it entered in 1880 sat near where, in the 1720s, James Franklin, with the help of his brother Benjamin, had printed The New-England Courant. In 1908 it moved to number 37 on the same street; after the Second World War the shop relocated from its then-location at 33 Court Street to 207 Washington Street, across from the Old State House. When that building was demolished in 1967, its final stop was 32 Tremont Street, adjacent to the city's oldest cemetery, King's Chapel Burying Ground. The mahogany display cases built for Court Street at the turn of the century were dismantled and reinstalled at each new shop, so the interior look was largely preserved across generations.

The centennial year of 1968 was marked by two separate events: the January issue of Antiques magazine carried an article by Wendell D. Garrett introducing the firm's collection of tobacco and pipe artifacts, and the Boston Public Library's Copley Square building devoted a twenty-five-case exhibition to the same collection that same month.
A Bench Behind the Window

Ehrlich's dealt in production as much as in sales. Raw material consisted of briar sourced from Algeria and meerschaum brought from Anatolia. The carvers' bench was positioned to face the shop window, turning pipe making into work that could be watched from the street; during the 33 Court Street years, the bearded master Gustave Fischer was the window's familiar face. Even after briar bowls moved to an electric lathe, meerschaum continued to be worked on an Austrian-made foot-powered wooden lathe. The firm is thus counted among the late links of American meerschaum carving, represented in New York by workshops such as F.J. Kaldenberg.

The use of amber as the mouthpiece material on premium pipes drew the firm into amber trading as a side business; since old pieces were also collected, it came in time to be known for a broad range of amber jewelry as well. The Boston Museum of Science holds a display case, donated by the firm, telling the story of amber.
Stamps and Grades

The EHRLICH name struck on bowls is usually accompanied by a grade name. At the top of the grades was Connoisseur, introduced around 1965-66 and seen only rarely; on this line, the number stamped on the bowl, such as 25, indicated the pipe's price tier at the time. Below it, in descending order, came Deluxe, Supreme, State, and Select; Special Grain and Boston sit at the bottom of the lineup. Early mouthpieces bear the PARA stamp, indicating the grade of vulcanite used; from the mid-1970s onward, standard vulcanite was used instead.
Leavitt & Peirce and the Last Masters

Both Ehrlich brothers were Harvard graduates; Richard A. was in the class of 1922 and William in the class of 1925. When Harvard Square's storied tobacconist Leavitt & Peirce went up for sale in 1956, they took over the shop and left its interior, including the metal ceiling, untouched. Founded in 1883 by Fred H. Leavitt and Wallace W. Peirce, that shop remains open in Cambridge today. The firm's last pipe maker, George Bushee, in the 1970s and into the early 1980s, found bowls that had been turned between 1903 and 1913 and forgotten in storage, and finished them with mouthpieces and ferrules matching the taste of his own day; since the bowls were not his own work, he did not stamp them with his "GB" initials. Bushee retired in 1986, continuing for a while afterward to make handmade briar pipes for the firm from home. According to his son Richard Bushee, who represented the firm at a 1980 Dunhill dealer meeting in London, retail operations continued into the 2000s.

r.x: Getz Pipes

is a one-man pipe workshop founded and run by Bulgarian designer Georgi Todorov under his own nickname. Working in Sopot, Todorov was for a long time regarded as Bulgaria's only internationally recognized pipe master, since the country has no established pipemaking tradition; he learned pipemaking not under a master but entirely on his own.
From Design to Pipemaking

Todorov's training comes from design, not craft. He began his studies at an art and design school in Kazanlak and continued in the industrial design department of the National Academy of Fine Arts in Sofia, graduating in 1995. Learning silverwork from a friend during his academy years underlies the metal bands and ornamental solutions later seen on his pipes. After graduation he worked for a time as a graphic designer at advertising agencies before settling in Czechia.

His introduction to pipes goes back to the late 1980s, to a cheap factory-made Czech pipe he acquired as a student. The idea of making pipes also matured in that same country, during the four years he spent in Czechia; according to the account, meeting Czech master Karel Hinger at a pipe shop in Prague, and the books he gained access to there, determined this direction. Records give both 1998 and 1999 as the starting date: craft records place the start of his profession in 1998, while in Todorov's own account he considered himself, above all, a pipemaker from the end of 1999.
Approach to Production

At Getz Pipes, production rests not on mass-produced molds but on lines the designer has developed over time. The workshop turns out both fully freehand examples that develop improvisationally on the block and hand-finished pieces that follow classical dimensions. The main material is briar; the materials used for the stem are not detailed in sources, but in general the stem materials common in handmade workshops are involved. Thanks to his knowledge of silverwork, metal details, too, can be worked in-house without being outsourced.

Todorov's industrial design background lends the workshop's formal language a measured order: even in pieces belonging to the freehand family, the proportion between bowl and shank is generally kept controlled. In this respect Getz Pipes sits at the narrowest end of the handmade-versus-machine-made definitional debate, as production run by a single master from start to finish.
A Lone Workshop in Bulgaria

The absence of an institutionalized pipemaking practice in Bulgaria has made Todorov's work both harder and more distinctive: there is neither an established master-apprentice chain nor a local material supply network. For this reason, the workshop has, from the outset, oriented itself abroad, particularly toward the collector circles of Western Europe and North America. Todorov's participation in the master gathering held in the Czech town of Kostelec in 2011 is one example of the workshop's ongoing ties to the Central European pipe scene. His entry into international craft records as Bulgaria's pipemaker is also a consequence of this isolated position. Todorov has stated that the country also lacks a pipe-smoking culture, and that this has made the work difficult from the start.

r.x: Eclesias Pipes

is the name of the one-man workshop belonging to Czech pipe maker Pavel Holub. The workshop operates in the village of Kašava, in the east of the country, part of the Zlín region; production runs on commission and in small series, passing entirely through the maker's own hands. Within the wave of Central European artisans that emerged after the mid-2000s, the brand is particularly noted for its hard, deep sandblast surfaces.
Surface Work

The trait that made Eclesias's name is the sandblast texture rippling in waves along the bowl and shank, made of deep rings with sharp peaks. At first glance this surface has been debated at length in the community, giving the impression that sandblasting and hand rustication were applied together. Reportedly there is no such combination at play: the texture is achieved solely at the sandblasting unit, and the details of the settings used remain known only to the maker and a few close colleagues.

The workshop's repertoire is not limited to this one texture. More measured, traditional-looking sandblasts and smooth finishes are also made. All three finish types are often accompanied by contrast staining; the colour scheme ranges widely, from plain black body-and-bit pairings to the vivid, experimental combinations especially conspicuous on sandblasted examples.
Material and Shape

Bowls are made of briar, bits from hand-cut vulcanite; horn is used occasionally for decoration and spacer rings. The maker also has a particular interest in bamboo shanks and works with different bamboo species. The shape repertoire can be grouped into three clusters: established artisan-tradition interpretations (Eskimo, oliphant, wasp), classic moulds (poker, billiard), and original designs built directly from the block.

This last cluster grows out of the workshop's working method. Rather than drawing the proportions of bowl and shank in advance, Holub examines the briar block in hand and decides from there; the flow of the grain determines both the shape and how the surface will be finished. This stance of letting the material speak before the design is considered a contemporary extension of the approach that settled in Danish workshops of the 1960s and 1970s.
The Maker's Path

Holub's interest in pipes arose through a doorway common in the community, reading J. R. R. Tolkien. He learned the craft outside a classic apprenticeship system, through watching online video sources and his own experiments; he tested his first products on himself and on pipe-smoking friends. This route is typical of the new generation of makers who have entered the artisan pipe field over the last twenty years. This same online network also introduced Holub to other makers in the country; reportedly the friendship and technical exchange he built with Jiřík "Biftek" Maczko, working in Bor, holds a particular place in shaping Eclesias pipes. Records indicate the workshop was founded in 2018, and within a few years demand grew enough for the maker to pursue the craft full time.

r.x: Baraccini

is the name not of a workshop but of a sales channel. This Italian-sounding name is used for pipes the US-based retailer Pipes and Cigars has made on its own account. The pipes are made in Italy; the records say production is handled by a large Italian factory, but that factory's name appears in no official statement. Because of this, the brand's country is usually treated as uncertain in country listings: design and marketing sit in America, manufacturing in Italy.
What It Means to Be a Retailer Brand

In pipemaking, having a well-known factory produce a batch on a retailer's behalf under its own name is an old practice; English and French pipe history counts such "house brands" by the hundreds. Baraccini is a current example of this tradition. Bodies are shaped on a series-production line, and briar is sourced from Italian suppliers; distinguishing elements such as the stamp and mouthpiece color are set according to the commissioning party's preference. The difference from pipes the same factory sells under its own name is often confined to finish and stamp alone.

The consequence for collectors is clear: it is not possible to tie a Baraccini to a single maker's hand. The pipes usually show only the brand name and the notation "Made in Italy"; the stamp on the shank is a plain, single-line inscription. Secondhand records also classify these pipes not by manufacturing workshop but by country, that is, as Italian-made.
Lines and Finishes

The brand's early period leaned toward small batches that were not repeated once sold out; in later years this approach was abandoned in favor of ongoing lines. Lines named in the catalogs include Copper, in smooth and sandblasted forms; Capriccioso, with multicolored acrylic mouthpieces and amaretto-toned bodies; Caffè con Panna, with its two-tone look; Leggero, in small sizes; and Strattura (Ebano and Naturale), with deep sandblasting. The Copper line is said to have returned to production in early 2019 after a hiatus; there is no independent record confirming this.

The distinction between lines rests largely on finish and color, while the shape repertoire draws on the usual classics of Italian series production: billiard, dublin, author, and their bent variants. Some models are also made with a 9 mm filter chamber. The same name has also been used for a line of pipe tobacco blends; these blends have no connection to the workshop that makes the pipes.
The Source Problem

There is no independent historical account of Baraccini. Nearly all the information available has been compiled from sales catalogs; basic data such as a founding year, registration date, or manufacturing agreement is not publicly available. A promotional page circulating online links the brand to a family workshop founded near Florence in 1947, while itself stating it has no official connection; since no trade record or independent source supports this account, it is not taken as fact here. Though the name gestures toward a past, the brand is one of many contemporary Italian-origin series-production brands with no documented history — in this respect it differs from workshops with a documented corporate history, such as Lorenzo or Brebbia.

r.x: Sixten Ivarsson

(1910-2001) was a Swedish-born pipe maker who worked in Copenhagen. His legacy lies less in individual pipes than in method: he placed at the center of his bench a hand-shaping technique that freed the bowl from the symmetry imposed by the lathe, and in the same years supplied models for a factory's mass production. In this way, pipe making in Denmark became both a craft capable of standing on its own and a design language recognizable from a distance; today it is regarded as the starting point of what is called the Danish school.
From Repair Shop to Independent Bench

According to records, he was born in the Skåne region of southern Sweden and settled in Copenhagen in the mid-1930s. The war had halted the entry of English and French-made pipes into the Danish market; the pipes people already owned were repaired again and again, and repair shops worked at an unusual pace. Ivarsson entered the trade under these conditions, at a repair shop called Suhr's; for years he did nothing but repairs, then began making new pipes on the same bench. The reason he left Suhr's was a disagreement with the workshop owner over how to share the royalty arising from shapes he had supplied to a pipe factory. When he opened his own workshop in the early 1950s, he became, according to records, the first person in Denmark to do this work independently.
Shapes Transferred to the Factory

Once word spread that new pipes were also being made at the workshop, his clientele widened; one of these was Poul Nielsen, who ran a small manufacturing operation in the countryside. Nielsen wanted to adapt Ivarsson's shapes for machine production, and a collaboration lasting more than forty years began. It is said that part of the shapes in the first regular catalogue of the Stanwell brand were the product of this partnership. The technical precondition for this was the copy-milling machines the factory acquired in the late 1940s: without lathes able to replicate a hand-shaped example exactly, it would not have been possible to carry the master's established proportions into mass production.
The Lathe, Freehand, and Necessary Materials

It is reported that until roughly 1957 he turned his bowls on a lathe, a method that by its nature produces circular, symmetrical bodies. Afterward he switched to shaping the bowl by hand against a rotating sanding disc. This technique, called freehand, allows the maker to follow the grain of briar and build asymmetrical, sculptural bodies; Ivarsson is considered the first master to regularly produce pipes designed this way. He is also credited with the idea of leaving the unworked bark at the upper rim of the chamber intact rather than cutting it away; this is the precursor of the plateau-top pipes that became widespread in the 1960s.

In the same years, briar was hard to come by. Ivarsson made full use of the material by cutting two or three bowls from a single block. This inevitably meant shorter shanks, and he completed the missing length with bamboo, buffalo horn, and bone. This solution born of scarcity gradually became a recognized part of his style.
Students and Stamp

From the early 1960s onward he trained apprentices: his son Lars Ivarsson grew up in the workshop, in later years Jess Chonowitsch and Jørn Micke worked there, and in the late 1980s his grandson Nanna Ivarsson joined the bench. The Swedish maker Bo Nordh also developed his approach to form after coming into contact with Ivarsson.

After becoming independent, he marked his pipes with the stamp "an Ivarsson product" arranged in a ring. It is reported that until around 1965 numbers were also struck inside the ring, with the leading one or two digits indicating the pipe's class and the final digit the year of production counted from 1950; in the later period the stamp carried only the year. It is said he made his last pipes in 1993-94.

r.x: Mastro de Paja

is a handmade pipe workshop that has operated since 1972 in Pesaro, on Italy's Adriatic coast. Over more than fifty years it has changed hands several times, and it has taken on its present character during the long tenure of Alberto Montini, who has run the business for many years. Production is carried out in Pesaro under the company Creazioni Italiane.
Founding and Name

Giancarlo Guidi made pipes as an enthusiast for a while before turning the business into a registered workshop in 1972. In the brand name, "mastro" means "master" in Italian; "de Paja" is the local dialect form of the nickname "Pajetta," which Guidi's friends gave him because of his curly hair. Shortly after founding, Giannino Spadoni, who also sold pipes among other products, joined as a partner; for a period the business was known as "Mastro de Paja di Guidi e Spadoni." From its earliest years the workshop was known for shapes that departed from classic molds.
Changes in Ownership

The partnership ended in 1981. Guidi left the business and, the following year, founded his own brand, Ser Jacopo, also in Pesaro. According to the record, Spadoni, who remained with the workshop, soon ran into financial trouble; Pesaro businessman Terenzio Cecchini took over management by acquiring a majority stake. After Spadoni also left, Cecchini put Alberto Montini, then an accountant in his thirties, in charge of the business. Montini went from employee to manager and partner, and after Cecchini's death became the workshop's sole owner. Under him, annual production volume was deliberately reduced, while sales spread beyond Italy. According to the manufacturer, about two thousand pipes are made a year today, the majority of which go abroad.
Stamps and Grades

At Mastro de Paja, quality information is conveyed through stamps burned into the body. The brand rebuilt this system from scratch around 2015, abandoning the old scheme on the grounds that it squeezed every pipe into a single finish group.
Current System

The mouthpiece of the ART, SPECIAL, and ELITE collections carries a silver or gold sun, while the Classica collection carries a silver or brass dot. The number of suns stamped on the body indicates the grade of beauty; the criteria assessed together include length, surface finish, difficulty of shaping the model, and decoration. Examples bearing no sun at all form the base grade of the series. Straight-grained bodies are called "fiammata" and are graded between one and three suns depending on the quality of the grain. According to the manufacturer's announcement, the year of production has also been marked on the pipes since 2025.
Pre-2015 Classification

Under the old system the catalog was grouped into three tiers: Limited Edition, comprising numbered and special commissioned pieces; Elite Collection, finished entirely by hand; and Classica Collection, machine-worked in its first stage and hand-finished thereafter. Surface information was given through combinations of letters and numbers:

rows: Smooth body with small rusticated sections
Naturally finished smooth body with good grain

r.x: The red-stained finish was called Ruber, the brown-stained finish Castanea. Examples decorated with silver, gold, or precious stones were further set apart by the letters P, N, L, S, and G.
Its Place in the Pesaro School

Mastro de Paja is considered the first link in the generation that turned Pesaro into one of the centers of Italian handmade pipe making; Ser Jacopo, which Guidi founded after leaving, also grew out of the same circle. Briar is used for the bodies. In terms of scale and working method, the workshop sits closer to the artisan pipe tradition than to the large Italian firms that mass-produce.

r.x: Dunhill pipe tobaccos

are a blend catalogue that grew from the shop Alfred Dunhill opened in 1907 on Duke Street in London's St James's district, first expanding and then contracting over eighty years. This entry covers the catalogue's course between 1907 and 1990. The individual characters of the blends, along with the brand's post-1990 period, are the subject of Dunhill Tobacco Blends; the pipes are covered in Dunhill (White Spot).
The Duke Street Counter and the "My Mixture" Ledger

In the shop's opening years the business was not selling ready-made tins but talking with each customer to build a bespoke recipe; the sign in the window read "Tobacco Specialist." Every recipe was given a number and entered into a ledger called "My Mixture." Records indicate that in the early years the leaf used in the blend came from George Dobie & Son in Paisley and a supplier called the Tobacco Supply Syndicate. The first crack in this arrangement appeared in the 1910 catalogue: ten "My Mixture" recipes were now listed openly for anyone, and nine of them carried the name of the customer for whom the recipe had first been prepared. 965, the longest-lived member of the series, had also been arranged for a single customer before 1910. The ledger tradition continued as the catalogue grew; it is said that by century's end more than thirty-six thousand recipes had accumulated in the Duke Street books.
The Birth of the Catalogue Blends (1912-1939)

The English regulation of the period kept the use of additives in blending far tighter than on the Continent or in America; flavour had to be drawn out of the character of the oriental tobacco and Virginia leaf themselves. The processes that achieved this — pressing, toasting, and ageing — could not be carried out at the counter, only in a workshop. In 1912 the firm released its first ready-made "named" blends: Royal Yacht, Cuba, and Durbar. According to catalogue records the list grew during the First World War with Ye Olde Signe (1915) and Harmony (1917); for troops at the front, temporary blends called Campaign Plug and Campaign Mixture were produced along with a plain pipe of the same name. In the 1920s, Standard Mixture, offered in three separate Latakia strengths, along with Three Year Matured and Prince of Wales, were added, followed by London Mixture in 1928. The name Prince of Wales was a token of gratitude to Edward, Prince of Wales, who granted the firm its royal warrant in 1921. In 1936 Throgmorton and Old Colonial were added; Throgmorton took its name from the firm's second London shop, run between 1923 and 1946. At the end of the same decade, when the assets of a tobacconist called Savory were acquired, Baby's Bottom and Savory's Mixture also entered the list. During this period the list only grew: from 1912 until the Second World War, no named blend was discontinued.
Post-War Culling and the Final Expansion

The shrinkage began after the war. Harmony, Throgmorton, and Old Colonial dropped from the list at the end of the 1940s, Super in the early 1950s. Against this, three new blends were introduced in 1951 — Aperitif, Early Morning Pipe, and Nightcap — and the latter two became among the brand's best-known names. Flake, a pressed Virginia, was added at the end of the 1950s, followed by Rough Cut Virginia in 1963. In the 1960s Prince of Wales, Savory's Mixture, and Three Year Matured were culled; the discontinuation of Cuba, blended with cigar leaf, in the same years is attributed to the American embargo on Cuba. The late 1960s and the 1970s brought a temporary expansion with names such as Elizabethan, Golden Label, Golden Hours, and Virginia Ready Rubbed; the culling that stretched from the late 1970s into the 1980s removed a series of names including Aperitif, Durbar, and Ye Olde Signe.
Leaf, Ownership, and 1981

Changes on the raw-leaf side played a large part in the catalogue's contraction. From the 1960s onward, oriental leaves began to be sold in bulk without regard to regional distinction, which made it harder to sustain recipes built on specific sub-varieties. The gradual replacement of Syrian-sourced Latakia by leaf produced in Cyprus is also counted among the developments that permanently changed the taste of English blends. Meanwhile the firm's ownership structure had changed, with Rothmans International taking over more than half the shares in 1967. Records indicate that in 1981 most of the tobacco-blending business, together with the named blends including 965, passed to Murray, Sons & Co., the same group's manufacturer in Belfast. At this long-established facility, dating back to 1810, ageing times shortened and some of the more complex recipes fell out of production; the first chapter of the story that had begun behind a counter in 1907 thus closed.
