r.x: Ludwig Lorenz

is the current name of a pipemaking tradition that has run for three generations in Austria's Tyrol region. The family's start in pipe production dates to 1886, and its present workshop is in the village of Götzens, a few kilometers from Innsbruck. The brand is not a mass-production factory but a one-person handmade workshop turning out a few hundred pieces a year; in Austrian trade records it appears under the name "Pfeifendesign Lorenz," with the occupation listed as pipemaker (Pfeifenschneider).
Three Generations of Family Tradition

Records indicate the family's first generation began making pipes in 1886. Credit for the business taking its present form, though, belongs mainly to second-generation Karl Lorenz: after the Second World War he opened a pipe shop in Innsbruck and ran both the production and sales side over a career spanning nearly sixty years. Born in 1963, Ludwig Lorenz entered the trade not straight from the pipe lathe but through an apprenticeship in wood sculpture, earning his master craftsman's certificate in that field; he learned the finer points of pipemaking at his father's side. He founded his own business in 1985 and ran the Innsbruck shop he inherited from his father until 2004. Since then he has carried on his work at his workshop in Götzens.
The Double-Filter Pipe

The feature that made the Lorenz name known beyond Austria's borders is the double-filter mechanism Karl Lorenz developed in the 1950s. The system has two separate filtering points: a filter plate set into the base of a removable chamber, and a second filter inside the shank. The aim is to trap moisture and condensation from the smoke in two stages, producing a drier, gentler draw. The maker says no other example of this system exists on the market; it is the feature that keeps the brand known outside Austria as well. Standard production is bored for a 9 mm filter; unfiltered bodies are made only on special order. The working principles of filter types and their effect on the smoke are discussed in detail in the entry on pipe filters and systems.
Production and Materials

The workshop turns out between one and two hundred pipes a year, and each piece is one of a kind; every stage, from rough cutting to final polish, passes through the same hand. The briar used comes from the Mediterranean basin, records say specifically from the Calabria region of southern Italy. Stems are hand-shaped from acrylic; gold, silver, and horn, among other materials, are used for bands and decorative elements. The maker says he completes a pipe in about thirty separate steps; in one report from Tyrol, he says the process from rough cutting to polish takes two to three hours per piece. Further detail on this working method can be found in the entry how a pipe is made.

The influence of his sculpture training also shows in the production range. Alongside classic shapes, unusual, figurative, and free designs are also known from the workshop; the maker says that even in these experiments, keeping the pipe smokable remains his basic criterion. In this sense, Lorenz stands at a point where the industrialized German-Austrian filtered-pipe tradition meets the freehand approach.

r.x: Golden Horn

is an export and distribution brand that shipped meerschaum pipes carved in Türkiye to the United States; records place California as the destination for its pipes. The brand's place in pipe history rests not on a model it developed itself but on a carver it introduced: it is known as the first company to bring the work of İsmet Bekler, later associated with CAO, to the American market. Its name is the English rendering of the Golden Horn, the inlet that borders Istanbul's historic peninsula on the north.
The First Link in the Bekler Chain

İsmet Bekler is among the most sought-after names produced by the Eskişehir meerschaum carving tradition; according to the trade, he died in 2018 at the age of eighty-four. Today his name is largely mentioned together with CAO. CAO is the company founded in Nashville by Cano A. Ozgener, a mechanical engineer born in Istanbul in 1937; the business began by improving the stems of Turkish meerschaum pipes with his own engineering knowledge, and celebrated its thirtieth anniversary in 1998. Ozgener left his engineering post in 1977 to devote himself entirely to this work.

Sources diverge on when the Bekler-CAO relationship began: one account says the master's pipes were sold through CAO from 1977, while another rests on an agreement made in 1980 covering all his output. Where the two accounts agree is that Bekler's habit of signing his pipes arose together with this relationship; work from before is unsigned. Golden Horn's place in this timeline is as the first promotional link, coming before all these dates.

One more name appears in the import chain of the same period. California-based importer Irving Korn is credited with discovering Bekler on one of his trips to Türkiye in the early 1970s; his family's company later issued authenticity cards for Bekler's unsigned works from those years. Sources give no direct record tying this line to Golden Horn.
Box Label and Signature

Golden Horn did not carry the output of a single workshop; work by different carvers came out of the brand's boxes. Even so, only Bekler's pipes are considered to have been signed with his own name. That signed and unsigned work stood side by side under the same roof also shows how blurred the distinction between workshop work and factory production could become in export channels.

The mark that actually identified the brand is not on the pipe's body but inside its box: a gold-foil label. On Bekler-signed examples, this label combines three pieces of information: the phrase "Exclusively by Golden Horn Genuine Bekler," a stylized letter "G," and, below the letter, the series name. Recorded series names include "Beyond Imagination" and "Imperial Heroes." Determining that a pipe separated from its box came through this channel is difficult, since the mark is not carried on the body.
Gaps in the Record

How little is known about Golden Horn is a typical example of the documentary scarcity seen throughout the meerschaum trade generally. The company's founding year, founder, headquarters, and the date it ceased operations do not appear in public sources. It is noted that the name was not registered as a trademark in the United States. By contrast, the name "Bekler" was entered into US trademark records in 2001; the master thus left a far more lasting legal trace than the very brand that first introduced him. Golden Horn is not active today; its pipes are seen only in secondhand and collector circulation, that is, in the estate market.

r.x: Directory of Israeli Pipe Brands

brings together, in alphabetical order, pipe names made in Israel or marked as Israeli-made in their stampings. The documented core of pipe making in the country is the Shalom Pipe Factory; the pipes this factory produced were made mostly not for the Israeli market but for export, especially to the United States. The entries below summarize only documented facts, and points left unclear by the sources are noted openly.
Brands
Alpha

— Born as a brand of the Shalom Pipe Factory, Alpha's entire output was earmarked for the United States market from the start; the factory's owner was Bernard Hochstein, a former senior executive of Mastercraft. Israeli-made Alpha pipes date from the 1970s through the 1980s, and one line from this period was marketed under the name "Citation." The name was sold to Mastercraft in the 1980s; its next stop was Lane Ltd., and in the late 1990s Lane released a very small number of pipes in five finishes, each named after a Greek letter. Mastercraft, having taken the brand back over, then offered finishes named Sierra, Delta, Mark V, Blue Ridge, Sabre, and Big Boy under the Alpha USA heading; some of these never carried the Alpha stamp at all.
Barilla

— All that is on record for this brand is a single Israeli-made pipe stamped "Barilla Elegy." Its maker is not known for certain, though based solely on its origin it is thought it may have come from the Alpha workshop. The records contain no information on the brand's founding, owner, or period of production.
Biltmore

— The Biltmore name was first used as a brand of the American National Briar Pipe Co., but examples marked as Israeli-made are also documented; it has been suggested these pipes may have come from the Alpha workshop. A collector has also reported Biltmore pipes made in Spain. These scattered traces point to the name having been commissioned from more than one maker.
Burl King

— Burl King was at one point used as a giveaway pipe in a coupon promotion for Borkum Riff tobacco. A pipe obtained this way by Seattle Pipe Club member Bob Taylor carries a postmark of 11 January 1978; the return address on the package was the town of Sparta, North Carolina. This address shows the shipment was linked to the Sparta Industries plant, maker of Dr. Grabow pipes. Since the same pipe also carries an Israeli-made stamp, Burl King pipes are considered to have been produced at the Shalom Pipe Factory and distributed through Sparta Industries.
Shalom Pipe Factory

— The country's only documented pipe factory; alongside its own eponymous Shalom brand, it drew its main strength from the Alpha name, well known in the United States, and directed the bulk of its output to export markets. Under the Alpha umbrella, the series Caprice, Citation, Classic, Pedestal, Regent, Region, and Rex are on record; some were sandblasted, others finished smooth. At least one of the factory's Citation shapes was also made for Carey's "Magic Inch" line; the records also mention, alongside the factory, the Danish pipe maker Muki Liebermann, known for his briar-bending technique and distinctive shapes, who later settled in the United States.

r.x: Zeman

is the name Jan Zeman used on the pipes he made while working in Nelson, on New Zealand's South Island. The workshop was a one-person operation, and production never grew to serial scale. Because pipe making in the country has remained a narrow circle, Zeman is counted among the few examples of New Zealand-made handmade pipes also known abroad. The workshop's founding year does not appear in known sources.
Catalogue and Series
The workshop's output is gathered into named groups. In the maker's own catalogue,
Signature
appears as the broadest group;
Smooth & Rustic
covers smooth-polished and rustic surfaces, while
Sandblasted
covers sandblasted examples.
Latitude 41
Lord of the Pipes
Old Sea Dog
, and
Club Pipes

are smaller groups. Of these, the name and unusual silhouettes of Lord of the Pipes are attributed to a reference to the Tolkien universe. The series names are sourced from the catalogue itself and are not separately documented by an independent record.

The bowl material is briar. On the mouthpiece side, the use of vulcanite and patterned cumberland rods can be traced through descriptions in secondhand sale records. Since only the maker's own promotional text speaks to which region the briar was sourced from, this detail is not given here as established fact. Pieces carry, besides the maker's name, a country-of-origin stamp reading "New Zealand"; in the secondhand market this is the main mark that links a pipe to Zeman.
Way of Working

Zeman's principal trade was tool and die making; he also worked for many years in photography. In workshop practice, both sides of this background are decisive: the precision of measurement that comes from metalworking and the sense of proportion that comes from visual work.

Working at a one-person scale takes production out of a delivery-schedule bind. Because a block can be left to rest for as long as it takes for the grain to reveal itself, the shape is often determined not by a preselected mold but by the wood's own pattern. This approach sits closer to the freehand outlook than to shapes faithful to classic measurements.
Current Status

According to records, Zeman has stopped making pipes; the date he stopped is unknown. The maker's website is an archive that carries no announcements of new products, only images of past pieces. The brand is therefore regarded not as an ongoing production line but as a completed signature represented by a limited number of pieces.

r.x: Brentegani Pipe

is the one-man pipe workshop run under his own name by Michele Brentegani, working in Verona, in the Veneto region of northern Italy. Recorded as born in 1989, the maker began making pipes in 2015 and turned it into his full-time profession in 2020. No mass production comes out of the workshop; every piece passes through the same hands from design to final polish.
From Wood to Pipes

Brentegani's diploma has nothing to do with pipemaking: he trained in traditional Chinese medicine and tui na massage. Woodworking, however, was a pursuit carried over from childhood; before pipes he made unrelated objects such as bows and bamboo flutes. In 2015, after seeing a friend's churchwarden pipe, he tried making one of his own. He managed to shape the bowl with the means available to him; the mouthpiece, however, remained a problem he could not solve, both in method and material. According to the account, this knot was resolved after correspondence with Brebbia, one of Italy's established manufacturers, resulted in three mouthpieces being sent to him. The next few years passed working part-time and largely through trial and error.
From Show to Academy

His period of self-teaching was followed by contacts established with other pipemakers; records mention the guidance of Ulrik Ash, known as Pipe Ulrik, at this stage. The workshop first announced its name to a wider circle in 2018, at the PipAlp gathering held in Triveneto. In 2020 he was admitted to the Accademia della Pipa, whose entry criteria are strictly maintained; the masters he worked with there are recorded as including Gabriele Dal Fiume, Davide Iafisco, Mimmo Romeo, and Gioacchino Sauro. The same year the workshop became full-time. This trajectory overlaps with the master-apprentice transmission tradition of Italian handmade pipemaking.
Material and Colour

The workshop's main material is the light-coloured variety of Italian briar; alongside this, bog oak and olive wood are also regularly worked. Materials such as horn, bamboo, ebony, snakewood, and tagua come into play as shank inserts, rings, and decorative elements. The brand's most easily recognisable trait, however, is colour. Azure or lapis blue is the maker's most frequently used tone on vulcanite mouthpieces; sea-foam green and magenta are also seen. Bowl staining is kept more restrained, and the colours of the bowl, mouthpiece, and any inserts are chosen relative to one another. The same sensitivity to colour is pursued equally in light Italian briar and in dark bog oak and olive wood.
Shape Repertoire and Lightness

Brentegani's interest extends both to English-French classics and to the Danish school that took shape after 1950. His catalogue includes established shapes such as billiard, brandy, and prince alongside freeform pieces. There is also an intermediate group where the two tendencies meet: pipes that retain the recognisability of the classic silhouette while departing from the rule in one or two details. The common thread is lightness. In Italian brand guides, Brentegani's work is found to have thin walls and measured composition; it is noted that most of the pipes stay under 35 grams.

r.x: Erik Hesse

is an American collector known for his collection concentrated on Dunhill (White Spot) pipes. According to his own account he was born in 1954 in Berkeley, California; no independent record has been found beyond this. Since he does not make pipes, his name is cited not as a manufacturer but as a researcher who has documented the product history of a single English brand in an orderly way. Because the listing of his collection is published on Pipedia, he is counted among the sources tied to the Dunhill entry.
Scope of the Collection

The pipes Hesse has assembled span the 1920s to the 2000s. The listing is organized into chronological clusters: the twenties; the thirties and forties; the fifties; the sixties; the seventies and after. This arrangement, since it allows period-by-period comparison of changes in a single brand's stamps, dimensions, and surface finishing, serves collectors not merely as a showcase but as a reference sequence.

Within the clusters are pieces of unusual size as well. According to the record, one of these is roughly twenty-eight centimeters long, has never been smoked, and is kept with its original box; the patent number in its stamp indicates the piece was made for export to America. The listing also includes a three-pipe set noted on the box as having been cut from the same briar burl. Boxed sets containing more than two pipes are considered rare; it is also noted that most such sets consist of small-size pipes.

Another notable point in the listing is the recording of a shape number with no counterpart in the catalogues. The number in question is described as an enlarged adaptation of a known shape. Such examples are specifically recorded because they show that lists such as the Dunhill Shapes List do not cover the entirety of factory production.
Place Within the Community

Hesse cites Edsel James as the name who guided him toward collecting. James comes from the first generation of Dunhill collectors and is known in the community by the nickname "Mr. Dunhill"; the profile written about him was published under Chuck Stanion's byline in the winter 1998 issue of Pipes and Tobaccos. According to the record, the two collectors corresponded for years but never met in person; a pipe James used for decades later entered Hesse's listing as well. This detail is a typical example of how, before online auctions became widespread, rare pipes largely changed hands through personal acquaintance.

In the listing, some pieces are credited as coming from the collections of other collectors such as John C. Loring. This habit of shared attribution points to the fact that documentation work on Dunhill is the product not of a single person but of a community that cross-references one another's records. The same listing gives particular weight to the deeply sandblasted early examples discussed under the heading The History of Dunhill Shell Briar.

Hesse's compilation is counted, alongside Loring's, among the most comprehensive private collections built around Dunhill in the community. That said, since almost all information about him rests on his own writing, personal details have not been independently verified.

r.x: Peretti

is the brand of pipes and tobacco blends sold under its own name by the Boston tobacconist L.J. Peretti Co. The shop was opened in 1870 by Libero Joseph Peretti, an immigrant from Lugano; records place it as the second-oldest tobacconist still operating in the United States, ranking behind only Iwan Ries & Co., dated to 1857.
From Cigar Workshop to Pipe Bench

The business's original form had to do not with pipes but with cigars. At the shop the founder opened in Boston's North End, he sold cigars he blended himself; a workshop set up in 1892 on Park Square employed around fifty rollers, and Cuban leaf cigars were rolled here for more than forty years. Pipes gained weight in the second generation, in the period of the founder's son, known at the shop by the nickname "The Major" — Joseph Peretti. Blending pipe tobacco began in this period, and the shop's first English-style blend — that is, a mix weighted toward Latakia — went on the shelf in these years under the name "British." In the same period, the shop became Boston's sole retailer of Peterson pipes brought over from Ireland, a distinction that reinforced the store's standing on the pipe side. According to a record on Pipedia, pipe production at the shop began in the 1920s, and third-generation Robert A. Peretti carried this work forward by his own hand from 1938.

The company at one point had more than one branch in the city's business district. The store on Massachusetts Avenue closed in the mid-1950s due to highway construction; the business today is gathered under a single roof, in the Park Square store just beside Boston Common.
Pipes and Blends

Peretti-stamped pipes do not carry the signature of a single workshop; they are briar pipes the shop had made under its own name and finished at its own bench. Simple, classic proportions were largely favored, and most of the smooth-polished examples were left unstained or in a light tone; the reasoning given for this preference is that the wood darkens on its own with use. In this respect Peretti, like Ehrlich's, its longtime rival in the same city, is counted a "shop brand" that defines its product through its own storefront.

The brand's real fame, however, lies on the tobacco side. According to accounts, the Thanksgiving blend prepared in the second generation in 1939 became one of the shop's seasonal traditions. Robert Peretti, who took over the business after the Second World War, created more than eighty house blends and was known for his blending until his death in 2019. These blends carry the shop's own name and are prepared at the Park Square bench; what the brand's name first brings to mind within the pipe community is likewise not a single pipe model but this list of blends. The business later passed outside the family, with management taken up by Stephen Willett, who had worked at the shop for many years.
Today

The company marked its 150th year in 2020, releasing a special blend for the occasion honoring its founding date. The Peretti name is recalled today in American pipe culture less as the name of a single master's workshop than as the name of an unbroken tobacconist tradition.

r.x: Goussard Pipes

is a contemporary signature South African pipe master Charl Goussard carries on single-handedly at his bench in Cape Town. Pipemaking in South Africa is not as established a craft as in Europe or North America; for this reason Goussard is counted among the few names representing the country within the international collector circle.
Founding the Bench

Goussard's interest in pipes began during his university years, and after making his first pipe the pursuit became a lasting one. The bench's founding is dated, according to records, to 2007. Again according to the same account, because sourcing briar blocks was initially expensive, the maker worked with whatever local species he could get his hands on, trying woods such as wild olive, guava, and African blackwood. This early period also lays the groundwork for the material variety that later became the workshop's distinguishing trait.

Pipemaking has not been Goussard's sole source of income. It is reported that his day job runs alongside the bench, and production is correspondingly limited in number. The workshop's current working pace has not been confirmed by independent sources.
Approach to Shape and Materials

Goussard's work, with its measured volumes and unbroken flowing lines, sits close to the Danish school. The maker cites, in his own words, Tom Eltang and Poul Rasmussen among his sources of inspiration. This kinship reads most clearly in his freehand interpretations, which follow the grain of the wood rather than a mold, and in his softened variations on classic shapes.

Most of the bowls are briar work. On the stem and ornamentation side, amber, acrylic, and horn are used; bamboo shank also comes through the bench. As a regional option, the tree known in Afrikaans as "waboom" — protea nitida — has been worked. This species is counted among the details that tie the workshop to its geography.
Assessment

The maker states that he gives priority to the unseen side of the pipe — the precision of the airway, the bowl base, and the stem channel. The trade's general view likewise holds that Goussard's strength lies not in showy ornamentation but in measured shape and clean internal work. Since part of his work has entered circulation through retailers outside South Africa, the signature has also become recognized abroad.

gathers pipe names originating from Armenia in alphabetical order. The single name on record belongs to a one-man bench; the directory therefore currently consists of a single entry. The summary below relies solely on documented facts.

Levon Asikyan

— The master behind this eponymous bench was born in the Republic of Armenia and spent his adulthood there as well. He worked much of his career as an engineer before turning to jewelry-making in later years; pipemaking was first taken up as a leisure pursuit, following the line of Danish school masters as a model. The repertoire leans heavily toward classic shapes: the molds do not stray from factory forms, though proportions are often kept slimmer, with lines finished off with tight cleanup. Algerian-sourced briar is preferred for the bodies; the mouthpieces are not factory-made either, each shaped by hand to fit its pipe. According to the record, the brand's pipes are offered in five distinct surface finishes.

r.x: Directory of Malaysian Pipe Brands

is a list gathering, in alphabetical order, pipe brands founded in Malaysia or run by Malaysian makers. Pipemaking in the country survives not as a factory-scale industry but as handwork carried on in one-person workshops; the number of recorded brands is accordingly small. What the two makers in this directory have in common is that both began the craft as a hobby before later turning it into a full-time occupation.
Brands
Abi Pipes

— The name behind the brand is Abdul Muttalib Md Sidik. He took up the lathe as a hobby in 2014, and a year later left his regular job to make pipemaking his living. As of a January 2019 record, 543 pipes bearing his signature had been made to that point, reaching buyers in the United States, Sweden, Thailand, and Singapore.
Johnsson Ooi

— The brand of a Malaysian craftsman working alone on Penang Island. Ooi began pipemaking as a side occupation in 2004, and devoted himself to it full-time after returning in 2007 from the Tyrol region of Italy. He learned both classic shapes and freehand work under Bertram Safferling. His workshop is open to custom commissions. Records indicate he won the Malaysian Good Design Award in 2013 and 2015, and the Malaysian Best Craft award in 2012 and 2013.

r.x: Tobias Kaffl

is a contemporary German pipe maker working alone in the Bavarian town of Bad Feilnbach. He produces his pipes under the "Kaffl Pipes" signature, bearing his own surname. Because his output remains limited in number, his name appears not among the major market brands but in compilations covering contemporary workshop masters.
A Bench Rooted in Woodworking

Kaffl's introduction to pipes came in the form of an already-established woodworking craftsman turning to a new field. The cutting, shaping, and surface-finishing habits carried over from carpentry have been decisive from the very start of his bench. Records indicate he began pipe making sometime in the 2020s; independent sources do not give a precise starting year.

His name spread relatively quickly within the German-speaking pipe community. His inclusion in German tobacconists' freehand pipe listings, along with coverage by publishers interested in the subject, has built a small but steady circle of interest. The maker communicates with those following his work mainly through social media.
Design Approach

The decisive influence on Kaffl's line is the Danish school; a flowing line, measured asymmetry, and a smooth transition from bowl to shank are common features of his work. A significant portion of the pipes he produces are interpretations that do not fit neatly into classic family names and can be considered freehand. This formal language, already well established for such a young bench, is, along with his craftsmanship, the trait most often cited about him.

The bowl material is briar. Fine woods, horn, and hammer-textured birch stand out in ornamentation and transition pieces. His use of bamboo shanks has become almost a signature in his work; the jointed texture of bamboo becomes the design's carrying element through the contrast it forms with briar's smooth surface.
Construction Details

For stems, he uses vulcanite and Cumberland rod from the German firm SEM; both are common choices in contemporary workshop production and are covered in detail in the stem materials entry. No single measurement is imposed on the smoke channel: depending on the shank's volume, a 6 mm or 9 mm filter chamber may be drilled. This dual preference is explained by the entrenched habit of filtered pipes in Central Europe: since a 9 mm filter has long been standard in Germany and its surroundings, most makers working for the region alternate between these same two measurements.

In a one-person workshop, where every pipe passes through the same hand from start to finish, annual output is small. Pieces are referred to as individual examples rather than by series number or model code; the same shape not being repeated identically a second time is a natural consequence of workshops operating at this scale. Kaffl is counted among the new generation of makers carrying the Danish influence forward in contemporary German pipe making.

r.x: Jan Andersson

is a Swedish researcher, collector, and club figure who put the Scandinavian handmade pipe tradition into writing. His name stands not for a brand but for a documentation effort: he recorded, through direct conversations with the makers themselves, the workshop culture that emerged in Denmark in the second half of the twentieth century and spread to Norway and Sweden. Today, much of what many reference sources know about Scandinavian makers derives, directly or indirectly, from material Andersson compiled.
His Books
Andersson's first substantial work was a monograph on Bo Nordh. According to trade records,
Bo Nordh, Pipemaker

was published in English in the late 2000s, with a later edition carrying the Briar Books Press imprint. The book stands out for gathering together nearly all of the shapes the maker designed; in this respect it functions as a collective shape catalog for readers who have no chance to see the pipes individually.
His second and more comprehensive work,
Scandinavian Pipemakers

, appeared in 2012 after four years of preparation. A heavily illustrated, substantial volume, the book brings together more than fifty makers from Denmark, Sweden, and Norway within a single narrative. The transition between generations is made especially visible here: the main thread the book follows is how the workshop ethos shaped around Sixten Ivarsson carried through to later names such as Jess Chonowitsch and Eltang. Andersson is also said to have prepared a standalone work devoted to Tom Eltang; the details of this book have not been confirmed in independent records.
Club and Magazine Work

Andersson's writing cannot be separated from his club activity. He served for many years as secretary of Svenska Pipklubben (Pipe Club of Sweden) and took charge of publishing the club's regular magazine,
Rökringar

. Some sources also list him among the club's founders; the club's own materials, however, list him only as secretary. By the club's own account it has a few hundred members, some of whom live outside Sweden. The association is known for adding English-language summaries to the magazine for its foreign members — a detail that shows how, from the start, Andersson's work looked beyond national borders. This international orientation of the club's publications occupies a distinct place within the tradition of pipe clubs.
His Place

Andersson's contribution comes not from his own pipes but from making the work of others visible; he has also made pipes himself, at an amateur level. He has spent much of his adult life smoking and collecting pipes, and has lived with his wife in Tyringe, a small town in southern Sweden. The fact that the body of knowledge built up around the Danish school can today be conveyed in an organized way owes a great deal to documentary efforts of this kind.

r.x: Shellcraft

is a series that emerged in the American pipe industry of the 1920s, known for its hand-carved exterior surface. The maker of the series, Reiss-Premier Pipe Co., had also absorbed the company that owned the Kaywoodie brand in the same years. Because of this tie, Shellcraft today draws mainly the interest of collectors tracking early Kaywoodie and pre-Kaywoodie production.
Its Maker and Period

Reiss-Premier was born in Chicago from the merger of Reiss Brothers and the Premier Briar Pipe Company; sources place its founding at different years between 1920 and 1922. The company registered the "Drinkless" name in 1926 and, in August of that same year, purchased the firm Kaufmann Bros. & Bondy. A year later, the Drinkless suction mechanism began appearing in Kaywoodie pipes. The company was taken over by S.M. Frank in March 1955.

Shellcraft is a product of exactly this transitional period. The series was offered under the wording "The Drinkless, Shellcraft" just before the Drinkless name became widespread across the Kaywoodie line. The brand name should therefore be understood not as a company but as a particular surface treatment and sales line.
Manufacturing Features and Dating

The most distinct technical marker of Shellcraft pipes is that the mouthpiece attaches to the shank with a wide, screwless fitting. Kaywoodie's screw-in Synchro Stem mechanism is recorded as having come into use, according to sources, from 1929 onward, with the name registered in 1947; in any case, a screwless Shellcraft points to earlier production that continued the classic push-tenon design, and dates roughly to the mid-to-late 1920s.
Other clues also aid in dating:
The white inlay on the mouthpiece resembles the shape of the Kaywoodie tenon piece.
On some examples, KB&B's leaf stamp appears on the shank.
Boxes and warranty documents carry the period-specific "Drinkless" slogan.
Surface Treatment

The Shellcraft surface that gives the series its name is achieved not by machine sandblasting the briar body but by carving it by hand, piece by piece. The carving forms a dense, regular pattern of indentations. This texture distantly resembles the Dunhill Shell surface that became widespread through sandblasting in England in the same years; up close, however, the regular mark left by the carving tool can be distinguished from the soft, random texture of a sand grain.

The same surface name is noted to have been reused, according to records, much later, in the 2000s, in a series around Kaywoodie; but since the texture in this later production was achieved through deep sandblasting, it differs from the original hand-carved surface. Since original Shellcraft examples are few in number and the stamps of the period vary, the series is counted among the more closely tracked small chapters of American pipe history.

r.x: Chheda Pipes

is the handmade pipe brand produced at Premal Chheda's bench in Columbus, Ohio, in the United States. The brand did not emerge from a standalone factory but from the back workshop of a tobacco shop: the Chheda family's Smokers' Haven. For this reason the Chheda name is known in the American pipe community both as a maker and alongside a well-established retail tradition.
From Shop to Workshop

According to the business's own records, Smokers' Haven's founding goes back to June 1940: the shop opened in downtown Columbus by Joseph Zieve, his wife Ina Zieve, and his brother-in-law Sid Ritter stayed in the same family's hands for more than forty years. Connections Zieve built in England during the Second World War brought Barling, Charatan, Dunhill, and GBD pipes, along with blends made specially for the shop, onto its shelves. The business was sold in 1983, then passed in 1987 into the hands of Arvind and Pushpa Chheda. Their son Premal Chheda took over in 1999; running the shop across from the Ohio State University campus, he turned the balance — which had shifted toward cigars in the 1990s — back toward pipes. The decisive step came in 2006: at the larger address the shop moved to, a workshop was set up equipped not just for repairs but for making pipes as well.
At Butera's Bench

Premal Chheda started working in the family's shops as a child and, by his university years, had handled nearly every task at the counter, including cleaning and repairing estate pipes being readied for sale. The idea of making his own pipe grew both out of this repair work and out of the high-quality artisan pipes he brought into the shop. In his first attempts he sought advice from Tim West and Steve Anderson, who supplied him materials and tools; but the name who set his direction was Mike Butera. Butera invited Chheda to his workshop in Texas and taught him the fundamentals of pipe-making. Having also trained names such as Steve Weiner, Larry Roush, and Michael Frey, Butera is regarded as a pioneer of the American high-grade pipe; this generation's portrait is drawn in the entry on Go West.
The Chheda and Buckeye Lines

Chheda made a limited number of pipes starting in 2003, but none of them carried his own name; the first Chheda-stamped pieces appeared around 2006-2007. The stamp reads "CHHEDA USA" and is accompanied by a three-digit serial number. Bodies are worked from select briar; for mouthpieces, quality materials are hand-cut, chief among them top-grade German ebonite. The repertoire ranges between classic shapes and freehand designs, and no two pieces are alike.

Between 2007 and 2016, the brand did not come from a single pair of hands. Bill Shalosky, who trained at the workshop, and later Jesse Jones, made some pipes alone and others together with Chheda through late 2014 and mid-2016 respectively; Shalosky moved to Tennessee's BriarWorks workshop at that later date. Chheda's wins at the Greater Kansas City Pipe Club's annual pipe-carving contest in 2013 and 2014 also fall within this period. After Jones's departure, the brand was again gathered under one pair of hands.

The Buckeye name was conceived in 2006 to make use of pieces that would not carry the Chheda stamp; over time it moved beyond a second-quality logic into a separate line that, while demanding less overall craftsmanship, still holds to the same standards for internal channel work. On this line the body is generally shaped by hand while the mouthpiece is typically adapted from a ready-made mold. In the mid-2020s the line was divided into tiers by degree of handwork, and, according to records, each tier began to be marked separately on the pipe.
The Workshop Circle

The Smokers' Haven workshop is known not just as a place that produces a brand but as a forge that trains makers; besides Shalosky and Jones, names such as Ryan Alden, Micah Cryder, and Reid Robertson worked there too. The workshop is also known as a gathering place for makers from different countries. In 2018 Premal Chheda also founded RawKrafted, a venture supplying briar blocks, mouthpieces, and tools for pipe-making.

r.x: Clarin

is a small clay pipe workshop working in Caxias do Sul, in southern Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul state. The workshop's founder and maker is craftswoman and musician Edna Bertin. The brand's starting point is to push back against the habit of treating the clay pipe as a cheap, disposable object, and instead to treat the body — as with briar pipes — as a piece worth handling individually and keeping. Records indicate the first model was introduced in 2023; the copyright notice on the brand's official site gives the same year. Promotional texts present the pipes as "the first true Brazilian clay pipe"; this description is the brand's own claim and does not rest on an independent record.
Name and Founding Team

According to the story told, the brand's name comes from the clarion, an old wind instrument, and is a tribute to the grandfather who introduced Bertin to music in childhood; for now, this origin rests only on the brand's own promotional texts. Bertin worked in music for many years, first approached pipes as a collector, and moved into making them as her interest came to focus on clay bodies. Shaping and finishing are her own work. Some brand materials also credit Alexandre Vichinheski as a design partner; since this partnership does not appear on the workshop's official page or in encyclopedic records, it is not treated as confirmed.
Production

The body is entirely clay, shaped as a single piece; there is no separately attached mouthpiece. On some models a separate glaze is applied to the shank tip. This distinction, which gives the impression of a detachable mouthpiece, is purely visual — there is no actual joint.

The process is defined by two separate kiln runs. The dried body is first fired in a ceramic kiln, then glazed and fired a second time; finishing and polishing steps fall between these two runs depending on the model. The glaze is a glass-like layer that fuses with the ceramic during the second firing. Based on quartz or silica that melts at high temperature, it both polishes and protects the surface.

The clay's color changes three times over these runs: the unfired body is chocolate brown, after the first firing it turns salmon, and after the second firing it becomes sand-colored with small black flecks mixed in. Encyclopedic records indicate one of the clay types the workshop uses carries the name "Tabaco"; this name has not been confirmed by an independent source.
Models
The lineup is deliberately kept narrow and built on classic shapes.
The Bulldog One:
Keeps the diamond-section shank of the Bulldog line. Its distinguishing feature is a double-walled chamber designed for heat insulation, along with an exterior surface that evokes stone texture.
The Canadian One:

Follows the proportions of the Canadian family with its long, oval-section shank; an oval shank is rarely worked in ceramic. Besides the smooth finish, there are rustic, tobacco-colored, and glazed-shank variants. For these terms, see the entry on surface treatments.
The Cutty One:
A plain interpretation of the cutty, one of the oldest clay pipe shapes. The forward-leaning chamber is kept, the heel preserved, and the dimensions and chamber volume enlarged.
Use and Care

The ceramic body differs from briar in terms of care expectations. A clay pipe requires no break-in period; nor is a thick layer of carbon buildup inside the chamber desired — cleaning the chamber after every use is expected instead. The body's gradual change in color, meanwhile, is regarded as the natural behavior of the ceramic.

r.x: Yashtylov

is the name for the handmade pipes Russian maker Viktor Yashtylov produces at his workshop in Saint Petersburg. The workshop was founded in the spring of 2005; since then, Yashtylov has become a name recognized beyond his own country both for the freehand shapes he designs and for the unusual solution he uses to join the mouthpiece to the body.
The Road to the Workshop

According to records, he was born in Saint Petersburg in 1971 and has lived his whole life in that city. He entered pipemaking in the very early 2000s, working first for himself; because his early years went into learning and setting up his bench, his work only reached a wider audience around 2004-2005. The workshop's formal beginning is cited as spring 2005. Yashtylov has accepted custom commissions alongside ready-made pipes from the start: making a pipe from a sketch or photo sent by a customer, producing a copy of a lost pipe, repairing a broken shank, restoring a worn chamber, and fitting a new mouthpiece are all among the workshop's services. The order period is stated to run one to two months depending on workload.
The Magnetic Connection

The invention that has done the most to spread Yashtylov's name is the magnetic connection that replaces the classic tenon-and-mortise arrangement. Small, high-quality magnets set into the end of the shank and the base of the mouthpiece let the two parts join smoothly, without relying on friction. This solution won him two things: the transition zone no longer had to keep the usual cylindrical cross-section, and the pipe could be taken apart even while still warm. In his early work he had experimented with the relationship between the shank end and the mouthpiece base, sometimes blending them with parallel lines, sometimes deliberately setting them against each other in disproportion; the magnets made it easier to carry this exploration into concave and wavy surfaces, and into faceted, paneled freehand shapes.
Material and Craftsmanship

He works with plateau blocks of briar rested for three years; sources cite blocks of Corsican and Spanish origin, and the workshop has also stated it plans to move to Algerian briar rested for ten years. For mouthpieces he mostly uses "A"-stamped ebonite, turning to cumberland, acrylic, and synthetic amber on request. In surface work he follows a graduated sequence from fine sandpaper to carnauba polish; the chamber's interior is also finished with sandpaper. He bores the smoke channel to roughly 2.8 to 4.5 millimeters depending on the pipe's size and the customer's request; inside the mouthpiece he shapes the airway as a cone narrowing toward the bit. The width and thickness of the bit are likewise adjusted with comfort in the mouth in mind.
His Place in the Saint Petersburg Circle

Yashtylov is regarded as one of the central names of the city's contemporary generation of makers. His workshop has been a site not only of his own production but of others' training: Andrey Grigoriev was a regular guest there for years, left engineering for full-time pipemaking in 2010 on Yashtylov's suggested apprenticeship, and learned the magnetic-mouthpiece technique at this same workshop. For other examples of Russian handmade production, see the Vladimir Grechukhin and Kharitonov entries.

r.x: Pirkenhammer

is a porcelain manufactory founded in 1803 in the village of Pirkenhammer near Karlsbad (Karlovy Vary) in Bohemia, and it continues operating today in the settlement now known as Březová. It is counted among the oldest porcelain concerns on Czech soil. Its name matters to pipe history because, in its founding years, it produced tobacco pipes alongside tableware; over the following two centuries, however, its product range was largely centered on table and decorative porcelain.
Founding and Chain of Ownership

The manufactory's founder, Friedrich Höcke, was a potter of Thuringian origin; records indicate he built two kilns and, with Thuringian workers he brought in, made both tableware and pipes. The business was known by its founder's name in its early years. Höcke is reported to have leased out the factory in 1806 and transferred it a few years later. The business was taken over by Johann Martin Fischer of Erfurt and a partner surnamed Reichenbach; the factory came to be known during this period as Fischer & Reichenbach. Sources give the year of the change of hands as anywhere between 1811 and 1822; the year the porcelain production privilege was obtained is given as 1822.

Fischer died in 1824; the business was run for a time by his widow, Sophie Friederike, and then passed to his son, Christian Fischer. When the partner withdrew from the business in 1846, the factory was gathered wholly under Christian Fischer. In 1853 the business was left to Christian Fischer's son-in-law, Ludwig von Mieg, and in later years it was known as
Fischer & Mieg
. The manufactory's distinguishing mark, the crossed-hammers stamp, is said to take its name from the village's blacksmithing past and is still in use today.
Products and Reputation

From the 1820s, Pirkenhammer was regarded as the finest porcelain producer in Bohemia. Its catalog included tableware decorated with landscape and floral motifs, vases, candlesticks, and, later, figurines and thin porcelain plaques that showed an image when held to the light (lithophanes). The business became the first Czech factory to receive permission for copperplate-print decoration in 1829. Medals won at international exhibitions cemented its reputation; the most cited is the gold medal won at the 1839 Vienna exhibition.

The porcelain pipe of the early period is a product shaped by the nature of the material. Because porcelain, unlike clay pipes, is not porous, it calls for a water chamber to collect condensing moisture and a long stem. For this reason the porcelain pipe type that became widespread in Central Europe was known more for its painted surface than for its smoking qualities. The German branch of the same tradition includes the early bowls of the Meissen Porcelain manufactory.
The Twentieth Century and After

After the First World War, the business became part of EPIAG, a joint-stock company that gathered the region's porcelain factories under one roof; the year it joined is given in sources as anywhere between 1918 and 1920. Following the Second World War, Pirkenhammer was nationalized along with the 1945 nationalization of Czechoslovakia's porcelain factories; it was successively folded into the Starorolský Porcelán and Karlovarský Porcelán structures and served as a research-and-development center. After 1989 it was privatized, and production went through an interrupted period. In 2006, with the appointment of designer Alexey Narovlyansky to lead the operation, a new product line was created. The manufactory operates today in Březová under the name Manufaktura Pirkenhammer.

r.x: The
Directory of German Pipe Brands

is an attempt to gather the scattered record of German pipe production in one place; this page holds the second part of the two-part directory, covering eight entries from Volker Bier to Wunderlich. Pipe making in Germany was never anchored to a single center: large factories and filter manufacturers worked alongside one-man workshops in small towns. The entries below are brief and factual; brands for which only a name is on record are kept in the list, with the gaps clearly noted.
Brands
Volker Bier

— The letters this German maker uses to mark quality tiers come from the initials of the heavy metal bands he listened to at the bench. The letters are ranked by surface: JP covers pipes fully or partly rusticated, IR smooth surfaces that may carry small spots, RA pipes with pronounced grain but a few flaws, and MA those with the cleanest, flaw-free grain. IE and BR fall outside this ranking; they are not tiers but line names, distinguishing pipes with bamboo shanks from those with bog oak stummels, respectively. Bier says the letters describe appearance only, and that there is no difference in workmanship between JP and MA. The logic of the distinction matches the framework laid out in the surface finishes entry.
Volz
— The pipes of Reinhardt Volz, working in the Inheiden district of Hungen in Hesse, are recorded under this name. No record exists on the nature of the production.
Waber
— Franz E. Waber's workshop in Augsburg produced handmade pipes. Neither the workshop's shape repertoire nor the years it was active are documented.
Werner Bürmann
— The business known as Pfeifenlädchen is run by Werner Bürmann in Besse, part of Edermünde in northern Hesse. Records go no further than the maker's name and address.
White Elephant

— Founded by Robert Maderholz in the Franconian town of Ettenstatt, the firm is today known mainly for pipe filters and pipe cleaners; it is the only company in Germany producing these cleaners, and one of three across all of Europe. Yet the business began at the pipe bench: Maderholz made pipes from 1945 to 1984, after which the firm shifted first to filter production and then to cleaners. Years later, pipes reentered the product line as well.
Wilhelm

— The work of self-taught maker Gerhard Wilhelm consists of freehand pipes with vulcanite mouthpieces, made either for a 9 mm filter or without one. He uses a stamp bearing the letter W as his signature.
Wolsdorff

— A passion for cigars led Hamburg merchant Emil Karl Ferdinand Wolsdorff to open a shop on Georgsplatz on May 7, 1907. His plan had two prongs: a line of own-brand goods made for him by quality manufacturers in Westphalia and Baden-Württemberg, and a network of branches spanning major cities. This network, which eventually spread nationwide, sold pipes, cigars, and tobacco; records put the store count at around one hundred seventy. Wolsdorff Tobacco GmbH passed in 1997 to Oettinger Imex AG, today known as Oettinger Davidoff AG.
Wunderlich
— Ralf E. Wunderlich's workshop in Weiterstadt is called Atelier REW. What shapes the maker worked in and in which years are not on record.

r.x: Christian Wolfsteiner

is a pipe maker who signed his pipes with the Tarock Briar stamp and worked in the German city of Ingolstadt. Born in 1961, Wolfsteiner came to the craft late and entirely on his own initiative, and never tried to scale up his output. His name is known not for series production, but for at most a few dozen unusual shapes a year.
The Road to the Workshop

By his own account, Wolfsteiner picked up a single pre-drilled briar block in the winter of 1997-1998 and started experimenting; this one-off impulse turned into a lasting pursuit. In 2001 he set up a small workshop and produced his pipes there. Output was never tied to a regular schedule at any point; the range the maker gave was anywhere from zero to forty pipes a year. This fluctuation is taken as the direct result of pursuing the work as a craft rather than a business.
Method and Materials

On the material side, the main body is briar; the maker is known to have made a small number of pipes from olive wood, and to have turned to different woods for the shank in three-piece designs. Mouthpieces are worked in acrylic, ebonite, or a synthetic compound combining the properties of the two; the majority of his pipes are unfiltered. For the mouthpiece material's share in a pipe's character, see the entry on mouthpiece materials.

Shaping at the workshop relies almost entirely on hand tools. Once the block is cut, the main tools giving it form are various files and rotary hand tools; the maker has stated he does not use sanding discs or belt sanders. This choice is credited with giving the surfaces a texture shaped by hand, far from machine flatness.

His approach to form owes less to classic molds than to the maker's own pursuit of line. The resulting pipes are designs that step outside conventional dimensions and are each named individually; in this respect his work is assessed within the German branch of the freehand tradition. His surface work, particularly his experiments with rustication and partial sandblasting, is considered distinctive among collectors.
Circle and Influence

Wolfsteiner was among the makers who set up a table at German pipe fairs. According to records on Pipedia, the first joint workshop, held at Uwe Maier's home in 2014, took the name Grainstorm at Wolfsteiner's suggestion; the gathering became a tradition in the years that followed. The same records name the core group as Roger Wallenstein, Steffen Mueller, Manfred Hortig, James Gilliam, and Martin Hansen.

The maker's influence on the younger generation is another point frequently raised within the same circle. Swiss pipe maker Yves Bäcksteiner, who met Wolfsteiner at the Speyer fair, says he considers him his own mentor.

The maker profiles on Pipedia report that Wolfsteiner died around 2016; the date is not documented in independent sources. The limited number of pipes he left behind appears in secondhand records under the stamp Tarock Briar, or simply Tarok.

r.x: Ron Powell

is an American hand maker who produces pipes under the signature RDPipes. The signature arises from the maker's initials, R.D., merging with the word "pipes" on a shared "P"; in the community it is most often read as "RD Pipes." This name became the identity of roughly a decade of limited but shape- and material-varied production. Powell arrived at the bench not through a classic apprenticeship but through collecting and then repair, in that order.
The Road to the Bench

By the maker's own account, more than twenty years of local and long-haul trucking left him with lasting back problems, which prevented him from continuing his old interest in handwork with heavy materials. The pipe stands out within this constraint as an object light enough to work with: first came collecting, then the repair of worn pipes. According to Powell's account, he joined an online discussion forum for pipe makers in 2013, completed his first pipe using knowledge gathered from posts there, and made production a lasting pursuit. Such late, self-directed beginnings are a typical result of the online flow of information that has made possible the worldwide spread of briar makers.
Style and Craftsmanship

It is difficult to tie RDPipes pipes to a single school. In texts introducing the maker's work, the style is described as a blend moving between Italian and Danish lines, occasionally returning to classic English proportions. Powell has tried both simple and ambitious shapes, using bamboo shanks, exotic wood rings, acrylic, and silver alongside sandblasted and smooth surfaces. He states that he uses Mediterranean-origin briar for the bodies and chooses, as far as possible, the highest-quality rod material for the mouthpieces.

In the maker's own description, the center of gravity of the work lies not in appearance but in engineering. The smoke channel in the shank is drilled at 9/64 inch (about 3.6 mm) and continues, narrowing, through the mouthpiece. Mouthpieces are not bought ready-made but hand-cut from vulcanite rod; the bite zone is reduced to a thickness of 3/32 inch (about 2.4 mm) to sit comfortably between the teeth. The polishing of the airway inside the mouthpiece is justified on grounds of ease of cleaning and airflow. These dimension-driven choices exemplify why mouthpiece craftsmanship is considered decisive in a handmade pipe; much of the part of the pipe-making process invisible from the outside consists of decisions of this kind.
The End of Production

According to records, Powell completed his last pipe on 15 March 2022 and gave up pipe making. No new production is being made under the RDPipes name; the maker's work can now only be followed through collections. Powell was also a guest on a pipe interview program, where he described his approach to production; this recording is one of the few sources offering firsthand information about him. His home state and city are not reliably documented and are therefore not given here.

r.x: Karl Erik

is the pipe brand Danish maker Karl Erik Ottendahl (1942-2004) built from his two given names. The Danish School usually brings to mind pieces made in small numbers, one-off and expensive; Ottendahl set his goal at the exact opposite and tried to turn the freehand pipe into a product a moderate-income smoker could afford. In doing so he built a distinctive system that did not conceal bench assistance, while leaving the final shaping to the hand. A production life spanning nearly forty years encompassed both a fifteen-person factory and a one-man workshop.
From Aalborg to Nairobi

Ottendahl was born in Aalborg, in the north of the Jutland peninsula. He encountered pipes at fourteen; after finishing school he began an apprenticeship in lithography at sixteen. Carving pipes was, in these years, a leisure pursuit; most of his early pieces were given as gifts to senior masters at his workplace. In 1962 he went to Nairobi, the capital of Kenya, to continue his trade; unable to find a pipe he liked there, he met his own need by hand. When he returned to his country three years later, lithography was not providing him enough income, so he began selling a few pipes to boost his earnings. He gave these pieces his two given names and stamped them with the letters "KE." When a few of Copenhagen's major tobacconists took the pipes onto their shelves, the direction of the business changed: Ottendahl acquired better lathes and moved into the trade full time. The brand's beginning is generally placed in the records at the mid-1960s.
Production Shared Between Lathe and Hand

As demand grew, a move to a larger space took place around 1967-68, and the first employees were hired. The real leap came through the relationship established with the New York-based Wally Frank Ltd.; the importer was looking for affordable freehand and fantasy pipes of Danish workmanship that could fit alongside the reasonably priced products in its catalog, without any compromise on craftsmanship. The workshop eventually grew to as many as fifteen people, production was divided into stages, and each craftsman specialized in a particular task. Bent Nielsen and Peder Christian Jeppesen, who passed through this staff, later became makers known under their own names.

Ottendahl's definition of "handmade" did not exclude having the rough shaping done on automatic lathes; where the hand came in was the final shaping and finishing stages, and the master would say so openly. What truly set the result apart was staying away from copy-milling: there are many KE pipes that resemble one another, but none is an exact copy of another. The majority of the mouthpieces came from Stanwell nearly finished, and the sandblasting work, too, was mostly done at the same firm.

The workshop's products were not sold only under its own stamp. For the Danish and US markets, production was also carried out under names such as Champ of Denmark, Knute, Larsen & Stigart, Shelburne, Garrick, Sven Egholm, and Wenhall. Because these names occasionally overlapped, and were even used together on the same pipe, making a clear distinction based on the stamp alone is not possible for most examples.
Quality Stamps

In the old system, quality was indicated by numbers rising from 4 to 1, with the "Extravagant" stamp applied to pieces made entirely by hand. In the later system, the numbers were replaced by letters running from D to A, while Extravagant examples were divided into the tiers C, B, A, AA, and AAA. Outside this system, the stamp "II S" has long been debated among collectors. None of the explanations circulating in the community have been confirmed; the only point that can be confirmed is that these pipes went only to the US market.
Return to Working Alone

Because the freehand fell out of favor worldwide and buyers pressed for lower prices, Ottendahl cut off exports to the US entirely in 1987. Running the factory left him no time to sit at his own bench; in 1990 he stepped back from management and returned to working alone once more. In this final period he moved toward more classic shapes, took the grain of the briar he used as the determinant of form, and hand-cut his mouthpieces. In the 1990s he designed several models for Stanwell's H.C. Andersen series. Around 1998-99 he transferred the German rights to the "Karl Erik" name to Planta Tabak-Manufaktur; from then on he signed his own work sent to the German market with his surname, under the "Ottendahl" stamp. After a thirteen-year gap, US sales reopened in 2000. Ottendahl died on 12 September 2004 at his home in Korsør, on the island of Zealand, following a stroke.
