r.x: K's Pipes

is a pipe brand, its life limited to a few years, founded by Japanese master Shin-ichi Kuwahara (1969-2015) in his small workshop in Kawasaki. Nearly all the information about the brand rests on the pipe community's own records; there is no independent institutional archive or official manufacturer record. According to these records, Kuwahara began pipemaking in the very early 2010s, in the hours left over from his main job; after placing in competitions held at Japanese pipe gatherings, he decided to continue production under his own brand.
Materials and Craftsmanship

The workshop's main material was briar blocks from Italian suppliers. Alongside this, Kuwahara also tried strawberry tree wood as a bowl material; for shank and stem joints he used thin insert pieces of various exotic woods. Strawberry tree is a bowl wood less common than briar, harder, and with a different grain texture; its selection as a bowl material is counted among the details showing the workshop's experimental side. What was most talked about regarding the brand, however, was its bamboo shank work. Mastery in bamboo requires the joints to fit the pipe's scale and the point where wood meets bamboo to be imperceptible by hand; the care Kuwahara showed on these two points is considered decisive in his work gaining recognition.

In surface treatment, detailed hand-applied rustication stood out from the start. In mid-2015 the maker also began trying sandblasting; this late-period work is noted separately for the maturity reached in such a short time.
Design Outlook

The workshop's shape repertoire drew mainly on the classic English school; it is said he reworked traditional molds in the Dunhill line with his own interpretation. But what made the brand's name most known was not these classics but very short-shanked "nose warmer" pipes that played with proportions. The best known among these are chimney shapes whose bowl rises taller than the pipe's total length; these designs, which deliberately upset the proportional relationship, also require a technically balanced weight distribution.
Aftermath

Most of production was made directly to order; in the brand's final years its work also began circulating through a few intermediaries. It is said that annual output did not exceed a few hundred pipes, though this figure rests on a single record alone. According to the same record, Shin-ichi Kuwahara died in a motorcycle accident in December 2015, and the brand ended with him. For this reason, K's Pipes is counted, within the post-2000 generation of Japanese pipemaking, among the names of which very few examples remain in circulation.

r.x: Georg Jensen

is a Danish pipe business founded in Copenhagen in 1954 by Per Georg Jensen and his wife. It is a separate concern from the famous Danish silver house of the same name; the resemblance stems from a very common combination of first and last name in the country. The brand grew during the years the Danish school was rising, and built a system that moved back and forth between series production and hand-shaped upper tiers.
Forty-Seven Years as a Family Business

The business remained in the same family's hands from its founding to its closure. From the 1980s onward, management was taken over by the founder's daughter Lis and her brother, who shared his father's name, Per Georg Jensen. Production scale, according to records, ran around two thousand pipes a year, positioning the brand as a mid-sized producer set apart from the era's giant Danish factories. The workshop kept both catalogue models multiplied at the bench and top-tier examples finished one by one under the same roof.
Lines and Stamps

The business used a tiered series system that ran on the logic of the factory pipe. From the lower tier upward, the names Danish Sand; Achat and Amber; Red Flame and Red Skin; Sunrise, Orange Ekstra, and Starline; Contrast, Bicolour, and Harmon; and, at the very top, Excellent and Masterpiece appear. Series pipes generally used acrylic stems, while upper-series pipes used ebonite or vulcanite.

Stamping progresses in step with this tier. The common body stamp consists of the model name, model number, and the phrase "Made in Denmark," with a red GJ mark on the stem. One tier up, the name "Georg Jensen" appears next to the model number in italic or ornate script. Hand-finished special series are set apart by a "Handmade in Denmark" stamp and a white GJ mark. At the very top sit individually shaped freehand examples, which carry a "Straight Grain" stamp along with a number grading grain quality from one to thirteen. Thirteen, according to records, is the highest tier, and examples bearing this stamp are extremely rare.
Closure and Aftermath

The workshop struggled with declining sales through the 1980s and 1990s, a period in which many small and mid-sized Danish factories experienced a similar contraction. The business ceased production in 2001. That same year, Per Georg Jensen moved to the tobacco house Mac Baren, where he began working on blend development and promotion, remaining for many years one of the company's well-known faces. There is no reliable record of the brand name being carried on by another manufacturer after the closure.

Today, Georg Jensen pipes are seen only in secondary circulation. The brand, alongside contemporaries such as W. Ø. Larsen, is counted among the second tier of postwar Copenhagen pipemaking. The tiered nature of its line names and stamp formats makes it comparatively easy to retroactively place any given example within its proper quality tier.

r.x: Satou

is the name Tokyo-based Japanese master Smio Satou (in Japanese order, Satou Smio) stamped on his pipes. What set the maker apart was combining European-derived briar pipe making with Japan's centuries-old
urushi
lacquer craft on the same bench. He carried out all his production by his own hand in a single-room workshop above his home. Satou died on 16 July 2023, at the age of seventy-nine.
A Craft Passed Down from Father

The craft entered the family through his father. The elder Satou was one of the first few craftsmen in Japan to make European-style pipes from briar in the 1940s. Until then, a pipe in Japan meant the thin metal-bodied, bamboo-shanked kiseru; Western-style pipes were smoked but not made locally. As Smio Satou told it, his father had even repaired General Douglas MacArthur's pipes during the postwar occupation years. In later years he did contract making and repair work for Tsuge, and his son's first stop was the same firm.
The Tsuge Years and Denmark

Smio Satou worked at Tsuge for around twenty-five years, mostly through the 1970s and 1980s. In the 1970s he was sent to Denmark twice with his colleague Kazuhiro Fukuda, learning the classic Danish handmade pipe approach firsthand. According to the account, the benches the pair stood at included those of Sixten Ivarsson and Jørgen Larsen. Fukuda later became the name who carried on Tsuge's hand-crafted Ikebana line.
Finishing with Urushi

He began making pipes under his own name in the late 1990s, and settled on his distinctive finishing method during this period as well. Adapting the urushi lacquer that Japanese furniture-making had used for centuries to pipes was an unusual choice for a craft accustomed to carnauba wax: lacquer is far more durable than wax and its finish does not need periodic renewal. The cost is patience. Ten coats of lacquer are applied to the bowl; each coat rests for two days in a cabinet kept at 70-75 percent humidity and 25 degrees Celsius. A single pipe thus takes about a month, and annual output stays between thirty and fifty. On some pipes, the stem carries a
tsuishu
inlay obtained by carving into layers of red lacquer applied one on top of another.
Bamboo and Mechanics

Satou's best-known shape is an arrangement in which a small bowl is extended by a long, thin bamboo shank. Two details make this delicacy possible: the bamboo's interior channel is lined with nylon, and a metal tenon is fitted at its ends. The seemingly fragile piece can thus both extend and bear load. The tenon is not glued to the stem; it locks in place via a metal pin descending from the stem surface. On pipes that don't use bamboo, a water-buffalo-horn band or gold and silver banding is preferred instead. Most bowls have smooth surfaces; sandblasted examples by the master are few in number.

r.x: Barclay Rex

is a tobacconist's shop opened in lower Manhattan in 1910 by Vincent Nastri, and kept in the same family to this day. Its founder was a pipemaker who had emigrated from Italy; records give his hometown as Salerno. In the shop's early years, part of what sat on its shelves was pipes made by Nastri's own hand. The name arose from a combination of two sources: Barclay Street, where the first shop stood, and Rex, Nastri's Great Dane.
The Story of the Name and the Early Years

How the second word in the shop's name became permanent rests on a story told within the family: as the account goes, rather than placing a newspaper ad, Nastri used his dog instead, fitting Rex with a cover bearing the shop's name and walking the animal around the neighborhood. This detail has no documented basis; what is certain is that the dog's name settled into the business's name.

The business built its early years on pipes and pipe tobacco, later broadening its range toward cigars. Its address did not stay fixed either. The shop moved more than once within Manhattan's financial district, with known addresses including Broad Street, 42nd Street near Grand Central, and Lexington Avenue; the opening and closing dates of these branches do not agree across sources. In later years the business consolidated into a single shop on Pearl Street. According to news sources, management passed in 2019 to Vanessa Nastri, a descendant of the founder; which generation of the family is now at the helm varies from source to source.
Barclay-Rex Stamped Pipes

The shop did not confine itself to selling other makers' pipes; it also ran a line under its own name. These pipes spanned a wide range, from plainly worked examples for everyday use to the carefully made pieces collectors seek out. By all accounts, the bodies used Algerian briar at least through the 1960s; Algerian briar was, until that time, one of the industry's main sources of raw material.

Some of the house-brand pipes were made elsewhere. One known example is the private-label pipes the English manufacturer Sasieni made for a time on Barclay-Rex's behalf; these carry Sasieni's own shapes and shape numbers. Arrangements of this kind were a common route for shops without a workshop of their own, or whose production outstripped their capacity.
The HGP Stamp Debate

The detail most discussed in collecting circles is the "HGP" stamp seen on some Barclay-Rex pipes. According to the account passed down within the family, these letters belong to a maker who worked for the shop for a time and set a small light-colored dot into the mouthpieces; because this dot detail directly calls to mind the Dunhill tradition, the story has attracted attention.

Against this, the same letters also appear in shop advertisements going back to 1920, where they look more like a commercial mark than a person's name. No document exists today to settle definitively between the two explanations. The stamped pipes are held to have been made in a single series, never repeated afterward; for this reason the HGP stamp is regarded as the main clue for collectors trying to trace the shop's early production.

r.x: Fuerst

is the small pipe output known under the name of an American amateur maker. The maker behind the name is Bernard William "Bill" Fuerst, born September 1, 1923, in Scottsbluff, Nebraska. The brand is not a regular business or catalogue but simply a limited number of hand-carved bodies the maker produced at the bench in the second half of his life. In this respect it belongs to the numerous generation of part-time makers who fill a large share of the history of pipemaking in the United States.
The Maker's Life

Fuerst was the son of William and Beulah (Koenig) Fuerst. During the Second World War he served in the Pacific theater in the U.S. Army's Signal Corps, holding the rank of first lieutenant. On August 6, 1946, he married Lorene Senne in Greene, Iowa. He completed his career as a marketing manager at Illinois Bell. He lived for many years in Villa Park, Illinois, moving in 1980 to Mountain Home, Arkansas, where he spent the rest of his life. His skill in woodcarving was known beyond pipes as well. He died on April 17, 2016, at the age of ninety-two.
Pipes and the Cellini Connection

Records of Fuerst's pipemaking are limited. According to his son Bob, the maker also produced pipes for a time for Cellini; however, the duration and scope of this collaboration are undocumented, and no independent record supports the account. Surviving bodies are dated between 1979 and the late 1980s; this range is drawn not from period documents but solely from the pipes that survive today. No reliable figure for total output is known.

A notable feature of the pipes is the brief descriptive note given to buyers. In this note Fuerst stated that he used Algerian-sourced briar for his bowls and English hard rubber for his stems. This information rests on the maker's own statement and has not been externally verified. The same note's claim that the wood was two to three centuries old is an emphasis common in the pipe advertising of the period; how such age claims should be weighed is discussed in the entry The Hundred-Year Briar Legend. For why hard rubber (ebonite) was favored, see the entry on stem materials.
Current Status

Production ended with the maker's death. Some of the surviving pipes have passed from the family to collectors, and most of what is known about the brand has been gathered by that route. The Fuerst name is therefore considered less a commercial brand than a documentary heading tied to the work of a single maker. Since most of what has been written about him rests on family accounts and the marks on individual pipes, the dates and details here should be read as the best available estimate rather than a firm record.

r.x: Briarlab

was a short-lived partnership in the US that tried to bring independently working pipe masters together in a single production space. The venture, led by Michael Lindner and Nate King, operated in Indianapolis, the capital of Indiana, and, according to records, closed in February 2017. It is remembered less for the pipes it produced than for the working model it tried out.
The Founding Idea

The venture's starting point was the most demanding part of handmade pipemaking: a master working alone has to set up an entire lathe, mill, sandblast cabinet, and dust-extraction system on their own budget. Briarlab was born from the idea of sharing this investment by setting up a shared bench accessible to everyone. Records indicate the workshop was founded in the summer of 2015; Michael Lindner, working in Michigan, and Nate King, based in Indianapolis, joined forces at that date. Sarah Steele is also said to have been part of the venture, handling sales and promotion outside production; no independent record documents this division of roles.

According to reported figures, the workshop had a floor area approaching two hundred square metres and a machine park that was extensive by the standards of the time. The founders envisioned this equipment not only for themselves: offering packages of bench time, tools, and shared experience to makers new to the trade, and even marketing their products online and at shows, was part of the plan. In this respect Briarlab was less a classic brand than an infrastructure service.
Closure and Its Legacy

The model did not achieve the expected financial balance. While the shared space's costs were fixed, the number of masters using the workshop and the sales volume never reached a level that could cover this cost. Another challenge of the shared-workshop model was that each master worked to their own arrangement and schedule; having to take turns on the machines narrowed the freedom a one-man bench normally offers. The venture ceased operations in February 2017. After the closure, Nate King continued producing under his own name; Michael Lindner is reported to have withdrawn from pipemaking not long after.

Briarlab's story is instructive for understanding the grey area between artisan pipes and factory pipes. On one side stand one-man benches, on the other structures such as BriarWorks that combine mass production with hand craftsmanship. Briarlab tried to settle into the space between these two, around the idea of a "shared workshop." The continued independence of examples such as Teipen Handmade Briar Pipes, working in the same circle for years, shows that Indiana's maker scene has continued to prefer personal workshops over a shared bench.
Assessment

Pipes bearing the Briarlab mark are few in number, and the venture did not live long enough to leave behind a school of style. It is nonetheless remembered as a notable example of the drive toward institutionalisation seen in the American handmade pipe community in the 2010s. Opinion within the community is widespread that while makers benefit from sharing knowledge and equipment, turning that sharing into a lasting commercial structure proves harder than it appears.

r.x: J. Bonet

is the signature carried by the pipes made by Mallorcan master Joan Bonet i Nadal (1929-2017). He is considered the best-known pipe bench of the Balearic Islands; the community often calls him not by his surname but by the Mallorcan nickname "Bonet de ses pipes." The brand rests on the long life the same man spent both at the bench and at the writing desk: Bonet was a craftsman who wrote as much as he produced, turning the pipe into a subject of Catalan literature.
A Bench Running from Manacor to Palma

The workshop's origin reaches back to the harshest years of the Spanish Civil War. Sebastià Bonet, arrested for membership in Esquerra Republicana following the 1936 military uprising, set up a small workshop with a few fellow prisoners at Manacor Prison during his detention, making handmade pipes. After his release he continued the work outside; production turned into a family business joined by his wife and son.

His son Joan, born in Manacor on 10 November 1929, left school at fourteen to take up the bench, and never left it again. After the family settled in Palma de Mallorca, the workshop found its permanent home in the city's Hostalets district; the master worked there until the end of his life. The work relied on pieces handled individually rather than series manufacture, placing it close to the small-scale Mediterranean branch of pipe making. Among Spanish workshops working briar, Bonet is counted an early link in a thin line of handmade work that later includes benches such as Labuenapipa. According to Pipedia, the pipes' distinguishing mark is an emblem giving the outline of the island of Mallorca.
Pen and Bench

What carried Bonet's name beyond craft circles was writing. In 1975 he translated Joaquim Verdaguer's book on the art of pipe smoking into Catalan; this work set his own pen in motion as well. In the narrative books that followed —
Les rondalles de la pipa
...I fumant en pipa!
Pipades i vivències
(1983) — the pipe is both subject and frame.
Las pipas: prontuario de pipología
La pipa en Baleares
(1980) are more reference works in nature; the 2004 book
Amb pipa i sense
is among the series' late entries. His advocacy for the Catalan language earned the master honorary membership in the Association of Catalan Language Writers.
His Place in the Community, and Afterward

He was a regular participant in international pipe-smoking competitions and served as president of the Spanish Pipe Club; some records list this role as honorary presidency. The work that brought him the most attention, though, was the giant pipe he made in 1982, designed so that a thousand people could smoke from it at once. Both Pipedia and the master's own writing records state that this pipe entered the Guinness Book of Records.

Joan Bonet died in Palma on 12 July 2017. The bench closed with him; what remains are the pipes bearing the island-silhouette stamp and a small number of books that turned the pipe into a literary subject.

r.x: Craig

is the name given to the pipes of the small workshop William D. Craig ran in Hurffville, in Gloucester Township, New Jersey, USA. Craig's signature reflects less a showy brand identity than a one-man shop's face-to-face way of working with its customers: pipes were both sold and repaired, and most were shaped to order.
From the Chemist's Bench to the Pipe Bench

Before turning to pipe making, Craig worked as a chemical operator at the Hercules Powder plant in Gibbstown. Wanting to get away from shift work, he learned the craft from an elderly Camden master named William Rodenbeck; records note Rodenbeck was ninety at the time. This transition's date is not fixed by an independent document: working from a 1973 newspaper article's mention of "thirteen years ago," it is placed around 1960. The transmission itself is a familiar pattern in American pipe making; as factory production spread, knowledge was carried hand to hand between individual makers.

Per the same article's phrase "eight years ago," Craig converted his home's two-car garage into a workshop in the mid-1960s; he added a brick-built shop section to his single-story wooden house and gave it the name Fireside Pipe Shop. The shop both sold his own briar pipes and took in repair work.
Material and Working Routine

One of the workshop's distinguishing traits was its choice of material: Craig sourced his briar from nowhere else, only from Greece. He also knew the preparation sequence there; blocks were cut, boiled in water to remove their resin, and dried before shipment. This detail is a concrete record of how briar traveled from the Mediterranean to America in the 1970s.

His working routine was communal. He would advance fifteen to twenty pipes at a time together, though this was often interrupted by incoming repair orders. He reduced the making process to a limited number of core stages — drilling, sanding, and finishing — and found the hundreds-of-steps recipes claimed in some accounts exaggerated. He counted the shapes he made to order, each remaining a single example, as a separate group of their own; among these is recalled a bowl carved in the shape of a molar for dentists. Such figural pieces are what set the workshop apart from mold-bound factory production, bringing it closer to a freehand sensibility.
Recognition and Current Status

Craig pipes are seen today mostly in secondhand circulation and appear regularly in estate pipe records. The stamp under the bowl is usually a script "Craig"; alongside it sometimes appears a short shape code (for example "S" or "D 2").

When the workshop closed is unknown; no record of it exists in either the period press or later compilations. Craig's name nonetheless still holds its place in lists of North American pipe makers as a maker from Hurffville. This last generation of one-man shops from the 1970s offers small but concrete examples of how handcraft survived in a market dominated by mass production.

r.x: Russ Alan Pipes

is a one-man pipe bench set up in the town of Greenville, in the US state of Rhode Island. The brand carries the name of its founder, Russ Alan; the earliest recorded promotion of it was made in the late 2000s, through the maker's own website. In scale it is less a workshop than a personal production kept up alongside a full-time career.
The Maker and the Scale of the Bench

According to records, Russ Alan was born and raised in Rhode Island and took up pipemaking in his early twenties. His actual profession lies in biomedical research; he makes his pipes on weekends and after work. By his own account, he turned to the craft shortly after he started smoking a pipe — meaning his time as a smoker and as a maker began at nearly the same point.

This profile is a familiar example of the American artisan bench, a category that multiplied in the 2000s thanks to the visibility the internet provided. At such benches, output is low, the relationship with the buyer is direct, and the brand name is bound straight to the maker's identity. A learning curve advanced by trial and error rather than a long apprenticeship under a single master is also a common feature of this generation.
Materials and Working Method

The bench's material range is not limited to briar; the maker has stated he also uses exotic wood species alongside briar. Working with species other than briar requires a separate body of knowledge about the material's resistance to heat and moisture; this is discussed in the entry alternative woods.

Two working principles stand out in the promotional text. The first is that every stage, including cutting the block and drilling the holes, is carried out by one hand rather than handed off to a machine line. The second is that no filler is used: flaws that appear in the bowl are not hidden with a putty-like filler, and are openly mentioned in the pipe's description. Working without filler is often taken as a sign, among small-scale makers, of a commitment to showing the material as it is; on the other hand, it raises the wastage rate when sorting through blocks.

The maker emphasizes that all of his pipes come from his own hand, made in the New England region. This emphasis is a promotional line small American benches of the period frequently used to distinguish themselves from imported bowls or semi-finished parts.
Limits of the Sources

Nearly all the information in this entry rests on the maker's own promotional text and the encyclopedia entry relaying it. No independent record has been found regarding the founding year, total production count, stamp form, or how long the bench remained active; the brand also does not appear in the common pipe-retailer and maker directories. The maker's website is not currently online; the latest dates on the copies found in web archives point to the early 2010s. The brand is therefore assessed as one of the many small benches that emerged in the 2000s wave of American pipemaking and faded away without leaving a wide trace.

r.x: Schulte

is the name of a pipe and tobacco shop that operated in the American state of New Jersey in the mid-twentieth century, and also of the pipes stamped with that same shop's name. Its founder, Max M. Schulte, is remembered less as a shopkeeper standing behind the counter than as a craftsman who spent most of his day at the lathe and polishing wheel. The name is occasionally misspelled as "Shulte."
Two Addresses

The business's known first address is 672 Springfield Avenue in Newark. The most solid document confirming this address is the record of the American patent Schulte filed for in 1960 and received in 1964; the applicant's residence is listed there under the same number. The shop later moved further along the same avenue to Maplewood, at 1628 Springfield Avenue. The move is said to be connected to the social unrest Newark experienced in 1967; this connection has not been confirmed by independent records.

Those who knew the shop consistently emphasize that at both addresses, the business centered not on the sales shelves but on the repair bench, which was set up where customers could watch the work in progress. Fuller descriptions of the interior layout rest on a single testimony.
Pipes and Tobaccos

Alongside the imported brands on his shelves, Schulte also sold his own hand-made briar pipes under the shop's name. These pipes are said to have leaned mostly toward classic shapes, and Schulte is reported to have embraced the Danish influence of the era early on. A complete inventory of the stamps he used has not been established.

The second arm of the business was tobacco; blending was done in the shop's basement. The best remembered product to come out of it was "Maritza." Sources differ on whether this was a Balkan blend or an Oriental tobacco sold on its own; what both versions agree on is that the tobacco is remembered for its strength. The spelling of the name is likewise uncertain.
Family and Legacy

Other family members also worked in the shop. According to accounts, most of the repair and blending work fell to Max's son Barry Schulte, while Max himself, in his later years, moved into a supervisory role. Howard Schulte, whose main profession was teaching, came into the workshop part-time. Sources disagree on how closely Howard was related to Max: in one account he is the son, in another the nephew.

The workshop's indirect contribution to pipe history comes from a figure who trained there. Retired attorney Jack H. Weinberger picked up his craft by watching Schulte work at the bench before he began making his own pipes; it is noted that the brand JHW Pipes rests on no other formal training than that.

Max Schulte's patent concerns not the pipe itself but an accessory that accompanies it: a holder with two spring-loaded arms that grips a pipe, cigar, or cigarette, filed on May 4, 1960, and registered on July 14, 1964, under number 3,140,782. In the patent drawing, these arms are likened to the silhouette of a seated kangaroo. The shop closed at some point thereafter; the closing date was never recorded.

r.x: Chapuis-Comoy

is a French pipe factory carrying the names of two related families from the Saint-Claude region, and it still produces today. The company's best-known product is the Chacom brand, whose name is drawn from the first syllables of the CHApuis and COMoy surnames. The family's branch on the other side of the Channel operated as a separate company, under the name Comoy's of London.
Founding and the Merger of Two Families

The company's official history traces the start of the business to 1825, to production the Comoy family carried on in Avignon near Saint-Claude. The dominant material at the time was not briar but boxwood; the products are also said to have been sold to soldiers in Napoleon's army. Briar bowls made their way into Saint-Claude's workshops in the 1850s, and the Comoy name is counted among the pioneers of that shift.

The partnership between the two families is, according to the story handed down, traceable to Henri Comoy's (1850-1924) meeting with his Chapuis relatives, who did the same work in Switzerland, during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-1871. The idea of a partnership was only put into practice after the First World War: Chapuis-Comoy & Cie was founded in 1922. After Henri Comoy's death, the company was run by his sons Paul and Adrien, alongside their cousins Emile and Louis Chapuis; the Chacom brand, registered in 1928, quickly became the backbone of the business.
The Depression Years and the Return of the Name

The economic depression of the 1930s shook Saint-Claude's crowded pipe industry. According to the company's own records, the factory joined a 1932 merger under the name La Bruyère, becoming one of the largest pipe businesses of the day. Once Chacom's success in the French market put the company back on its feet, it reverted to the name Chapuis-Comoy & Cie in 1957. Generational change within the family continued over the same period; records note that Louis Chapuis joined the business in 1938 and Pierre Comoy in 1947.
The Grenard Era

In 1971, as the London branch went its own independent way, management of Saint-Claude production passed to Pierre Comoy's cousin Yves Grenard. During this period the company set out to gather closed or changed-hands French brands under its own roof; in 1994 the Ropp brand was added to the catalog. Management passed in 2007 to Yves Grenard's son Antoine Grenard. In 2013 the factory received France's "Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant" award for deep-rooted craft businesses; in 2016 it moved to its new facility in Villard-Saint-Sauveur, right next to Saint-Claude, which also houses a museum and exhibition space.
Its Place Today

Chapuis-Comoy is counted among the few deep-rooted pipe manufacturers still standing in the Saint-Claude region. Keeping hand-finished top-tier lines and series production under the same roof has allowed the brand to be recognized among both collectors and everyday users.

r.x: Alinetu

is a pipe workshop run alone by Daniele Carbini, working in the town of Tempio Pausania in Sardinia's Gallura region, Italy. The brand name comes from the Alinetu locality in Gallura, tied to Carbini's family roots; sources describe it variously as a mountain near Aggius or as a settlement name within the boundaries of Bortigiadas. The same region is one of the natural growing areas of the briar root used in pipe making, so the name carries both a sense of belonging and a mark of the raw material.
Workshop and Production

Born in 1972, Carbini, according to records, began making pipes in 2017 after roughly a decade of preparation and study, opening his workshop the same year in Tempio Pausania. Production is entirely handmade and small in scale: published profiles put annual output at forty to fifty pipes. At this scale, every stummel can be individually selected and shaped; there are no series molds or a fixed model catalogue.

The briar he uses comes partly from blocks selected locally in Gallura and partly from supplies provided by the maker Mimmo Romeo; blocks from this second source are said to be seasoned for at least a year, and often two to three. Mouthpieces are not bought ready-made but turned from vulcanite, cumberland, and methacrylate rod. Horn, hardwood, bone, or acrylic rings are used at the transitions between mouthpiece and stummel. These choices, in terms of mouthpiece materials, place the workshop close to the classic Italian school.
Approach to Shape

The brand's most cited trait is lightness; small and medium stummels are kept at a weight that can be comfortably carried in the teeth for long periods. Shapes stay true to classic lines: round bowls with preserved proportion, plain shank lines, and understated bands free of flourish. In block selection, pieces with a prominent flame grain are sought, making grain direction one of the criteria that determines the shape; finishing is done both smooth and rusticated. According to the Pipedia entry, the workshop's emblem is an "A" enclosed in a circle.
Influences and Circle

Carbini started out self-taught, later receiving technical training at the workshop of Mimmo Romeo and his wife Karin; he has explicitly said he considers this training decisive to his development. Records also note that in his early years he exchanged views with Augusto Spanu of the Spanu family and, through correspondence, with Maurizio Tombari. The workshop is associated with the circle around Accademia della Pipa, the association of Italian handmade pipe makers.

Alinetu is considered a typical example of the small-scale workshop generation that has become more prominent in Italy since the 2000s: an approach that, instead of competing with factory production, makes a limited number of hand-shaped pipes, each decided according to the character of its own block. Its Sardinian location, offering the ability to select raw material directly from the land it grows in, is highlighted as one of the elements that defines the workshop's identity.

r.x: Ebenhart's Handmade Pipes

is a small handmade pipe workshop operating in the town of Calitzdorp in South Africa's Western Cape province. The name behind the workshop is Ebenhart Botha; according to its official presentation he has been carving pipes since 1993. Since few pipe workshops on the African continent have survived to the present, this one-man shop in Calitzdorp is counted among the continent's rare examples of pipe production.
The Maker and the Workshop's Establishment

The person who trained Botha is the German-born pipe maker William Mattner. According to records his training period under Mattner spans 1993 to 1995; this information rests largely on the maker's own account and has not been supported by an independent document. Even so, the Central European working habits of the Mattner line can be traced in the proportions and finishing sensibility of the Calitzdorp workshop.
Over the years the workshop grew into more than just a bench. Today the same address is known as a mixed venue holding a pipe workshop alongside a dining section and other crafts such as knives.
Woods Used
Briar is not alone on Botha's bench; the region's hardwoods are also regularly worked. Foremost among these are the leadwood tree, known locally,
Combretum imberbe
, and
Dalbergia melanoxylon

, known as mpingo or African blackwood. Both yield extraordinarily dense, heavy, dark-coloured wood. This choice makes the workshop a living example of alternative woods used in pipe making; the question of how non-briar species behave under heat is answered by trial in workshops of this kind.
Afrikaans Names and a Dotted Grading

The workshop's best-known trait is the names it gives its shapes. Every form in the catalogue carries an Afrikaans word: Uitspan, Appel, Bakkie, Plaasbrak, Kommando, and Calitzdorp, taking the town's own name, are a few of these. The naming carries an intent to foreground the local language. That said, these names are not a production template but guides that flex as the piece is shaped by hand; as a result, visible differences can exist between two bodies bearing the same name. Hand carving on the bowl and body surfaces is common, and dark, vivid colouring that brings out the grain texture is also frequently used.

The workshop also has its own grading system: two, three, or four dots placed on the bit show the pipe's rank in the order, with four dots corresponding to the top tier. It is stated that these dots are made from wild-boar tusk; since this detail rests solely on the workshop's own presentation, it should not be taken as confirmed. Botha also says he uses a condensation mechanism of his own design; solutions of this kind are an example of the workshop-specific experiments covered under the heading pipe filters and systems.

r.x: Northern Briar Pipes

is a small-scale pipe workshop born around Stockport in Northwest England and kept in the hands of the same family for three generations. The name today is synonymous with Ian Walker; the brand's entire output comes off a single maker's bench, and every pipe is shaped by hand from start to finish. Factory-scale production has never featured at any point; the workshop has remained a family business making its living from craftsmanship.
A Three-Generation Line of Craft

The family's tie to the pipe trade was established when Ian Walker's grandfather, George Walker, began working at Duncan Briars in 1922. Records show George Walker was made the factory's foreman in 1931 after a long apprenticeship, responsible for training pipe makers and finishers. After a total of thirty-six years at the factory, he left Duncan in 1958, and that same year set up, with his son Peter Walker, a workshop offering pipe repair services to tobacconists across the United Kingdom. This repair workshop is the origin of the Northern Briar name.

Ian Walker joined the trade in 1972, straight out of school. The family's purchase of a tobacconist's shop in the Heaton Moor area of Stockport in 1983 was the step that changed the business's direction: by then handling all the repairs, Ian Walker tried making his own pipes for the shop's shelves. When the trial caught on, production spread first to nearby shops, then across the country. His meeting with Bill Taylor, maker behind the Ashton brand, and the support he received from him, is often cited as the turning point at which the workshop found its own voice.
Production and Grades

Northern Briar pipes are made from Italian-sourced briar; the block supply is reported to come from the same source Bill Taylor used. Mouthpieces are not bought ready-made but cut by hand from vulcanite or Cumberland rod; the maker's standing in the community rests to a large degree on this mouthpiece work.

The workshop's best-known surface is a rustication called Rox Cut: a deep, pronounced texture considered the brand's signature. Products are split into two grades, Premier and Regal; by the maker's own definition, Premier is the higher group, while Regal's standards are held a little more loosely. The shape range leans heavily on English classics — the billiard and its relatives — with the maker's contribution lying in the measured tweaks he makes to those lines.
Recognition and Status Today

The workshop began appearing at UK pipe shows and club events from 1999 onward. By one account, the order for fifty identical pipes prepared for the 2005 British pipe-smoking championship was also given to Ian Walker. His first appearance abroad came in 2006 in Chicago; the brand's recognition in North America accelerated after that date.

The workshop's address today is not fixed. Ian Walker lives with his wife on a canal boat and keeps his bench there as well; since British mooring rules do not allow staying more than two weeks at the same spot, the home and workshop move along the country's canals and rivers. The brand remains active today, and production still runs at a one-man scale.

r.x: Blatter & Blatter

is a Canadian pipe workshop founded in Montreal in 1907 and carried on by the same family for five generations. It was known in its early years as "Blatter Bros."; today it is considered the last workshop in the city to finish briar pipes entirely by hand from start to finish. The workshop's line rests not on ornament but on plain shapes proportioned for use.
From Europe to Montreal

Which founding figure the family should be credited to varies from source to source: the common account says the family was founded by French-born Frédéric-Georges Blatter, while some accounts place the brothers Ernest and Henri-Georges directly at the head of the business. What is consistent is that the craft was learned in France and carried outside Europe. Records indicate the family ran a pipe workshop in London in the late 1890s; when the workshop burned down, they moved to South Africa, producing and selling in both Cape Town and Durban. In 1907 it was Montreal's turn; a workshop and an attached shop were opened in the city.

Working alongside Frédéric-Georges were his son Ernest and Ernest's half-brother Henri. The business expanded rapidly: by the 1930s it is reported the workshop employed around fifty people and supplied pipes to five separate points of sale. The Great Depression and the years of the Second World War pulled this scale back; in the early 1950s production and retail were merged under one roof. Having remained on the same street for sixty-three years, the business moved in 1970 to another street in the city, its current location.
Generations and Workshop

Ernest's son Henri-Georges joined the business in the 1930s and held the management until his death in 1967. His son Pierre, who had been working alongside his father since 1964, took over management at that point. Pierre's brother Robert joined the firm in 1968 and took charge of pipemaking; the handmade "Select" pipes have been associated with his name since that date. In 1997, Pierre's son Patrick began training alongside his uncle, and over time moved to the bench himself.

The bond with Saint-Claude, France's pipe city, continued at both the raw-material and reputation level: a significant portion of the briar blocks come from that town's suppliers. Pierre and Robert Blatter were admitted to Saint-Claude's guild of master pipemakers (Confrérie des Maîtres-Pipiers) in 1982; the same honour is reported to have later been granted to Patrick as well. According to records, the firm was recognised among businesses noted for service quality in Quebec in 1993.
Approach to Shape and Marks

Production is limited to a few hundred pieces a year; bowls are shaped by hand in the workshop behind the shop, and repairs and maintenance are carried out at the same benches. Although demand has exceeded production capacity, the workshop has not expanded, continuing instead to turn out a limited number of pieces. In this respect it is a concrete example of the distinction between artisan production and factory production. The shapes lean heavily on classics such as the billiard and Canadian; Dublins, Rhodesians, and freehand pieces also appear. All three surface treatments are used: smooth polish, sandblast, and hand rustication.

The shank mark is generally "Blatter" with "Montreal" beneath it; "Blatter Bros." and Robert Blatter's signed "Select" mark are also known types. The brand's most distinctive marker, however, is the small red dot placed on the body. Accounts of the dot's meaning disagree: one version holds that a single dot indicates the standard grade and a double dot the Select tier, while another version ties a single dot to machine-assisted shaping of the body. On pipes prepared for the founding's centenary in 2007, the shank was stamped with "1907 – 2007" alongside Robert Blatter's signature mark.

r.x: Brakner

is a Danish name that emerged within Copenhagen's handmade pipe scene in the postwar years, owing its fame almost entirely to a single surface treatment. The master's civil name was Peter Micklson; he later changed his surname to Brakner and stamped his pipes under that name. Neither his birth year nor his death date is clear in the records; his output, however, is dated to the early cohort of what is known as the Danish School.
Workshop Circle

He entered the trade at Suhr's Pibemageri in Copenhagen, that is, the Teofil Suhr workshop. That workshop's foreman at the time was Sixten Ivarsson, who shaped the design language of Danish pipemaking. According to a piece of information passed down in pipe literature, Brakner is said to have facilitated Poul Rasmussen's entry into the workshop, showing him the basic fundamentals of the craft in a short, intensive course; since this detail rests only on secondary sources, it should be treated with caution. Brakner's period working for someone else did not last long; he went into production under his own name at an early date.
A Lost Surface: Antique

The master's real signature is the extremely fine-grained rustication he developed himself and called "Antique." The pits are small and regular compared to the era's habit of coarse carving; for this reason it is mostly described in the literature as "micro-rustication." Brakner kept the method hidden from his fellow makers. According to an account attributed to Kai Nielsen, he showed the technique to only one person; with that person's departure as well, the details of the method are unknown today. Kent Rasmussen, of the following generation, has stated that he considered this surface his starting point when developing his own rustication method. Smooth-finished Brakner pipes are rare; known examples include a plateau-topped type and one marked "Jewel of Denmark."
Series and Marks

A significant portion of Brakner's pipes were distributed through the tobacconist W.Ø. Larsen; the master was a close friend of shop owner Ole Larsen, and this relationship lasted until Larsen began employing his own staff carvers. The shop's 1960/61 export catalogue lists three separate series: Antique, Bella Danica, and Royal Danois. All three are listed with either the tan (fawn) or black variant of the Antique surface. The name of Royal Danois, which forms the top tier of these series, comes from the Royal Danish Guard regiment founded in 1689; the shank mark on these pipes carries the phrases "Hand Cut" and "Denmark" alongside the brand name.

Considered one of the names to first bring top-tier Danish handmade pipes to the United States market, Brakner found notable recognition there in the early 1970s. Production ended with the master's unexpected death (the date is not recorded in sources). Though his name has receded somewhat over time in the shadow of the longer-lived workshops of the same generation, his pipes continue to be mentioned in the collecting literature because of their surface craftsmanship and the connection they carry to early Danish design language.

r.x: Samuel McLardy

is the firm founded in Manchester in the second half of the 19th century that grew into one of the era's largest British clay pipe manufacturers. The company's namesake, Samuel McLardy, was born in Glasgow in 1842, the son of a tobacconist who also made pipes, and learned the trade in his father's shop. In his early twenties he moved to Manchester and set up his own business, and records show he adopted 1865 as the founding year.
From Miller Street to Shudehill

The firm's first address was 16 Miller Street in Manchester; what began as a small workshop reached factory scale before 1880. Moving to 67 Shudehill in 1890, the business continued to operate there for a stretch reaching well into the 1910s. The company's address in its final years was, as far as can be gathered from its liquidation record, 20 Swan Street.

The scale of production gives a good sense of the clay pipe industry's golden age. Around 1895 the factory reportedly held more than five hundred molds, and it was noted that, used efficiently, these molds could produce as many as five million pipes a year. This figure is comparable to the capacity of the large Dutch manufacturers of Gouda in the same years.
Product Range and Stamps

Period manufacturer catalogs display numerous McLardy-signed clay models; the firm's more than five hundred molds meant a wide variety in bowl shape and shank length. Though clay was the main line of business, production was not limited to it: silver-mounted calabash pipes also carried the firm's name. In one known example, the hallmarks on the silver band show the Birmingham assay office and the date letter for 1907; in such pipes the bowl was traditionally lined with meerschaum.

As a manufacturer's mark, the letters "S Mc L" set within a triangular cartouche were used. Because British hallmarks appear alongside this mark on the silver-mounted examples, such pieces can be dated to the year. For how British industrial and trade records are used in pipe research, see the Grace's Guide entry.
Decline and Liquidation

As briar increasingly displaced the clay pipe at the start of the twentieth century, McLardy too was forced to change direction. To offset falling revenue the product range was expanded beyond pipes, and over time the firm came to resemble a trading house more than a manufacturer. The market squeezed by the First World War, the fading interest in the clay pipe, and the financial shock following the 1929 stock market crash left the business unable to stay afloat.
The official record of the end appears in
The London Gazette

: an extraordinary general meeting held on 13 January 1930 at 20 Swan Street in Manchester resolved on the company's voluntary liquidation and appointed a liquidator. Sixty-five years of manufacturing history thus came to a close. Today the McLardy name is remembered, through stamped stem fragments found in collections and archaeological digs, as one of the names documenting the last great era of the British clay pipe industry.

r.x: Sabina Santos

is a Portuguese handmade pipe maker who signs her pipes "Sabina." She is recorded as having been born on 20 May 1985 in Tiel, the Netherlands, and has lived in Portugal since the age of three. Working in a craft where women makers are few has contributed to her name becoming known early on.
Coming to the Craft

Santos trained in communications and spent the first years of her working life in finance. She has said herself that she turned to woodworking in search of balance against a desk job; according to the record, this search dates to around 2013. Her husband, a longtime pipe smoker, had a keen interest in the handmade pipe world, and this drew her into the same field. Santos left her job after the birth of her son, and carved her first pipe during this period.

For the following three years she taught herself, learning through trial and error on every pipe. Once she saw the limits of working alone, she traveled to Denmark for training and spent seven weeks there. Fellow Portuguese maker João Reis became her guide there; during this period she also gathered knowledge at the bench from masters such as Tom Eltang, Kai Nielsen, Kurt Balleby and Tao Nielsen. It is said that in her work in Denmark she focused especially on surface treatments, bamboo-shanked bodies and drilling geometry.
Sense of Shape

Santos's designs sit distinctly within the Danish school line. By her own account, her sources of inspiration include Scandinavian masters such as the Ivarsson family, Bo Nordh, Poul Ilsted and Jess Chonowitsch. She is known to prefer taking classic shapes as a base and giving them a contemporary reading.

The maker's own emphasis is that aesthetics do not come before engineering: drilling accuracy and internal geometry matter as much as the body's proportions. She uses Italian and Algerian briar as her main material; stems are hand-worked from German ebonite. For decoration and transition rings she uses bamboo, horn, exotic woods, and treated mammoth ivory and bone. She is also recorded as having experimented with material recovered from recycled plastic bottles for ornamentation.
Stamps

All pipes carry the "Sabina" stamp. On some of these, a single additional letter "G" stamp also appears; the maker applies this mark only to the examples she considers, by her own standards, the most successful, and the letter refers to the name of her son Gil. The "G" is thus not the name of a series or a surface treatment, but an internal grading mark the maker applies to herself. Because the workshop is small in scale, annual production is limited and each piece is finished individually by hand; as a result, no two pipes are expected to be identical.
Recognition
Santos's name has become known at international gatherings such as the Chicago and Chengde pipe shows, and she has also been a guest on the radio program hosted by Brian Levine.

r.x: Lord Davenport Pipes

is an American pipe brand marketed through New York during the Second World War years, named for its inventor, Henry Davenport Bellin. What sets the brand apart is not a cutting or polishing technique but a mechanical stem assembly fitted into the pipe that could be removed and cleaned by hand. The mechanism was protected by two separate U.S. patents, and the brand's entire marketing was built around this invention.
Patents and the Mechanical Assembly

Bellin, listed in patent records as being from Providence, Rhode Island, filed his first application on 16 February 1938; it was granted on 7 February 1939 as U.S. Patent No. 2,146,613, titled "Smoking Device." The design has two telescoping tubes: when the stem is pushed forward, a needle at its tip cleans the mouth of the airway where it opens into the chamber; a one-way flap inside lets smoke pass while blocking saliva from reaching the chamber, and accumulated moisture is expelled through drain holes that align when the tubes are rotated.

The second application is dated 10 February 1940 and was granted on 18 February 1941 as No. 2,232,092. This time the aim was to simplify the mechanism: a sleeve with one short and one long longitudinal groove holds a tongue on the smoke tube that keeps the stem in its normal position within the short groove. When the user pushes the stem forward against a spring and rotates it, the tongue moves into the long groove and the stem comes off entirely. The first patent was assigned to August A. Thomen of New York, the second directly to the Providence-based Davenport, Ltd. Inc.; by this date, then, the brand had taken on a corporate structure. In the pipe industry of the period, a patent served as both a dating tool and a marketing device, as discussed in the entry on pipe patents; Lord Davenport is a textbook example of this.
Product Range and Marketing

The pipes were made of imported briar; known shapes include billiard and panel billiard, Dublin, apple, Lumberman, and Rhodesian. Records indicate four separate lines were marketed: the sandblasted "Shell," two Lord Davenport lines with saddle and taper stems, and "Drury." Secondary sources compiling period advertisements report that the removable assembly was called the "Magic Stem" in ads; where stem materials are concerned, what sets it apart from the era's usual vulcanite construction is not the material but the metal mechanism.

The company advertised in widely read magazines such as Fortune and Esquire between 1944 and 1947. Sales are said to have run through a showroom on Lexington Avenue in New York and wholesale catalogues such as Bennett Brothers. Advertisements were built on two promises: the pipe would not clog, and moisture would not build up in the stem. Alongside this came a purely image-based line such as "a pipe to suit every face type."
Aftermath

No definite record has been found of when the brand closed; traces of advertising stop in the late 1940s. The complex mechanical stem's need for maintenance, together with major manufacturers of the same years such as Kaywoodie dominating the market with far simpler filter and tenon solutions, appears to have shortened the brand's life. Today, Lord Davenport pipes are regarded as a witness to their era, with the rare surviving examples whose mechanism remains intact sought after by collectors.

r.x: Thomas Kalmar

is a Hungarian-born maker who works in a one-person workshop in the Bavarian Forest and has signed handmade pipes under his own name since 2022. He is a relatively new name among German makers; even so, having spent years repairing old pipes before taking up the bench means he began the work already familiar with the material.
Workshop and Working Practice

The workshop is a small wooden structure standing at the edge of the forest, at the foot of the Falkenstein hill. Production runs entirely by one hand: there is no series, no mold, every pipe comes from the same person's hands from start to finish. Kalmar has had no master's apprenticeship or workshop training; he works as a self-taught craftsman. He and his wife attend pipe fairs regularly and show his work directly to collectors.
Material Selection

Only briar is used for the bowl. Blocks come from two sources: from Mimmo Romeo's quarry in Italy, and plateaux and ebauchon pieces of Greek origin. On the decorative side he sticks to natural material, using native or exotic wood and horn — including deer antler — for shank rings and transition points. Plateau is the cut that carries the outer surface of the root and shows the most pronounced natural grain pattern; ebauchon is a more economical block taken from the interior of the root, with a calmer pattern. Using both together lets a one-person workshop move between freehand and more measured work on the same bench. Mouthpieces are ebonite or acrylic. He opens the 9 mm filter socket expected in the German-speaking market as an option.
Shape Approach

The weight of the work lies in a mold-independent freehand approach: the shape is determined by what the block's grain allows, and the resulting bowl remains a one-off. Both smooth-polished and rustic finishes are seen in surface treatment; whether the rustic surface counts as a distinct signature has no independent assessment available.
Before the Pipe

Kalmar was born in Hungary in 1978, studied horticultural engineering at university, and after graduating worked seven years in public service. He settled in Germany with his family in 2009. A year later he and his wife set up an online business trading restored old pipes. He learned the basics of making technique during this repair work. Having smoked pipes for more than twenty years, Kalmar put the idea of making pipes under his own name into practice in March 2022.

r.x: Dunhill Special Series

is a heading gathering Alfred Dunhill's pipes that fall outside its ordinary catalogue production. These pieces are known not by an individual shape or finish name but by the reason for their release: an award, an anniversary, a merchant's special commission. What they share is a low production run, numbering, and often metalwork added to the body. To become familiar with the brand's standard production and stamping conventions, see the entries Dunhill White Spot and Dunhill dating guide.
Microphone (1981)

The "Pipe Smoker of the Year" title, awarded by the British Pipesmokers' Council between 1964 and 2003, was not just a title; a pipe was also commissioned for that year specifically for the winner. The 1982 holder of the title was BBC radio presenter Dave Lee Travis, and the commission went to Dunhill. Made to resemble a studio microphone as a nod to the presenter's profession, the pipes were completed in 1981; a total of fifty were made and stamped from 1 to 50. Records indicate that the series' first number went to the display case of the Alfred Dunhill museum in London, and the second to Travis. The rest gradually entered collector circulation over time; because of its unusual form, it is counted among the brand's most easily recognized commemorative pieces.
Longitude (1999)

Longitude, prepared to mark the arrival of the new millennium, was released in 1999 and its production was capped at 2,000 pieces. The body chosen was a Shell-finished billiard in the size-5 group; the sandblasted surface and the most familiar shape were thus brought together in one pipe. The real innovation was a gold-plated, rotating stainless-steel band placed at the rim of the bowl. The world's major cities are engraved on the band according to their time zones, and a red marker is positioned to show the point of rotation; when the marker is aligned with the desired city, the time there can be read off. The mechanism was also built to account for daylight-saving offsets. Each piece was individually numbered.
Classic Series and Special Commissions

Not all the commemorative pipes are tied to a single event. The Classic Series, released in limited numbers in the 1990s, aims to bring back into circulation shapes that survive from the brand's production dating back to the workshop opened at Mason's Yard in 1910. It is less a search for a new design than a selection that looks back at its own catalogue.

One-off commissions fall entirely outside the notion of a series. The most-discussed example in this group is a pipe made in 2005 for the Cologne pipe merchant Peter Heinrichs, depicting the city's cathedral. Records indicate that an XL-sized, four-star straight-grain freehand body was used, with a cathedral-shaped cap worked in 925 sterling silver placed on top. Because the cap's perforations and the main door opening allow smoke to pass, the piece is technically functional, but its purpose was not to be smoked; records indicate it was put on display at the Cologne City Museum. Works at this scale are counted among the boundary examples where the briar body becomes a canvas for jewellery work.

r.x: Rocheleau Briar Pipes

is the name of a small pipe workshop that Canadian painter John Rocheleau ran single-handedly. The workshop remained active for only a few years in the 2000s; nevertheless, the small body of work it left behind continues to be remembered in the North American artisan pipe community for its surface craftsmanship. Rocheleau is reported to have worked in western Canada, in British Columbia; since this detail of location rests on a single secondary source, it is not considered certain.
The Craftsman's Background

Rocheleau's primary pursuit was not pipes but painting. He worked in oil and acrylic on landscapes and also sculpted in stone, metal, and wood. Pipe making became the work of a limited interval between these two pursuits. Since no other master or assistant worked in the shop, annual output was low; this is also why examples in circulation on the secondhand market today are relatively rare.
Shape and Surface

The technical detail most emphasized in sources is that shaping was done mainly with hand tools: the block was opened with a file and sandpaper, and the final shape was adjusted as the grain pattern became apparent. The material used is described as high-quality briar.

The surfaces include both smooth-polished and rusticated work. Restoration write-ups note that the rough texture was opened with a cutting-bit rotary tool (a Dremel), with a result resembling sandblasting. Leaving thin smooth bands at the shank-mouthpiece junction and around the bowl rim was a common preference.

Coloring was not finished in a single coat; color applied in several successive stages was used to emphasize, rather than mask, differences in the wood's grain. Mouthpieces were made from hand-worked vulcanite; for how this material differs from other options, see mouthpiece materials.
Stamp and Closing

The pipes carry a handwriting-style "Rocheleau" stamp on the underside of the shank. On some examples a short code of letters and numbers appears alongside the stamp; since no published chart explains what this code indicates, it is not reliable for dating purposes.

Rocheleau was forced to give up pipe making because of ailments in his hands and wrists. In his closing announcement he stated that he was shutting down the business and that the workshop's website would go offline sometime in 2007; the exact closing date is not supported by any record beyond this announcement. In later years he turned to painting and writing. The workshop is remembered as short-lived but distinct alongside multi-generational Canadian houses such as Montreal-based Blatter & Blatter.

r.x: Gurra

is the brand under which Swedish pipe maker Lars-Göran Markunger (b. 1960) signs his pipes. Markunger, who lives in Halmstad, works his day job at a glass factory; according to accounts he turned to pipe making in the mid-2000s out of a curiosity for combining different materials. He was not a pipe smoker at the time; taking up the pipe himself came only after he began making them. The brand has earned a small but recognized place in the Swedish pipe scene through its extremely limited output and unusual material combinations.
Origin of the Name and Stamping

In Swedish, "Gurra" is a common shortening of the name Lars-Göran, and the maker has gone by it since his youth. The fact that his full name would not fit on a stamp was decisive in marking the brand with the short nickname. The suggestion came from Per Billhäll, who introduced the pipes to collector circles. Markunger works with an engraving tool rather than a steel stamp. The grading system is based on a deck of playing cards: a sequence rising from "10" to "Ace" is used, with the "Queen" marking the middle grade. In recorded examples, the stamp consists of the brand name, the country name, and the grade mark.
Bo Nordh's Encouragement

Two prompts are cited as having drawn Markunger to the pipe: a newspaper article about a French pipe factory, and a television program featuring Bo Nordh. According to the account, he took his first attempts straight to Nordh, met with both harsh criticism and detailed suggestions, and received clear approval when he returned with a second batch of pipes. That Markunger, on Nordh's guidance, passed a series of pipes to Per Billhäll is considered the starting point of the brand becoming known among collectors; the brand has been associated with the Nordh circle from its very beginning.
Workshop and Material Experiments

The workshop is set up in an old house Markunger has renovated himself; he built a significant share of the machines he uses. According to records describing the situation in 2008, the workshop had no lathe at that time, and these operations were carried out on an acquaintance's equipment instead. Experiments that go beyond classic mouthpiece materials like briar and ebonite are the brand's distinguishing feature. Records indicate that he has used Damascus steel on some army-mounted pipes (where the mouthpiece fits over the tenon end of the shank), and on two of his pipes he has used birch bark, which can only be found thick enough in northern Sweden. For coloring he favors acid-based methods rather than traditional dyes, and on some pieces he applies sandblasting using the equipment at the glass factory where he works. His formal vocabulary moves between classic shapes and freehand forms.

Production scale has stayed low from the start. According to a February 2008 workshop-visit article, the total number of pipes made up to that point was around twenty-five; no total figure is known for later years. For this reason, Gurra-stamped pipes are considered rare finds among collections.

r.x: Skovgaard

is the name of the pipes stamped under his own name by Danish pipe maker Lasse Skovgaard Jørgensen. Born in 1983, the maker works in the southern part of the island of Sjælland. His reputation spread beyond Denmark's borders fairly quickly, thanks in part to his apprenticeship years at his father's workshop and to the factory discipline he gained at one of the country's long-established pipe firms.
An Apprentice Trained at Larsen's Bench

His father, Benni Jørgensen, is also a pipe maker, and Lasse's first contact with the craft was established at this workshop. His entry into the trade, however, came not through pipes but through accessories: at sixteen, he was carving tobacco tampers from buffalo horn for W.Ø. Larsen. By eighteen he was working on the same firm's "select" and two-tone lines; at nineteen he was assigned to what is considered Larsen's most demanding work, the making of straight-grain pipes. Having practiced, while still in high school, on a production line regarded as a benchmark of Danish pipe making is considered the source of the technical confidence in the master's later work.
The 2004 Chicago Debut

The decision to begin production under his own stamp was made at the encouragement of master Teddy Knudsen, a friend of his father's. In 2004, Skovgaard went to the Chicagoland international pipe show with twelve smooth-surfaced pipes bearing his own name; this first batch sold out over the course of the show. The following year he returned with seventy-five pipes, this time mainly sandblasted bodies, and the result was the same again. These two appearances are considered the turning point that built the workshop's buyer network outside Denmark; the master's work has reached many countries since that date.
Approach to Surface and Shape

Skovgaard's work carries both the freehand line of the Danish School and the measured craft discipline learned at a factory workshop. Sandblasted surfaces make up a distinct portion of production; in deep sandblasting, the annual rings of briar stand out like relief. Alongside classic shape families, there are also bodies named by the maker himself; sources mention shapes called "Whale" and "Elephant's Foot."

At the top of the grading scale is the premium stamp reserved for the small number of bodies whose grain or shape is judged exceptional; sources refer to this stamp as "Lion." The workshop is a one-man operation with deliberately limited annual output; since every pipe comes from the same hand, production volume is set by the master's own working pace.

The stamping arrangement also follows the common practice among independent Danish masters: the maker's name is struck under the bowl, alongside a mark indicating the piece's grade. Unlike the model-number-based system of mass-production brands, this arrangement points to a mode of production in which each piece is assessed individually. Skovgaard's name is counted among the young generation of Danish masters who emerged with their own stamp in the early 2000s; this generation is regarded as the representatives of a transitional period, moving from the country's large workshops into small independent shops.

r.x: Dunhill tobacco tins

are considered one of the sturdiest foundations for dating in English pipe-tobacco collecting. Even though a blend's name stayed the same for decades, the size of the tin, the shape of the lid, the base stamp, and the royal-warrant wording on the label were renewed at set intervals; the period of a tin is largely established by reading these four details together. The first study to lay out the criteria in an organized way is John C. Loring's 1997 review. For the history of the blends themselves, see Dunhill Pipe Tobaccos: 1907-1990.
The Shape and Size of the Tin

Records indicate the earliest tins were not vacuum-sealed; a photograph dated to 1909 shows half-pound and one-pound tins under two closely related "My Mixture" labels. During the First World War, the switch was made to the knife-lid (cutter-top) tin. The distinguishing feature of this design is its double lid: a thin metal inner lid seals the tobacco airtight, and the outer lid that fits over the body has a small sliding knife at its edge for cutting the seal. Once the seal is cut, the outer lid serves only as a cover. This arrangement, well suited to long-term storage and overseas shipping, is credited with playing a part in the brand's spread. The most common size was four ounces; eight- and two-ounce tins were also made, with pressed flake blends usually going into the two-ounce size.

In the examples Loring studied, the four-ounce tin from the 1920s through the 1950s measures roughly four inches in diameter and two inches in height; a few blends used a narrower, taller tin. At the end of the 1950s and into the 1960s the metal thinned, the diameter dropped to 3.75 inches, and the outer lid took on a bright gold colour with a pronounced curl at its lower edge. Somewhere in the mid-to-late 1960s, the packaging changed fundamentally: the paper-labelled knife-lid tin was replaced by a painted, coin-twist-capped tin. The transition was gradual; the 1968/69 wholesale catalogue lists the two types side by side.
Label and Base Stamp

The paper label wrapping the body was printed separately for each blend, while the outer lid was fastened to the body with a paper band bearing Alfred Dunhill's signature, often along with a facsimile of a red seal. With the move to the coin-twist cap this seal disappeared, and the "My Mixture" label gained the long-tailed "dunhill" script. On the limited-distribution "My Mixture" tins the label is uniform, with the blend number written by hand on a side label. The address section on early examples shows telephone and telegraph details; once the New York and Paris branches opened in the 1920s, branch addresses filled this space.

The base stamp is a separate clue: tins from the 1940s and 1950s carry only the wording "MADE IN GREAT BRITAIN," and a weight stamp was first struck on the four-ounce tin only in the 1960s. In the 1970s, as part of adapting to the common market, the stamp switched from ounces to a paired ounces-and-grams format, and by the end of the decade the four-ounce tin had become a 100-gram tin.
The Timeline of the Warrant Wording
The royal-warrant wording alone also gives a rough date range:
The warrant obtained from Edward, Prince of Wales, in 1921 appears on the labels of some blends in the 1927 catalogue; it was never added to the label of the blend called Prince of Wales.
The warrant lapsed with the 1936 abdication, and records indicate that by 1938 a new warrant obtained from George VI brought wording for a king onto the label.
Tins from the Second World War years also carry a "wartime packaging" mark.
After the war the warrant moved from the side label to the top label.
Following the king's death in 1952, direct reference to the sovereign was dropped, a few years later the wording "the late king" was adopted, and this was used into the early 1960s.
With the coin-twist cap, the wording was renewed for the queen, and by the early 1990s it was removed from the label altogether.
The Manufacturer Wording

When blending was outsourced at the end of the 1970s, the label's "blended by Alfred Dunhill" wording disappeared, replaced by forms noting only the country of production. The identity of the manufacturer that took over the work is not certain; the two names most often cited are Murray, Sons & Co., founded in Belfast in 1810 and folded into Carreras and later Rothmans International after 1953, and McConnell. After the warrant fell away, the wording first became forms meaning "under licence from Alfred Dunhill Ltd.," and around 1994, "in association with Dunhill Tobacco of London." The blends' course after this date is covered in the entry Dunhill Tobacco Blends.

r.x: Shaabi Pipes

is the pipe workshop Manuel Shaabi opened in Hamburg in 1998 and has run single-handedly from start to finish. In the German handmade pipe scene, its name is associated both with unusual details of its production method and with the fact that its founder came to pipe making from a completely different branch of woodworking.
From Wood to the Pipe

The founder was born in Lebanon in 1950; he entered the trade through an apprenticeship in wood sculpture and furniture craft. In 1979, while the Lebanese Civil War was underway, he moved to Germany and settled in Bavaria, where he both produced one-off furniture pieces and worked on the restoration of old wooden figures in churches and cathedrals. His daughter's asthma was the deciding factor behind the family's move to Hamburg in 1984. These two dates are said to appear consistently across biographies that corroborate each other.

When he struggled to find steady work in Hamburg, he went back to school to complete his professional training. Even though he won awards in furniture work, he came to feel it did not meet his creative expectations, and according to records he gave it up entirely in 1993. He found his new pursuit at the well-established Hamburg firm Dan Pipe: he first did pipe repair, then began carving his own bodies. These years laid the groundwork for his move into independent work in 1998.
The Workshop's Method

Shaabi's working method deliberately departs from the standard steps of mass production. He is said to avoid drilling the tobacco chamber, on the grounds that a drill bit does not make a clean cut in briar, and to use a knife he prepares himself instead. He is reported to favor a 4-millimeter measurement for the smoke channel, and to argue that the channel should meet the chamber not right at the bottom but a few millimeters above it; his stated reason is that this keeps tobacco residue from working its way into the channel and mouthpiece. These two technical details have not been confirmed in an independent source.
Mouthpieces are cut by hand one at a time and are mostly made of lucite; mouthpiece work is considered as significant a stage in this workshop as carving the body.
Shapes and Aftermath

His shape repertoire moves back and forth between classic European molds and carvings drawing on Middle Eastern ornamental language. In secondary-market records, straight and bent egg shapes, brandies, Rhodesian variants, and carved work with plant motifs stand out. Examples aimed at the German market show a 9-millimeter filter chamber, a detail reflecting the local habit around filter systems. Some of the pipes have also been recorded under the Dan Pipe name because of the ongoing relationship with his former employer.

Because production stayed tied to a single person, annual output was never high, and it stopped in 2007 due to health issues. Whether the maker returned to production in later years is not clear; Shaabi-signed pipes are today seen mainly in estate collections and secondary-market channels.
