r.x: Fat Bastard Pipes

is a small pipe workshop run single-handedly in Denmark by a maker named Alex Goojvin. The workshop's output consists of large-bodied freehand pipes not tied to any mold or model number. The brand's unusual name also nods to this scale; it is a nickname carried over from the maker's youth.
Founding of the Workshop

According to the record, Goojvin began making pipes around 2009-2010, producing his first pieces without any intent to sell, purely for his own use. The business took on a commercial identity only in later years, and the workshop is still not a full-time operation today.

By the maker's own account he was born in California; he has lived with his family in Denmark for a long time and carries out his production there. This dual background makes it hard to place the brand within a single national school. Even so, its mold-free way of working, with proportions determined piece by piece, shows a kinship with the workshop habits of the generation that followed the Danish school.
Approach to Making

The workshop's defining choice is that it does not use a wood lathe. Both bowl and mouthpiece are shaped by hand on a grinding wheel and sandpaper; automated machinery is left out as much as possible. The practical result is that no two pieces ever match exactly: even for custom requests, the aim is a close shape rather than an identical copy.

Working without a lathe also sets the workshop's pace. A symmetrical bowl or a smooth conical mouthpiece is something a lathe can produce in minutes; doing the same work on a grinding wheel requires constant measuring, turning, and re-checking. This method also makes small asymmetries in individual pieces unavoidable, and these are treated not as flaws but as a mark of the hand behind them.

According to the maker's own account, finishing a single pipe takes five to eight hours; in a productive month around twenty pieces can be turned out. Since production is run part-time, this number varies noticeably from month to month.
Material

The main material is Italian-sourced briar blocks. For large-volume bodies, black cherry wood comes into play; the reasoning is that large briar blocks are both expensive and hard to find. One reason cherry stands out among non-briar woods is its low density: on a large pipe, the difference in weight directly reduces the load on the teeth. This information rests on the maker's own account and has not been compared against an independent technical study.
Assessment

Fat Bastard Pipes is less a producer with a catalogue and model series than a sum of pieces coming from a single pair of hands. The brand's lasting trait is a workshop stance that deliberately rejects standardization.

r.x: Dobbelmann

is a German brand that made tobacco and pipes in the town of Rees, in the Lower Rhine region, for a little over thirty years. Its founder was not a local workshop but Louis Dobbelmann, the Netherlands' established tobacco firm: based near Rotterdam, this company set up a branch factory in Rees on 8 April 1929 to gain a direct foothold in Germany, one of the era's largest tobacco markets. Production began that same autumn with twenty-five workers, producing pipe tobacco alone.
A Tobacco Factory in Rees

The factory was built on grounds vacated by the town's closed margarine industry, and within a decade grew its workforce to forty. The Second World War cut this progress short; by 1945 more than ninety percent of the factory buildings had been razed to their foundations. The reconstruction carried out between 1946 and 1948 covered not only the production buildings but housing for the workers as well. The new workshop building, completed at the end of 1947, was considered advanced by the standards of the time.

In the same town of Rees, just a few hundred meters away, the Oldenkott factory was operating. The two firms standing side by side allowed a small provincial town to become one of Germany's pipe manufacturing centers.
Move into Pipes

The company entered pipe making in 1946/47, under the shortage conditions of the postwar period. The first pipes were made from apple, cherry, and beech wood; these were forced solutions resorted to because briar was unavailable, a widespread practice across postwar Europe. When briar supply from the Mediterranean again became possible around 1950, the factory quickly returned to it.

The decade that followed became the brand's most productive period. Tight coordination between production and the sales organization, delivering products fresh to dealers, and rigorous quality control were the hallmarks of the era. Staff numbers reached around seventy by around 1950. According to records, the firm's tobacco turnover roughly quadrupled between 1953 and 1959; it won an honorary certificate at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair and rose to become Germany's third-largest pipe and tobacco manufacturer in the industry ranking. The rhyming advertising slogan meaning roughly "Great and small, everyone smokes Dobbelmann" even made it into the German press of the time.
Closure

This rise did not escape the notice of the industry's big players. The Bremen-based tobacco company Brinkmann bought Dobbelmann in autumn 1962; its aim was not to continue the business but to eliminate a rival. Tobacco production was halted on 15 September 1962, while pipe production continued at a reduced level until year's end. Eighty people lost their jobs. The remaining machinery and stock are said to have been transferred to Oldenkott. According to records, the company's legal entity persisted on paper until spring 1964.

The brand survives today only among collectors. The sole visible trace left of the factory in Rees is an old company emblem on a building's façade. Dobbelmann-stamped pipes are considered short-lived but quality examples of postwar German series production, and are covered under this heading within the Germany pipe brands index.

r.x: Amiel

is a pipe brand that operated in Philippeville (renamed Skikda after 1962), the port city of French colonial Algeria. The facility, considered the country's first pipe factory according to records, takes its name from its founder, engineer Raoul Amiel. What makes the brand notable beyond its own scale is that it set out to produce finished pipes in a country that otherwise only exported briar as a raw material.
Founding and Algerian Briar

Accounts say the Amiel family came from Nancy, France: they left the city in 1870 during the German occupation, stayed for a time in Florence, and eventually settled in Philippeville. The factory is reported to have opened its doors in 1932, with founding capital supplied by a local family. The plant's layout and machinery were Raoul Amiel's own work, and it is described as a modern workshop by the standards of its time.

The factory's location here was no accident. The adoption of briar as a pipe material in the second half of the nineteenth century had made Saint-Claude, in France's Jura region, the center of world pipe making; this process is covered in the Briar Revolution and Saint-Claude entry. As the century turned, the old Mediterranean collection grounds could no longer keep up with rising demand, and the search shifted to North Africa. Records show that after 1905, Algeria's briar forests were seriously explored as a source. The extracted root burls were cut into rough blanks (ebauchons) and shipped by sea to France, especially to Saint-Claude. Amiel can be read as an attempt to keep the final link of this chain within the country itself.
The Saint-Claude School and Unstamped Exports

Both the factory's bench layout and its processing methods were carried over from Saint-Claude, which is why the products stay close to French pipes in shape and craftsmanship. A significant portion of production was shipped finished to France, where it was stamped with a French mark before being distributed to the world market. This arrangement limited the brand's recognition under its own name: some of the examples that survive today are unstamped, and attribution to Amiel is more often drawn from comparing shape and craftsmanship than from a stamp.
Shapes and Craftsmanship

The bulk of the brand's production falls between the mid-1930s and the mid-1950s. The backbone of the catalogue consists of classic bowl shapes such as the billiard, the pot, and the boule, along with various bulldog variations. Alongside these are plump bowl shapes derived from the streamline fashion of the 1930s. A craftsmanship technique that spread after 1940 also appears: flat facets are shaved around the bowl, and these polished surfaces give the pipe a distinct look. Mouthpieces are made of hard rubber (vulcanite); the differences between mouthpiece materials are compared in the Mouthpiece Materials entry.
The Brand's End

The factory is said to have stopped production toward the end of the 1950s, with the brand name possibly surviving for a while longer under other hands. Amiel-stamped pipes disappeared entirely from the market around 1980. This quiet disappearance is viewed alongside the changes in Algeria's industrial order after independence and the general decline in interest in pipes. Today Amiel is counted among the sparse production traces the briar trade left behind in the countries that supplied its raw material.

r.x: Carlson

is the name signing the pipes of Sweden's Bengt Carlson (born 1938). Carlson came to the craft in middle age, repairing and reshaping pipes he already owned; after retirement he became a maker turning out only a few dozen pipes a year in a one-man workshop. His work is known abroad, particularly among collectors in the United States.
Stamp and Scale of Production

Carlson's pipes carry a single stamp: "BC Sweden." Requests — mostly from American buyers — that he add further marks such as a year of manufacture, a quality tier, or a shape number, have been recorded, but the maker has not obliged them. Production has stayed small-scale from the start; sources give the annual figure as between twelve and twenty-five. Demand has long run above this number, yet Carlson has continued working to his own pace rather than to an order list. His view of himself as a hobbyist rather than a professional is tied to this stance.
Entering the Craft

The habit of altering factory-made pipes served Carlson as a kind of apprenticeship: records dated to 1993 mention that he gave an old Stanwell pipe an eight-sided bowl and thinned its shank and bit. In the same period he began visiting Bo Nordh's workshop regularly. Nordh culled the top-grade briar blocks he obtained for his own work and passed on what he set aside to enthusiasts around him; Carlson's first blocks came from there too. Once ordinary hand tools proved insufficient, a lathe was bought first, and the workshop was completed step by step over the years. Being able to retire at sixty in 1998 markedly increased the time he could devote to the work.
Finish and Shapes

Only smooth and rustic finishes are used; according to a record from 2002, he had not tried sandblasting up to that date. The rustic texture is opened with a dental drill and resembles a ring-grained sandblast. Smooth pipes are either simply oiled and left in their natural colour, or stained a medium brown; in both cases a black undercoat is applied first and sanded back to bring out the grain. The mould he returns to most often is what he calls the "Bun": round-bowled, thick-walled, and gently proportioned. Second in mention is the blowfish, a difficult mould put forward by Lars Ivarsson, son of Sixten Ivarsson: since horizontal grain is wanted on the flats and birdseye on the sides, a suitable block is scarce, and the body is left asymmetric so as not to disturb the grain. Around 2002 he tried bamboo and horn for the first time; because tightly spaced growth rings are sought in bamboo, the material is hard to find.
Standing Among Swedish Makers

Carlson's name in Sweden is tied not only to his own work but to the support he has given those around him. He has taken part in preparing the Swedish Pipe Club's magazine, Rökringar, and helped Love Geiger find equipment, above all a lathe, when setting up his workshop. It is recorded that after seeing the early work of Ronny Thunér, who began in 2005, he took on, at his own suggestion, a role as teacher and design advisor, and that he has also hosted new makers such as Jonas Rosengren at his workshop. It is reported that, after Bo Nordh's death, he remade in a small number of copies a Nordh pipe left to him for repair. Available records concentrate in the 2000s; the pace at which the workshop operates today cannot be confirmed from independent sources.

r.x: The Directory of Pipe Brands of Uncertain Origin

brings together pipe brands whose country of manufacture cannot be documented, or whose records point to more than one country. Most of these brands never built their own factory; instead they had their products made by large workshops, or entered the market simply under a mail-order retailer's name. Since the stamp usually carries only the brand name, the place of manufacture can no longer be traced. The twelve entries below make up the second and final part of the directory.
Brands
Turbo Flo

— considered a derivative of Viking and Falcon designs, this is a pipe with an aluminum body and a screw-in briar bowl. It carries cooling fins set at an angle along the shank; although its stem's teeth resemble Viking's, it does not accept Viking bowls. Records date the brand to around 1956.
University

— a brand name distributed by Pipesandcigars.com; there is also a line of the same name under Comoy's. The first University pipes were unvarnished examples made from old briar. Later, a batch made decades earlier in France from natural-surface Algerian briar was released under the "University Deluxe" stamp; these pipes have vulcanite mouthpieces and were made in three shapes — a six-sided panel, a standard billiard, and a lovat.
Vibel

— very little documentation survives. The only known detail is that the pipes were made from briar in the Czech Republic for the Danish distributor C. B. Møller. Known examples include a billiard stamped "Real Briar."
Victors

— a brand encountered with the stamp "VICTORS, HAND MADE; ALGERIAN BRIAR." Online records suggest the name is likely tied to Jost's, a pipe shop in St. Louis that also sold Comoy's-made pipes under its own name. The Algerian briar stamp suggests the piece in question may have come from Comoy's French factory.
Webco
— pipes bearing this stamp came out of the Weber Pipe Co. workshop. Known examples include models stamped "WEBCO FILTER," fitted with the same type of filter used in Dr. Grabow and Medico pipes.
Western

— a Japanese brand made in Tokyo; the same maker also produced cigarette holders with nearly identical stamps. The pipes have briar bowls and vulkanite mouthpieces, finished in a dark walnut tone. Stamps include the wording "OLD BRIAR," along with "DENICON TOKYO," thought to indicate the manufacturer and its location; on the side there is a circled number, presumed — as with Dunhill — to denote a size group. Another stamp is a triangular banner-shaped frame reading "G" at the top and "UC" below.
White Flame
— according to
Who Made That Pipe
records, made by both Imperial and Civic, with both England and France cited as places of manufacture. Known surviving examples are of French make.
Whitman

— known only from pipes stamped "WHITMAN MADE IN ENGLAND" on the stem. The documented example is a medium-sized pipe with a straight shank and a dark brown rustic surface. Nothing is on record about its maker; only the stamp has been documented.
Willard

— its pipes were made between 1963 and 1975 at the Sparta Industries plant in Sparta, North Carolina; records state that weekly output reached sixty thousand pipes. Some were distributed through army sales units serving soldiers during the Vietnam War years, and some were made for R. J. Reynolds. The brand's emblem is a large "W" set within a five-pointed star on the mouthpiece; the name Lord Abbott is said to have been a sub-brand or series of Willard.
William Anderson Pipes
— the name given to the briar pipes made, each as a one-off, by William Anderson Crawford, who worked in Virginia's Blue Ridge Mountains.
Wiltshire
— known from the stamp "Wiltshire Made in London England"; manufacture was undertaken by Comoy's.
Yorkshire

— a brand sold exclusively through Sears Roebuck catalogs; it appears in the 1941-42 catalog. The pipes were made in France from Algerian briar and, being neither stained nor varnished, retain their natural honey color. Known model names include Bond Street, Royal, Aristocrat, Natural, and Straight Grain.

r.x: The
ODB 831 stamps

are a set of marks gathered on the shank of a small, unassuming pipe from the 800-series OD line Dunhill introduced in 1950 — marks that, read together, do not agree with one another. Three separate year codes, two grade-4 marks, two "A" letters, and an "H" of unknown meaning sit side by side on the shank. John C. Loring, who compiled and interpreted the sequence, concludes that this writing records not a single moment of production but several separate operations spread across roughly six years. This pipe is cited as an example of why Dunhill stamps need to be read layer by layer rather than all at once.
A Price Cut Twice Over

The key to the sequence is a factory note from December 1952 that Loring cites. According to the note, a batch of Italian briar obtainable in 1948 was used in shapes between 806 and 832, these pipes were priced as ODB, and after 1953 the same shapes would be counted as ODA. With this information, the "(4) A" cluster on the shank face stops being a single grade or finish stamp. Loring's inference is that the "A" marks the unsold pipe's downgrade from ODB to ODA in 1953, and that the "(4)" marks the same pipe being pulled down once more, this time to grade-4 pricing, in 1956. The reading rests on three observations: the letter is too large for a Bruyere finish stamp but exactly the right size for an OD grade stamp; the "6" and the "(4)" on the other face of the shank appear struck tightly together, as if at the same time; and later-dated 831s came out from the start already carrying a grade-4 stamp. This reading has no documentary confirmation; it is presented as the only consistent explanation put forward for the stamp sequence. For the series' price tiers, see the Early Dunhill OD Pipes article.

The most disputed element in the sequence is the earliest year code; the mark read on the shank was at first taken for a "3," which would place the pipe in 1953. That the 800 series began in 1950 does not by itself rule out such a date, but three other marks argue against it. It is accepted that the brand stamped a patent number on the shank up until 1954, dropping the practice from 1955 onward; on this pipe, however, no patent number appears at all. The LONDON line under the DUNHILL wording fell out of use around 1951-1952, yet here it sits right where expected. Moreover the shape number, which under the 1953 arrangement should sit directly beneath the OD stamp, is here not on the face bearing the brand wording but on the shank's other side. Reading the code as "50" rather than "3" removes all three inconsistencies at once and places the pipe in the series' first year. The possibility of forgery, meanwhile, was ruled out on physical examination of the pipe: its workmanship, including the mouthpiece, matches the brand, the stamps are correctly struck one by one, and the writing is noticeably worn, unlike the crisp stamps typical of forged examples.
What Remains Unanswered

Why the patent number is missing still cannot be explained. It is accepted that the brand did not stamp a patent mark on pipes without an inner tube during the 1910s and 1920s, and stamped it independently of the inner tube from the late 1920s onward. No sign of an inner tube is visible on the pipe in question, yet its date does not fit this exception. In a note he later added to his article, Loring notes that a 1949-dated LC of his also lacks a patent number, and that LCs were not fitted with inner tubes. What the "H" stamp stands for remains unknown. For the general method of reading years from stamps, see the Dunhill Patent Stamps and Dating article.

r.x: Aircool

is a metal system pipe brand launched in Canada immediately after the Second World War. Records indicate the pipe was manufactured and distributed domestically by a Toronto-based company called Essential Agencies Limited; no document firmly establishes the exact year the brand came to market. The brand was not a workshop in the classic sense but a single-product venture built around one mechanical solution and sold for a limited period.
Design

Aircool's defining feature is the finned aluminum shell that wraps the bowl area. Designed on radiator logic, these fins are meant to spread the heat released during combustion over a wide surface and dissipate it. A separate briar inner chamber sits inside the shell; the tobacco itself burns inside this wooden piece, with the metal serving only as a cooling jacket. The finned shell screws onto a shank made of aluminum alloy, and the mouthpiece at the end of the shank is hard rubber. Beneath the mouthpiece is the stamp "AIRCOOL MADE IN CAN."

The product's design treats the inner chamber as a consumable: pipes sold boxed came with a spare briar chamber, and when the chamber wore out the user removed it and fitted a new one. The rear end of the shank is closed with a removable cap in the similar Airflow design, while on the Aircool it takes the form of a screw-in plug; collectors use this detail to tell the examples apart. In shape, the pipes have a plain, straight, industrial look.
Related Designs

Aircool was not an idea that arose in isolation. In the same years in the United States, the Imperial Smoke Kooler, made by Edlund Co. of Detroit and distributed by the March Corporation of Chicago, carried an almost identical structure; a version of the same body sold under the name Airflow, with different company initials attached to the front, is also known. Collectors regard Aircool as the Canadian adaptation of this family; some sources suggest the design originated with Edlund, though the details of the production relationship are not documented.

All of these designs continue the path opened in the 1930s by brands such as Kirsten. Aluminum's lightness and its ability to dissipate heat quickly, combined with the wartime growth in metalworking capacity, gave rise to a brief "machine aesthetic" wave in the pipe world. The most lasting product of that same pursuit was Falcon, patented in the United States in 1936 and moved into series production after the war; this design, rising alongside Aircool, would go on to keep the same idea alive for decades.
Today

There is no reliable record of how long Aircool was produced or of its sales volume. The brand disappeared leaving neither a continuation nor a succession story; all that remains are examples circulating on the secondhand market. In most of these examples the briar inner chamber has either been lost or replaced. Today the brand is overshadowed in Canadian pipe history by established names such as Brigham, but it is counted as a footnote carrying the postwar metal-pipe fashion's northern trace.

r.x: London Meerschaum

, despite what its name suggests, was not based in London at all but produced its pipes in the town of Cowbridge in the Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. The business was founded by Alistair McKay Mitchell and his wife Anne Mitchell, a couple who had worked in the meerschaum trade in East Africa before settling in Britain; the brand's story therefore begins with the mines at the foot of Kilimanjaro.
From Africa to Wales

According to family accounts, the couple had first set up a meerschaum-processing operation in Nairobi's industrial district in Kenya, and later in Arusha, Tanzania. Raw material was sourced from blocks quarried in the Amboseli region at the foot of Kilimanjaro. The Tanganyika Meerschaum Corporation, which worked the same deposits, was founded in 1955 and introduced East African meerschaum to the world market; the account also links the Mitchells' venture to that name, though the relationship between the two enterprises has not been independently confirmed. The region's stone is considered harder and less porous than Eskişehir stone, and is also distinguished by tones running from deep yellow to brown. English pipe companies of the period followed this source closely; GBD's block meerschaum series is said to have arisen from the same connection.

Once access to raw blocks was cut off following Tanzania's independence, the family moved to Britain. According to the account, a Somali intermediary was found and supply shifted to Somali-origin stone; every pipe that came out of the Cowbridge workshop was worked from these blocks.
Production and Products

The workshop in Cowbridge was small in scale but relied on machinery as well as handwork. Bowl blanks were roughed out on an Italian-made copy lathe, and the black plastic stems fitted to the pipes also came from the same country. Darkening the bowl rim on a hot plate to give it a dark band was a practice carried over from the Arusha years, and it is this detail that gives the brand's pipes their recognizable look.

The product range was not limited to solid meerschaum. The workshop also made models with a meerschaum bowl set into a wooden body; such pipes are known to have found favor in England. A corncob-shaped model is also mentioned in the records.
The BELT Stamp and Closure
London Meerschaum is also reported to have made pipes stamped
BELT
or
THE BELT

. Known examples have both smooth and sandblasted bowls and carry the inscription "Genuine Block Meerschaum" on the bowl; some feature English silversmith's hallmarks on the silver bands. In line, the series recalls the fully curved shape of Peterson system pipes, and the stems resemble the P-Lip; but the smoke hole is bored at the tip of the stem rather than on top of it. The series appears to have been on the market at latest by the 1950s. Some sources link the brand to Pomeroy & Cooke Ltd., though this link has not been confirmed.

After Alistair Mitchell's death, Anne Mitchell chose not to carry on the business, and the workshop closed. The closing date is not given clearly in the records. London Meerschaum is remembered today as one of the few brands to carry the short-lived trace of African meerschaum in British pipe production.

r.x: Alexa Pipes

is a one-man workshop run under his own nickname by Serbian woodworker Dragomir Aleksić. Aleksić was born in 1956 in Belgrade's Zemun district and trained as an engineer; according to his personal résumé he completed his degree in agricultural machinery in 1980. This measurement- and bench-based technical grounding, combined with the woodcarving he pursued for years as a hobby, forms the two threads that shape the workshop's identity today.
From Engineering to Carving

The year Aleksić changed direction was 1995; by his own account, this is when he made woodworking his main profession, beginning to work as a designer and carver at a workshop producing period-style furniture. Portfolio records show that during this period he made sculpture, church commissions, ornamentation, and interior work — meaning that before coming to pipes, he spent a long time observing how wood behaves at both large and small scale.

Pipe making was added on top of this accumulated experience only later. The sources do not record exactly which year he began this work; what is known is that from the late 2000s his pipes reached a wide circle through his own website and social media accounts. Aleksić has been known as an independent pipe maker since that time.
Approach to Shape

What sets Alexa pipes apart is that they follow a freehand line rather than sticking to the classic shape repertoire. Pieces are mostly one-off; rounded and undulating stummels, plateau rims, carved ornamentation, and faux-bamboo transitions are frequent features. The main material is briar, though he is also known to work with other woods such as olive wood; this second point rests on only a limited number of records. The weight of carved ornamentation varies from piece to piece: some stummels are left entirely plain, while on others most of the surface is worked. The pipes are frequently presented together with matching custom stands from the same hand, which pushes the work closer to small-scale sculpture than to plain pipe making practice.
Standing

Serbia does not have an established briar-pipe tradition on the scale of Denmark or Italy, which is why Aleksić is counted among the few Balkan representatives of the worldwide network of independent artisans. Output numbers are limited, and since each piece is individually shaped, the workshop's output is regarded not as a series but as a total made up of independent works.

r.x: Lanier

is the signature carrying the name of French pipe carver Paul Lanier. Lanier is remembered as one of the few masters who kept figurative pipe carving alive in an era dominated by series production, and is counted among the most recognized figures of the late twentieth century in the town of Saint-Claude, the craft's center.
From Wood Sculpture to Pipes

Lanier was born in Pierre-de-Bresse, in the Saône-et-Loire département of Burgundy; sources give his birth year as either 1931 or 1932. He began not with pipes but with furniture carving: at fourteen or fifteen he entered an apprenticeship in Chalon-sur-Saône, spending four years on modeling, drawing, and carving, and earning a vocational qualification in wood sculpture. This training would prove the defining trait of his later work; Lanier approached the pipe less as a smoking implement than as a small-scale sculpture.

He set up his own business in 1955; in the early years what he produced was not pipes but carved gift items. He learned to adapt the craft to pipes under a maker named Epely in Saint-Claude. He then worked for a long stretch as an independent subcontractor: he is said to have produced around five thousand pieces a year for Butz-Choquin, doing the rough and intermediate work at his own bench and leaving the finishing to the factory. From the 1980s on he moved to working entirely under his own name.
Master Titles and the Confrérie

What brought Lanier's name to prominence in France was his success in the Meilleur Ouvrier de France competition, the country's most respected craft examination. He won the title in two separate categories: pipe carving in 1991, and pipe turning in 1994. He is held to be the only pipe maker to carry both titles at once; combining a carver's hand skill with a turner's measuring discipline in one person is credited with keeping his work consistent both figuratively and technically.

In 1983 he took Denis Vincent's place in Confrérie des Maîtres-Pipiers, Saint-Claude's guild of pipe masters. From that date on, carving a pipe bearing the portrait of whoever the guild chose each year as "France's Foremost Pipe Smoker" became Lanier's task; each of these one-off pieces is said to have required up to three weeks of labor. Lanier also exhibited work at venues such as Paris, Tokyo, and Amsterdam, and took commissions built to a client's own design.
Material, Shape, and Legacy

The workshop's main material was briar, though auction records show that Lanier also carved other hardwoods such as boxwood. He is said to have used ebonite, acrylic, and horn for mouthpieces. His subject matter follows the classical carved-pipe tradition: human faces and portraits, animal figures, vanitas motifs such as skulls, and narrative scenes. In this work the chamber is often hidden within the composition — that is, the figure is not an ornament added on top of the bowl but the bowl itself.

Paul Lanier died on 11 June 2015, and his workshop was not carried on. A portion of his work is exhibited at the Pipe and Diamond Museum in Saint-Claude. Lanier is regarded today as one of the last great representatives of hand carving in the town where the briar revolution was born.

r.x: Kurusu

is the brand of handmade pipes produced by Japanese pipe maker Reiichi Kurusu under his own name. Known in the West as "Ray," the maker was born in Osaka in 1977 and entered the trade in his thirties at a small bench he set up in his home city. The brand is not a workshop but a one-man operation: the number of pipes made each year is limited, and both the bowl and the mouthpiece of every piece come from the same hand.
Material and Method

The briar used in the bowls comes exclusively from the Italian supplier Mimmo Romeo; the maker considers sticking to a single source a way of coming to know how that wood behaves. No ready-made mouthpiece blanks are used — every mouthpiece is cut and shaped by hand from rod stock. According to available accounts, the smoke channel is kept wide to give an easy draw; the figure of 4 millimeters rests on a single retailer's information. Secondary materials such as boxwood and bamboo appear frequently in shank bands and decorative elements.
The Road to the Bench

Kurusu's first thirty-odd years had nothing to do with pipes; by his own account, they were spent traveling abroad, pursuing music, and working at a tattoo shop before he entered the trade late in life. The turning point came in 2011, when he met Hiroyuki Tokutomi at a pipe gathering in Tokyo. He soon applied to study under the master and, in the years that followed, made regular trips to Tokutomi's bench.

By the maker's own account this apprenticeship lasted roughly two and a half years, with the real progress coming in the final months; this account has not been independently verified. What is certain is that around 2014 his work began drawing the interest of retailers outside Japan, and his pipes started reaching Europe and North America on a regular basis. Kurusu thus came to be counted among the new generation of the Japanese workshop tradition beyond Tsuge.
Design Vocabulary

Kurusu's work sits at the point where Japanese workmanship discipline and Scandinavian free-form sensibility intersect. Among the influences the maker cites, alongside Tokutomi, are Kei'ichi Gotoh, Bo Nordh, Jess Chonowitsch, and the Ivarsson family. This dual heritage reads clearly in the catalog: on one side, bowls faithful to classical dimensions; on the other, free-form bodies shaped by following the direction of the grain. Rounded shapes such as blowfish and acorn are among the forms the maker returns to often. Restraint also stands out in surface work: polished smooth surfaces are left as such wherever the grain shows itself, leaving no need for further decoration.

kunyeTam: Mimmo briar, individually crafted mouthpieces, boxwood and bamboo accents

r.x: Labuenapipa

is a small handmade pipe workshop that operated in Jerez de la Frontera, the Andalusian city known for its wine. The workshop was run single-handedly by Luis Wiesenthal, whose birth year is recorded as 1951; the founding date is not clearly documented, and the information available dates mostly to the early 2010s. Given how narrow a circle pipe making occupies in Spain, the workshop is counted among the country's few independent ventures.
Founding the Workshop

By what is reported, Wiesenthal's working life was spent not in pipes but in wine: he ran a business in Jerez's cellars for many years, dabbling in oil and watercolor painting on the side. He founded his pipe bench as a continuation of this interest in handcraft, at a later stage in his career. What began as a hobby is said to have turned into full-time work over time. The workshop's scale never went beyond small-batch production at any point; every piece came from a single hand.
Material and Method

The workshop's chief distinguishing feature is that the material was overseen by the same person from start to finish. Wiesenthal has said that he selected his own briar blocks and cured them himself, so that he could set the drying time as he wished. This is a different way of working from workshops that buy ready-made blocks, and it directly limits production speed.

Besides briar, it is also recorded that he occasionally cut bodies from the burl of the olive tree. Olive root is not a common alternative to briar in pipe making; in Mediterranean workshops it appears more as a regional preference. The workshop's range also included electronic pipes at one point. These pieces are said to have been developed with former smokers who had quit tobacco in mind, and are noted to have not departed from traditional methods in the body's craftsmanship.
Design Line

Wiesenthal's work sits somewhere between set classical shapes and full freehand: free lines are used, but classical proportions are not fully abandoned. The standard the workshop emphasized was not appearance alone but also the consistency of the smoke path and chamber measurements. This emphasis is a common stance among one-man workshops: because the piece count is low, the interior dimensions of every body can be checked individually, and shape can be built up without letting it override function.

Wiesenthal is known to have named Scandinavia, in particular the Danish school tradition, as his own points of reference; he is associated with Tom Eltang on account of the importance he placed on surface work.
Current Status

Whether the workshop remains active cannot be confirmed. The web address used for a long time now belongs to a commercial site unrelated to pipes; the workshop's name also does not appear in current directories of Spanish pipe makers. For this reason, what is known about Labuenapipa largely remains frozen at a small workshop from the early 2010s.

kunyeTam: Free-form design, self-cured briar, olive root

r.x: Jean Alexis Handmade Pipes

is one of three brand names used by maker Richard Baggenstos, said to work in Switzerland. Baggenstos turns out two kinds of work at the same bench, distinguished by method: freehand pipes go under the names White Dog and Glen Ben, while those built around a classic mold are known as Jean Alexis. What changes the name is not the maker's identity but how the bowl comes into being — which makes this line one of the frequently cited examples of how, in small workshops, naming itself can become a statement of method.
The Method the Name Signals

The only criterion determining the split is which bench shapes the bowl. In freehand lines the block is opened on the grinding wheel and with carving knives; the shape grows wherever the wood's grain allows. In Jean Alexis pipes, however, the bowl and shank are turned on a lathe, so the result is either a mold like the billiard or a variant worked from that mold's measurements.

Drawing this kind of line is not as purely technical a matter as it might seem. Where the phrase "handmade" begins and ends in the pipe community varies from workshop to workshop, as seen in the debate over handmade versus machine-made. Baggenstos's solution has been to run the two methods under separate names from the start rather than argue over the definition.
Wood and Finishing Philosophy

The briar blocks used in the line are set aside from long-cured stock. The most talked-about aspect of the line is that no putty is used in finishing: small flaws found in the wood are not filled and hidden but left as they are. When a flaw grows too numerous or too large, the bowl is not discarded but salvaged through sandblasting; roughly a tenth of surfaces are finished this way, the rest left smooth and polished. The same approach continues in the tobacco chamber: it is left uncoated with a break-in cake, leaving the interior surface's condition visible to the buyer.

Most stems are pulled from ebonite, a smaller share from acrylic. Colors range from natural wood tone to black, red, light orange, and dark brown contrast finishes. According to records, filter-seated bowls make up a very small portion of total production; the maker is said to favor the filterless bowl for ease of use and maintenance.
Stamp and Grading

Each bowl is placed on a scale from zero to nine, based on the quality and freedom from flaw of its grain. This number is stamped on the underside of the shank right next to the brand name; so reading the stamp is enough to place a Jean Alexis within the workshop's own hierarchy. While small workshops usually keep grading to a few tiers, extending the scale here to ten steps and stamping it directly onto the bowl gives the line its own identity. In keeping with this same approach, it is noted that Baggenstos does not work to order or from a customer's drawing; he decides for himself which shape will come from which block.

r.x: The China Pipe Brands Directory

brings together, in alphabetical order, pipe brands and workshops founded in China. Briar pipe-making is a late-arriving tradition in the country: records indicate the first briar pipe makers became visible in 2007, and in the years since, both freehand workshops following the Danish line and manufacturers geared toward series production have been established. As a local feature, buckthorn (Rhamnus) wood, native to northern China, is used as a body material alternative to briar. The entries below simply summarize the facts on record.
Brands
Daadou Pipe

— Works in Beijing's Haidian district. Production runs on two tracks: briar pipes, and pipes made from buckthorn (Rhamnus) wood, which has a deep history in northern China. Because buckthorn's hardness keeps it off the lathe, the brand's pipes on this line are shaped entirely by hand from start to finish; this same difficulty also explains why few makers have tried the material.
KingCheng

— A manufacturer that has produced corncob and wood pipes since 2009, headquartered in Shijiazhuang, Hebei province. Because its product range is close to that of the American manufacturer, it is often referred to in the community as China's counterpart to Missouri Meerschaum.
Leizhou pipe tribes

— The name of a collective bringing together five art-trained pipe makers. All five use the character "lei" (雷) as a shared brand mark; which piece belongs to whom is indicated by the maker's name struck beneath this mark.
Mister Pipe

— Founded in 2008; its output is confined to handmade pipes. Bodies are made predominantly from northern China's buckthorn wood. By the brand's own account, its design line combines the Danish-derived freeform approach with elements specific to Chinese culture; it states it works with a young team and aims to bring recognition to Chinese handmade pipes.
Road Town

— Its pipes come not from a single workshop but from various makers across China; distribution runs through Wilson Pipe Studio. Most of what is known about the brand rests on promotional copy in sales listings: according to this, the studio was founded in 2011, its founder Wilson is a pipe agent coming from an architecture background, and the roster includes more than twenty professional makers. The catalog splits into two series: "Classic," which follows traditional shapes and carries the "HS STUDIO / ROAD TOWN" stamp, and freeform "Freehand." Beyond this, no verified record exists.
Zhiputang

— A craft workshop founded and run by Yang Zhimin. Besides producing pipes under his own name, the workshop also teaches the craft to new makers, functioning in part as a school. The best-known name to have come through it is Hangzhou-based Xin Li, who worked alongside Yang and signed numerous Zhiputang pipes.
Zhishan & Mindong Pipe

— The joint brand of Zhishan and Mindong Wang, who work in Tianjin, near Beijing. Records identify this pair as the first two Chinese briar pipe makers to become known, in 2007. No detailed assessment of the pipes themselves exists in the archive.

r.x: The Directory of Polish Pipe Brands

gathers, in alphabetical order, pipe brands established in the country or run by Polish makers. The center of gravity of Polish pipe making is the southeastern city of Przemyśl; records trace this tradition back roughly a century, to the work started by Wincenty Swoboda. The chain of makers who trained in the Walat brothers' workshop extends down to today's one-man workshops, and some of the entries below can be traced to this family tree. Brands with no detailed information in the records are also listed by name. Swiss Pipe, included in the list, is not of Polish origin; it appears in this compilation because of its place in brand catalogs, and this is noted in its entry as well.
Brands
B&B

— A workshop run since 1996 by Artur and Mariusz Bednarczyk, based near Przemyśl. Alongside pipes, cigarillos are also made; materials used include briar as well as pear wood and other wood and shrub species. Most production steps are not left to machinery, so no two pieces turn out exactly alike. Natural wood stains and waxes are preferred for surface finishing; the workshop considers itself a continuation of Przemyśl's roughly century-old pipe-making tradition.
Dominik Pipes

— Carries the signature of Dominik Kobryń. Kobryń's first contact with pipes came through a piece he bought at a flea market in 1993, and he finished his own first pipe in December 2016. He names Wojtek Pastuch as his teacher. He sources his briar from Mimmo Romeo, and shapes his mouthpieces mainly from ebonite and Cumberland rod, occasionally acrylic. Technically solid, he focuses on one-off pieces that do not resemble one another.
Filar

— Ryszard Filar is counted among the senior makers of Polish pipe making. He entered the trade at the Walat brothers' workshop, where he worked alongside Ryszard Kulpiński. After Ludwik Walat's death, the two founded their own firm in 1981, then split in 1983 to continue on their own; the two workshops are located on the same street in Przemyśl. Filar favors classic-leaning shapes over freehand ones, producing in small batches with smooth or fully or partially textured (rustication) surfaces. He stamps his pipes with an "F" inside a circle.
JSG

— Belongs to a Polish maker who signs his pipes with the letters "JSG." The maker presents himself not as an experienced craftsman but as someone at the start of the road; he highlights his interest in briar's grain and the inner drive that led him to handwork, stating that each new pipe turns out better than the last. Alongside making, he also takes on repair work, and does not shy away from taking on the most difficult jobs as long as there is a chance of saving the piece.
Parol

— Marek Parol has been firing clay pipes in Przemyśl since 1991–1992, reviving this forgotten craft as a second occupation. He uses a type of clay that takes on a reddish tone when fired. His range includes historical shapes ("Reprints") remade from old molds he was able to rescue from the Gambier factory in Givet, France, as well as his own models bearing figures and portraits of well-known contemporary people. He worked for a time alongside Ryszard Filar; his pipes adapting classic wooden shapes to clay are counted among his most notable work. These pipes have double-walled bowls and are said to deliver a cool smoke.
Rogrus

— The signature of Robert Gruszczyński, who works in Warsaw. A fine arts graduate, the maker has at different times worked as a sculptor, painter, and restorer of antique sculpture and furniture. He works with stone and clay alongside briar, producing carved and free-form compositions with dense ornament and measured construction. His sources of inspiration include the work of Kent Rasmussen and Hiroyuki Tokutomi. The brand emblem is the stylized letters "rg" inside a circle.
Stokkebye

— Names the pipe wing of Peter Stokkebye International Ltd., known on the tobacco side; the company's parent, Orlik Tobacco Company, is considered Denmark's largest tobacco firm. Making of the pipes has been undertaken by Jørgen Larsen since the 1970s. The top grade in the ranking is marked "AAA"; on the stamp, the letters "PS" nearly overlap.
Swiss Pipe

— Traces back to 1941, to a cooperative founded by a group of craftsmen who split off from the Bru-Bu factory. The brand later passed to Stich, a company making wooden furniture and craft goods; this company also produced a limited number of pipes, mainly replicas of older pieces. As its name suggests, the brand is of Swiss origin, and it enters this list not because of a Polish connection but because of its place in brand catalogs, as noted in its entry as well.
Worobiec

— A family workshop founded in Przemyśl; the business was started in 1954 by Paweł Worobiec and continued single-handedly after 1979 by his son Henryk Worobiec. Over Henryk Worobiec's more than half-century as a maker, his awards include honorable mentions at the national craft exhibitions held in Kielce in 1985 and in Kraków in 1986 and 1987, and a certificate of recognition given in 1989 by the Polish Federation of Pipe Smokers' Clubs.
Wozniak Pipes

— The brand Rafał Woźniak has run since 2014. He uses mainly briar and ebonite, occasionally also bog oak and acrylic mouthpieces. Each pipe is shaped individually with basic hand tools. Woźniak mostly follows his own design ideas, occasionally trying his hand at interpreting other makers' approaches to shape. He marks his pipes with the signature "R.Woźniak."
Zembrowski Pipes
— The name for pipes signed by Tomasz Zembrowski. No further detail about the brand appears in the records; the only documented facts are the maker's name and the brand's existence.

r.x: Anne Julie

is the most frequently cited woman maker in the Danish handmade pipe tradition. She did not come to this work by choice but after an unexpected loss: her husband, Poul Rasmussen, one of the well-known makers of his day, died in October 1967 at the age of forty-six, leaving behind a tobacco shop and a fully equipped workshop. Twenty-seven-year-old Julie was raising a two-year-old child at the time; rather than sell the machinery and stock, she chose to take her place at the bench, and that choice marked the beginning of a body of work under her own name that would span more than fifty years.
Taking Over the Bench

According to the records, up to that point Julie had never even held a pipe; her husband belonged to a generation that regarded carving as men's work. During the days she went to sell the Copenhagen shop, she ran into one of Rasmussen's former apprentices, Hans Nielsen — a maker the pipe community knows by the name Former. The briar blocks sitting on the shelves drew the two of them into a shared undertaking; Julie carved her first pipes from these very blocks under Nielsen's guidance. In the years that followed, by her own account, she learned how the material behaved and how a shape was built on the job.
Shape Language and Metalwork

Anne Julie's work falls into two veins. On one side sit classic shapes made in generously large dimensions; on the other, freehand examples built around the wood's own grain. In the freehand pieces, volume is used generously and the lines are kept legible; some pipes present a slender, balanced look while others are finished with a nearly untouched, raw-looking surface.

The use of metal is one of the most distinctive marks of this output. Caps covering the bowl rim, plates set onto the body, and rings are commonly seen; the silverwork was handled for a long time by Klaus Bjerring Andersen. The mouthpieces (stems) are not left plain either — they are worked with beads, rings, and contours that tie into the design of the body. In finishing, a ruby-tinged red stain and black are the most frequent choices. The shank carries the "Anne Julie" stamp along with a single red-and-white dot; this dot mark was inherited from the stamp Poul Rasmussen used.
The Læsø Years and Transmission

Over time the workshop stopped being merely a place of production and turned into a center of instruction. Tom Eltang, who first appeared before Julie at age sixteen with pipes he had made himself, began his apprenticeship here in 1974 and worked for roughly three years; the balance of shape and the sense of staining seen in Eltang's later work is often traced back to this period. In this respect Anne Julie is counted among the links within the Danish School that carried knowledge from one generation to the next, as much as she is counted as a maker in her own right.

In the following period the maker moved her production to the island of Læsø in northern Denmark. The island became the address both of the workshop and of a gallery where she gathered her paintings; pipemaking continued for her as part of an artistic practice spread across several disciplines. Because her annual output remained limited, her work is counted among the pieces sought by collector circles not only in Denmark but also in Japan, Germany, and the United States.

r.x: Verteramo Pipes

is the one-man pipe workshop of Matías Verteramo, working in Argentina's southern Río Negro province. The scale of production is small: every pipe made to order comes from the same hands, from the selection of the burl to the final polish of the mouthpiece. Since briar craftsmanship in South America has a much shorter history than in Europe, workshops like Verteramo's are examples of the handmade pipe circle that has gained visibility on the continent in recent years.
Founding of the Workshop

Verteramo's start is said to rest on experiments he carried out with non-briar woods, particularly fruit-tree burls he could find locally; this is how he learned how each species behaved. After this trial period, correspondence he built up with makers abroad changed the direction of the work; among these names, records cite the Austrian maker Ludwig Lorenz. Records also give 2020 as the year the pursuit turned into a full-time job; in the same period the first comprehensive stock of materials was assembled, made up of Italian briar, Ukrainian-sourced morta, and olive wood.
Shape and Technique

The catalog's weight falls mostly on bent bodies and freeform shapes close to the Danish School approach; rather than the measured repetition of classic English molds, shaping each piece to its burl is fundamental. The smoke channel and bowl holes are opened at the bench itself, without the aid of a mold; the work left to machines is limited to rough shaping.

In surface finishing, a weathered look through rustication stands out. Rather than alcohol-based stains, finishes that preserve the wood's natural tone are preferred, so the grain pattern remains visible even beneath the rustic surface.

The most talked-about part of the workshop is the mouthpieces. It is said that Verteramo casts the acrylic himself, coloring it through a process that takes months of preparation using pigments he obtains from plants. Although this claim rests on a single source, the result is described as producing tones that vary from piece to piece, something not seen in mass-produced mouthpieces.
Current Status

The workshop remains active. Its buyer base is said to have grown over time beyond Argentina's borders, reaching North America and Europe; records note that demand also comes from other continents. Verteramo's design philosophy rests on placing the function required by the act of pipe smoking ahead of formal display, and on never considering any piece flawless.

r.x: Jost's

is the name of a long-lived pipe and tobacco shop in St. Louis, Missouri, and of the pipes sold under that shop's name. The business began as the umbrella stand of a wood turner who had emigrated from Germany, stayed in the same family from founding to closure, and shut down in the 1980s. The bulk of Jost's-stamped pipes were made in London by Comoy's, with a portion carved on the shop's own bench.
From Umbrellas to Pipes

Founder Henry Jacob Jost was born February 7, 1870, in Germany's Hesse region, learned his craft there, emigrated to America in the early 1890s, and was naturalized in 1895. Known by the nickname "Duke," Jost appears in St. Louis city directories as a turner from 1899 on. The shop's founding year is uncertain: a 1939 newspaper article gives 1892, while a family obituary points to 1905; both were written well after the events in question.

Directory records show more reliably how the business evolved. In 1909 Jost is listed solely as an umbrella maker; by 1914 pipes are added to the listing and a second address appears downtown. By 1921 umbrellas had disappeared entirely, leaving only pipes. The product line changed while the bench stayed the same; umbrella handle, cane, and pipe all relied on the same turning craftsmanship, and the shop kept canes on its shelves until the 1970s. The business took the name "H. J. Jost & Son" around 1936; the "son" here is Louis William Jost, born 1901.
Adah Jost and Harvey Raspberry

When Louis died young in 1940, his widow Adah became co-owner of the business alongside her father-in-law; after Henry's death in 1954 she held it as sole owner until it closed. It has been suggested that Adah was the woman referred to in the St. Louis press of the era as "Mrs. Henry A. Jost," noted as a pipe-smoking woman operating the business; this is an inference drawn from comparing family history with press records rather than a direct document. Adah is also said to have given customers pipe-smoking lessons in the shop.

From around 1960, day-to-day operations were entrusted to Harvey Newell Raspberry (1914-2007). Born in Arkansas, Raspberry is recorded in the 1940 census as a clerk at a pipe shop; if that shop was Jost's, he would have worked there for over forty years. His obituary states he retired in 1984. Before him, a local pipe man named Bill Collins had handled the shop's repair and making work. Raspberry's name also appears as the registered agent in the state incorporation record of H. J. Jost & Son, Inc., established in 1983; though sources sometimes describe his role as manager and sometimes as owner, no document confirms a claim of ownership.

When its original building was demolished, the shop moved in the 1960s to a new location downtown, beneath the parking ramp of the Famous-Barr department store. Sources give the closing date anywhere between 1984 and 1988.
Stamps and Pipes

Most pipes sold under the Jost's name are Comoy's-made, and distinguishing this from the stamp is relatively easy: one face of the shank reads "Jost's" with a curved "Olde England" beneath it, while the opposite face carries "Made in England" and a shape number. The "J" prefix on the number is the most reliable sign of Comoy's origin; the mouthpieces also carry a circled J stamp. The catalogue was divided into several tiers: Old English De Luxe and Supreme at the top, Virgin Briar Supreme in the middle, entry-level Thames Briars along with sandblasted models, and Dukes Briars, carrying the founder's nickname, at the bottom tier.

The way to distinguish pipes finished on the shop's own bench is the absence of a stamp: examples that carry no England mark are attributed to Raspberry. In these, the chamber top is often left with the unworked plateau surface of the briar root, and the shank is kept in its knotty state rather than reduced to a smooth cylinder; the result is immediately unfamiliar to an eye accustomed to factory molds. Long-shanked Canadian examples are among the known shapes in this group. The shop also had tobacco blends prepared under its own name; customer accounts mention names such as Virginia, Deluxe, and Old English, though no catalogue record confirms these.
